InterviewOS

InterviewOS automates initial round interviews at scale. AI conducts adaptive interviews without a recruiter present, giving hiring teams structured, evidence-backed insights for human review.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

What it does

InterviewOS: Scaling Initial Round Interviews with AI

Inspiration

Every year, companies receive thousands of applications, but conducting the initial round interviews takes an enormous amount of time, thus causing a lot of potentially great employees to not even reach the first round of interviews. Recruiters repeatedly ask similar questions, coordinate schedules, and screen candidates before moving them forward.

We asked ourselves: What if AI could conduct personalized initial round interviews at scale, without requiring a human interviewer to be present? This could allow companies to conduct a way larger amount of first round interviews where they can choose from a greater pool of candidates where this time they know a lot more about them then their resumes.

That's why we built InterviewOS, an AI-powered platform designed to make initial interviewing more scalable, accessible, and consistent while leaving hiring decisions to humans.

What It Does

InterviewOS is designed to automate the first round of hiring through structured, adaptive AI interviews.

Candidates answer interview questions through a webcam and a mic, review and confirm their responses, and receive follow-up questions generated using their actual answers. The system validates evidence and organizes insights that hiring teams can review afterward.

Our approach combines several technologies:

AMD-powered AI: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, accelerated with ROCm and llama.cpp, generates adaptive questions and evidence-backed feedback.
NVIDIA edge AI: A Jetson Orin Nano runs OpenCV face detection and YOLO11 pose estimation using TensorRT, keeping webcam frames local.
Google Gemini multi-agent exploration: Specialized ADK agents explore evidence extraction, identifying missing details, question generation, and quality review.
Full-stack interview experience: A React frontend and FastAPI backend handle interview interactions, confirmed transcripts, session management, and AI integration.
Privacy-conscious design: Video remains on the edge device, with a metadata-only architecture and safeguards against unsupported candidate judgments.

How We Built It

We built the frontend using React, TypeScript, and Vite, and the backend using Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic.

For our core language model, we used Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on AMD ROCm, running through llama.cpp. This enables follow-up questions based on candidate responses and feedback grounded in direct transcript quotes.

We deployed YOLO11n-Pose on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8GB, exporting the model and optimizing it with TensorRT for real-time webcam inference.

We also built an experimental Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) pipeline with six specialized agents, exploring how multiple AI components could collaborate to produce more reliable interviewer-facing insights.

The system's components were developed across multiple devices, with backend contracts and network communication designed to connect them.

Challenges We Faced

Getting AI Models Running on Real Hardware

Deploying computer vision on the Jetson meant working through CUDA compatibility, TensorRT optimization, model exports, camera capture, and Linux GUI issues.

After extensive debugging, we successfully ran live YOLO11 pose estimation at 1280×720 resolution.

Preventing AI Hallucinations

A convincing AI response isn't necessarily a correct one. We implemented deterministic validation to verify that cited evidence comes directly from a confirmed candidate answer and to reject unsupported feedback.

Connecting Different Systems

Our architecture spans AMD-accelerated inference, NVIDIA edge hardware, FastAPI, and React. Coordinating different machines, environments, API contracts, and network configurations was a major engineering challenge.

Building Trust Into Interviewing

Automating interviews raises serious questions about privacy, fairness, and transparency. We focused on explicit consent, local video processing, evidence validation, and keeping AI observations separate from actual hiring decisions.

What We Learned

We learned how to deploy and optimize machine learning models on specialized hardware, build reliable AI-backed APIs, and design safer workflows around generative AI.

More importantly, we learned that the hardest part of an AI product often isn't generating an answer. It's ensuring that the answer is grounded, useful, and appropriately delivered.

What's Next

Our goal is to expand InterviewOS into a complete autonomous first-round interviewing platform that organizations can use at scale.

Next steps include completing end-to-end hardware integration, expanding adaptive interview conversations, and connecting validated insights to secure dashboards for authorized hiring teams.

InterviewOS isn't about replacing human hiring decisions. It's about allowing every applicant to complete a meaningful first-round interview without requiring a recruiter to conduct each one personally.

A.D.A: Autonomous Device Assistant

LLMs can't really interact with the physical world, and most other AI robotics are unable to learn and improve in deployment, but A.D.A can! She is able to scan new objects, build models, and improve!

Like
1

Comment

Calibration Hell when I was at lowes getting a baseboard

I have been doing some customized home assistant and embedded work in my personal life, and I could use something like this. able to clean and remember and actually understand what is going on. in the environment. I was always fascinated at the principles of 3d scanners and wanted to firmly believe that AI are able to improve the tools they can use to do work. Just like how we create scripts to automate deployment, or more. I decided to give an LLM the ability to iterate on itself by being able to control a robotic arm, use custom fine tuned CV models with synthetic data and real life data that can bridge the gap. ADA is able to scan objects close up with her arm to inspect items in her field. Then it gets processed by gather data and doing research, which gathers data from know parts and 3d model libraries, and is actually able to generate them via all sorts of connections. On her first try, she was able to identify a 8 year old arduino board, and build and compile a kicad schematic and export it perfectly! 

Scanning items and finding them is one thing, but the most important part about any robot is its ability to see and manipulate. In order to see, she is able to use a synthetic dataset replication system that uses ray tracing and other details to bring the most realistic data as possible. She is able to spin up RGB, Depth, Pose, and theoretically reflections via ray tracing to plug into CV training models to grow her own 'vocabulary'.  The CV Pipeline uses 6 different models, ranging from on device yolo, Dinov2, and some cutting edge open source pose predictions that allows Ada to even showcase a 'ghost' obj and check for overlap and accuracy. This then feeds into other ML algorithm pipelines.

For manipulation, using the generated 3d render a grasp physics simulation is attempted to try and find the best angle and interactivity for grasping the the object and building a database of optimal grasping strategies for manipulation. 

CUDA Accelerated, distributed processing, and a heck of a lot of compute towards getting this jetson to be one of the best processors to run anything this town can see. 

It was fun doing this one, and i wish I had more time to flush out the scanning algorithms and rendering parts, but I ran into multiple issues with doing the distributed networking, China ping for AMD compute, and most painful of all, real to sim sensor and arm calibration that makes it difficult to work in practice with cheap servos that are the absolute bane of my existence.

title: AuditPilot — Internal Audit Policy Navigator
text:
Notifications

Loading...

AuditPilot — Internal Audit Policy Navigator

Bring your policies home — get answers without sending your documents to external AI services.
Your policies. Your machine. Your answers. Private, local, and built for trust.

Like

Comment

GIF

Inspiration

I work as a data science associate at Mitsubishi Power Americas, and I deal with policies a lot. Policies are long, full of numbered clauses, and the answers people need are small and specific: a time limit, an approval requirement, an escalation rule. Finding them means searching through pages of text, and it is easy to land on a similar-looking clause and get the wrong number.

I wanted a tool where someone can simply ask, "How long does AP have to review a potential duplicate invoice?" and get an answer taken directly from the policy. That became AuditPilot: Internal Audit Policy Navigator.

Why RAG, and why locally

Many general-purpose AI tools run in the cloud. Pasting a policy or any internal document into them means sending that text to a third party, which can expose confidential information. They also answer from their general training, so they can sound confident while being wrong about your policy.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps address the problem: the model is only shown the passages retrieved from the actual document and is told to answer from them, or say it doesn't know. I handled the first problem by running every piece locally:

the embedding model runs on my machine,
the search index is a local file,
the language model runs through Ollama, so no document text is sent to an outside service.

RAG gives grounded answers, and running it locally keeps the document private.

What it does

AuditPilot answers plain-English questions about an Accounts Payable policy. It finds the most relevant parts of the policy, writes an answer using only those parts, and says when the answer is not in the document. Users can download the full policy from the app to check the answer themselves.

How I built it

Extract: read the 19-page policy PDF with PyMuPDF and removed the repeated page headers.
Chunk: split the text into chunks of 1200 characters with 150 overlap, using LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.
Embed and index: turn each chunk into a vector with the BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embedding model and store them in a FAISS index.
Retrieve: embed the question the same way and fetch the 3 closest chunks. By default, FAISS ranks chunks by distance, where a smaller distance means a closer match:

$$d(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{c}) = \lVert \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{c} \rVert_2$$

Answer: send the question and the retrieved chunks to a local qwen2.5:7b model through Ollama, with rules to answer only from the excerpts and not to invent policy names or numbers.
Interface: a Streamlit app with a question box, an answer card, information cards, and a sidebar that shows whether the index and the model are ready.

Challenges I ran into

No cloud subscription. The tutorial I followed used Azure AI Foundry. I replaced it with free local models.
Chunk size. My first setting of 800 characters could split one rule across two chunks. Many clauses in the policy are longer, so I moved to 1200.
PDF noise. PyMuPDF put a line break inside every page header, so my first cleanup pattern matched nothing. Fixing it removed about 1,000 characters of noise.
Model choice. A small 3B model can pick the wrong number from similar clauses. I compared it with a 7B model and used the larger one.
Tooling problems. I worked through a misplaced requirements file, a missing package, a stale PATH that hid the Ollama command, and a Streamlit crash caused by its file watcher.
Wrong policy names. In early testing, the model could mix up a section heading with a policy name, so I added explicit rules to the prompt.

What I learned

I gained a clear understanding of the complete RAG workflow and learned which models and tools to use at each stage, from embeddings and retrieval to answer generation.
Test retrieval before adding a language model. If the wrong chunks come back, no model can answer correctly.
Chunk size and PDF cleanup affect answer quality as much as the model does.
The embedding model used to build the index must be the same one used for questions.
A "say you don't know" rule matters for policy work, because an unsupported answer is worse than no answer.

What's next

Show the section or page behind each answer, which means keeping page information on each chunk.
Support several policy documents at once.

Knight Study Space

Turn handwritten notes into LaTeX, find cheap eats near campus, and keep your lofi playing on every tab. Everything a UCF student needs to study smarter, all in one place.

Like
2

Comment

Top half of the landing page of the website!

Bottom half of the landing page of the website!

Sign up page prior to user accessing dashboard or functionality.

Login page prior to user accessing dashboard or functionality.

Users dashboard with shortcuts and nav bar.

Notes upload page with a filtering system

Lofi page with multiple tracks for the user to pick from and volume settings.

Map page that uses the students location to provide information about local deals and restaurant ratings. 

User settings with function that allow them to alter their profile settings and site layout.

More settings options for the user including accessibility features, updating their password, or deleting their account.

The settings page displayed in dark mode.

Inspiration

What inspired us to create this project is being a UCF stressing out for midterms or finals and wanting a late-night munchie to take that stress away.

What it does

Knight Study Space is an all-in-one study companion for UCF students:

Dashboard: a home screen with quick actions, counts of notes converted and restaurants saved, and recent activity.
Notes: converts handwritten notes into LaTeX.
Lofi player: a study-music player with a mini player in the sidebar, so your music keeps playing as you move between tabs.
Food finder: shows restaurants near campus on an interactive map, with distance, ratings, price estimates, and a link to each menu or offer. You can filter by cuisine and price, set your location with GPS or a ZIP code, and save favorites.
Accounts and settings: sign up and log in, a display name, light, dark, or match-device themes, adjustable text size, and a reduce-motion option, all saved on your device.

How we built it

We worked together as a team to plan out the website, design the interface, and build its features. We split up different responsibilities and used what we knew about web development to bring our ideas to life.

Frontend: React and TypeScript with Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS.
Backend: Python and Fastapi.
Map: React-Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles, plus browser geolocation with a draggable pin to correct your position.
Shared audio: a single audio element lives at the app root, and the Lofi tab and sidebar mini player both control it through shared state.
Reusable components: a shared Card and Button keep every tab consistent, with CSS modules for buttons.
Dark mode: a data-theme attribute on the app wrapper, with a theme stylesheet that swaps the light colors for dark ones.
Responsive layout: a flex-wrap layout that collapses the sidebar into the page on small screens.

Challenges we ran into

Along the way, we had to do a lot of testing, troubleshooting, and figuring things out as we went. One of our biggest challenges was getting everything to work the way we wanted it to, especially for the AI. It struggled a lot with understanding the user's handwriting. However, we mostly overcame this curve.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Three different tools in one polished, consistent interface.
A mini player that follows you across every tab without interrupting your music.
Accessibility built in from the start: text sizes, reduced motion, keyboard-friendly controls, and clear focus states.
Integrated external APIs to pull live data into the site, connecting our React + TypeScript frontend to outside services instead of relying on static content.
Worked hands-on with AI models for the Notes page, which converts users' uploaded handwritten notes into clean, formatted LaTeX files.
Improved the AI's accuracy through iterative testing, running trial-and-error rounds on real handwritten samples and refining our approach based on where the output fell short.
Built a location-aware interface that uses the user's location to show nearby college food deals on an interactive map, so each student sees results relevant to their area.
Designed and developed a full user flow, from the landing page and sign-up/login through to a dashboard with navigation to the Notes, Lofi, and Food Deals pages.

What we learned

This project taught us a lot about web development, problem-solving, and teamwork. We realized that building a website involves more than just writing code. It takes planning, communication, patience, and a lot of trial and error, but it was an amazing experience and we loved doing it.

What's next for Knight Study Space

Finish the account features because we had more that we wanted to implement, but didn't have time
Add more lofi tracks and playlists, including shuffle and repeat.
Add verified student deals and discounts for the food finder.
Add more study tools, such as a focus timer and a way to organize notes by course.

title: ADACVA
text:
Notifications

Loading...

ADACVA

An accessible piano tutor for learners who can’t rely on visual sheet music.

Like

Comment

About the project

Inspiration

Learning piano often starts with reading sheet music and following visual demonstrations. We wanted to explore a different starting point: learning through listening, playing, and conversation.

We built ADA Piano Teacher for learners who cannot rely on visual sheet-music interfaces, with blind and visually impaired learners as our intended audience. Our goal is to make practice guidance easier to hear, understand, and act on.

What it does

ADA combines a MIDI-connected piano, spoken interaction, score import, and camera-based hand tracking in one desktop prototype.

Learners can ask piano questions aloud and hear ADA’s responses. For guided practice, they can import MusicXML or convert a PDF score, review and approve a passage, listen to a reference performance, and practice its notes and chords.

ADA uses MIDI events to check what the learner actually played. The AI coach receives those measured results and suggests a small next practice step. Camera hand tracking is also available, though it does not yet assess fingering or technique.

How we built it

We built the application in Python with a Tkinter desktop interface. Mido and python-rtmidi connect the application to a digital piano, while a local evaluator checks note and chord accuracy.

Audiveris converts PDF sheet music into MusicXML. Imported passages require review and approval before they become practice material.

The AI coach uses OpenAI’s Responses API. Linux voice input uses recorded audio and OpenAI transcription, while text-to-speech produces spoken replies. OpenCV and MediaPipe provide camera capture and hand-landmark tracking.

We use uv to manage Python dependencies and GitHub Actions to run automated checks.

Challenges we ran into

One challenge was keeping musical feedback grounded in evidence. We separated performance evaluation from AI coaching: MIDI determines which keys were played, and the model explains the results.

Another challenge was coordinating microphone input, spoken replies, reference playback, and the interface without blocking interaction or letting ADA hear itself. We added background processing, cancellation, and microphone pauses during spoken output.

Score recognition introduced another source of uncertainty. Instead of treating every converted PDF as correct, we built a review-and-approval step before practice begins.

Accomplishments that we’re proud of

We connected score import, audible reference playback, MIDI-based practice, and conversational coaching in a working prototype.

We also implemented Linux voice interaction and verified microphone capture, cloud transcription, spoken playback, and live agent responses. Our local verification included 217 passing automated tests.

What we learned

An accessible learning experience needs more than spoken interface text. Instructions must be concise, controls must remain predictable, and feedback must distinguish measured facts from assumptions.

We also learned the value of keeping local practice independent from cloud services. Learners can continue basic note and chord practice even when AI coaching is unavailable.

What’s next for ADA Piano Teacher

Our next priority is testing the complete workflow with blind and visually impaired learners, especially score review, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader compatibility.

We also want to improve voice interaction, add rhythm assessment, and investigate calibrated finger-to-key tracking. The current prototype evaluates note and chord attacks; it does not yet grade rhythm, posture, or fingering.

title: Nod & Read
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Nod & Read

An accessible comic reader for blind, low-vision and dyslexic readers. Panels play one by one with character voices, controlled by your face.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Comics are one of the most visual kinds of storytelling, and that makes them one of the least accessible. A blind reader can listen to an audiobook, but there's almost no way to listen to a comic. Dyslexic readers struggle with dense speech bubbles, and anyone who can't easily use their hands has to fight with tiny page-turn buttons. We wanted a comic to feel like a show you watch, one you can control just by moving your head.

What it does

Nod & Read turns comic pages into an accessible, hands-free experience:

🎬 One panel per screen. It finds every panel, puts them in reading order, and a camera glides across the page from panel to panel, like a motion comic.
🗣️ A voice for every character. Each character gets their own voice, with emotion ("[whispers]", "[urgently]"), plus sound effects under each panel.
🎧 Audiobook mode. A narrator describes the setting, the action, and each character's expression and body language.
🙂 Face control. Turn your head right for yes / next panel, left for no / back, close your eyes to toggle the narrator, and look up to pause. Face tracking runs entirely in your browser, so no video ever leaves your device.
❤️ A heart meter. Smiles and nods fill it, shakes drain it, and it picks what to watch next: more of what you liked, or a change of mood if you didn't enjoy it.
♿ Accessibility built in. Dyslexia-friendly and low-vision fonts, colour-blind correction applied to the artwork itself, emotion labels for readers who find expressions hard to read, full screen-reader and keyboard support, and translation into 7 languages, voiced by the same cast.

The library is curated: only public-domain and Creative Commons comics, like Little Nemo in Slumberland (1905) and Pepper&Carrot.

How we built it

Every page goes through an AI pipeline:

Magi v2 (Hugging Face) detects the panels. It was trained on manga, so we re-sort its right-to-left order into Western rows read left to right.
Google Gemini reads the whole page once to build a consistent cast list, then writes each panel's script in parallel: scene description, narration, dialogue with speakers and emotion tags, and sound-effect prompts. If one model is overloaded or rate-limited, requests fall back to another Gemini Flash model.
Gemini casts one ElevenLabs voice per character. ElevenLabs v3 performs the dialogue and generates the sound effects, and edge-tts voices the narrator in each language.
Everything is stored in Neon (Postgres plus object storage). Pages are cached by their SHA-256 hash, so nothing is generated twice.
The FastAPI backend streams pipeline progress over Server-Sent Events into a live visualization of the comic being read, which zooms seamlessly into the reader.

The front end is React 19 + TypeScript + Vite. MediaPipe Face Landmarker tracks 478 face points on-device, and three.js renders an animated 3D guide that teaches each gesture.

Head turn (yaw) comes from the face's rotation matrix:

$$\text{yaw} = \operatorname{atan2}!\left(-m_{8},\ \sqrt{m_{9}^2 + m_{10}^2}\right)$$

$$\text{yaw} = \operatorname{atan2}!\left(-m_{8},\ \sqrt{m_{9}^2 + m_{10}^2}\right)$$

During setup you hold each turn until a bar fills, and we set your own threshold from how far you held it:

$$\theta = \operatorname{clamp}!\big(0.6 \cdot \operatorname{median}(\text{held}),\ 10^\circ,\ 24^\circ\big)$$

That way, people who can only turn a little can still use the whole site.

Challenges we ran into

Gestures are noisy. Head turns were misread as shakes, the "neutral" position drifted, and talking or another face walking into the frame set off false triggers. We added re-arming, grace periods, a stillness check, and auto-pause when you look away.
Winks didn't work for everyone. Many people can't wink with one eye, so we switched to closing both eyes for one second.
Too many gestures. We first had nods, shakes, gaze and winks all issuing commands. It was confusing, so we cut it down to two simple ones: right = yes, left = no. Nods now only fill the heart meter.
Left and right got flipped. The webcam image is mirrored, so we flipped head-turn direction more than once before confirming it on real hardware.
Old comics broke panel detection. Little Nemo's ornate 1905 layouts confused Magi, so we marked those panels by hand.
Keeping voices consistent across pages and separate uploads of the same comic took a whole-page cast list with stable character IDs.
Hosting cheaply. PyTorch is huge, so we made the server reading-only: it serves everything already stored, with no PyTorch and no model API keys, in about 1–2 GB of RAM.
Licensing. We dropped every comic we couldn't legally use, so the library is public domain and Creative Commons only.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

You can watch a full comic with character voices, sound effects and a narrator without touching anything.
Face tracking is private by design: it runs entirely in the browser.
Per-user calibration makes face control work for people with limited movement.
The live visualization shows the AI reading the comic, then zooms straight into the reader with no cut.

What we learned

Accessibility features help everyone. Captions, narration and hands-free control made the app better for all of us, not only the people we built it for.
Fewer, clearer gestures beat clever ones. Every gesture we removed made the app easier to use.
Testing on real webcams, real faces and real lighting catches bugs no simulation will.
Caching AI output by content hash keeps costs down and makes replays instant.

What's next for Nod & Read

A bigger library, through partnerships with public-domain archives and Creative Commons creators.
User testing with blind, low-vision and motor-impaired readers.
A mobile app with the front camera as the controller.
More languages and more expressive narration.
Letting creators submit their own licensed comics for review.

title: SketchSensAI
text:
Notifications

Loading...

SketchSensAI

SketchSensAI is an AI drawing coach for all ages, offering personalized drawing tips and custom reference images to help everyone learn, improve, and bring their creative ideas to life.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Drawing has always been a passion of ours, and we believe everyone should have the chance to experience its joy. That’s why we created SketchSensAI, an AI-powered drawing coach that guides users step by step in bringing anything they imagine to life. Our mission is to make drawing accessible to everyone, build confidence, and inspire creativity through art.

What it does

SketchSensAI is an AI-powered drawing tool that helps users improve their artistic skills through interactive practice. Users can draw with a mouse, touch, or stylus, choose preset subjects or describe their own, and practice using reference images and customizable shape guides. With step-by-step outlines, real-time AI feedback, and side-by-side comparisons, SketchSensAI makes learning to draw more engaging, accessible, and intuitive.

How we built it

We built the app with a JavaScript frontend and a Node.js backend. The drawing canvas handles input, undo and redo, and guide overlays. Hugging Face image generation creates Freehand references, while a vision model provides drawing feedback. The app can connect to a local vision model over Tailscale.

Challenges we ran into

Turning generated images into useful tracing guides was challenging. We needed to extract clean contours, split them into manageable parts, and keep the reference and guide aligned. We also had to handle slow or unavailable model responses without losing the user’s drawing.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We brought the full practice flow together: start with a preset or an original idea, get a reference, work through a guide, and compare the result. We’re proud that people can choose how much guidance they see while keeping their own sketch at the center.

What we learned

We learned that useful AI feedback depends on the full experience around the model: clear controls, helpful timing, reliable error handling, and a drawing flow that still feels good when a model is slow or unavailable. We also learned how to combine generated images with vector contours for interactive tracing.

What's next for SketchSensAI

We’d like to improve the guide and feedback quality, make it easier to use across devices, and add secure accounts and cloud-based sketch storage. We also want to explore ways for people to share practice sessions and learn from each other.

The Hackathon Oracle

Divine your project's future. 
Change your fate and claim the win.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

After the long sleepless nights during the hackathon it's finally time to make your DevPost. Your presentation is arguably the most important part of the project but not many teams give it the proper amount of time to get it right (we sure didn't). The Hackathon Oracle is here to put your DevPost to the test, and foresee whether your project has what it takes to win big.

What it does

The Oracle predicts your odds of winning, the category you stand the best chance in, and tries to provide helpful advice so that you can alter your fate before it is too late.

How we built it

The Oracle is trained on 3,526 projects studied across 17 in person hackathons within the last 3 years. The Oracle judges a project's chances of winning using a two stage classifier. A text model estimates how "winner-like" the project write up is. Then a model combines that score with project completeness and technology features gathered from the DevPost.

Challenges we ran into

We lost a lot of time coming up with ideas and didn't start until the second day. This put us on a pretty substantial time crunch and taught us the importance of preparing some ideas before hand.

What's next for The Hackathon Oracle

Looking deeper into a project's description: A project's description has a lot more info than we were able to parse through in our limited time. While the sentence transformer inherently learns this and uses it in scoring, having more data from the description like the type of project: finance, video game, etc. would be a great insight into what sort of projects win hackathons.

title: Knight-Wagon
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Knight-Wagon

fast and efficient campus food service delivery robot 

Like

Comment

Robot

NVIDIA and robot

Touchscreen Display Monitor

Attaching Cameras

Inspiration

We found that UCF's campus is huge, and getting food isn't always easy. For example, a student with a disability, someone stuck in a lab or a long study session, or anyone without a car on a hot Florida day. Food delivery apps either don't reach inside campus or cost a lot for a short trip. We wanted on-campus delivery that's accessible and cheap: order from your phone, and a robot brings it to wherever you are.

What it does

Knight-Wagon is a self-driving delivery robot with a full ordering app around it. With this, a person can order from a phone, browse 18 UCF campus shops and their menus in the iOS app, build a cart, and check out with the current location becoming the drop-off point. The whole point is that the robot comes to the customer. The order goes to the robot, which drives itself along sidewalks using cameras, depth, lidar, and GPS. It stops for obstacles and people, and treats crosswalks carefully. Live tracking is also available, following the robot on a map in real time, with order status from "placed" through "on the way", "arrived," and "delivered". In contact between the person and robot, a secure hand-off takes place. Each order gets a PIN. Enter it on the robot's touchscreen to release your food. Five wrong tries lock it for 10 minutes. There are apps for every role: customers order and track, shop staff accept orders and send the robot, and operators see the robot's position and battery, and can emergency-stop or resume it from their phone. Safety is always a priority. Every motion command passes a motion gate that blocks driving without fresh localization and a clear path ahead. Speed is hard-capped. Physical buttons on the robot latch a stop that no remote command can override.

How we built it

We built the robot on a Hiwonder JetAuto, a four-wheel mecanum base with an STM32 motor board (buttons, buzzer, OLED, IMU), driven by an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB running ROS 2 Humble. For sensing, it carries an Orbbec Astra Pro Plus RGB-depth camera in front, an RPLidar A1 for 360° range, three ELP AR0234 global-shutter fisheye cameras (left, right, rear) on a powered USB 3 hub, an iFlytek six-microphone ring array with a USB speaker, a 7-inch touchscreen kiosk for the PIN hand-off, and GPS from the hotspot phone riding on the robot after the USB GPS puck proved deaf. Everything runs on the robot itself: RTAB-Map visual odometry fused with wheel and IMU data by an EKF, NVIDIA's X-Mobility model as the local driving policy (ONNX on the GPU), and a motion gate with lidar clearance checks that has the final say on every wheel command. A single GPU vision server runs YOLO26n-seg plus a fine-tuned person detector (TensorRT), and three models from Hugging Face: Depth Anything V2 Metric-Outdoor-Small for depth from the color image in daylight, NVIDIA's SegFormer-B0 (ADE20K) as the night-time ground model, and Facebook's Mask2Former Swin-Large (Mapillary Vistas) with our own adapter to tell sidewalk from road, crosswalk, and grass. A Vosk speech model listens for "help" and "stop that," saves video from every camera, and announces a simulated 911 call, and a FastAPI backend (Postgres, Redis, Firebase, Cloudflare tunnel) and an iOS app send orders to the robot over a WebSocket bridge. We also evaluated VILA 1.5, Qwen-Drive, SmolVLM, and SmolVLA from Hugging Face but did not deploy them, and used NVIDIA Isaac Sim for early simulation and reinforcement-learning experiments.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges and the greatest thing we realized is that GPS is hard on a small robot. Our USB GPS receiver heard no satellites, so we switched to the iPhone's GPS and compass. That meant designing for about 5 m of error: arrival requires three consistent position readings, not just one. There were real-time limits. On the robot, visual odometry ran about 300 ms behind, while our motion gate requires a pose under 200 ms old. We had to tune the robot to meet that rather than loosen the safety rule. Bringing the simulation into reality was a tough job. We started with reinforcement learning, then found our simulator's obstacle model was measurably wrong. We threw out the learned pipeline and rebuilt navigation as deterministic, testable obstacle avoidance. Networking in the field with QuickTunnel's address changes every restart. The robot booting offline with its clock at 1970 broke HTTPS. Campus Wi-Fi's captive portal silently swallowed connections. We built automatic reconnection, clock-setting from GPS time, and plain-language connection errors. Integration was complicated. We merged robot, backend, and app work from several branches. One of our bugs was a .gitignore rule that hid the app's whole data layer on case-insensitive file systems.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

As a team, we are incredibly proud of a full order-to-robot pipeline. We were able to build an ordering app that becomes a route the robot drives, with live tracking and a PIN-secured hand-off. Autonomous delivery through the full safety chain in simulation was able to handle people crossing its path, barrier detours, and a hidden destination it had to search for. On the real robot, the motor path and safety checks pass, the motion gate is deployed, and localization meets its timing target.

What we learned

Throughout this process, we learned that measuring the real robot before trusting the simulator is key: wheel radius, sensor latency, and GPS error are all very realistic things. We also had to adjust to the fact that hardware projects are mostly integration with clear interfaces between robot, backend, and app, letting a team build them in parallel. Planning ahead and designing for failure was one of the best things we did in this process. Then dropped connections, restarted servers, and bad GPS fixes all happen, so every part needs a safe default.

What's next for Knight-Wagon

Our goal is to definitely set up smooth real-world tracking in the app, as well as making it accessible to campuses all around the nation. There are things we want to build on and improve, like creating a temperature-adjustable, lockable compartment that opens only with the right PIN. Subsequently, side and rear fisheye cameras feeding obstacle checks and person detection running entirely on the robot.
Integrating businesses and the concept of campus dining is also a bullet point on what is next for Knight-Wagon. Real menus, live prices, and payment with student meal plans.

text:
Notifications

Paralassist

Helping paralyzed patients communicate when their voice cannot

Like
4

Comment

Inspiration

Paralyzed patients are unable to control the majority of their bodies, sometimes including their voice. However, they still retain the function of their brains. Paralassist turns these brain signals into a voice, allowing them to request help and make commands. 

What it does

Paralassist uses an electroencephalogram (EEG) with a visual stimulus to convert a user's brain signals into messages. Users gaze at flickering tiles associated with messages, and generative AI is used to bring meaning to their responses.

How we built it

Visual Frequencies: The human brain will attempt to replicate visual frequencies from flashing lights with Steady-State Visually Evoked Potentials (SSVEPs). We use these to associate them with meaningful messages and allow users to communicate with a glance.
EEG Acquisition: Electrodes placed at the occipital lobe receive SSVEPs that are emitted when the user is exposed to specific visual frequencies associated with messages.
AI Interpreters: Two AI models, a TRCA model and a model using the EEGNet neural network, calibrate themselves to the user’s brain waves and then interpret their SSVEPs into meaningful messages or commands. 

Challenges we ran into

Training data was scarce, and the public SSVEP datasets we found varied in experiment type and had small inconsistencies with our needs, making them hard to unify. Developing the model was also a learning curve for our team, and working through preprocessing, feeding data, and model tuning deepened our understanding of the field.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Half of our four-person team were first-time hackers, so the event was as much a learning experience as a build. We picked up new skills along the way, from training a machine learning model to learning how to navigate GitHub for version control, and collaborated effectively throughout. We’re also proud of bringing together our unique interests and fields of study into a single project.

What we learned

Through this project and the development of two AI models, we learned a lot about the workings of machine learning, such as how TRCAs and convolutional neural networks function. This is also the first hackathon for two of our teammates, and they learned a lot about GitHub and aspects of web design. 

What's next for Paralassist

Paralassist has strong potential in medical field, where it can give ALS, spinal cord injury, geriatric, or locked-in syndrome patients a reliable, signal-based way to communicate basic needs. The same principle extends well beyond the hospital. Any setting where a person’s hands, voice, or attention are already occupied could benefit from a hands-free, silent control channel. Surgeons, pilots, and machine operators could issue commands without using their hands, and technicians could work in noisy or hazardous settings where speech and touch aren’t practical.

Watchdog

Watchdog transforms Boston Dynamics SPOT robot inspection data into actionable insights, helping power plant operators detect hidden anomalies, monitor equipment, and prevent overlooked failures.

Like
4

Comment

Inspiration

Inspired by NextEra Energy's challenge at Knight Hacks 2026, we developed Watchdog, a platform that transforms synthetic Boston Dynamics SPOT robot inspection data into actionable insights.

Our goal was simple: A completed inspection should never mean an overlooked problem.

What it does

Watchdog helps operators monitor robotic inspections through an interactive dashboard. Users can replay missions, follow SPOT's movements, identify hidden equipment anomalies, and prioritize maintenance decisions.

Our platform also provides equipment histories, performance analytics, interactive facility maps, and simulated scenarios involving extreme weather and obstacles.

How we built it

We built Watchdog using Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, with the interface designed in Figma.

Our custom simulation engine uses A pathfinding and Canvas 2D* to animate SPOT navigating inspection routes.

The backend uses Node.js, Express, and Neon PostgreSQL to manage inspection records, sensor readings, anomalies, and operator decisions.

We also explored AI integration using a Hugging Face summarization model, allowing users to generate draft mission summaries with validation checks against inspection records.

The application is deployed using Vercel and Railway.

Challenges we ran into

Our first challenge was defining team responsibilities, designing the architecture, and coordinating development. Some team members were unfamiliar with GitHub workflows, adding to the learning curve.

We also faced challenges integrating the frontend, backend, and simulation engine within the hackathon's limited timeframe.

Another challenge was implementing an open-source AI model. It sometimes generated information that wasn't supported by our inspection data, teaching us the importance of validating AI-generated responses.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud of transforming our initial idea into a deployed, full-stack application in one weekend.

We successfully integrated a custom robotic simulation, interactive dashboard, cloud database, mission analytics, and operator decision tracking.

Most importantly, we created a system that demonstrates how robotic inspection data can help operators recognize problems that might otherwise go unnoticed.

What we learned

We strengthened our skills in GitHub collaboration, full-stack development, relational databases, API integration, simulation, and AI experimentation.

We also learned the importance of planning, defining responsibilities, communicating across different development areas, and managing our time effectively.

Above all, we learned that building a successful application requires both technical skills and teamwork.

What's next for Watchdog

We hope to connect Watchdog to live robotic inspection systems, improve the accuracy of AI-generated insights, and expand predictive maintenance capabilities.

Our vision is to help energy operators identify problems earlier, improve inspection efficiency, and strengthen infrastructure reliability.

title: BlackBox
text:
Notifications

Loading...

BlackBox

It’s a black box for your car that runs on your phone: it detects a crash, saves the evidence, and reconstructs what happened in 3D within seconds.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

After a car crash, the most important evidence disappears in seconds. What's left is two drivers with two different stories, and whoever decides what happened has to rely on memory, guesswork, and whatever a bystander happened to see. Planes have black boxes. Most cars don't, and the ones that do keep their data locked away from the person who was actually in the accident.

We wanted a reliable source of truth for accident situations: something that records what really happened at the moment of impact so the people sorting it out afterwards (drivers, insurers, attorneys) are working from evidence and not recollection.

What it does

The crash re-enactor turns the phone already in your car into a crash black box. The phone keeps a rolling buffer of motion data and video. When it detects an impact, it saves the 10 seconds before and the 5 seconds after, checks whether the driver is okay, and can alert an emergency contact.

Seconds later, our web app shows a 3D replay of the crash with the video synced to the sensor data, plus a report with the impact force, direction and speed change. An AI model describes the scene from the video and writes the report narrative. Every number is labelled as an estimate, and the report never assigns fault. It presents what was recorded.

How we built it

The capture side is a web page that uses the phone's motion sensors and camera, so there is no app to install. You scan a QR code and tap Start. The web app is built with React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind, with the 3D replay in three.js. The AI runs locally through Ollama, using moondream to read the video frames and Gemma 3 to write the narrative, so crash footage never leaves our own hardware. Incidents sync to Supabase and the site is hosted on Vercel.

We built a crash simulator first so we could develop the whole pipeline before any hardware worked.

Challenges we ran into

Our hardware died halfway through. The original design was a sensor pod built on an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense, mounted on a Lego car and streaming data over Bluetooth. It worked, and we had live data flowing into the app. Then midway through the hackathon the Nano stopped being detected by our computers entirely. Nothing we tried brought it back, and we had no spare.

That failure made the project better. We asked what else has an accelerometer, a gyroscope, a camera and a radio, and the answer was in our pockets. Moving the black box onto a phone gave us video, which the Arduino never could, and that made the AI scene description and the synced replay possible. It also meant the product went from a device you would have to manufacture to a link anyone can open.

We also dropped two other approaches along the way, an overhead tracking camera and phone LiDAR scanning, when they turned out not to fit. And we learned that phone sensors are slow compared to how fast a real crash happens, which is why we are upfront that our numbers are estimates.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The full chain works on real hardware. Crash the car, and a replay and report appear on the laptop about 20 seconds later, then on the hosted site. We lost our core hardware mid-hackathon and still shipped something better than the original plan.

What we learned

Build the simulator first. Because our pipeline ran on simulated crashes from the start, losing the Arduino cost us a sensor and not the project. We also learned that constraints improve designs. We would not have chosen the phone if the Nano had kept working, and the phone was the right answer.

What's next for BlackBox

A native app with faster sensor access for better measurements, signed records so a report can be shown to be unaltered, and reconstruction of both vehicles when both are running it.

title: Here
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Here

Here is a spatial awareness platform for the deaf and hard of hearing. It identifies the sounds and voices around you and tells you where they are with a haptic belt.

Like
3

Comment

Hear & There

Here dashboard

Haptic belt internals

Inspiration

Caption apps turn speech into text. They don't tell you who said it, or where that person is standing. Sound alerts say "doorbell" and leave you to figure out which way to turn.

Deaf and hard-of-hearing people miss more than words. They miss where a sound came from, who in a group is talking, how it was said, and that anything happened at all while they were looking the other way. A car behind you is a direction problem before it's a vocabulary problem.

What it does

HERE fuses a microphone array, a camera, and a haptic belt into one spatial picture of the room.

🗣️ Captions on the right person. Each line floats above whoever said it (Person 1, 2, 3) with a tone chip: whispering, laughing, loud.
🔔 Sounds with a direction. Doorbell, your name, a car, footsteps, an alarm. A card names the sound and a ring points to it.
🧭 A belt that turns you. Someone speaks behind you, the belt buzzes on that side of your waist, you turn, and their caption slides into view. Works with the phone locked in your pocket.
🧠 Attention, not noise. An AI layer decides whether a sound is ambient, notice, important, or urgent. A fan doesn't buzz you. A car behind you always does.
🗺️ Memory. HERE Now shows the room live. Hear & Now replays your days on a 3D map of campus, answers questions like "when did the doorbell ring?" with evidence, and surfaces patterns across days.
🔒 Private by design. No audio or video ever leaves a device. Only text, labels, and bearings travel.

How we built it

The rig

Part
Role

ReSpeaker XVF3800 mic array
The ears: direction of arrival + two focused beams

Laptop with RTX GPU
The hearing module: speech, sound, and attention models

iPhone on a chest mount
Stands in for AR glasses: its camera is the glasses' camera, its screen is the display

ESP32 haptic belt
The output: tells your body where to turn

Relay on Vultr
Connects everything, on any network

The belt (built from parts)

We soldered and wired the belt ourselves and tested after every stage with a multimeter.

Controller: 30-pin ESP32 in a screw-terminal breakout. It only switches; it never powers a motor.
Driver: ULN2803 Darlington array, with COM tied to +5 V so its built-in flyback diodes absorb the motors' kick.
Motors: 3 V coin motors, each bonded to a 2.5 cm plate cut from a plastic card. A bare coin motor shakes a spot you can miss through a shirt; the plate spreads it over skin you can't miss.
Power: an Anker power bank through a cut USB cable into Wago lever connectors as +5 V and ground hubs, with a 1000 µF cap so the ESP32 doesn't brown out when motors spin up. Every motor gets its own home-run wire pair with strain relief.
Motor safety: a firmware duty cap on the PWM so 5 V never cooks a 3 V motor.
Bluetooth LE: one write-without-response characteristic. A 3-byte command fires one motor; a 4-byte bitmask command fires several at once; 0xFF stops everything.
Fail-safe: the firmware owns the off-timers, so Bluetooth jitter can't smear a pattern, and a disconnect stops every motor.
Mounting: motors on Velcro inside a tactical belt, electronics in a notched project box at the back, wires taped along the top edge and never across the buckle.

The phone decides where to buzz, not the belt. The array reports where the sound is in the world, the phone knows which way you're facing, and the belt gets the direction relative to your body. Turn around and the buzz stays pinned to the sound.

The mic array is embedded work too. We mask the XVF3800's two beams to separate two people talking at once, and drive its LED ring so it glows toward the sound. Even with the wearer standing off to the side of the array, bearing error stays inside one motor's sector at normal conversation distances.

The AI stack

HERE is a stack of models, each doing the one job it's good at, on a strict latency budget.

🎯 Attention with JEV, the part we're proudest of. Detecting a sound is easy. Knowing whether to interrupt a person is hard. We turn each event into one short state sentence:

Sound: doorbell (confidence 0.71). The wearer was in a conversation. No repeats in the last minute. Focus mode off.

Then we ask JEV-9B, an open decision model from AutoTrust, a typed question with fixed options: ambient, notice, important, or urgent, plus "was this said to the wearer?" It answers with calibrated probabilities, which decide between a small cue and a full card plus a belt buzz. Quantized to 4-bit so it fits beside the speech model on one laptop GPU: 208 ms median per decision.

🛡️ A safety rule around the model. The model can raise an alert. It can never lower one. Under 0.5 confidence or over its time budget, the next tier decides: a DeBERTa zero-shot classifier, then deterministic rules. A vehicle behind you is urgent no matter what any model says, and every event records which tier made the call.

Sound classification: audio-event models label what the array hears, and the phone's on-device sound analysis acts as a second sensor that has to agree.
Speech: streaming transcription with words appearing as they're spoken, a tone estimate per line, and filters that stop the model from inventing text on noise.
Fusion: the phone matches each line's bearing to a tracked face in the camera view, so the caption lands on the right person.
Context: Gemini writes a one-line context for a caption and phrases Ask HERE answers from the evidence rows.

Sponsor technology

🎙️ ElevenLabs

Scribe v2 Realtime powers streaming speech-to-text, the core of what a hard-of-hearing user reads. It sits behind a single transcriber interface with automatic mid-sentence failover to a local model, so a network drop never blanks the captions. On the live API we measured a 0.04 word error rate with first words in about 1.2 s.

☁️ Vultr

Our relay is a WebSocket service on Vultr behind Caddy for TLS. The laptop publishes events and Vultr fans them out to the iPhone in real time, on any network, no shared Wi-Fi required. It carries only text, labels, and bearings. We also built a one-command deploy script, a live status page with message rates, and session export to Vultr Object Storage using a dependency-free SigV4 client.

🤗 Hugging Face

HERE runs on open models from the Hub, and a lot of them:

Attention: JEV-9B (4-bit via transformers, peft, bitsandbytes) and MoritzLaurer/deberta-v3-base-zeroshot-v2.0
Speech: Whisper large-v3-turbo for local fallback
Sound: a real bakeoff on 254 clips of mispeech/ced-mini, AST, and laion/larger_clap_general (zero-shot with our own per-sound prompts) against PANNs CNN14

Every backend is one config line apart, and we report results as measured: CED-mini was 2.3× faster at a third of the memory, while PANNs caught more doorbells under crowd noise. Every event names the model that produced it.

🧱 Databricks

The live system answers "what's happening now?" Databricks answers "what keeps happening?" A serverless job reads the exported event log from a Unity Catalog volume, aggregates it in Spark into Delta tables, and writes ranked insights back:

where your name was called from behind and you missed it
the crosswalk where danger comes from the rear
who you talk to most
your quietest window and the loudest place-hour

These become the pattern cards in Hear & Now on a 3D map of UCF, each stamped with the run that produced it. ~4,500 events → 13 insights in 83 seconds. A plain-Python fallback means the dashboard never blocks on the cloud.

🐘 Neon

Memory lives in Neon Postgres: sessions, every event, final utterances with full-text search, and the Databricks insights. Ask HERE is a SQL question first (full-text search plus time and bearing filters), then a phrased answer linked to the evidence. Campus Wi-Fi blocks port 5432, so we wrote a small shim that talks to Neon's SQL-over-HTTPS API on port 443.

Challenges we ran into

Two motors didn't survive. We designed for eight motors and coin motor leads are hair-thin. We ended up with six working channels, remapped the firmware, added the bitmask command so two neighbors can fire together to point between them, and re-tuned the direction mapping.
Three models, one GPU. JEV-9B is 18 GB at full precision; the laptop has 16 GB shared with speech and sound. 4-bit got it to ~6 GB. Cold, it missed our latency gate (496 ms). Warm, it passed (208 ms).
Speech models hallucinate on noise. In a loud hall the transcriber wrote sentences nobody said. Now we only trust a segment if the array heard a talker long enough, and drop segments the model itself doubts.
Campus Wi-Fi. It blocks Postgres and isolates devices from each other, which is exactly why the relay and HTTPS database driver exist.
Four ideas of "forward." The array, the compass, the camera's field of view, and the belt all disagreed. Nothing worked until everything became a bearing in one shared frame.
Overloading the user. The first version buzzed for everything. Most of the attention work is deciding what to leave out.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The turn-around: someone speaks behind you, the belt buzzes, you turn, and their caption is waiting on them.
A hand-built belt a stranger can put on and understand in seconds.
An AI layer with a real safety rule: models can escalate, never suppress.
A full system that runs without any of its hardware, from fixtures and mocks, with one message contract shared across Python, Swift, and TypeScript.

What we learned

Direction is the missing half of accessibility for sound. A label without a bearing leaves the user searching.
Haptics should carry direction and nothing else. Short patterns, never continuous buzzing.
Commit fast, then refine. Show something immediately and let slower models fill in.
Measure before you claim. Our benchmarks changed our minds more than once.
Soldering: put the heat shrink on before you make the joint.

What's next for HERE

Real AR glasses in place of the chest-mounted phone, with the mic array on the wearer
All eight motors, then a slimmer belt on a custom PCB
Testing with deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and tuning attention to each person
A phone-only mode for walking outside, where a car behind you matters most

Mimisis

Low-cost robot teleoperation with just two webcams and your bare hands

Like
2

Comment

Inspiration

Mimesis started with a goal: make it cheap for robots to learn from human demonstrations. Robots pick up new skills from recordings of an operator guiding them through a task, but the tools for capturing those recordings are expensive and hard to use. Affordable research arms like the open-source SO-ARM101 are normally driven with a second "leader" arm, which doubles the hardware cost and takes practice to operate.

We wanted any student, hobbyist or researcher to be able to control a real robot arm with nothing more than a laptop, two webcams and their own hands.

What it does

Mimesis is an end-to-end, vision-based teleoperation system for the SO-ARM101. It works as follows:

Hand Tracking: Two consumer webcams and the WiLoR neural network find 21 keypoints on each hand. We triangulate them into a 3D hand pose.
Two-Hand Control: The right hand moves the gripper through 3D space. Twisting the left hand rotates the wrist, and making a fist closes the gripper.
Motion Control: A custom inverse-kinematics solver turns the hand pose into joint angles. A 50 Hz driver moves the arm with safety checks on each joint.
Research Ready: Sessions can be recorded and replayed exactly. A ROS 2 interface lets researchers plug in their own trackers, controllers or AI policies.

How we built it

Mimesis combines stereo computer vision, Kalman filtering, inverse kinematics and real-time servo control, connected through ROS 2.

The Hardware: 
An SO-ARM101 arm with six Feetech STS3215 servos, plus two Elgato Facecam MK.2 webcams at 1080p and 60 fps.

The Vision Pipeline: 
A YOLO hand detector and WiLoR (a vision-transformer hand model) run in PyTorch. An IMM Kalman filter then smooths the triangulated hand position.

Core Optimizations: 
Fixing how the driver handled messages cut command-to-arm latency from 700 ms to ~220 ms. A PyTorch upgrade and a multithreaded pipeline doubled tracking to 20–21 updates/s. The new filter cut smoothing lag from ~90 ms to 20–40 ms.

AMD Cloud Server: 
For laptops without a GPU, WiLoR runs as a FastAPI service on an AMD GPU with ROCm. We sped it up by batching both camera views into one FP16 model call, running the detector only every third frame, auto-tuning GPU kernels with TunableOp and keeping several requests in flight.

Challenges we ran into

Network latency was our biggest challenge. The cloud server needs only ~20 ms per frame, but network transit adds about 300 ms per round trip, which we can't reduce from our side. We therefore support two modes: local GPU (~50–60 ms) for the most responsive control, and the AMD cloud server for machines without a GPU. On the hardware side, we had to correct a misfocused camera that caused wrist glitches, joint limits narrower than the robot model's, gravity sag in the shoulder, and a wrist encoder that couldn't rotate past a fixed point.

Accomplishments

We're proud of building a full-stack system that drives a physical robot arm through pick-and-place tasks using only two webcams and natural hand motion. We also cut its latency by more than half and ran hand tracking on NVIDIA, Apple and AMD GPUs.

What we learned

High-Performance Computing: GPU inference with PyTorch on ROCm, CUDA and Apple MPS, including kernel tuning and FP16 precision.
Robotics: Inverse kinematics, Kalman filtering and servo tuning on real hardware.
System Integration: Combining computer vision, a cloud server, ROS 2 and a physical robot into one application.

What's next

Record demonstrations in the LeRobot format and train AI policies that do tasks on their own.
Move the cloud server to a region with lower network delay.

Special Thanks to AMD

We thank AMD for access to the AMD Developer Cloud GPU that powers Mimesis's cloud mode.

Certifi

Good music. Good people. Great nights.

Like
1

Comment

GIF

Inspiration

Each of us in the group are avid music enjoyers - over 100,000 minutes each on our yearly Spotify Wrappeds and dozens of concerts attended. So we feel that being able to experience the vibrations of the stereo and the harmonics of both old or newly discovered artists coursing through your body at a venue is a sensation that everyone should get a taste of in their lifetimes. Unfortunately, finding concerts that match our interests, schedules, and budgets can be a hassle, and any potential plans between us always ends up falling through.
We created Certifi to make to concert-going process easy, collaborative, and fun. Instead of searching for events individually and coordinating flimsy plans afterward, we wanted to help friends discover concerts together and identify options that fit the group.

What it does

Certifi is a social concert discovery platform that helps users find live music they and their friends may enjoy. Users can create a music profile by connecting Spotify or entering artists they like. The platform uses those preferences to surface concert recommendations.
Users can create groups, invite friends, and request recommendations based on a shared musical interest or event preferences. Group members can vote on suggested concerts, and a unanimous choice becomes a plan with event details and calendar links. Certifi aims to make it easier to move from discussing a concert to choosing one and coordinating attendance.

How we built it

We developed the web application with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The Next.js App Router serves the website and its API routes. Neon Postgres stores application data, including user profiles, groups, and concert plans, while Neon Managed Auth supports account creation, session management, and Google and GitHub sign-in.
A Python FastAPI service handles music analysis and recommendation tasks. It uses Sentence Transformers to generate embeddings, Last.fm to enrich artist information, Gemini to create artist descriptions and interpret group requests, and Ticketmaster to retrieve concert listings. The Next.js API communicates with FastAPI, allowing browser requests to remain on the same origin while connecting the interface to the recommendation service.

Challenges we ran into

Integrating authentication across the application required careful debugging. Email sign-in worked before social sign-in reliably appeared in the user session, so we investigated how OAuth callbacks, cookies, and local app origins interacted. We also learned that editing a schema file in the repository does not update the live Neon database; new profile-photo fields required a database migration before the API could use them.
We also encountered issues at the boundaries between services and the browser. Failed API responses sometimes caused JSON parsing errors in the profile page, which led us to improve its error handling. These experiences reinforced the importance of examining logs and tracing errors frequently during the development process.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud to have built a functional experience that brings music discovery and group coordination together. Users can create a music profile, receive recommendations, form groups, invite friends, and vote on concerts. The app can also turn a group decision into a plan with event details and calendar links.
We are especially proud that Certifi addresses a problem our team has experienced firsthand. Concert discovery is shaped by individual taste, but attending a show is usually a group activity. We designed the project to support both, and believe it could help other people make plans around the music they enjoy.

What we learned

Developing Certifi gave us practical experience with Neon Postgres and Neon Managed Auth, including how authentication sessions connect to application data and how database schema changes must be applied to a live environment. We also learned how to connect a Next.js application to a separate FastAPI service while keeping the browser-facing API in one place.
We learned that effective prompting needs more than a few sentences at a time; an application needs to also handle ambiguous requests and flawed results. Throughout the project, we saw how essential error handling and debugging are to software development. Tracing issues across the browser, API routes, authentication, database, and Python service helped us understand how the system works as a whole.

What’s next for Certifi

We plan to improve concert recommendations by adding more precise date, price, and travel constraints. These options would help groups find events that fit their schedules and budgets, while giving Certifi more information to consider when ranking shows for multiple people.
We are also interested in adding a map view so users can explore recommended concerts by location, improving event and venue details, and supporting trip planning around shows. Our lonr-term goal is to make Certifi a useful place for friends to discover concerts in any area they're in, make decisions together, and coordinate the plans that follow in a simple and highly effective manner.

CodeSquire

Custom trained LLM Coding Agent, cheaper than Claude & Codex

Like
2

Comment

Inspiration

Agentic AI has made a break through in technology in the past few years, but chief among the use cases of generative AI has been coding. Those who do not know how to code become empowered with a new innovative skill and those who already knew became even more efficient. 

But not all models are easily accessible. Some people cannot afford the rising token prices. Some companies  have data that is far too sensitive to share over the internet with an LLM provider.

In August of this year, Pinterest has reported over 92% savings in LLM transaction costs. Uber has reported 52% savings per AI agent session. Lyzr.ai, Axis, Factory, and OpenPipe are other companies that have reported  similar results. All savings from hosting open source models on their own infrastructure rather than relying on the tech giants' expensive models.

What is CodeSquire

CodeSquire is an open source, lightweight coding agent leveraging the harness mini-swe-agent. After installing, users are able to run the command "codesquire" to open up the CLI tool and prompt the agent, approve of actions, and watch it solve complex coding issues within the terminal.

How we built it

Our team trained the LLM using Hugging Face's TRL library (Transformer Reinforcement Learning). The base model was Qwen-3-8B, which we then performed supervised fine-tuning on a RTX PRO 6000 WS (96 GB VRAM) GPU, using a dataset of reasoning traces and tool calls from a larger model of the same family (Qwen-3-Coder-30B). We trained it on a total of 18.6 million tokens across 2 epochs.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We evaluated our agent on a subset of a benchmark called Swe-Bench, we used 25 samples hand picked for their ranges in difficulty and uniqueness. The benchmark asks the agent to read through a given open source git repository and address a prompt in the form of a github issues to resolve a bug or implement a new feature. 

Results

Our agent achieved 200% improvement in github issues resolved over the base model (Qwen-3-8B) on the 25 sample subset as well as a 100% reduction in format errors. We have our full evaluation report on our Hugging Face repo.

What we learned

We learned how to work with a variety of state of the art open source frameworks such as vLLM, LiteLLM, TRL, and swe-agent.

What's next for CodeSquire

To continue our SFT training as we could have trained it on much more data, as we only used 1,000 training samples out of nearly 400,000. We also would love to implement RLVR using GRPO on Transformers Reinforcement Learning, the Hugging Face framework.

Lenny Roasts

Let Lenny roast your hackathon idea, rank it against simulated competitors, and help you sharpen your pitch before judging.

Like

Main Page - Knight Hacks Location UCF ENG2

Inspiration

We were brainstorming ideas, researching them, and even starting to build one before realizing it probably wasn’t worth pursuing. By then, we had already spent part of our hackathon finding out what we wished we had known earlier.

That made us wonder: what if we could get a rough feel for the competition and judging before committing to an idea? Would our project stand out? Does it actually fit the sponsor track? Is the pitch hiding a weak idea behind nice wording?

That’s where Lenny Roasts came from. We wanted a place to test an idea, hear the uncomfortable feedback early, and give it another shot while there was still time to change direction.

What it does

Lenny Roasts turns your hackathon idea into a practice submission. You describe your project, choose your sponsor tracks, and let Lenny evaluate it against a simulated field of competitors.

You get scores, category eligibility, a placement range, rival projects, and suggestions for improvement. The experience takes place in a 3D UCF setting, with sponsor classrooms, Lenny hosts, and a simulated awards ceremony.

The placements are practice results, not predictions of who will win. The goal is to help you spot weaknesses and make better decisions before the real judging starts.

How we built it

We split the work into three parts: preparing the competition, building the judging backend, and creating the frontend.

We used past public Devpost projects as seeds and GPT-6 Luna through Codex to create variations for our simulated field. Our final field contains 106 accepted projects.

Qwen3-32B, served through Hugging Face and DeepInfra, evaluates both those competitors and new user submissions. Each applicable category gets three scoring runs, and our code calculates the averages, eligibility, and rankings. We keep the judging settings consistent so users and competitors are compared on the same basis.

The backend uses FastAPI and Neon PostgreSQL. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js to bring the campus, classrooms, and ceremonies to life.

Challenges we ran into

Our biggest challenge was deciding which tracks we could simulate fairly. We wanted to include more, but had to leave out NVIDIA, AMD, OneEthos, Figma, Adobe, and others.

Some tracks involved hardware, where a written submission alone cannot show whether something actually works. Others depended heavily on the UI or design, which our text-based judge could not properly assess. For some sponsors, we also couldn’t find enough past hackathon examples to understand their judging expectations or build a useful field of simulated competitors.

That limited our scope more than we expected. Each track needed enough context to guide the judge and enough relevant projects to make the comparison useful. We focused on the categories we could support with the data and evaluation approach we had.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We’re proud that we turned a problem we were experiencing ourselves into a working practice tool during the hackathon.

We built and scored a 106-project simulated field, connected real Qwen evaluations to our backend and database, and verified the submission-to-report flow locally.

We also gave the project a setting that feels like our own hackathon. Walking through UCF, pitching to Lenny in a classroom, and watching a practice ceremony made the experience much more personal than a plain score dashboard.

What we learned

An idea deserves more than one enthusiastic conversation before implementation. Looking at it from the user’s perspective, the sponsor’s requirements, and the competition can reveal problems that brainstorming alone misses.

We learned how to work with open-source models more effectively: test model choices on concrete cases, give them clear rubrics, keep responses manageable, and check what they return.

We also learned that valid JSON can still contain bad judgment. Getting the format right was only the beginning; we had to question the scores and explanations too.

What's next for Lenny Roasts

We want users to revise a pitch and compare versions, so they can see how their changes affect the feedback.

We also want to support more hackathons with their own tracks and competitor fields. The biggest next step is comparing our evaluations with feedback from real judges. That would help us understand where Lenny is useful, where it is too generous, and where it still misses the point.

title: Golden Egg
text:
Notifications
