Golden Egg

A brainstorming and idea validation app that helps teams compare ideas with 57,000+ hackathon projects, question their assumptions, and decide together what to build.

Like
4

Comment

Inspiration

We were brainstorming what to build for this hackathon. I had three ideas, and my teammate had three more. Before we had written any code, we already had a problem to solve: how do we choose?

We could explain why we liked our own ideas, but we needed more than opinions. What had other people already built? Were we solving a real problem? What would make one direction worth pursuing over another?

That conversation became our idea. We built Golden Egg to help teams work through the same decision we were facing.

Choosing a project shapes everything that follows, yet teams often make that choice with scattered searches, incomplete information, and whoever makes the most convincing argument. We wanted a shared place to explore possibilities, find evidence, and reach a decision everyone had helped make.

What it does

Golden Egg helps teams take an early idea through research, criticism, revision, and a final decision.

It starts with an interactive 3D map of more than 57,000 real hackathon projects. Each star represents a project and links back to its source. Teams can explore what people have built, discover related work, and find inspiration.

Type an idea or speak it aloud, and Golden Egg finds projects with similar meaning. Comparison cards explain what overlaps, what differs, and which existing project presents the strongest alternative. The map helps you explore, while the underlying search determines which projects are actually relevant.

Teams can then investigate the questions that matter before committing:

Does evidence suggest this problem exists?
What related tools are already available on GitHub or Hugging Face?
Which assumption would a judge, potential user, or engineer challenge?

The critic asks one question at a time, giving the team room to respond and rethink. Teams can accept a revision, keep their original idea, or branch into several directions.

When it is time to choose, both teammates vote privately. Their choices remain hidden until both have voted. The selected version becomes a fixed decision snapshot, with a read-only link and QR code for sharing.

Finding a similar project does not have to end an idea. It can help a team identify a more specific user, a missing capability, or a better approach.

How we built it

The foundation is a searchable collection of real projects. Our Python pipeline collects public Devpost pages, removes duplicate and near-empty records, and converts project descriptions into numerical representations of their meaning using BAAI/bge-m3. We store those vectors in Neon Postgres with pgvector.

New ideas use the same embedding model. We compare them against the stored projects using cosine similarity. Separately, UMAP projects the collection into three dimensions for visualization. Keeping these calculations separate matters: a star's position on the screen is not a reliable measure of how similar two ideas are.

We built the app with Next.js and TypeScript. React Three Fiber and Three.js render the galaxy, with the stars stored in a single GPU point buffer.

Gemini generates comparisons, critiques, revisions, and branches, while Google Search grounding supports problem research. Model responses must pass schema validation before reaching the interface. Claims carry labels distinguishing source-supported information, inference, and unverified statements.

ElevenLabs provides live speech transcription. The server issues a single-use session token so the API key stays out of the browser.

The engineering extends beyond asking a model for feedback. Golden Egg maintains a searchable project collection, retrieves relevant evidence, tracks idea versions, coordinates two participants, enforces private voting on the server, and preserves the final decision as a fixed snapshot. Those behaviors require application state, database logic, and verification alongside the model.

Challenges we ran into

Expanding the collection from 8,409 projects to more than 57,000 initially made our search worse.

Near-empty project pages were appearing as matches for unrelated ideas. Their vague descriptions placed them close to many short queries in the embedding space. We filtered out 187 low-information records and checked the results against known queries. That experience taught us that collecting more data only helps when the data is useful.

The larger collection also increased exact similarity search time from roughly 36 milliseconds to about 0.8 seconds. We kept exact search for this version because relevant results were worth the extra wait.

Coordinating coding agents across two laptops presented another challenge. We used written specifications, pull requests, ownership checks, CI, and verification before merging. When two agents attempted competing production updates, a safety check caught the changed state and prevented the second write. We learned why release coordination needs one clear source of truth.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We built a working path from an uncertain idea to a shared decision. A two-browser verification run with live Gemini covered idea entry, evidence, criticism, revision, branching, private voting, and the final shareable snapshot.

We also made important promises enforceable. Vote privacy is checked at the API response level. Later edits cannot change a shared decision snapshot. Missing evidence remains visible, and empty space on the map is never presented as proof that an idea is original.

What we learned

Useful feedback needs evidence and a clear next step. A question about one specific assumption gives a team something to investigate or change.

We also learned to distinguish passing automated tests, successful live API calls, and verified production behavior. Each answers a different question about whether the app works.

What's next for Golden Egg

We want to expand the project collection while keeping search accurate and responsive, add current event projects alongside past submissions, and let teams compare ideas against sponsor challenge requirements.

The goal stays close to the conversation that started this project: help a team with six possible ideas understand which one they want to spend their weekend building, and why.

title: Apprentice
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Apprentice

The universal tutor for humans and robots

Like
5

Comment
3

Inspiration

Kids learn by watching someone do a thing once, then trying it themselves. Robots are supposed to learn the same way, from demonstrations, but today that usually means thousands of training videos. Recording and training on all of that takes a huge amount of computing power and energy, which is not friendly to the environment. We kept asking: what if one demonstration could teach both? A parent or teacher builds something once, and then a child and a robot each try to repeat it, graded by the same camera with the same rules. Nobody has to hover over the child, and the robot gets honest feedback too.

What it does

Apprentice turns one demonstration into a lesson that two very different students can learn: a person and a robot arm.

Teach: someone builds a pattern with blocks on a 3x3 board, or records a video of it. Apprentice watches with an overhead camera and turns the build into a step-by-step lesson.
Learn: a student rebuilds it while a monitor shows a 3D view of the board. A holographic intro replays the build first. Then, as the student places each block, the camera checks it and gives kind, specific hints like "Close! Move the yellow block one cell to the right", with an arrow on the 3D board.
Repeat: press one key and the SO-101 robot arm builds the same lesson. The same camera grades the robot's work with the same checker. When the arm misses, it measures its own error and corrects the next try.
Play: Apprentice Buddy is a kids' version on a tablet. Picture Recall shows a pattern, hides it and asks the child to rebuild it from memory. Take Turns has the child and our robot character, Pip, build a picture together. Pip can point at a square for a hint, or take wrong blocks off.
Learn from the data: every placement, mistake, hint and timing goes into a journal. A Databricks pipeline turns the journals into tables and a dashboard, such as which steps are hardest and which cells cause the most mistakes.

How we built it

Hardware: an NVIDIA Jetson runs the overhead webcam, the vision pipeline, the robot API and the Buddy server. The board is a printed sheet with four AprilTags at the corners. The arm is an SO-101, driven through LeRobot.
Perception (OpenCV, on the Jetson): we lock the board's position once, using the tags on an empty board. Then we read the board cell by cell: for each of the 9 cells, the system draws what every possible stack (empty, or 1 or 2 blocks of each color) would look like from the camera's angle, compares that with the live image, and keeps the best match. It corrects for the camera's angle, reads stacks from the colors on their sides, votes over a few frames, and treats a hand over the board as "wait", never as a pass.
The brain (Python): a stabilizer waits for a steady board. Then a deterministic checker compares it with the lesson and returns a verdict: pass, wrong cell, wrong color, wrong level, missing, or extra. Unknown is never a pass, and no language model ever decides pass or fail. A session tracks progress straight from the board, so lifting off a finished block moves the lesson back a step.
Lessons from demonstrations: the extractor watches a live build or a video, turns the settled boards into steps, and runs a gate that refuses lessons it can't trust. Gemini only names a color when our camera and color memory can't, and only while processing a recording, never in the live checking.
The robot: a FastAPI service wraps our executor. It plans each pick and place from what the camera sees, clears blocks in the way, verifies every placement with the camera, and learns a correction from where its blocks actually land.
Interfaces: a three.js 3D monitor with a lesson picker, the intro replay and live hints, and Buddy's tablet app, which reuses the same 3D board.
Data: an append-only journal for every session, with each session tagged real (graded by the camera) or simulated, uploaded to Databricks and turned into bronze, silver and gold Delta tables plus a dashboard.
Team process: four people, frozen shared contracts, and a fake camera feed and fake robot, so everyone could build without waiting on hardware.

Challenges we ran into

Our cell names were the mirror image of the printed sheet. Only the three diagonal cells meant the same square in the camera code and on the paper and robot side, so the arm and the hints disagreed with the paper. We switched everything to the sheet's convention.
The blocks hid the corner tags. Our silicone blocks are 47 mm, so a block in a corner cell always covers part of a tag, and the board kept "disappearing". We lock the board's position once on an empty board and then only check the tags we can still see.
Tall towers broke the view. Our camera sits only 432 mm above the table, so the top of a 3-block tower leans a full cell over in the image. In real sessions, the 3-high lesson left 45% of boards unreadable, versus 8% on a flat lesson. We used that data to cap stacks at two blocks.
The arm knocked over its own towers and pressed down on blocks as it released them. We raised its travel height above the tallest stack, stopped it pushing on release, and made retries learn the arm's error at each height.
Lag stacked up. Four separate waits (the camera's vote, its stack memory, the brain's stabilizer and the UI's celebration) added 3 to 4 seconds. We shortened each one without weakening "unknown is never a pass".
Speeding things up broke safety. One of our speed-ups made a hand over the board read as unknown blocks instead of a hand. A test caught it, we reverted the change, and we added a guard: several unreadable cells at once means a hand.
Colors: under the venue lighting, orange and yellow, and teal and light blue, read as the same color, so we play with four colors that the camera separates clearly.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

One camera grades a human and a robot with the exact same deterministic rules.
A cell-by-cell vision model that reads stacks and stays honest: it says "I can't tell" instead of guessing.
A robot arm that checks every placement with the camera and corrects itself.
A full path from a physical build to a lesson to a game to analytics
Our design decisions came from our own data: the stack cap came straight from measured session results.

What we learned

In physical AI, the hard part is the boring part: lighting, camera angle, line endings, which way the grid is named.
Determinism builds trust. Letting language models write hints but never grade made the system predictable enough to put in front of a child.
Measure before arguing. Our journal and Databricks tables settled debates that opinions couldn't.
Fakes and frozen contracts let four people build one system without blocking each other.

What's next for Apprentice

Learn from any video: a parent films a build, and Apprentice turns it into a lesson at home.
More than blocks: cooking steps, chemistry lab setups, physical therapy exercises, anything with steps a camera can check.
Adaptive difficulty and parent reports built on the learning data: memory span over time, hints needed, common confusions.
A camera mounted higher, for taller stacks and bigger builds.
Robots that keep improving with every lesson they repeat.

text:

CampBuddy

This is a local AI assistant for campers/hikers or individuals needing informational assistance for survival/camping contexts such as identifying a plant, safety tips, hiking/camping tips, etc.

Like

Comment

Default Landing Page Light Mode

Default Landing Page Dark Mode

Sample Prompt and Response

Inspiration

We were inspired to provide a solution to a real problem that real people face in a real time constraint. Many of us use AI today but take for granted our internet access that allow us to use these powerful tools. Some individuals in remote locations like campers or hikers need the assistance of these tools but do not have the internet access that we do. 

What it does

This app provides a local AI assistant to users without wifi such as hikers and campers. Users can ask survival, first-aid, and gear questions and get answers grounded in locally stored manuals, with the source document and page shown so they can verify the advice, and with a clear label whenever an answer comes from the model's general knowledge instead.

Additionally, a computer vision model is also run locally aiding users with visual tasks such as identifying different species of plants. Users can then ask follow up questions about the images they've uploaded.

How we built it

We built this app using a React-based frontend (Vite and Tailwind CSS) and a FastAPI backend that passes each user question through a LangChain RAG pipeline, which retrieves the most relevant passages from a ChromaDB vector database of survival documents and feeds them to Llama 3.2 3B running locally on Ollama. This way, inference and document search stay on-device, and each user's chat history is saved privately in their own browser.

Challenges we ran into

One of the struggles we initially faced was determining which AI model to use for our local LLM. We had to prioritize capability while still taking into account RAM usage and limits that are most common in commercial laptops. 

We faced a similar challenge when choosing our computer vision model. We faced roadblocks where potential computer vision models that we wanted to use would completely misidentify plants and had to adapt to change of plans in a short notice. 

We also struggled with initially setting up our model and integrating it into our backend API routes. We also struggled with integrating the computer vision element for scanning plant types. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are particularly proud of the RAG integration and offline Computer Vision capability of CampBuddy.

What we learned

We learned LLMs can be run locally on laptops and how Retrieval Authenticated Generation (RAG) works to improve the local LLMs accuracy. Additionally we learned more about how computer vision works, what the potential downfalls are with certain models and how using models specifically trained for a specific identifications work better than models trained for general identification. 

Furthermore, we learned how starting a project with a clear design vision can actually turn general design concepts into concrete architecture and to use AI-tools to help maintain rapid development pace. 

We ultimately learned how to take our development expertise and not only integrate them into an effective team setting, but use them to guide AI tools and actively control them rather than simply relying and being controlled by such tools.

What's next for CampBuddy

CampBuddy's future lies in our vision to enhance our dedication to making a local, wifi-independent assistant that can offer robust camping/survival advice. Our next endeavors involve enhancing our model's supporting resources in breadth, depth, and reliability and enhancing the user experience with features like modifying chat history and accepting voice input.

title: Glint
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Glint

Real eyes. Realize. Real lies.

Like
3

Comment
2

The Project

Meet the Team

Obtaining the Jetson

Wow

EOG Sensors

Whimsy

Logo

⛰️ Walkthrough

https://youtu.be/K2ZkGaDlyeU

💫 Inspiration

ALS gradually takes away a person's ability to speak and move, but eye movement often lasts long after other control is gone. We wanted to turn that into a voice: glasses that let someone pick and speak phrases using only their eyes, so they can keep talking with the people they love.

👓 What it Does

Glint is an eye-movement communication prototype for people who can't speak or use their hands. It reads electrooculography (EOG), which is the small voltage changes your eyes produce when they move or blink. A person can pick a phrase or sentence and have it spoken aloud without touching anything.

BioAmp EXG Pill sensors on the face feed an Arduino Nano R4. A Python host turns those signals into commands:

Glance left, right, up or down to move around a four-slot phase ring.
Double blink to select.
Long blink to go back.

Glasses with a built in OLED screen displaying the four-slot phase ring. The HUD is in constant access for the person, allowing them to make their decisions without needed a laptop or phone to showcase the web application.

The web application showcases Glint interface and customization in it's entirety, with access to the four-slot phase ring, different ways to speak, the community page, and more. This is where users can change different aspects of how they communicate with others and also see in a more detailed light on how it works.

Finally the Jetson Orin Nano. This small AI computer allows Glint to process beefier aspects of the prototype like the AI output, speech transcription, and more.

🔨 How We Built it

Two BioAmp EXG Pill sensors on the glasses pick up the electrical signals from eye movements. An Arduino Nano R4 samples them 250 times a second and sends them to our Python backend, which turns glances and blinks into navigation through an eight-phrase ring. An ESP32 shows that ring on the glasses' OLED screen, and a Jetson runs local Qwen models that transcribe what the other person says and suggest replies. ElevenLabs speaks the chosen phrase, with the browser's built-in voice as a fallback.

Hardware:

BioAmp EXG Pills go into the Nano R4's inputs. 
Customized Glasses with an OLED Monitor displaying the phase ring at all times.
Jetson Orin Nano powering our more difficult software processes.

Software:

The application itself is a Python server with a vanilla-JavaScript companion. 
Qwen through Ollama is our main AI model that allows the users options to change during the conversation.
ElevenLabs to utilize the person's voice during any situation.

📊 Challenges We Ran Into

Everything.

Getting the EOG sensors was an exciting but terrifying experience due to how different they were from the rest of the project.

Blinks and glances look alike. Looking up and blinking both show up on the same vertical sensor as a similar pulse. Left and right were dependable; up and down kept getting mistaken for blinks. We ended up redesigning the wheel so the two replies sit on left and right, the directions we could trust.
The signal drifts. Our detector matches each eye movement against example movements we recorded. Examples recorded in the morning matched poorly by the evening as the electrodes shifted and dried, so correct glances were being thrown away as "uncertain".
A double blink we could not see. Our first double-blink detection failed in live use even though the blinks were clear. Replaying the recording sample by sample showed the detector went briefly "deaf" right after the eyes returned to center, exactly when the blinks happened. We added a second detector that watches for blink pairs continuously.
Telling a return from a command. Looking right and then back to center produces a second pulse in the opposite direction, which was being read as "left". The detector now remembers the outward glance and treats the opposite pulse as the return.

Building the glasses to allow people to see the phrases they can say while also connecting with other components was challenging.

The glasses. Designing and building glasses that hold the EOG electrodes firmly against the face and a display in view, while staying comfortable to wear, took many rounds of trial and error.
The OLED screen. Mounting a tiny 128×64 OLED into the glasses and fitting an four-option phrase ring onto it meant cutting every label down to a few characters and still keeping it readable right in front of the eye.
Connecting it with an ESP32. Getting the ESP32 to mirror the website's live state onto the OLED, so the glasses and the companion app always show the same screen, took a lot of debugging across firmware, serial and our Python backend.

The Jetson Orin Nano was super fun to learn, orchestrate, and build with; but it also came with a lot of it's own issues. 

It's utility. During the learning and implementation process, we as a team had a variety of scenarios and questions on how the Jetson could even be useful for the prototype. Burger.
Setting it up. Every phase of getting the Jetson running was a struggle and a great learning process. The start where we had issues figuring out where the micro SD card went, in the middle when we did not have the right cords and ports to connect the jetson to a monitor. Lots of trips were made to best buy.
It just does it's own thing sometimes. We implemented a major upgrade where the speech transcription could finally be utilized with the Jetson, but after inputting the terminal commands... Everything went black. Very scary moment for the software side of the team, but it took a good amount of troubleshooting, reading some documentation, and the power of Momo.

Networking, debugging, and portability were the main software issues throughout the project. Figuring out as a team how every piece should connect with each other or how was difficult, committing bug fixes constantly to new features was time consuming, and maintaining the portability of the project was an important goal for us.

🥇 Accomplishments that we're Proud of

It works. A full loop runs end to end: someone asks a question out loud, it is transcribed on the Jetson, the reply model suggests answers, they appear on the wheel in the glasses, the wearer looks at one, double blinks, and it is spoken aloud. Nothing is ever spoken without that deliberate double blink.

EOG. We went from a detector that missed every movement in replay to one where left, right and double-blink selection work in live use. We also built the tooling to get there: every session is recorded, and any decision the detector made can be replayed exactly to find out why. We are honest about the limits: up and down are still unreliable, and this has been tested on one wearer, not on the people it is meant for.

Glasses. The glasses show the live wheel, the current status, and a full-screen "DOUBLE BLINK" cue at the exact moment a blink will be accepted, so the wearer does not need a laptop in view. On the website, the whole screen frame changes colour by state (green to choose, blue to return to center, purple to blink, red to retry), because text in your peripheral vision is impossible to read while your eyes are busy steering.

Jetson. Connecting Jetson to hardware proved to be difficult, but being able to provide computing power to our systems like the ESP-32 and R4 Nano was well worth the challenge. With it, we were able to have our project take the next step in becoming more mobile and accessible to those who need it.

📦 What we Learned

We learned that building wearable hardware means balancing comfort, fit and visibility all at once. Blending together an OLED screen with a pair of glasses was a different frontier of embedded software we weren't used too.

We learned that EOG signals drift and are noisy, so we had to detect quick eye movements and blinks instead of tracking exactly where someone is looking. Constant trial and error of trying to make eye movements perfect for the user caused a lot of time.

Learning how to set up a Jetson Orin Nano for the first time was very fun. Even with all the hiccups, being able to use and play with a portable AI computer was exhilarating.

Connecting all of these pieces together was an insurmountable effort by everyone and it helped us learned a lot about every frontier of making a project on this level.

🌎 What's Next for Glint

Glint is a powerful proof of concept, and we have plenty of ideas and upgrades. We're focused on truly creating the best experience for people who need it most.

Full portability: Right now Glint needs a lot of different devices to have it working. We want one small, battery-powered unit you can mount on a wheelchair or a bed and the glasses with EOG capabilities. The Jetson already runs our offline speech and reply models, so the next step is putting the eye-control on it too. A caregiver should be able to set it up from a phone.
Optimized networking: We want the whole loop, from eye movement to spoken word, to feel instant. Today our screens ask the server for updates over and over, so we’ll switch to live updates that push the change the moment you look. We’ll also trim the trip your voice takes to the Jetson for speech recognition, and cache or pre-generate the voice for the phrases you use most.
Improved hardware: Today it’s DIY glasses, EOG sensors, and a random Jetson Orin Nano. We’d like a wireless headband or glasses frame with more electrodes, which should make up and down much easier to tell apart. It would also get a built-in screen and speaker. Then we’ll test it with the people who would actually use it.

title: RiskDiff
text:
Notifications

Loading...

RiskDiff

RiskDiff is the Git Diff of companies' 10-Ks. Every year, publicly traded companies publish a 10k outlining their risk factors. RiskDiff compares this year’s 10-K report to last year’s.

Like
3

Comment

RiskDiff Home Page

RiskDiff Analysis of Adobe's most recent 10k fillings

Inspiration

We were challenged with building something useful for financial services. Every public company files a 10-K, an annual report required by the SEC that runs hundreds of pages, and the changes that matter are easy to miss. The Risk Factors section is where a company has to tell investors what could go wrong, but most of it is copied over from the year before. Analysts who want to know what changed often paste two years of text into a diff tool and read it line by line, which is slow and easy to get wrong.

We also saw that AI summarizers struggle with trust in finance, because a summary is hard to rely on if you can't see where it came from. We wanted to solve both problems, for the analysts covering these companies and for the risk teams who need proof of what was reviewed.

What it does

The idea

RiskDiff takes a company's two most recent 10-Ks, compares the Risk Factors sections sentence by sentence, and shows you exactly what changed.

Type in a ticker

RiskDiff pulls both filings straight from the SEC, finds the Risk Factors section, and splits it into individual risks. It then matches each risk to last year's version, even if it was reworded or moved, so wording that changed slightly but means the same thing doesn't show up as a new risk. What changed is always decided by fixed rules in code, so the same two filings give the same result every time. AI only helps with the matching and with short summaries that are clearly labeled.

What it shows you

A label for every risk factor: new risk, dropped risk, expanded, scaled back, major update, or essentially unchanged. For NVIDIA, 6 of 29 changed meaningfully, so you know which 23 you can skip.
Potential to Actual: our favorite part. It flags a risk described as something that could happen last year that is described as something that did happen this year.
New figures and new names: like the $4.5 billion charge NVIDIA disclosed this year that wasn't in last year's filing.
An easy way to read it: new words are highlighted and removed words are crossed out, side by side or inline.
Proof: every quote is word for word, and a link opens the SEC filing with that exact sentence highlighted.

Trends

The Trends page looks across every company in our library. It ranks the topics that the most companies newly added this year. Expanding a topic shows the exact sentence from each company, and a heat map below shows how many sentences changed for each company in each risk area.

Briefing

Seeing the changes is useful, but someone still has to turn them into a report. On the Briefing page you pick up to 20 companies and RiskDiff builds a 4-page Disclosure Briefing you can download as a PDF, print, or share by link. It has a one-page summary of what to read first, the themes across your list, what became actual along with new figures and new and dropped risks, and an audit trail of the filings used. A credit analyst can use it for the annual review of a borrower, and a risk team can keep it as a record that the review happened.

How we built it

We started with several ideas and kept refining them until we landed on one the whole team understood before any code was written.

The backend is a Python pipeline that runs in stages. It fetches the filings from SEC EDGAR, extracts the Risk Factors section, splits it into individual risks, and matches each risk to its counterpart from the prior year. It then compares them sentence by sentence and runs rule-based checks for new figures, new names, and potential-to-actual wording. The results are published as reports and served through a FastAPI backend to a Next.js frontend. A shared report library on Databricks keeps every teammate's laptop on the same set of reports.

Challenges we ran into

Pulling clean text out of real SEC filings was harder than we expected. The "Item 1A" heading appears twice in a filing, once in the table of contents and once in the real section, so we had to figure out which one was actually the Risk Factors.

We also had to be careful about how risks were matched, counted, and displayed so users would not be misled. Section headings were being counted as new risks, some before-and-after pairs didn't belong together, and the counts on different pages didn't always agree. Tracking these down meant auditing our own data against the filings.

Our first frontend was also hard to read for anyone who wasn't technical. We redesigned it around plain-English labels and a color system that only shows direction (more language or less language), never "good" or "bad."

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Running RiskDiff on real filings and watching it surface real changes was really cool, like NVIDIA's $4.5 billion charge showing up as a figure that wasn't in last year's filing. We're also proud that every quote in the app and in the briefing can be traced back to the filing, and of how we scoped the project. We chose to do the year-over-year comparison well instead of trying to rate or rank stocks by risk.

What we learned

Partway through, we found quotes in our own app that didn't match their source. Fixing that taught us that a tool for finance is only useful if every claim can be checked, and it shaped the rest of our decisions, from keeping quotes word for word to labeling anything written by AI. We also learned that explaining the project in plain English matters as much as building it.

What's next for RiskDiff

The next step is making the briefing fit more of the people who would use it. One idea is offering different export formats from the same data: a one-page summary for portfolio managers, the full briefing for analysts, and a single-company version for credit reviews. We would also like the briefing's links to jump to the exact sentence in the filing, the way the rest of the app already does, and to expand the library to more companies and more years so trends can be tracked over time.

title: Waverio Studio
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Waverio Studio

Music DAWs can have a steep learning curve. Waverio Studio is a browser DAW for beginners. Record vocals, describe the sound you want, and AI builds effects tailored for your voice. 

Like
1

Comment

Inspiration

When I was in my senior year of high school, my passion for music recording began. Going through a tough patch in my life, I listened to a ton of music as a way to disconnect from reality and feel more grounded. Listening to bigger artists such as Drake, Don Toliver, and Teezo Touchdown showed me how music can reach the hearts of millions around the world, and I was influenced to try music production myself.

When I first started making music, vocal mixing was probably the toughest part. Understanding how to use a DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) felt like operating a plane, I was bombarded by knobs, sliders, and controls, and I had no idea where to even get started. Getting my vocals to sound even halfway decent on any song was a complete challenge. A couple of years later, I can now say that I can comfortably use various effects such as autotune, reverb, and equalizers to mix my vocal takes with a beat, and I consider myself somewhat experienced. Understanding all the pain and frustration it took to get to this point, I built Waverio Studio alongside my partner, who has supported me in every way throughout my music journey, as a way for beginner artists to be able to produce music without the hassle of spending months learning vocal mixing, but as a way where they can learn it as they go.

What it does

Waverio Studio is a Digital Audio Workstation where artists are able to place beats, record vocals, and utilize an AI assistant to help with the engineering of their vocals. This AI assistant reads a written description of the sound they want, along with measurements of their recording, and builds a custom preset they can still edit.

How we built it

This project uses a React and TypeScript interface to run on a web browser, and uses libraries such as Tone.js to run the audio locally through the Web Audio API. The browser stores data locally through the use of localStorage and IndexedDB, which are used to store sessions and clip audio.

When a user records an audio clip, that snippet is analyzed in the browser by mixing the audio down to one channel, then cutting it into short overlapping frames of 2,048 samples. These frames are analyzed for different measurements such as loudness, noise floor, peak, crest, pitch, etc. The user can then input a prompt describing what they would like their vocals to sound like. These measurements, along with the prompt, are then sent to the server.

A small Node API is in charge of sending this data over to a Hugging Face model (Qwen/Qwen3-8B), as well as information such as a few example presets and a catalog of available effects. These effects were given as Tone.js nodes, but several others, such as autotune, are either custom made or utilize other libraries (such as Rubber Band). The AI returns a preset (which is a chain of vocal effects) in a JSON format, which is then validated and clamped before being utilized.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges that we ran into while developing this project was the overall workflow. Considering that this was our first hackathon, we didn't understand how to go about tackling our problem. One specific issue that we learned how to solve as we went along was the use of GitHub and the creation of a repo. Other challenges we ran into included challenges with the actual architecture, one of which being the AI model not fully understanding how to create the right preset. Providing it with proper seeding and syntax allowed it to be far more effective. Another challenge was the actual implementation of certain effects, such as autotune. The pitch correction in both Tone.js and Rubber Band is very limited, and sounds a lot rougher compared to those used in professional DAWs. This is a problem we still aim to tackle in our future solutions.

Accomplishments that we're proud of, and what we learned

We are proud of the fact that we stayed dedicated to the task, regardless of challenges that popped up. We successfully created a web app where users are able to record or upload vocals, prompt AI, and generate a customized and editable preset. At some points, it felt as if completing this project would be impossible in the time given, however, we pushed through and gave it our all. On the behavioral side, we learned a lot about teamwork, working collaboratively, time management, delegation of tasks, and consistency. On the technical side, we learned about proper prompting of AI, GitHub, creating task specs, and hosting of web apps.

What's next for Waverio Studio

We aim to improve upon this application by exploring potential implementations of better effects, which would overall create better sounding vocal presets. We also aim to explore possible fine-tuning of the model we had utilized in order to provide it with more knowledge of vocal mixing.

title: StoryForge
text:
Notifications

Loading...

StoryForge

Draw a hero, and watch an AI storybook bring them to life.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

We wanted to create an interactive storytelling experience that combines creativity, artificial intelligence, and technology to make reading more engaging for children. Traditional storybooks have a fixed storyline, but we wanted children to become active participants by creating their own characters and deciding what happens next. This inspired us to build StoryForge, a picture-book maker that transforms children's imagination and drawings into personalized adventures.

What it does

StoryForge allows children to draw their own hero or type an idea to begin a personalized story. A locally running language model generates the story one page at a time, allowing children to influence the plot through interactive choices or their own ideas.

Each page features an AI-generated illustrated background, the child's character animated on top of the scene, and audio narration. Children can tap difficult words to see and hear their definitions, making the experience both entertaining and educational. The application supports different reading levels, from pre-readers to confident readers.

How we built it

We built StoryForge around the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit, using a locally hosted AI model to generate stories while integrating cloud services for additional creative features.

AI storytelling: We used Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct, running locally through llama.cpp, to generate structured story outlines and individual pages.
Character creation: We developed a drawing interface that allows children to draw their own heroes. Image processing separates the character from the background so it can be animated within the story.
AI-generated illustrations: We integrated FLUX.1-schnell through Hugging Face to generate illustrated backgrounds, with local image-generation and preset-image fallbacks.
Narration: We integrated ElevenLabs for audio narration, with local Piper and browser speech synthesis as fallback options.
Reading assistance: We used word-frequency analysis and readability tools to identify difficult vocabulary and generate child-friendly definitions.
Animations: We used HTML Canvas, CSS animations, SVG filters, and JavaScript to bring characters and story scenes to life.
Ambient lighting: We connected an ESP32 running Arduino code with FastLED to control a WS2812B LED strip that changes colors to match the illustrations.
Backend: We used Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, and asynchronous processing to coordinate the AI models, illustrations, narration, and story progression.

Challenges we ran into

One of our biggest challenges was running AI models on the Jetson Orin Nano's limited shared memory while maintaining a responsive experience. Generating stories, illustrations, and narration requires several components to work together without making children wait too long between pages.

Another challenge was ensuring that AI-generated stories remained appropriate, coherent, and consistent. Smaller language models can produce malformed responses, repeat information, or generate unexpected content. To address this, we used structured JSON outputs and Python validation to check, repair, and filter generated responses before displaying them.

We also had to coordinate multiple services with different response times. To improve responsiveness, we started generating page backgrounds as soon as the scene description became available instead of waiting for the entire page to finish. We implemented fallbacks for image generation and narration so the application could continue working when external services were unavailable.

Finally, animating a child's drawing over generated backgrounds required image processing to separate the character from the original background and make the character fit naturally into different scenes.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of building an interactive storytelling application that combines locally hosted AI with cloud-based creative services on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.

Our biggest accomplishment is bringing multiple technologies together into one cohesive experience. Children can create a character, generate a personalized story, explore illustrated scenes, listen to narration, learn new vocabulary, and influence the plot through their decisions.

We are also proud of implementing safeguards and fallback mechanisms. Rather than displaying raw model output, StoryForge validates structured responses and checks story content before presenting it to children. Generating illustrations and narration asynchronously also helps reduce waiting time.

What we learned

We learned how to integrate locally hosted language models with cloud-based AI services and hardware peripherals into a single application. Working with the Jetson Orin Nano taught us to consider memory constraints, model quantization, and performance when designing AI-powered experiences for edge devices.

We also learned the importance of structured outputs, input validation, and fallback mechanisms when building applications around language models. AI-generated content cannot always be trusted to follow instructions perfectly, so robust validation is essential, especially when developing for children.

What's next for StoryForge

We would like to expand StoryForge with more drawing tools, richer character animations, additional story choices, and more interactive elements. We also want to improve the speed and consistency of locally generated illustrations to reduce reliance on cloud services.

Future improvements could include more personalized reading recommendations, progress tracking, additional languages, and expanded educational features. We would also like to enhance the physical experience with more responsive lighting effects and explore other ways to connect digital stories to the real world.

Dancify

Transform any video into an interactive dance game, making learning choreography fun, engaging, and accessible to everyone!

Like

Comment

Hand-drawn limbs were used to create the generative pictographs without the use of AI. 

Inspiration

We wanted to play Just Dance, but we didn't have a Wii, so we had to follow along on YouTube instead. 
Because of the lack of feedback, it was hard to know whether or not our dances were correct, and it was becoming frustrating. But not just that, we also thought the same thing about dances on other platforms, like TikTok and Instagram.

That's how Dancify was born! We envisioned a platform where anyone could turn their favorite dance videos into personalized, interactive games, making learning choreography feel less like practice and more like play.

What it does

Dancify transforms any dance video into an interactive dance game. Users can upload a video of their choice and follow along with the choreography while the game tracks their movements and evaluates their performance.

By combining movement tracking with interactive feedback, Dancify encourages users to improve their dancing while having fun. Whether you're learning a viral dance, practicing choreography, or jyst having plain fun, Dancify gives that opportunity to play, learn, and improve.

How we built it

We built Dancify by combining computer vision and joint tracking to transform ordinary dance videos into interactive gaming experiences.

We used Python alongside OpenCV to process uploaded videos and analyze individual frames. MediaPipe enabled us to identify and track body landmarks, allowing us to interpret choreography as a sequence of movements that could be compared against a player's performance.

For the frontend, we used React and TypeScript to develop an interactive interface that allows users to upload videos, learn choreography, and receive performance feedback. We also used Figma to design and prototype a visually engaging user experience.

By integrating these technologies, we developed the foundation for a platform that transforms virtually any dance video into a personalized, interactive choreography-learning experience.

Challenges we ran into

One of our biggest technical challenges was translating dance movements from a two-dimensional video into something that could be accurately compared with a player's real-time movements. Differences in camera angles, body proportions, timing, and movement speed can make evaluating choreography difficult.

Another challenge was designing an experience that balances accuracy with enjoyment. We wanted Dancify to reward players for their effort without making the game overly strict or discouraging, especially for beginners.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We have many accomplishments that we are proud of when it comes to this project, but there is one that really stands out, which is our 3D-printed wearable with a built in metronome used to help assist clients align with the beat to be able to match the dance with practice.

What we learned

Building Dancify taught us how computer vision and motion tracking can bridge the gap between digital entertainment and physical movement.

We also gained a greater appreciation for the challenges involved in evaluating human motion, particularly when accounting for differences in body types, movement styles, and skill levels.

Beyond the technical aspects, this project reinforced the importance of designing technology around the user experience. An effective dance game isn't just about tracking movements accurately, it's about making people excited to keep dancing.

What's next for Dancify

Our vision for Dancify extends beyond a single dance game. We want to build a platform that makes learning choreography more accessible, social, and personalized.

Future improvements could include real-time movement feedback, adaptive difficulty levels, multiplayer dance battles, leaderboards, and personalized recommendations based on player performance.

Ultimately, we envision Dancify becoming a platform where anyone can discover new dances, learn choreography, challenge friends, and express themselves through movement all through the videos they already love.

text:
Notifications

Loading...

SteadyForum: A Form-Correcting, Gym Journey, Social Media

Everybody has a cell phone, and personal trainers are expensive and only available at set times. Introducing SteadyForum, a new way to learn how to go to the gym without injury, hassle or humiliation.

Like
8

Comment
2

Our Logo

Critique on the workout to improve form, 45 seconds until the next set

One of our five pose-estimation model supported workouts, other workouts can be logged, just won't be pose-tracked

a user doing shoulder press, dots show key pieces of body. Amber dots show potential strain in parts, no strain is visible

Inspiration

Nearly everyone who steps into the gym enters with ambition, but without proper guidance on form, that early drive can easily turn into wasted effort and frustration. 

Existing fitness apps are either great digital logbooks or have vision but make the mistake of shouting audio cues that disrupt bracing and focus. They also dont focus on players coming back from injury. Fitness apps such as Fitbod or Hevy record the numbers the user types in for their sets and reps, but they aren't monitoring if you're moving safely or correctly. While current vision apps may shout mid-set audio cues to encourage you, this can distract you during your workout. We built SteadyForum to bridge the gap: an intelligent training companion that silently supervises your form, respects camera privacy with on-device inference, and gives you actionable coaching during rest.

Whether you're building a consistent routine as a beginner or coming back from an injury, lifters deserve to know immediately that their movement is effective and safe without second-guessing themselves. 

What it does

SteadyForum is an AI-driven mobile app that acts as a coach, removing the guesswork from gym training and physical recovery, and as a social platform, giving users motivation from other gym-goers. Using real-time computer vision, it silently tracks your movement during a set and delivers brief, actionable feedback during rest periods.

Core Features

Smart Rest Cards & Scoring: The app silently computes joint angles and rep criteria, providing a clean score and a targeted corrective coaching card when you rest. 
Injury & Recovery Workflows: Designed alongside physical therapy protocols, the system enforces prescribed range-of-motion limits and tracks objective rehab milestones. 
Privacy-First On-Device Vision: Runs 17-point pose estimation locally on iOS via Core ML and YOLOv8n-pose. The raw camera footage doesn't leave your phone; only lightweight joint coordinates and telemetry are logged.
Social Community: Social feeds and buddy matching built around verified movement quality as opposed to vanity metrics.

How we built it
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. YOUR PHONE (React Native / iOS)                          │
│  [Camera] ──> [Pose AI (Core ML / YOLOv8n-pose)]            │
│                       │ (17 joints/frame)                   │
│                       ▼                                     │
│  [Silent Screen] <── [Form Engine & Rep State Machine]      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│ (Finished set: joints & rules)   ▲
▼                                  │ (Rest note & score)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. STEADYFORUM API (Node.js + Express)                      │
│  Coordinates session data, authenticates, and routes to ML  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│                   │                      │
(Saves sets)                │ (Syncs session)      │ (Requests notes)
▼                   ▼                      ▼
┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
│ 3. NEON POSTGRES │  │ 4. DATABRICKS    │  │ 5. HUGGING FACE │
│ - User Accounts  │<─┼─(Syncs Gold      │  │ - Text Inference│
│ - pgvector (RAG) │  │  table insights) │  │   (Rest Notes)  │
│ - Social Feed    │  │ - Lakehouse      │  │ - Cloud Pose AI │
└──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘

Client/Edge Inference

React Native & Expo: powers interactive lifer UI, workout screens, and camera feed. 
Core ML & YOLOv8n-pose (Swift Native Plugin): runs on-device pose estimation on iOS at high frame rates, extracting 17 key joints in real time whilst keeping the frames of the camera private on the phone. 
Apple Vision: native fallback pose-detection framework on iOS when Core ML models are not active. 
Rule Engine & Rep State Machine (TypeScript): smooths incoming joint coordinates, tracks rep angles, and flags form breakdowns without interrupting the set. 

Backend & Storage

Node.js, Express & TypeScript: central REST API layer managing authenticated requests, workout session lifecycle, and coordinating external services. 
Neon Postgres & Drizzle ORM: primary serverless database storing user accounts, workout set records, historical baselines, and social feeds.
pgvector: manages vector embeddings inside NEON to power RAG retrieval for exercise specifications and physical therapy guidelines. 
Neon Auth: handles user authentication and secures token validation across server and mobile requests.

Data Pipeline & Insights

Databricks Pipelines: ingests exported workout telemetry to build a multi-tier lakehouse processing raw logs (Bronze), validated set metrics (Silver),  and aggregate process summaries (Gold)
Hugging Face Inference Endpoints: hosts specialized language models to generate contextual rest-interval coaching notes
Hugging Face Hub: manages model versioning, testing checkpoints, and deployment artifacts used throughout the pipeline

Challenges we ran into

There was a steep learning curve connecting external inference services and data warehouses (Databricks and Hugging Face) into our backend. Getting exported session metrics fed into Databricks without slowing down client response times took a lot of trial and error. 
We ran into a lot of friction connecting our mobile app to the backend server, making fetching and re-rendering workout data on the frontend inconsistent during testing. 
Packaging all the finished workout data to send off to the backend and Databricks pipeline was a major headache. We had to figure out how to properly compress the per-frame joint tracking data and calculate per-rep aggregates so the mobile app, database, and Databricks lakehouse all shared the same data schema without breaking the payloads. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

End-to-End Edge Pipeline: successfully deploying on-device YOLOv8n-pose via Core ML to extract 17 keypoints at high frame rates on iOS, completely maintaining lifters' privacy.
Coaching Experience: designing Rest Card workflow, ensuring lifters are given clear, actionable form corrections during rest instead of disturbing them mid-set. 
Bridging Fitness and Rehab: implementing our JSON-driven exercise rules with RAG-powered physical therapy guidelines (pgvector), enforcing safe range-of-motion thresholds for lifters that are currently recovering.
Data Architecture: connecting mobile session exports through Neon Postgres directly into a Databricks Medallion lakehouse for deep telemetry aggregation. 

What we learned

We were able to gain first-hand experience deploying and querying models through Databricks and Hugging Face. We learned how to serve inference endpoints alongside an operational database and how enterprise data lakes structure multi-tier session data. 
We learned what it takes to run ML models locally on mobile devices. Deploying YOLOv8n-pose via Core ML taught us how to handle tensor data, manage device memory, and process high-frame-rate camera feeds natively on iOS to preserve user privacy. 
Building the rep state machine taught us how to take raw, occasionally jumpy point coordinates, smooth them out, and apply strict geometric rules to evaluate phases of human movement in real-time. 

What's next for SteadyFlow: A Form-Correction Gym Journey Social Media

Our current JSON specs do not cover many exercises. We want to map out thresholds and form rules for a wider variety of lifts, especially complex compound movements like deadlifts and barbell rows, where tracking spinal alignment and hip-hinge mechanics is highly technical but very important for injury prevention. We also plan to map out specific mobility and physical therapy drills to deepen our rehab workflows.

scap! sprout

SCRAP! is a first-person browser boxing game that turns your webcam into the controller. Jab at the screen, lean to slip punches, and duck strikes with your real body. 

Like
2

Comment

Inspiration

Every boxing game ever made asks you to memorize which button throws a hook. We wanted to know: what if you just threw the punch? SCRAP! is our answer — an immersive first-person boxing experience running entirely in your browser where your webcam acts as the controller, your head movement dictates spatial dodges, and your fists deliver real strikes[cite: 1].

Deployed live on a custom domain registered via GoDaddy Registry, SCRAP! turns everyday webcams into serious gaming hardware without requiring specialized peripherals[cite: 1].

What it does

Step straight into a stylized ring and fight using physical perception and real-world movement[cite: 1]:

Punch the camera — A fist surging toward the lens registers as an authentic strike, dynamically scaling hit power and knockback by real-world velocity.
Physical head and body tracking — Lean forward to pressure inside, lean back to make rivals swing at air, or duck and slip beneath telegraphed combinations[cite: 1].
Dynamic AI commentary & rival dialogue — Rivals taunt, adapt, and react with realistic vocal personalities powered by ElevenLabs, driven by round-by-round fight intelligence orchestrated with the Gemini API[cite: 1].
Serious game & perception simulation — Full 3-round bout simulation tracking stamina consumption, guard blocks, combo streaks, knockdowns, and ringside scoring under Full Sail's Pathways & Perception challenge guidelines[cite: 1].
Unlockable career progression — Climb the ladder against unique procedural archetypes, from sharp counter-snipers to towering heavyweight brawlers.
Accessible controls — Seamless fallback support for mouse and keyboard controls alongside a sparring tutorial mode.

How we built it

Everything is hand-rolled web tech engineered for lightweight, zero-dependency performance:

Open-Source Computer Vision (Hugging Face): Deployed open-source computer vision and pose-estimation models from Hugging Face directly in the browser to extract 21 hand landmarks and 6-DOF head poses for real-time punch recognition, slips, and dodges[cite: 1].
Intelligent Audio & Strategy (ElevenLabs & Gemini API): Fighter dialogue, corner coaching, and play-by-play commentary are dynamically generated using the Gemini API and vocalized via ElevenLabs' expressive speech synthesis[cite: 1].
UI/UX & Visual Identity (Figma & Adobe): The visual aesthetic was prototyped and designed in Figma, with custom-crafted shaders, bold stylized UI, and vibrant visual effects built to Adobe design standards for an arcade look[cite: 1].
Deterministic 3D Simulation (Three.js & Full Sail Challenge): Built a custom 2D-to-3D ring simulation with lane-pull steering, reach calculations, and spatial boundaries in Three.js to address the Full Sail Pathways & Perception serious games and simulation challenge[cite: 1].
Deployment & Production: The platform is hosted and served live on a dedicated custom domain using GoDaddy Registry[cite: 1].
Procedural Sound & Headless CI: Procedural WebAudio handles glove impacts, bells, and rope creaks, while Puppeteer automated tests run headless bouts to verify tracking accuracy.

Challenges we ran into

Client-Side Open-Source Vision Inference: Running Hugging Face vision models directly inside the browser at high frame rates required aggressive optimization, frame skipping, and quantization to avoid frame drops on integrated GPUs[cite: 1].
Webcam noise & punch gating: Distinguishing standard hand movement from high-velocity strikes required pairing bounding-box expansion heuristics with strict fist-closure thresholds.
First-person perspective tuning: Keeping agile opponents framed inside a front-facing viewing cone while they circle and pivot required an intelligent lane-pull steering layer inside the ring simulation[cite: 1].
Synchronizing real-time voice and gameplay: Streaming ElevenLabs voice commentary alongside the Gemini API's fight analysis without interrupting active Three.js rendering loops[cite: 1].

What we learned

Game feel relies heavily on micro-feedback: hit-stop freezes, rope jolts, telegraph flashes, and dynamic ringside banter[cite: 1]. We also discovered that pairing open-source AI with deterministic simulation makes vision-driven physical gameplay fully testable in automated pipelines[cite: 1].

What's next

Dynamic difficulty adjustments tailored live to player reaction speeds.
True southpaw stance toggles and branching tournament ladders.
Expanded AI coach commentary with deeper post-fight strategy breakdowns[cite: 1].

Bin-It

Residents report overflowing bins from their phones. Staff get a dashboard that corrects for reporting bias and ranks the best places to add bins, shown as estimates and never as measured outcome

Like

Comment

Report submit screen

Report Map on Mobile

Landing page for dashboard

Dashboard main map

Recommended bin locations

Inspiration

As people who live/used to live deep in The Bronx, NY, we're very used to seeing trash and the like on the streets of NYC. After reading OneEthos' challenge, we were inspired to find a way to tackle this issue, leading us to make Bin-It.

What it does

Bin-It is a two part app: one side mobile app, one side web dashboard, that allows for the people of a city and it's government to collaborate to clean up trash! Citizens can take pictures of overflowing trash that they want to be cleaned up in the app and make a report. That report is then visible to the city administration on the dashboard, and with multiple reports + map data for the city, Bin-It can calculate the most trash heavy points in a city, AND where new trash beans need to be installed!

How we built it

We used a wide tech stack to build Bin-It, for the mobile app we used React Native and Expo. For the dashboard Next.js and React and Typescript were used, and that covers both front ends. For the backend, our pipeline combines Python scripts, Neon, Hugging Face, Databricks, Docker, Ngrok, FastAPI, and Vercel. Neon holds photos and reports taken from the app, trash bin info, and other things. 

Once a user takes a photo, it is sent to our Hugging Face classifier which is trained on trash data and classifies it using OpenAI's CLIP model, and gives it a severity ranking based on how bad the trash pileup is. Ngrok is used to create a tunnel between the docker container that the classifier is stored in and our Python scripts. Databricks then takes in geolocation, bin, place, and 311 complaint data and processes it by training it with NYC's and Chicago's highly accurate and extensive 311 data, which is then used to predict high trash points in any other applicable city, as long as the geolocation data is there. Using that data, the top 20 best potential bin locations are ranked for that city and stored. That info is then fed back into the Neon database, which Vercel pulls from to create the Next.js app, completing the cycle.

Challenges we ran into

We tried to set up Hugging Face Spaces in order to host the classifier, we believed there was a free tier for that but since we didn't have a Pro account we couldn't. We had to go around that by setting up a Docker container to host the classifier and use Ngrok to help it communicate. Another challenge was just setting up the backend as a whole. For us, this was the largest amount of frameworks/libraries we've used in one project, so getting them all to communicate was quite the challenge.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud of the fact that we learned how to use so many different frameworks together, especially as it was our first time working with most of them.

What we learned

We learned how to make an multi-platform app that communicates together with many different moving parts.

What's next for Bin-It

Spreading the data to include more cities, making sure that each city is cleaner than the last.

title: ArchAI
text:
