ArchAI

ArchAI is an architectural intelligence layer within the construction industry's operating system, orchestrating design, material engineering, execution intelligence, and lifecycle optimisation.

Like

Comment

3D visualization

ArchAI — Engineering Intelligence for the Construction Lifecycle

Inspiration: A National Construction Intelligence Gap

Construction is one of India's most consequential economic and engineering activities, yet the decisions that shape a building are often fragmented across architectural design, structural engineering, geotechnical assessment, building services, regulatory guidance, material estimation, and construction execution. These disciplines are deeply interconnected, but project information frequently remains scattered across disconnected tools, documents, and professional workflows. This fragmentation can create coordination gaps, repetitive revisions, cost uncertainty, and difficulties translating a design concept into a coherent, actionable construction plan.

The consequences of inadequate building safety and structural oversight can be devastating. According to the National Crime Records Bureau's Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India 2024 report, India recorded 1,435 structure-collapse cases resulting in 1,525 deaths, including 922 dwelling-house and residential-building collapse cases associated with 988 deaths. These figures establish the scale of reported structural-collapse incidents, although they do not establish a single cause for every incident.

Source: NCRB, Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India 2024.

The urgency was underscored by the September 2026 building collapse in Satya Niketan, Southwest Delhi, which killed seven people. According to reporting on a Delhi Police submission to the Delhi High Court, the building owners had failed to ensure structural safety and had not obtained advice from qualified structural engineers or architects before undertaking repair and structural-modification work.

Source: LiveLaw — Satya Niketan building-collapse case.

These incidents illustrate the importance of appropriate engineering assessment, professional oversight, and accountable construction decisions. AI alone cannot guarantee building safety, but a well-designed intelligence platform can help organise project information, expose missing inputs, connect relevant considerations, and facilitate timely professional review.

The challenge extends beyond safety. Homeowners must navigate site constraints, architectural choices, local regulations, engineering dependencies, and uncertain construction costs—often without a unified way to understand how these factors influence one another. Professionals, meanwhile, can spend substantial time transferring information between applications, recreating drawings, coordinating revisions, and preparing technical documentation.

We envisioned ArchAI as an engineering intelligence layer that connects these fragmented decisions into one coherent construction workflow. Our central question is: How can AI make construction planning faster, more connected, and more accessible while preserving the technical rigour and professional accountability that buildings demand?

What We Built

ArchAI is an AI-powered architectural intelligence platform designed to streamline early-stage residential planning and construction decision-making. It transforms plot information, site context, user requirements, architectural preferences, and budget constraints into architectural concepts and preliminary construction intelligence.

At its core, ArchAI follows the principle of shared project context and coordinated intelligence. Rather than treating every task as an independent prompt, the platform aims to preserve relevant project information across the workflow so that subsequent decisions build upon the same underlying requirements.

Our system brings together several complementary intelligence layers:

Site and project intelligence: Organises plot dimensions, site information, geographical context, user requirements, and budget constraints.
Architectural intelligence: Supports preliminary space planning, layout exploration, architectural concept generation, and visualisation.
Regional architectural intelligence: We have organised our architectural framework around 20 architectural styles across 8 geographical regions of India, recognising the country's diverse architectural traditions and regional design contexts.
Knowledge intelligence: Uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to retrieve relevant information from a knowledge base, grounding AI-assisted reasoning in available reference material.
Engineering intelligence: Establishes a coordinated workflow connecting architectural intent with structural, geotechnical, plumbing, electrical, HVAC, and other building-system considerations as the relevant modules develop.
Construction cost intelligence: Supports preliminary quantity estimation, BOQ-oriented workflows, and cost-related decision support where implemented.
Visualisation and documentation: Connects project information with visual outputs and a longer-term vision for automated, context-driven technical documentation.

The fundamental distinction is that ArchAI does not treat an architectural concept as the final product. The concept is the beginning of a broader engineering workflow.

How It Works

1. Project Context Formation

The workflow begins with project information such as plot dimensions, site imagery, location, intended occupancy, spatial requirements, preferred architectural direction, environmental priorities, and budget.

These inputs establish a structured project context that informs subsequent planning and decision-support operations.

2. Context-Aware Architectural Planning

ArchAI uses available project information to support architectural concept generation and preliminary floor planning. The objective is to explore alternatives in relation to user requirements, site constraints, and regional context rather than optimise solely for visual appearance.

3. Knowledge Retrieval and Engineering Coordination

The intelligence layer combines AI-assisted reasoning with retrieval from a structured knowledge base. It is designed to connect architectural decisions with relevant engineering considerations, including structural systems, geotechnical information, plumbing, electrical installations, HVAC, and applicable regulatory guidance.

These disciplines require different types of information and validation. Geotechnical recommendations, for example, must rely on verified site investigation data, while structural adequacy requires appropriate engineering calculations. ArchAI aims to coordinate these considerations rather than infer safety-critical facts from insufficient information.

4. Preliminary Construction Intelligence

Where supported by the available modules, ArchAI connects design decisions with preliminary material quantities, BOQ preparation, and cost-oriented insights.

The broader objective is to reduce the disconnect between architectural design and construction planning, helping users understand the potential implications of their decisions before committing to execution.

Preliminary quantities and estimates remain subject to input quality, project specifications, current prices, and professional verification. They are not presented as substitutes for detailed quantity surveying or final procurement documents.

5. Dynamic CAD Automation Engine

One of ArchAI's most important development priorities is a dynamic CAD automation engine that converts structured project inputs and accumulated project context into detailed, project-specific technical drawings.

Conventional drafting workflows can require repetitive manual work to transfer dimensions, room geometry, doors, windows, annotations, circulation, and other project parameters into drawing software. ArchAI aims to automate as much of this repetitive translation as reliably possible.

Rather than treating CAD as a separate downstream task, the intended engine will use the project's existing information to generate coordinated drawing outputs and systematically update them as requirements change.

Our objective is to generate extensive CAD documentation in seconds for supported workflows, reducing repetitive drafting effort and enabling professionals to spend more time on engineering judgement, refinement, and verification.

The long-term goal is context-driven CAD generation, in which technical documentation remains connected to the underlying project data instead of being recreated independently at every stage. Dependable production-grade output requires geometric consistency, dimensional validation, appropriate drawing standards, coordination checks, and professional review.

6. Refinement, Validation, and Professional Handoff

Project outputs must be evaluated against available constraints and information. Missing inputs, unresolved engineering questions, uncertain estimates, and items requiring specialist assessment should be explicitly identified.

Our objective is to establish a pathway from preliminary AI-assisted planning to structured, professionally reviewable project documentation.

What Makes ArchAI Different

ArchAI's central proposition is engineering-oriented integration rather than isolated content generation.

A conventional generative design tool may transform a prompt into a floor plan or architectural rendering. ArchAI aims to connect the decisions surrounding that output: what the user needs, what is known about the site, which assumptions remain unresolved, how design changes influence downstream considerations, and what information is required before a project can proceed.

Our approach rests on four principles:

1. Persistent project context

Relevant project information carries across the workflow, reducing the need to reconstruct the same context for every task.

2. Engineering-oriented orchestration

Architectural planning is connected to broader construction considerations instead of being treated as an isolated visual output.

3. Regional architectural intelligence

Our framework encompasses 20 architectural styles across 8 geographical regions of India, providing a foundation for regionally informed architectural exploration.

4. Context-driven automation

Our CAD development direction aims to convert project information into technical documentation, reduce repetitive drafting, and improve continuity between planning and documentation.

Together, these principles position ArchAI as a potential intelligence and coordination layer for the construction lifecycle.

Long-Term Vision: A Connected Construction Ecosystem

Our ambition extends beyond architectural planning software. We envision ArchAI evolving into an integrated platform connecting homeowners, architects, civil engineers, geotechnical experts, contractors, and other construction professionals.

1. AI Intelligence Combined with Human Expertise

We plan to build an in-house team and professional network of experienced architects, civil engineers, geotechnical specialists, and other relevant experts who can review project-specific outputs within their respective areas of competence.

AI will help organise information, prepare preliminary outputs, automate repetitive tasks, and accelerate coordination. Qualified professionals will provide engineering judgement, perform necessary verification, and issue certifications, seals, or approvals only where they are appropriately authorised under applicable regulations.

For homeowners, this could create a clearer pathway from initial requirements to professionally reviewed project documentation. For professionals, it could provide an environment to discover relevant projects, collaborate with clients, review project information, and manage their workflows more efficiently.

Our intended model is not AI replacing professional expertise. It is AI reducing repetitive work so that qualified professionals can concentrate on specialised analysis, verification, and accountable decisions.

2. Dynamic CAD as a Productivity Engine

We aim to make CAD automation a central part of ArchAI's engineering workflow.

By converting project requirements and structured context into coordinated drawings, the platform seeks to reduce repetitive drafting and the manual transfer of information between design stages. As project requirements evolve, the intended system would update supported drawing elements systematically, helping reduce avoidable rework.

The long-term objective is to deliver extensive, standards-aware technical documentation in seconds for supported cases, with validation and professional review before construction use.

3. A Marketplace for Homeowners and Professionals

ArchAI also aims to create a connected marketplace where homeowners can discover suitable architects, engineers, contractors, and other construction service providers, while professionals can find relevant projects and collaborate with prospective clients.

The platform could connect preliminary planning, technical documentation, professional verification, and service discovery within a common project environment.

This would help bridge the gap between understanding what needs to be built and finding the qualified people needed to design, verify, and execute it.

4. Construction Lifecycle Intelligence

Our longer-term roadmap extends from site understanding and architectural planning to dynamic CAD automation, professional verification, construction coordination, and eventually post-construction building operations.

We envision a system in which project information remains connected across these stages, creating greater continuity between design intent, technical documentation, professional decisions, and construction execution.

Challenges and Learnings

The central technical challenge is bridging generative AI with the precision, consistency, and accountability demanded by construction engineering.

A visually convincing output is not necessarily dimensionally accurate, structurally adequate, compliant with local regulations, or ready for execution. Reliable construction intelligence requires structured information, relevant knowledge, explicit constraints, geometric consistency, transparent assumptions, and validation appropriate to each discipline.

This has reinforced an important principle in our development: AI-generated outputs must remain distinguishable from verified engineering results. Structural safety, foundation design, geotechnical conclusions, regulatory approval, and construction-ready documentation require appropriate evidence, calculations, and qualified professional oversight.

We see this distinction not as a limitation of the vision, but as a fundamental requirement for building a responsible engineering platform.

What's Next

Our development priorities include strengthening the connections between architectural geometry, engineering systems, regional knowledge, regulatory guidance, quantity estimation, and cost intelligence.

We aim to advance dynamic CAD generation, improve consistency between design outputs and project parameters, introduce stronger constraint-validation mechanisms, and develop professional review and project-collaboration workflows.

As the platform matures, we intend to build the professional network and marketplace needed to connect homeowners with qualified experts and relevant construction services.

Our long-term goal is to transform ArchAI from an early-stage architectural intelligence platform into a comprehensive construction intelligence ecosystem that supports better-informed decisions throughout a building's lifecycle.

Our vision is to make the journey from an initial plot to a well-coordinated, professionally reviewed construction project faster, more transparent, and more intelligent.

ArchAI — Engineering Intelligence for the Construction Lifecycle.

Hakit

Hakit is the OS for hackathons. It generates project ideas, matches tasks to teammates' skills, tracks live progress through GitHub, and uses AI to keep your team on track and ahead of deadlines.

Like

Comment

Plan review

Team capability

Tasks

Mission control

Inspiration

Friday night, we sat down to find an idea. After talking about what everyone was good at, we started throwing some ideas around, but nothing stuck. And that's when the idea for Hakit hit us. An app to help solve the exact problem we were facing. An app to help you figure out what ideas to pursue based on the collective experience of the group. An app that helps you form an idea, distribute work, and execute that idea, inside the tight timeframe a hackathon demands.

What it does

Hakit starts with a team. Your team. Sign up with your GitHub account, and invite everyone the same way. Hakit will analyze the skills and technical familiarity of each team member. 

After onboarding, you can either bring in an idea or have Hakit help you find one based on your team's skills and any interests you may have. A refined idea turns into a plan, where Hakit uses a combination of AI and fixed algorithms to determine the feasibility of the project inside of the event's deadline given the team members' defined availability and sleep hours.

After the project's plan is decided, Hakit splits it into tasks and milestones, then assigns tasks to teammates based on their respective skillsets and past experience with different frameworks.

During development, Hakit tracks commits live, and links them to tasks when it can, automatically tracking progress. It can identify potential issues with the timeline, and suggest changes to the plan/tasks using AI. For instance, if the development of core code took longer than expected, Hakit can surface that and recommend the removal of a few auxiliary features to meet the deadline. 

To accomplish these tasks, Hakit uses embedding models through inference provider HuggingFace, as well as using the Gemini API for more advanced AI text-generation steps.

How we built it

It certainly would have been nice if we had Hakit to build Hakit. We discussed the strengths of each team member, and divided the work accordingly. Each team member built in slices, asynchronously, employing the use of agentic harnesses like Claude Code and Codex.

│ Updates │ │   Jobs   │ │  Drafts   │

│

│                                     │

▼

│                                     │

└─────────────────────────────────────┘

One deployable app: a single Cloudflare Worker serves the React app and the Hono API, written in TypeScript end to end.
Shared contract: every endpoint is defined once with Zod and checked on both the client and the server.
Real time: each project gets its own Durable Object, which pushes live updates over WebSockets.
Background work: Cloudflare Queues and a cron job process webhooks, embeddings and adaptive re-planning.
Data: Tiger Cloud Postgres, reached through Hyperdrive and Drizzle. TimescaleDB stores activity history and pgvector stores skill vectors.
AI drafts, the engine decides: Gemini drafts plans as structured JSON. A deterministic engine then computes scores, task assignments, hours and the critical path.
Skill matching: Qwen3-Embedding, served through Hugging Face, matches people to tasks by meaning.
Fallbacks: templates stand in for Gemini and keyword matching stands in for embeddings, so the app keeps working when a provider fails.
Integrations: a GitHub App handles sign-in and repo activity. A Claude Code plugin sends opt-in coding-agent activity to the team’s live view.
Team process: four parallel workstreams, coordinated through a full mock mode so nobody had to wait on anyone else. Typecheck, lint and tests ran in CI on every pull request.

What's next for Hakit

Next, Hakit will support deeper integrations with coding agents, so that it can allow coding agents to understand the project as a whole, as well as what teammates are working on. We already support monitoring agents' progress from Hakit.

Hakit can also be easily extended to support small team sprints, which are essentially what hackathons are anyway.

Argos

Argos is an Anti-Cheat monitoring tool designed to help exam proctors spot potential cheating Live. Using cameras and RF detectors it can find hidden smart devices and usual student activity!

Like
1

Comment

Team picture

First eye track attempt

RF detector

Video StoryBoard

KnightHacks Leaderboard

Final UI Tracker

Looked Away

Inspiration

"Honesty is the Best Policy!"  Or at least that's what we tell ourselves, but in reality, cheating has become a growing epidemic in the last few years with AI at the forefront of the problem. However, cheating on tests and exams has and will always be around so long as there are people wanting to take a shortcut. Although their shortcuts put every other honest person behind, and discourages real learning, so to bring back proper education we need to combat academic dishonesty. 

What it does

Argos allows exam proctors to track students visual patterns and flag if they look away from their test too many times or for too long in a short amount of time. While also having the ability to spot iPhone, earbuds, and smartwatches both visible and not visible using both a camera and RF detector rig. 

How we built it

We used an open-source AI face detector to help us track where students are facing and looking at all times. Then we then took those pre-determined positions and coded actions that check if this person is potentially cheating. As well as implementing an RF detector to check the radio-signals in the air that find out whether a device is being used in the area, and its approximate location.

Challenges we ran into

Changing AI models halfway into our build really through us off track for a bit, but it was necessary since the previous model lagged our app so bad we only reached around 3fps. Then we had trouble with our RF-detector because it kept picking up signals from across the building, along with previous signals that were already there. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

As a team we are so proud of all the hard work we were able to accomplish in 36 hrs, from the software in the code to the hardware we camped out to rent. 

What we learned

"Perfection is overrated", sometimes you can't work out every bug, or implement every cool feature you want. Maybe that's because of time constraints, memory, or some other reason that stops you from perfecting your build, and maybe that ok too. 

What's next for Argos

Taking Argos to the next step would lead to more features, such as overhead cameras, heat maps, ink sensors and more. So next time we would need better hardware, more budget, and more time to perfect our software and present it in front of real investors.

title: Blurr
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Blurr

Ask for the blur. Local AI video redaction on one AMD GPU.

Like
2

Comment

Homepage

Blurr works with photos too! 

Multiple mask options

Inspiration

Anyone who posts street footage, bodycam clips, a vlog or a school event has to hide bystanders' faces and license plates first. Today that means one of two things: scrubbing through an editor and keyframing boxes by hand, or uploading the footage to a cloud service, which is the opposite of protecting the people in it. We wanted redaction you can ask for in plain language, check frame by frame, and run without a cloud.

What it does

Blurr hides people, faces and license plates in video (and photos) from a plain-language request.

Ask in plain words. "Blur all plates and the person in the red hoodie around halfway." "Everyone except the woman." "Pixelate faces in the first 10 seconds." "Unblur the plates." "Undo."
Or draw a box around anything, and it's tracked through the clip.
See what the agent did. Each reply lists its steps in plain words: the yes/no question it asked about each person ("Is this a man wearing a red hoodie?"), how many said yes, no or unsure, and what it masked. A coverage strip shows when each target is masked.
Preview before you export. Source shows every box the detectors found (solid if masked, dashed if not), and Program shows the frame as the export will render it.
Fix any mask by hand. Mask, unmask, restyle (blur, pixelate, black box) or drag a box to the right place and it's re-tracked from there. Every change is a version, and undo is one click.
Fail closed. If the vision model is unsure about a person, or the tracker loses someone, they stay blurred. Errors mean more blur, never less.
Photos too, exported with no metadata (no GPS position, camera serial or capture time).
Fully offline. Inference never touches the network.

How we built it

The agent never touches pixels. It edits a mask timeline (which object is masked, when, and with which effect) through a small set of typed tools, and a deterministic renderer applies that timeline to the video.

Scan at upload. A background scan finds faces and plates with Meta's EgoBlur models and people (and any other named object) with YOLOE, and tracks them across frames.
Understand the request. Plain requests are parsed by a template in milliseconds, with no model. Anything else goes once to Qwen3-VL-8B, which writes the whole plan as JSON. Plain code validates and runs it. The model never handles track ids.
Check who's who. "The woman" becomes a yes/no question that the same Qwen3-VL model answers about each tracked person, from crops across the track. Above 0.65 is yes, below 0.35 no, in between unsure, and unsure stays masked.
Render. Plain code applies the timeline: blur, pixelate or a solid box, with padding, interpolation between detections and a hold after a track is lost.

Built on one AMD GPU with ROCm. PyTorch 2.9.1+rocm7.13, transformers, Ultralytics, OpenCV, FastAPI and a single-file web UI. We built and measured on a Radeon AI PRO R9700 (32 GB), then moved to a Radeon 8060S Strix Halo (64 GB shared) when the Dublin hub went down. Same ROCm, same code. Detection, the 8B vision-language model and the planner all share one card: 17.9 GB peak on the R9700, 19.3 GB on the Strix Halo. fp16 cut each EgoBlur call about 3x with the same boxes (0.147 s to 0.049 s per 1080p frame on the R9700, 0.376 s to 0.129 s on the Strix Halo). On the R9700 a 720p clip scans at 1.12x real time, 24x faster than a 64-thread Threadripper PRO CPU. On the Strix Halo the full face + plate + person scan runs at 105 ms/frame at 720p.

Private by construction. ./run.sh puts Hugging Face and Ultralytics in offline mode, and an egress guard refuses and logs every outbound connection or DNS lookup. The log stays empty through our demo, and /health reports "offline": true.

Challenges we ran into

Checking our own benchmark. On the night-crowd clip most failed requests were label errors: face boxes half a face off, a plate box left on a frame after the plate drove away. We corrected the 28 boxes we could verify, left every ambiguous one as drawn, and report both scores (13/20 before, 14/20 after).
Plate false alarms. At a low threshold EgoBlur flags tail lights, signs and shoes. Requiring two confident detections took one clip from 232 plate tracks to 49 while keeping every real plate.
Small, fast plates. A 13 px plate moving 10 px between checked frames doesn't overlap itself, so the tracker split it. Linking by size and distance and starting masks a few frames early took plate coverage from 72% to 94.6% of frames.
Step-by-step agents are slow. Our first LLM loop picked one tool at a time and took over two minutes for "everyone except the guy in the red hoodie". One JSON plan per request, run by plain code, does it in 7 s.
Fragmented person tracks. The tracker sometimes loses a pedestrian and starts a "new" person. A stitcher joins tracks by position, heading, size and color (15 to 11 person tracks on one clip). We checked every join by eye, because merging two different people is worse than leaving a piece.
ROCm quirks. MIOpen couldn't read its kernel database on the cloud image, so every new crop size triggered a ~15 s kernel search per VLM call. Fixed-size crops plus MIOPEN_FIND_MODE=FAST fixed it. Asking the model for only the last position's logits avoided a 16 GB memory spike.
Moving GPUs mid-hackathon. The Dublin hub went down on Sunday. We re-measured on the Strix Halo and kept the numbers separate rather than copying them across.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

It really is offline. An empty egress log after a full demo, enforced by code, not by promise.
Fail-closed behavior we measured. With fail-closed on, 14/20 real-clip requests pass; with it off, 11/20. A keyword-only baseline gets 7/20.
Plates (Strix Halo): 100% of plate frames masked on a 1080p street clip and 93.7% on a 720p one, with 2.5% and 0.06% mean over-blur.
Labeled boxes at least 90% masked (Strix Halo): faces 0.95, plates 0.98, people 0.99. Our face labels are head boxes, so this undercounts faces.
An honest benchmark. Every number comes from one script over hand-labeled real clips, and we published our label corrections.
Four people, one contract. The typed mask timeline let us build the agent, detectors, renderer and UI in parallel against a stub, and the full test suite runs in about 15 s with no GPU.

What we learned

Keep the model out of the pixels. A typed mask timeline between the agent and the renderer made every result checkable, undoable and testable without a GPU. Measure before you optimize: the GPU, not decoding, was the limit, and fp16 was the win. And treat benchmark labels as suspect before blaming the model.

What's next for Blurr

Live mode: a standing rule ("blur any plate that appears") on a stream behind a short delay buffer, then an OBS virtual camera. On the Strix Halo, detecting every 5th frame at 720p behind under 0.8 s of delay would keep every mask in place, but it isn't built yet.
Pixel-accurate masks with SAM 3 instead of padded boxes.
Fewer vision-model checks per request in crowds.
More categories: screens, on-screen text, documents.
Better recall on dim, motion-blurred faces in masks, which EgoBlur misses even at a 0.05 threshold.

Limits: no nudity or graphic-content detection, masks are padded rectangles rather than outlines, offline speed on the Strix Halo is 0.4x real time, and photos support JPEG, PNG, WebP and BMP but not HEIC.

title: SPOTlight
text:
Notifications

Loading...

SPOTlight

An operator console for SPOT: open Hugging Face models on AMD ROCm flag and explain each anomaly live or after a mission, backed by Neon, so plant operators know what to do next.

Like
4

Comment

Fine Tuning a System 1 0.4B Laya Model for Quick Decisions

System Architecture

The Tech Stack

CI/CD Pipeline to push to github and have it immediately deploy on Vercel and Neon

Qwen 3 0.6B Embedding Model we chose and downloaded on hugging face

Qwen 3.8 27B GGUF LLM we chose and benchmarked on the 5 domains the SPOT dog encounters.

Inspiration

NextEra asked us to help plant operators understand what SPOT is seeing, live and after a mission, without having to become technical experts. Before designing anything, we loaded NextEra's challenge kit (27 synthetic SPOT missions) into pandas. One number set the direction: 26 of the 27 missions are marked COMPLETED, yet 21 of those 26 contain failed actions, and 14 of the 15 HIGH or CRITICAL anomalies happened inside "completed" missions.

$$\frac{21}{26} \approx 81\% \text{ of green missions were hiding a failure.}$$

That is the "wall of green dots" operators see in Orbit today. We wanted a console that shows what actually went wrong, explains why in plain language, and says what to do next. It should earn trust by showing its evidence instead of asking for it.

What it does

Live patrol: start one of five 8-stop routes and watch SPOT walk the plant blueprint. Each stop pings red or green. At photo stops, the image is read and Qwen's explanation types itself into the card as the model writes it, then the checked answer replaces it. The patrol is a simulation: it re-sends kit data as live events, and its photos are labelled as simulated.
Mission replay and review: replay any recorded mission on the map and rewind its timeline. Work through a priority queue of flags. Open a flag to see its readings, photo, cited evidence and recommended action. Acknowledge, escalate, resolve it or add a note.
Analytics: fleet charts by category, such as hidden failures, the battery cliff, the worst waypoints and how reliable each inspection type is, with drill-down.
SPOTbot: a chat assistant grounded in the plant's records. Every citation and number in its answer is checked against the sources, and the answer gets a grounding badge.

Status is never shown by color alone: every status has a color, an icon and a word.

How we built it

Our rule was gates first, model second. Explainable rules and a small classifier decide what deserves attention, a large model explains it, and a deterministic checker decides whether that explanation is shown.

System 1, triage on every event. Laya (421M, ModernBERT-large) answers typed questions in a single forward pass, with calibrated probabilities: escalate? priority? category? can this reading be trusted? It never generates text, so it can't hallucinate. Next to it runs a rules validator modelled on alarm rationalization (ISA-18.2: consequence × urgency). Simplified:

$$
\text{priority} =
\begin{cases}
\text{P1} & s = 4 \;\lor\; (s = 3 \land c \ge 3) \;\lor\; (\text{failed} \land b \le 15\%) \
\text{P2} & s = 3 \;\lor\; (s = 2 \land c \ge 3) \;\lor\; (\text{failed} \land c \ge 3) \;\lor\; b \le 25\% \
\text{P3} & s \ge 1 \;\lor\; \text{failed} \;\lor\; b \le 35\% \
\text{P4} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Here $s$ is anomaly severity, $c$ is asset criticality (both 1 to 4) and $b$ is battery. The battery thresholds come from the data: actions succeed 33% of the time at $b \le 25\%$, against 80 to 90% above it. Either Laya or the rules can escalate, and the rules' priority is a floor that Laya can raise but never lower.

We fine-tuned Laya with PyTorch on ROCm, on an AMD Radeon 8060S. The data is split by mission. A simulator fitted only on the training missions adds more cases, and counterfactual pairs (one-field edits that flip the label) teach it that battery or criticality alone can change the answer. Untuned Laya is near chance. Our best fine-tune reached a macro-F1 of 0.805 on held-out real missions and 0.846 on counterfactuals.

System 2, explanations for escalated flags. Qwen3.8-27B (8-bit GGUF) runs in llama.cpp, which we built with HIP for an AMD Radeon Pro W7900D, at about 22 tokens/s. It gets one prepared context packet from our read-only MCP server and makes no tool calls. It answers in Orbit's format: question, answer, cited evidence, a recommended action from a fixed list, and a confidence. A deterministic checker then requires, for every claim $k$ citing the rows $R_k$:

$$\text{numbers}(k) \subseteq \text{numbers}(R_k) \quad\land\quad \text{ids}(k) \subseteq \text{ids}(R_k)$$

A rejected answer is retried. If the retry also fails, the operator gets a template labelled as a template. We tested it on 38 held-out flags from 8 missions it had never seen. 36 answers (94.7%) were accepted on the first attempt, the other 2 fell back to the template, and every answer served passed the schema, citation, number and name checks. Latency was 11.2 s at p50 and 15.0 s at p95.

Streaming. An empty box for 10 to 15 seconds kills trust. System 2 streams llama-server's partial JSON as draft snapshots over SSE, through the FastAPI backend and Next.js to the browser. Drafts, labelled "unverified", appear in about 3 seconds. The checked answer then replaces them, and only checked answers are ever stored.

Retrieval. We use Neon Postgres with pgvector. It holds 503 documents (the kit, the Spot manual, incidents, policy and operator notes), embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B running on the AMD box. Search combines vector and full-text matching. It also uses a 574-node knowledge graph stored as plain tables and walked with WITH RECURSIVE, because Neon has no graph extension. Chat drops matches below cosine similarity 0.50, unless they also match the question's text or IDs:

$$\cos(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{d} \rVert} \ge 0.50$$

Operator notes are embedded too, so later explanations can cite what a human wrote.

Vision. Code, not a vision-language model, computes every number taken from a photo. Readers for dial gauges, thermal colorbars, spectrograms and Orbit screenshots turn an image into citable readings and an annotated picture. Published results put VLMs at 25 to 30% on gauge and thermal reading.

The stack.

The Next.js frontend, FastAPI backend and MCP server run on Vercel.
Neon is one database for operations, the RAG documents, the knowledge graph and the audit logs. The MCP server connects with a read-only role.
On the AMD box, the LLM, the embedding model, Laya and System 2 run under supervisord.
The compose stack adds a LangGraph orchestrator and a LiteLLM gateway.
SPOTbot answers through the Gemini API.
Every service has a Dockerfile, and one docker-compose.yml with profiles runs it all.
We wrote each API contract in docs/ before its code. CI runs 14 checks on every PR.
We built with Claude Code as a pair programmer, with separate agents for implementation and validation.

Challenges we ran into

The GPU box fought us.

It had no Docker, and Hugging Face was blocked. We pulled the 29 GB model through a mirror and checked its SHA-256 against Hugging Face's API.
The pip ROCm install had no HIP CMake files, so we installed the developer package by hand to build llama.cpp.
Kubernetes wouldn't run (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN), and sshd refused port forwarding. We bridged the services over stdio on one SSH connection, then added Cloudflare tunnels so Vercel could reach the GPU.

15 seconds is a long time. At 8-bit, the 27B model's p95 missed our 15 s budget by 3 ms (15,003 ms). We kept the 8-bit quality and fixed the experience with streaming instead of shrinking the model.
Silent failures.

llama.cpp once got stuck returning "Unexpected empty grammar stack" while /health still said OK, so every explanation quietly became the template. /health now runs a real one-token model probe.
In another bug, one provenance note sat in the wrong field (gaps instead of facts), which made the model refuse every live stop.

Our checker was too strict. It rejected correct answers because it read flag:14 as the number 14 and action:A0030 as an unknown name. It now masks cited IDs and the flag's own subject, but still checks every number.
Gauges are hard.

Our first code reader was right on 22% of 87 real gauge photos. It also marked 7 readings as trusted, and 6 of those were wrong.
Untuned Qwen got 46% right, but said "ok" to all 47 of its wrong answers.
So we shipped an acceptance policy. A photo reading counts only when two independent readers agree within 2% of the dial's span, $|x_{\text{geo}} - x_{\text{qwen}}| \le 0.02\,(x_{\max} - x_{\min})$. Otherwise the operator sees the photo and is asked for a retake or a human reading.

Small data. The kit has 27 missions and 40 anomalies. We split by mission, fit the simulator on training missions only and report mission-level bootstrap confidence intervals. We also pre-registered a fresh gauge test so we can't fool ourselves.

What we learned

Read the data before designing. Our best feature came out of a pandas notebook, not a brainstorm.
Gates first, model second. Rules people can audit and a calibrated classifier decide what matters. The LLM explains, and a checker decides whether the explanation is shown.
Fine-tuning teaches format, not facts. Qwen is not fine-tuned: its facts come from retrieval, and the checker holds it to them.
A 200 from /health doesn't mean the model is answering. Test a real request.
Perceived latency is a design problem. Streaming made a 10-second answer feel immediate without changing the model.
Evaluations have bugs too. Our first gauge scorer assumed every gauge read psi. Keep every run, report coverage next to accuracy, and pre-register the test that counts.
ROCm handles real workloads. We fine-tuned Laya with PyTorch on a Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and served a 27B model with llama.cpp on a W7900D (gfx1100).

What's next for SPOTlight

Continue to develop the pipeline and improve the QWEN model for better output and more trustworth responses.

Aria Vision

An AI-powered assistant for Meta Aria glasses that describes your surroundings, answers questions by voice, and provides spoken warnings to help you navigate the world with greater confidence.

Like
1

Comment
1

Inspiration

Understanding your surroundings can be challenging, especially for people who are blind or visually impaired. Everyday activities, such as recognizing objects, understanding what is nearby, or getting oriented in an unfamiliar place, can require extra effort.

We wanted to explore how AI and wearable technology could make this experience easier. That inspired us to build AriaVision, an AI-powered assistant that uses Meta Aria glasses to help users understand their surroundings through spoken descriptions and answers to their questions.

Our goal was to make interacting with the world more accessible by letting users get information through audio instead of constantly looking at a screen.

What It Does

AriaVision connects Meta Aria glasses with an AI assistant that helps users better understand what is around them.

With AriaVision, users can:

Receive spoken descriptions of their surroundings.
Press the Space key to ask questions, such as “What is in front of me?”
Ask for help understanding their environment or figuring out where to go.
Hear the assistant's responses instead of needing to read them on a screen.

The project explores how wearable cameras and AI can work together to provide more accessible, hands-free environmental assistance.

How We Built It

We combined wearable hardware, AI, and software to create our application.

Meta Aria glasses: Capture visual information from the user's surroundings.
Gemini: Powers the AI experience by interpreting visual information and helping generate responses to questions.
TypeScript, HTML, and CSS: Support the website's interface and interactive features.
Python: Runs a bridge that connects the glasses to the application and transfers camera information.
Project Aria Client SDK: Helps the application communicate with the Meta Aria glasses.
WebSockets: Allow the Python bridge and website to exchange information.

We also worked on connecting the glasses to a computer through USB so the application could receive information from the device. Our goal was to combine this visual input with spoken responses to make the experience simple and intuitive.

Challenges We Ran Into

One of our biggest challenges was getting the hardware and software to communicate properly. Connecting the Meta Aria glasses required setting up the Python environment, installing dependencies, and troubleshooting the USB connection.

We also ran into network restrictions that interfered with our wireless connection attempt. Using USB gave us another way to connect the glasses to the computer. Additionally, a port conflict on the computer required us to choose a different port for communication.

Another challenge was bringing the different parts of the experience together. We wanted the assistant to provide environmental descriptions while also allowing users to ask their own questions. Working through these challenges taught us how much coordination is required when combining AI software with wearable hardware.

Accomplishments We're Proud Of

We're proud to have explored how Meta Aria glasses can be used as part of an AI-powered accessibility tool. We connected the glasses to our application, created an interface for user questions, and developed spoken environmental guidance.

We're also proud of the idea behind AriaVision: making information about the surrounding environment easier to access through audio. This project let us explore how AI can go beyond a traditional screen-based experience and become part of a wearable, real-world interaction.

What We Learned

Throughout this project, we learned that building an AI application involves more than simply connecting a model to a website. Hardware integration, device communication, network limitations, and the user experience all play important roles.

We also learned how important it is to design with accessibility in mind. An assistant is more useful when its information is easy to understand and doesn't require constant attention to a screen.

Most importantly, we learned the value of troubleshooting, adapting when our original approach did not work, and testing individual parts of a system before bringing them together.

What's Next for AriaVision

AriaVision still has room to improve. In the future, we would like to:

Improve the accuracy and usefulness of environmental descriptions.
Expand the types of questions the assistant can answer.
Explore more advanced navigation assistance.
Improve reliability across different network and connection setups.
Test the complete experience more extensively with the physical glasses.
Gather feedback from people who could benefit from hands-free environmental assistance.

Our long-term vision is to make AriaVision a more reliable and useful accessibility companion that helps people better understand their surroundings and move through unfamiliar environments with greater confidence.

title: Doorway
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Doorway

Lost in a UCF building? Point your phone, pick a room, and follow a glowing AR path on the floor to the door. Doorway finds you from walls and room signs, fully offline.

Like
3

Comment

Inspiration

As a freshman at UCF we all had difficulties navigating through campus and finding the rooms for classes, clubs, and meetings. That's why we built Doorway to solve our problems with campus navigation. 

What it does

Doorway is an AR app that gives turn-by-turn directions inside campus buildings, where GPS stops working. It works the way Google Maps does outdoors.

Open the app, pick where you're going, and Doorway draws a glowing route on the floor through your phone's camera, all the way to the room. An outdoor campus map connects them: tap the other building to load its floor.

Finds where you are indoors, without GPS. It combines AR tracking, step counting and the building's walls to work out your position. It also reads room-number signs ("121", "107A") through the camera to pin down exactly where you are.
Guides you in AR. A route on the floor and a turn banner tell you where to go next. It recalculates if you go a different way.
Talks with you. Say "take me to room 107" or "where's the bathroom?" to set a route. Doorway reads each turn aloud, so you can keep your eyes up instead of on your phone.
Lets you browse the building. Search or scroll a directory of rooms, bathrooms, elevators, stairs and entrances. A floor map you can zoom and a minimap show where you are and where you're headed.
Works without a connection. Floor plans, routing and sign reading all run on the phone.

How we built it

The app. Doorway is built in Unity 6 with C#, using AR Foundation and ARCore on Android. ARCore tracks the phone's movement and senses depth, so the app can tell walls from floor. A Java plug-in brings in Google's ML Kit text recognition, which reads room-number signs in the camera feed, fully on the phone. Voice commands and spoken directions use Android's built-in speech recognizer and text-to-speech. We call both directly from C#, with no extra plug-in.

Finding you indoors. With no GPS inside, our localizer combines several weaker signals into one position. It uses AR tracking, steps from the phone's step sensor, a match between the walls ARCore sees and the walls on the floor plan, and every room sign the camera reads. A router finds the shortest path through a walkable grid of the floor. A navigator turns that path into turns, then reroutes or re-aligns when you drift.

Turning floor plans into maps. We started from floor plans traced by Knight Hacks and archived UCF floor plans. Python pipelines with OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy, Shapely and Pillow pull walls, rooms, doors and walkable space out of the images. They then produce the floor data and themed map images the app loads. The outdoor campus map comes from OpenStreetMap, downloaded through the Overpass API and lined up with the floor plans.

Training a voice model. We generated labelled voice commands from the building's own rooms. We added more natural wordings using Hugging Face Inference Providers, then fine-tuned Google's FunctionGemma 270M on Hugging Face Jobs to turn speech into app commands. A rule-based parser in the app handles commands instantly and offline.

Testing with real walks. We walked the buildings with the app, which logs every position it estimates. We then replayed those walks and generated synthetic ones in Unity to measure positioning error and tune the localizer. The logs go into Databricks, where tables and maps show how far off the app was and where on each floor it struggles.

Keeping it working. GitHub Actions runs our pytest suite on the data pipelines. Through GameCI, it also runs Unity's tests and builds a test APK.

Challenges we ran into

We faced lots of difficulties figuring out how to make our AR tracking more accurate. One of the biggest causes to this problem was the outdated floor plans that UCF made publicly available. Due to this constraint, our AR tracking would have difficulties navigating through furniture, new pathways, and people.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're happy to have learned AR tracking for the first time and implimented it into an application that serves a very useful purpose to students, faculty and others on campus. not just for UCF but for other institutions in the future

What we learned

We learned to perform more efficiently in a group of 3 throughout the course of 36 hours to completely start from zero and end up with a working proof of concept. We also combined a lot of technologies such as Unity, AR Foundation, ARCore, Google's ML Kit, Android's speech recognition and text-to-speech, Python with OpenCV and NumPy, OpenStreetMap, Hugging Face with Gemma, and Databricks into one app, and learned how to make them all work together.

What's next for Doorway

Next up is scaling into instutitions that will benefit from this more, including but not limited to hospitals, retirement homes, and many others.

title: KYU-BOT
text:
Notifications

Loading...

KYU-BOT

A disaster management system leveraging 3D city physics and multi agent AI to synthesize incoming casualty reports, plan optimal dispatch routes, and score situational awareness against ground truth.

Like
2

Comment
1

Dashboard Screen

Inspiration

In the terrifying aftermath of a massive earthquake, the most agonizing tragedy isn't just the crumbled buildings, it's the helpless silence. Thousands of people remain trapped beneath rubble while calls flood emergency centers, leaving first responders blind to who needs help first and how to reach them before time runs out. We build this platform out of a simple belief: that technology should stand between life and loss. By grounding AI in real Japanese seismic physics rather than guesswork, we can cut through the noise and chaos of a crisis and guide rescue teams directly to trapped victims, ensuring that when seconds mean everything, no one if left waiting in the dark. 

What it does

KYU-BOT generates a high fidelity earthquake around Shinjuku, Tokyo using real 3D city data, soil amplification maps, and Japanese seismic engineering formulas. It calculates the exact hidden truth: which builds collapse, which roads are blocked by debris, and where people are trapped or hurt. 

Then, it streams a chaotic feed of around 120 calls, social media posts, and eye witness texts. These reports include real world noise such as duplicate calls, exaggerated injury counts, wrong locations, and false rumors. 

Next, a team of specialized AI agents process the incoming report stream: 

Medical Agent: Filters injury reports into a prioritized triage list showing trapped / critical victims per location.
Verification & Assessment Agents: Merge duplicate reports and verify claims against existing evidence.
Routing & Resource Agents: Find eligible rescue teams and plot routes around blocked streets using road graphs. 
Planning Agent: Generates actionable rescue plans.

Later, the proposed rescue plans, responder locations, and route updates are displayed on a 3D MapLibre interface for a human operator to review and approve. If a road collapses mid run, the AI automatically detects the blockage, reroutes the responders, and explains why. 

Finally, at the end of the simulation, the system compares what the AI agents believed was happening against the hidden physical reality stored in the backend. It outputs a scorecard rating how accurately the AI found trapped victims, filtered rumors, and routed teams through open roads. 

How we built it

Frontend:

React + TypeScript for the dashboard, built and served with Vite.
MapLibre GL for the 3D map of Shinjuku: extruded buildings, road layers and report dots.
OpenFreeMap / OpenStreetMap for the background map tiles.
lucide-react for icons.

Backend:

FastAPI (Python), the API that the simulator, website and agents all go through. It checks input with Pydantic and runs on uvicorn.
psycopg connects it to the database.

Databases:

Neon (Postgres + PostGIS):
the static map: buildings, roads, facilities
everything agents may see: runs, reports, incidents, road restrictions, units, decisions
PostGIS handles the locations and geometry
Databricks: the hidden truth (real damage, people, the answer key) and the scorecards. Agents have no access to it.

Simulator (Python):

Shapely for geometry, like which roads are under a collapsed building's debris.
NetworkX for the road graph and routing (A* routes, nearest units).
SciPy for matching units to incidents.
OSMnx to build the road graph from OpenStreetMap (run once, on a laptop).
Its own small FastAPI service on port 8100, which the map calls for Generate and the live clock.

AI:

Gemini (through the google-genai SDK):
writes the report wording, which is what we built
planned for the agents
The agents may run on an open model (Qwen via Hugging Face) instead.
Whisper (Hugging Face) is planned for turning emergency-call audio into text.

Data sources:

Project PLATEAU (Japan's 3D city model) for buildings.
OpenStreetMap for roads.
J-SHIS for soil.
Published earthquake research for the damage formulas.

Tooling:

pytest for tests.
dev.sh (Mac/Linux) and dev.ps1 (Windows) start everything.
Git + GitHub with pull requests.

Challenges we ran into

Lots of Merge Conflicts, Unfamiliar with Neon and had a hard time assigning permission and roles since each agents had a different role, the simulation needed access to the database directly and that made it difficult to learn, getting everything merged into the 3D rendering simulation and getting everything to work simultaneously without having to click a button.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of the fact that we were able to create and use a very complex database schema on a new database. Furthermore, we were also able to successfully fuse real 3D building data from PLATEAU, soil amplification models and road networks into one unified map. 

What we learned

We learnt a lot about how to use a Databricks and Neon, and were able to delve into the world of 3D modeling and simulations. We also learnt how to orchestrate multiple AI Agents. We were also able to learn a lot about how to create systems and pipelines to ensure that we have efficient workflows. 

What's next for KYU-BOT

While Japan has an incredible national disaster communication infrastructure, a catastrophic earthquake can still fracture internet connectivity. That's why our natural next step for KYU-BOT is local, edge native deployment. This would allow the entire multi agent pipeline to run entirely offline on local hardware, ingesting radio and mesh network traffic to coordinate life saving rescues even when the grid goes completely dark

title: Beacon
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Beacon

Every face has a story to it. Remember it.

Like

Comment

Every recognized face gets a card: who, where, when. AMBER alerts in red. Today’s path is drawn on the map; click it for Street View.

Beacon dashboard: live glasses feed, lens display, people met nearby, AMBER watchlist, and a Street View of your walk.

Inspiration

Beacon was inspired by a simple question: what if smart glasses could help you remember the people you meet and where you last saw them? We wanted to explore how wearable technology could assist with memory, navigation, and locating someone during situations such as a missing-person alert—all while keeping the wearer’s hands free.

What it does

Beacon turns Meta smart glasses into a wearable visual-memory assistant. The glasses stream camera frames through an Android phone to our backend, where faces are detected and converted into embeddings. Beacon can recognize someone it has seen before, display their name or notes on the glasses, and record where and when they were encountered.

Users can name people, add notes, create watch alerts, and ask where somebody was last seen. Beacon also builds a map from the wearer’s movement and can guide them back to a person’s last known location. Full frames and face crops are stored privately so users can review and correct recognition results.

How we built it

We built the Android application in Kotlin using Meta’s Wearables Device Access Toolkit for camera streaming and glasses display output. The phone sends frames and location information to a Python FastAPI backend.

For face recognition, we use the AuraFace v1 model from Hugging Face through InsightFace and ONNX Runtime. Faces are represented as 512-dimensional embeddings.

Neon powers the data layer. Neon Postgres stores people, embeddings, sightings, locations, map nodes, and routes. The pgvector extension performs similarity searches between face embeddings, while Neon Object Storage privately stores face crops and complete sighting frames. The backend connects each stored image to its corresponding database record.

Our navigation system builds a graph from the wearer’s movement and uses A* pathfinding to guide them toward a person or location. The final result is displayed as simple, readable instructions on the glasses.

Challenges we ran into

Combining real-time camera streaming, face recognition, database writes, object storage, location tracking, and glasses output created several integration challenges. We had to control latency so processing one frame would not block incoming frames or make the display feel delayed.

Face quality also varies significantly with distance, lighting, motion blur, and viewing angle. We created quality thresholds and training sets so Beacon only saves useful face images.

Migrating from local SQLite and filesystem storage to Neon required redesigning the database layer, adding Postgres migrations, configuring pgvector, and replacing local image paths with private Object Storage keys. We also had to prevent embeddings generated by different recognition models from being mixed together.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We created an end-to-end system that works with real smart-glasses hardware rather than only a simulated interface. Beacon can detect a face, generate an AuraFace embedding, compare it through Neon, store the sighting and its images, and return useful information to the glasses.

We are especially proud of connecting face recognition with location-aware memory and navigation. Beacon does more than identify someone—it remembers the context of the encounter and can help the wearer return to that location.

We also added practical privacy and correction features, including anonymous identities, configurable retention, manual merging and reassignment, private image storage, and a complete data-reset option.

What we learned

We learned that a machine-learning model is only one part of a useful AI product. Data quality, storage design, latency, model compatibility, privacy, and user experience are equally important.

We also learned how Neon Postgres, pgvector, and Object Storage can work together as one backend for structured records, vector similarity searches, and private media. Working with wearable hardware also taught us how important graceful failure, concise displays, and real-device testing are.

What's next for Beacon

Next, we want to deploy the backend to scalable cloud infrastructure, improve recognition accuracy through additional real-world testing, and optimize inference for lower latency. We also plan to add authentication, encryption, consent controls, and stronger automatic retention policies.

We would like to use Neon database branching for safe development and demonstrations, add more advanced location understanding, and evaluate hosted GPU inference for supporting multiple wearers. Our long-term goal is to turn Beacon into a reliable and privacy-conscious memory assistant for accessibility, safety, and everyday use.

title: Rate That Slop
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Rate That Slop

Sniff out the slop. Stitch with confidence.

Like

Comment

Image Ratings of Sewing Patterns on Etsy with badges

Extension Score Tab (top half)

Extension Score Tab (bottom half)

Extension Login tab (signed out)

Extension Manual tab 

Extension Settings tab (signed in)

Extension Login tab (signed in)

Image ratings are also compatible with other Etsy listings

Inspiration

Etsy used to be a great place to find unique, fun sewing patterns. But with the rise of AI, we've gone from discovering amazing designs to scrolling through slop after slop. Listings can look great at first glance, only for the actual pattern to have inconsistent measurements, questionable fabric recommendations, or instructions that clearly weren't made by someone who knows how to sew.

We wanted to make it easier to find patterns worth stitching. So we built Rate That Slop to help sewists sniff out the slop before they buy, and stitch with confidence.

What It Does

Rate That Slop is a Chrome extension that helps you spot potentially AI-generated sewing patterns on Etsy before you buy them.

Sniff Out the Slop: Uses an open-source AI detection model to analyze listing images right in your browser.
Look at the Whole Picture: Combines image scores with listing descriptions and reviews to give each listing an overall risk rating.
See the Red Flags: Etsy badges flag potential concerns, while the popup shows a detailed breakdown with individual scores and explanations for images, descriptions, and reviews, plus whether a seller is recognized as trusted through manual admin review.
Keep It Private: Image analysis runs locally in your browser, and image bytes aren't uploaded during ordinary server interactions.

How We Built It

We wanted to go beyond checking whether a single image looked AI-generated, so we brought together several different signals to get a better picture of each listing.

We integrated an open-source ONNX image-detection model that runs directly in the browser.
We built a weighted scoring system in Javascript that combines results across listing images and other available evidence.
We used Google's Gemini models to evaluate descriptions and reviews for additional context.
We built a backend hosted on DigitalOcean to support shared listing data and account-based features.
We designed a high-contrast interface with separate tabs and customizable settings, so users can choose what matters to them. We built it using Javascript, HTML, and CSS.

Challenges We Ran Into

Getting everything to work together was definitely harder than we expected!

Getting the Pieces to Talk: Connecting the browser extension, AI models, and backend without breaking something along the way took plenty of debugging.
Caching and Syncing: Storing results and getting them to sync reliably with the server took some trial and error.
Branching Out (Literally): With different team members working on separate branches, merging everything together came with its fair share of headaches.
Unexpected Bugs: We ran into errors we hadn't planned for and had to add more error handling and spend time tracking down what went wrong.

Accomplishments That We're Proud Of

We're proud that Rate That Slop grew beyond a simple AI image detector into a tool that looks at listings from multiple angles.

A More Complete Picture: Combined image analysis with other listing signals to create an overall risk rating.
AI That Runs Locally: Got image inference working in the browser without needing a separate inference server.
A Working Full-Stack Setup: Connected our extension to a hosted backend for shared features.
Putting Users in Control: Built a customizable interface that lets users decide which features they want to use.

What We Learned

This project taught us that getting an AI model to work is only half the battle. Turning its output into something people can actually use takes a lot more thought.

One of our biggest takeaways was that building a browser extension is very different from building a web app. We had to rethink how we approached several things:

Storage and Caching: We needed to cache results and avoid repeating expensive image analysis wherever possible.
Thinking Beyond Local Development: A server running on our own machines works during development, but isn't a long-term solution for other users. We learned the importance of hosting our backend so server-dependent features can work outside our local environments.
Designing for a Different Interface: A browser extension isn't a standalone website. We had to rethink how to organize information, display our ratings, and make everything feel intuitive within the extension's popup.
Working Within an Existing Website: Instead of designing an entire page ourselves, we had to integrate our features into Etsy's existing interface without getting in the way of the shopping experience.

We also learned how important it is to test everything together rather than assuming that individually working components will automatically make a working product.

Most importantly, an AI score isn't proof that a listing is a scam. We want to help sewists spot potential red flags and make informed decisions, not make snap judgments for them.

What's Next for Rate That Slop?

We've got plenty more we'd love to do!

Make Detection Better: Test and refine our scoring against real, manually reviewed sewing patterns.
Catch Fewer False Alarms: Improve our ability to distinguish AI-generated images from legitimate product photos.
Build a Stronger Community: Expand shared ratings and community reporting to help sewists learn from one another.
Keep Improving: Make the extension faster, more reliable, and clearer about why a listing gets its rating.

Our goal is simple: help people find patterns worth stitching, without having to dig through endless slop to get there.

Outfox the slop. Stitch with confidence.

Gatesmith

A unified pipeline for quantum circuit development that slots into any researcher’s Qiskit workflow

Like

Comment

Web UI

GitHub bot

cat of an Improved Circuit

cat of overview of a run's GPU performance

Inspiration

Bioinformatics has had a suite that holds the field together for decades: Rosetta. One shared score function, reused by every protocol, keeps researchers speaking the same language. Quantum computing has nothing like it. Circuits get written in one framework, compiled in another, benchmarked in a third, and judged differently at every step. Gatesmith is our step toward a unified, Rosetta-inspired pipeline that keeps quantum researchers on the same page and streamlines how they develop circuits.

What it does

Give Gatesmith a GitHub repository link, a local folder or a single OpenQASM file. It finds the quantum circuits without running your code, lets you pick which ones to score, and drafts a manifest describing what must stay the same in each.

The scoring engine, qscore, then:

Validates first and explains before running. Every input problem is reported at once with a location and a fix, and nothing runs until you confirm what Gatesmith understood.
Compiles across multiple seeds for a hardware target (IBM's 133-qubit Torino layout by default) and reports the best result along with the spread, not one lucky run.
Measures 20 metrics in four groups: resources, hardware cost, optimization opportunities and research. It places each one among 119 public benchmark circuits from QASMBench and MQT Bench.
Diagnoses where the cost comes from. Ten rules turn metrics into located findings, such as "routing dominates this circuit" or "this block can be re-synthesized", each naming the qubits, the gates and the fixes that apply.

From there, researchers can ask the CLI to improve a circuit with one of two layers: deterministic Qiskit resynthesis, or open-weight models from Hugging Face. Every proposed rewrite must pass exact equivalence checking and be re-scored with the same seeds. It counts only if it's strictly better and breaks no constraint.

Our guiding rule: AI proposes, the scoring engine decides.

On top of the pipeline sits a research platform: a web app, and a GitHub review bot that brings Gatesmith's results into pull requests, with Gemini turning the findings into review comments.

How we built it

Engine: Python 3.12, Qiskit 2.x and OpenQASM 2/3, managed with uv.

Strict Pydantic schemas, with seeds, versions and hashes recorded on every result.
Five code layers whose import direction is enforced in CI.
Equivalence is decided by exact methods only, such as Qiskit operator comparison. Random tests count as supporting evidence, never as proof.

Improvement layers:

reference-qiskit wraps Qiskit's own synthesis passes, so the same input always gives the same output.
hf sends only the flagged region of a circuit to four pinned open-weight models through Hugging Face Inference Providers: gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Coder-30B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and gpt-oss-20b. Replies must be strict JSON at temperature 0, within call and cost budgets.

AMD: we built Qiskit Aer for ROCm on a Radeon PRO W7900. qscore bench measured statevector simulation at 6.7× faster than the CPU at 28 qubits in double precision.

Platform: an always-on Vultr server running Docker Compose. Caddy serves the web app over HTTPS and forwards /api to a FastAPI service backed by a durable SQLite job queue. Workers pull jobs over HTTPS, so no machine ever has to accept inbound connections.

GitHub review bot:

A GitHub Action scores the base and head of a pull request inside the repository's own CI, so repository code never runs on our servers.
A GitHub App checks the results' checksums and provenance, then posts one summary and a check.
Gemini, opt-in, adds line comments that must cite recorded evidence. Every number comes from the engine, never the model.

Frontend: React, Vite and TypeScript, designed in Paper and built screen by screen to match the designs.

CI/CD: GitHub Actions runs linting, type checks, import-layer checks and close to 1,000 tests on Python 3.11 and 3.12, plus the bot's own suite. It then deploys the exact tested commit to Vultr.

Challenges we ran into

Models can't do exact quantum bookkeeping. Across our evaluation runs, 102 of 104 AI-proposed rewrites were not equivalent to the original circuit. A typical mistake was adding gates to "convert" one gate into another without undoing them. The verifier caught every one. Getting replies parseable at all took its own work: reasoning models spent 4,000–6,000 tokens thinking before writing any JSON, and few-shot examples were what got invalid replies to zero for three of the four models.
Qiskit is already very good at small regions. The regions our diagnostics flag are usually 2–6 two-qubit gates, where Qiskit's synthesis is near-optimal. Commutation-aware routing made one circuit 35% worse, so we dropped it. IBM's RL synthesis models won big on synthetic circuits but found no gain on any of 68 QASMBench circuits.
Sandboxing differs by OS. Our builder sandbox caps memory with RLIMIT_AS, which macOS rejects, so circuits built from Python code need Linux, and CI runs there. We kept the limit rather than weakening it.
Qiskit edge cases. Classical control hidden inside nested gate definitions slipped past validation until we walked definitions recursively.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The scoring engine works end to end. It finds circuits from just a repository link or path, scores them on 20 metrics and pinpoints where the cost comes from. It has scored 119 circuits from QASMBench and MQT Bench, two widely used open-source benchmark suites.
A real, verified improvement. The deterministic layer cut QASMBench's fredkin_n3 from 12 to 10 two-qubit gates (−17%). It's proven equivalent and reproduces on 20 fresh seeds.
Zero false improvements. Every wrong AI rewrite was caught, and the engine never claims a gain it can't justify.
The GitHub bot works on real pull requests. On a demo PR, it caught a change that took a circuit from 1 to 6 two-qubit gates and added a SWAP. It failed the regression check and posted a Gemini review comment citing the evidence.
The research platform turns Gatesmith from a standalone tool into the start of a Rosetta-esque suite.

What we learned

Creating deterministic diagnostic tools is harder than it looks, especially for a team entirely new to quantum circuits and quantum computing. This project was a chance to really learn the field and where it's heading. Funnily enough, some of the repositories we looked at were bioinformatics projects. One of our example circuits is a QAOA circuit for protein side-chain packing, because quantum algorithms could speed up searching that enormous conformational space.

The improvement loop was less straightforward than we expected. To show meaningful improvements, we'd need many examples of badly written circuits that can't be fixed deterministically, since the goal is to let any AI improvement layer slot in, as is common in current pipelines. That isn't an inherent limitation, just a matter of scope for 36 hours.

What's next for Gatesmith

Deeper AMD ROCm acceleration. We've laid groundwork for ROCm acceleration and want to push it much further. We chose AMD because ROCm is open source end to end, the same openness we want for quantum research.
Circuit maps, not just single circuits. Researchers' repositories hold many circuits, often nested inside one another. We want to score the whole map and use AMD hardware to run many more optimizations. That would show how optimizing one circuit affects the rest, and which circuits to target first.
A graph learning layer that screens out noisy candidates during optimization to speed up processing, once we've assembled the training data.
The full multi-round loop, GPU verification on the W7900 and an open leaderboard on Hugging Face that ranks models by verified-improvement rate under identical budgets.
More frameworks, starting with Cirq and PennyLane.

title: UltraFit
text:
Notifications

Loading...

UltraFit

When working out most people have difficulty on ensuring that they perform the exercise with the right pose or right angle. Well look no further with this app that can easily help you correct that. 

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Our main inspiration for this project came from when we faced the issue of when we began to notice people around in social media or even in our own gyms who wanted to perform an exercise but weren't informed on how to maintain the correct posture or form. Most people work out or practice a sport without anyone watching their movement, and it’s hard to know what your body is actually doing. We wanted a simple tool anyone could use with just a phone video.

What it does

UltraFit is an AI-assisted web app that estimates your exercise form from a video. You choose an exercise (squats), upload a short video, and the app detects your body and measures the angles of your knees or elbows. It shows the smallest, largest, and average angle, a chart of the angle over time, and a frame with your detected body points drawn on it, along with general practice reminders. It also states its limits plainly. The app gives estimates only, can’t guarantee correct form, and can’t diagnose injuries.

How we built it

We built it in Python, with Streamlit for the website, MediaPipe to detect 33 body landmarks in each video frame, and OpenCV to read and process the video. For each joint, we take three body points (for example hip, knee, and ankle) and use basic trigonometry to calculate the angle at the middle point. We skip any frames where the AI isn’t confident about a joint, so the app doesn’t guess. We split the code into three files (the website, the pose-detection logic, and the exercise information) so new exercises are easy to add. We stored the project on GitHub for collaboration.

Challenges we ran into

Getting set up: we hit errors using git in Windows PowerShell and worked around them by uploading through the GitHub website.
Version conflicts: the newest MediaPipe release removed the interface we were using, and MediaPipe doesn’t support the newest Python versions, so we had to pin specific package versions.
Pose detection isn’t perfect: results depend heavily on the camera angle, lighting, and whether the whole body is in view, so we had to handle missing or low-confidence detections gracefully.
Being honest about what AI can do: we had to design the app’s wording carefully so it gives measurements and reminders without claiming to judge form as “right” or “wrong.”

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We have a working prototype that goes from an uploaded video to real, measured joint angles.
We tested the angle math and the video pipeline, so it isn’t just a mockup.
We built the app with clear safety messaging from day one.
We’re beginner programmers, and we turned an idea into a working AI app.

What we learned

How pose-estimation models work, and how to turn their output into useful numbers.
How to use Streamlit, OpenCV, and MediaPipe together.
That real-world software needs careful handling of bad input, such as blurry video, hidden limbs, and no person in frame.
That collaboration tools like GitHub, virtual environments, and package versions matter as much as the code.
That responsible AI means being upfront about uncertainty.

What's next for UltraFit

Automatic rep counting from the angle data.
More measurements, such as hip and back angles.
A workout log and progress tracking over time.
Calorie estimates based on exercise type, duration, and body weight.
Exercise recommendations based on a user’s goals and preferences.
Putting it online so it works smoothly on phones anywhere.
