title: Spot-a-Vibe
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Spot-a-Vibe

Ever wonder what vibe you give off? Or are you looking for new music that suits you? Look no further than Spot-a-Vibe! Upload a photo of yourself and get a suggested genre that matches you!

Like

Comment

Inspiration

We wanted to create a fun and interactive way to combine artificial intelligence, computer vision, and music discovery. Since people often express themselves through their clothing and accessories, we wondered whether AI could use someone's visual style to guess their music taste.

That idea led to Spot-A-Vibe, a web application that turns a webcam snapshot into a personalized music vibe. Instead of answering a questionnaire, users simply step in front of their camera and let AI guess their musical identity. We wanted to make AI feel more approachable by turning it into an entertaining experience that could also help people discover new music.

What it does

Spot-A-Vibe uses a person's clothing and accessories to predict their music genre and sub-genre. When someone steps in front of the camera, the application detects their presence, starts a countdown, and captures a snapshot. Users can also capture a photo manually.

The AI predicts one of nine music genres: Pop, Rock, Metal, Rap, R&B, Country, Electronic, EDM, or Jazz. It then identifies a sub-genre within the predicted category, producing results such as Rap · Trap.

Users can view confidence scores and ranked probability breakdowns for all nine genres and the five sub-genres associated with their top result. If they connect their Spotify account, Spot-A-Vibe recommends songs that match their predicted vibe and allows them to save those recommendations as a Spotify playlist.

How we built it

We built Spot-A-Vibe using Python, Flask, JavaScript, and several machine learning technologies.

For person detection, we used OpenCV.js and a MobileNet-SSD object detector running in the browser. This allows the application to detect when someone enters the camera's view without continuously sending video frames to a server. Only captured snapshots are uploaded for genre analysis.

For music genre prediction, we integrated Cloudflare's Clef-Flash vision-language model. The model analyzes clothing and accessories through a multiple-choice classification process. We use two inference passes: the first predicts the most likely genre from nine options, and the second predicts a sub-genre from five options within the selected genre.

We developed the backend with Flask to process snapshots and return the model's predictions and probability scores. For deployment, we separated the web server from the GPU-powered Hugging Face Inference Endpoint, allowing the application to serve web requests without requiring a GPU on the web server itself.

Finally, we integrated the Spotify Web API to recommend songs based on the predicted genre and sub-genre probabilities. Users can connect their accounts, browse recommended tracks, and save their selections as private Spotify playlists.

Challenges we ran into

Integrating multiple technologies into one cohesive experience presented additional challenges. We needed browser-based person detection, automatic snapshots, model inference, confidence scores, Spotify authentication, and playlist creation to work together smoothly. We also had to account for camera permissions, Spotify redirect configuration, and the time required to initialize the model.

Another challenge was designing a meaningful classification system for something as subjective as music taste. Clothing does not reliably determine what someone listens to, so we approached the project as a playful AI prediction rather than a definitive assessment of a person's preferences. We also designed sub-genre descriptions to account for visual style as well as musical identity, helping the model make more specific predictions.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of turning an unconventional idea into a functional AI-powered music discovery experience. Spot-A-Vibe brings together computer vision, a vision-language model, a web backend, and a music streaming API in one application.

We are particularly proud of implementing automatic person detection and snapshot capture, making the experience interactive without requiring users to repeatedly operate the camera. We also went beyond a basic genre prediction by including sub-genre classification, probability breakdowns, and Spotify song recommendations.

Another accomplishment is our deployment architecture. By separating the lightweight web server from GPU-based inference, we made it possible to host the application without requiring dedicated GPU resources for every web request. Supporting scale-to-zero on the inference endpoint also helps limit GPU costs when the application is not being used.

What we learned

Building Spot-A-Vibe helped us gain practical experience integrating computer vision, multimodal AI, backend development, and third-party APIs. We learned how to use a pretrained vision-language model for classification, process model outputs into meaningful results, and connect those results to a music recommendation experience.

We also learned how important infrastructure decisions are when working with large AI models. Model size, startup time, GPU memory, and deployment costs all affect how an application performs in practice. Separating inference from the web server helped us better understand how AI applications can be structured for deployment.

Most importantly, we learned that building an AI-powered application involves more than getting a model to produce an answer. The surrounding interface, data flow, user experience, and limitations of the model are just as important in creating something useful and engaging.

What's next for Spot-A-Vibe

We want to continue improving Spot-A-Vibe's accuracy, usability, and music discovery features. One area we would like to explore is expanding the range of visual styles and sub-genres the application can recognize while refining the prompts and classification process.

We would also like to improve the recommendation system by offering more diverse song selections and giving users greater control over the music that ends up in their playlists. Additional features could include saving past vibe results, comparing predictions across different outfits, and sharing results with friends.

Ultimately, we want to keep experimenting with ways to make AI-powered music discovery more interactive, personalized, and fun. Spot-A-Vibe is a starting point for exploring how visual AI can connect self-expression with music in unexpected ways.

Dottie

An interactive, multi-modal braille learning system that helps young, blind learners build literacy through touch, voice, and storytelling.

Inspiration

National Braille Press reports that only 10% of blind schoolchildren receive Braille instruction. Learning Braille can help children build literacy, confidence, and independence, yet access to equipment and teaching support remains a barrier. Source We wanted to make learning Braille more accessible and playful by connecting the letters children feel to everyday objects and stories, with guidance that adapts as they learn.

What it does

Dottie is an interactive, multi-modal braille learning system designed to help blind learners build literacy. It combines a refreshable braille character with voice-based interaction, intelligent storytelling, word-reading exercises, a camera, and a web component to create an engaging, interactive learning experience.

How we built it

Challenges we ran into

Learning Hardware from Scratch: All of us were first-timers with CAD, 3D printing, and servo power requirements. Building a compact Braille cell meant thinking about printed tolerances, moving parts, and electronics together.
Connecting the Pieces: Object recognition, Braille translation, and Arduino control each had to agree on what to send and when. We needed clear boundaries between software commands and actual device acknowledgements.
Making Personalization Useful: Databricks was new to us, but connecting services was only part of the challenge. We also needed learner insights to be grounded in confirmed observations and give instructors something actionable.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Turning an Idea into a Physical Prototype: We designed a six-dot Braille mechanism, built its firmware, and developed an object-to-Braille software pipeline while learning the tools along the way.
Connecting Braille to Everyday Curiosity: We brought objects, stories, and practice into one learning experience, giving children more ways to connect letters with things they care about.
Building Beyond a Chatbot: Our companion combines learner evidence, cited research, and evaluated teaching proposals. We’re proud of building the foundations for personalization while keeping confirmed observations separate from AI guesses.

What we learned

Physical Design Changes Everything: A mechanism that looks right in CAD still needs testing for fit, friction, power, and movement.
Structured Outputs Matter: AI proposals need clear schemas and validation before they become app actions or hardware commands.
Personalization Starts with Evidence: A transcript or a correct answer alone does not establish mastery. Useful guidance needs context and traceable observations.
Research Needs Review: Retrieving a passage does not make it approved teaching advice. Citations and review status matter.
Accessibility Shapes the Whole Experience: Tactile feedback, spoken instructions, pacing, and navigation all need to work together.

What's next for Magneto

Immediate Roadmap (Next 3 Months)

Validate the six-dot cell: Print and assemble the mechanism, calibrate each servo, and test dot spacing, reading comfort, power requirements, and repeated movement.
Complete object-to-Braille interaction: Connect the cane camera, Jetson Nano, and Arduino so a selected object is spoken aloud and spelled on the cell, with device acknowledgements and retry handling.
Connect personalized teaching: Supply confirmed learner profiles and approved research to the teaching planner. Activate evaluated prompts through MLflow Prompt Registry.
Test with educators and families: Work with Braille instructors and blind or low-vision children to review tactile readability, spoken instructions, pacing, and navigation.

Long-term Vision (Next Year)

Build a multi-cell prototype: Move from one-letter presentation to short words, testing the eight-cell design for reliability and reading comfort.
Expand the curriculum: Add numbers, punctuation, and instructor-reviewed activities that progress from letter recognition to reading words.
Evaluate learning over time: Study retention and independent reading with educators, then use reviewed examples to improve teaching prompts.
Make the hardware reproducible: Publish tested CAD, firmware, wiring, and assembly instructions with a measured bill of materials, so others can build and improve Magneto.

text:

Hold Short

An air traffic control safety enhancement software suite. Includes, MAPF route pathfinding, a controller fatigue monitor, and incident avoidance. 

Like
1

Comment

Home Page

Simulation Page

GIF

Demonstration GIF

Drowsiness Monitor

Monitor Awake

Monitor Drowsy

Inspiration

Air traffic control is an incredibly demanding responsibility, requiring controllers to make quick decisions while managing dozens of moving aircraft, changing runway conditions, and the constant possibility of human error. Even a small mistake in communication or ground routing can lead to significant delays or dangerous runway incursions. We wanted to explore how artificial intelligence and modern software could help air traffic controllers make safer, more informed decisions while reducing the mental workload associated with managing busy airports.

This inspired us to create Hold Short, an interactive airport ground-control simulator that demonstrates how intelligent routing, real-time conflict detection, and controller monitoring can work together to improve aviation safety. Rather than building a purely automated system, we wanted to place users in the controller's position, allowing them to interact with aircraft, make routing decisions, and experience firsthand how difficult managing airport ground traffic can be.

What it does

Hold Short is an interactive, AI-assisted airport ground-control simulator built around a digital representation of Newark Liberty International Airport (KEWR). The simulator dynamically introduces aircraft into the airport environment, calculates taxi routes, and tracks their movement across a network of real airport taxiways. Users can observe aircraft moving throughout the airport, intervene in routing decisions, and issue commands to manage traffic.

One of Hold Short's central features is its ability to detect potentially dangerous situations, including aircraft separation conflicts and runway incursions. The system analyzes aircraft and vehicle movements to identify hazards and support timely controller intervention. Our project also explores incorporating fatigue detection to monitor controller attentiveness and adjust the urgency of warnings accordingly.

Through interactive gameplay, Hold Short aims to demonstrate both the complexity of ground-control operations and the potential for intelligent software to assist human decision-making.

How we built it

We developed Hold Short using a full-stack architecture with React and TypeScript on the frontend and Python with FastAPI on the backend. The frontend provides an interactive airport visualization, displaying aircraft positions, taxiway routes, and simulation information. Communication between the two systems uses WebSockets, allowing the interface to receive continuously updated aircraft positions and game-state information.

For the simulation environment, we constructed a connected representation of Newark Liberty International Airport using real-world OpenStreetMap geographic data. Airport taxiways are represented as a graph of nodes and edges, allowing the backend to calculate paths between different locations. We implemented A* pathfinding alongside more advanced space-time routing and reservation systems to support aircraft movement and account for shared taxiway resources.

Our backend manages aircraft spawning, movement, route assignment, runway scheduling, and conflict detection. The simulator updates continuously, tracking aircraft as they travel through the airport and checking for potential safety hazards. We also structured the project to support historical taxiway data analysis, fatigue detection, and additional AI-assisted functionality.

Challenges we ran into

One of our biggest challenges was translating real-world airport infrastructure into a usable simulation environment. Airport taxiways are much more complex than simple paths between points, and we needed to ensure that the graph used for routing matched the airport layout displayed on the frontend. Maintaining consistent geographic identifiers between the backend and visualization was essential to prevent aircraft from appearing in incorrect locations or following invalid routes.

Another major challenge involved coordinating multiple moving aircraft while accounting for shared taxiways, runway access, and potential conflicts. It wasn't enough to find the shortest route between two locations; our routing and simulation systems also needed to consider when different aircraft would occupy specific segments of the airport.

We also encountered challenges integrating separately developed frontend and backend components. Working across different GitHub branches introduced merge conflicts involving dependencies, configuration files, and API functionality. Resolving these issues required us to establish consistent data structures, clarify which components each team member was responsible for, and ensure that changes to one part of the application didn't break another.

Finally, the limited timeframe of a hackathon required us to carefully balance technical ambition with having a stable, demonstrable application.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

One of our proudest accomplishments was transforming real geographic airport data into a functioning, interactive ground-control simulation. Rather than relying on a completely fictional airport layout, we developed a system that represents actual taxiway connections and allows aircraft to navigate through them.

We're particularly proud of implementing an integrated backend capable of automatically spawning aircraft, assigning routes, updating their positions, and detecting potential conflicts as the simulation progresses. Seeing aircraft move across the frontend's airport map using routes generated by our own algorithms was an important milestone because it demonstrated that our routing, simulation, and visualization systems could operate together.

Another accomplishment was designing Hold Short around meaningful user interaction. Instead of simply displaying aircraft movements, we wanted users to participate in managing airport traffic and understand how their decisions could affect operational safety. This helped transform a technically complex simulation into a project that could communicate its purpose through an engaging, hands-on experience.

What we learned

Developing Hold Short gave us valuable experience working with graph algorithms, real-time simulations, geographic data, and full-stack software integration. We learned how to represent a complex physical environment as a connected graph, apply pathfinding algorithms to real-world routing problems, and synchronize continuously changing backend data with an interactive frontend.

We also gained a greater appreciation for the complexity of airport ground operations. What initially appeared to be a straightforward routing problem quickly became much more challenging when considering multiple aircraft, runway restrictions, scheduling, and conflict prevention. This reinforced the importance of combining efficient algorithms with carefully designed simulation rules.

From a software engineering perspective, we learned the importance of modular architecture, consistent API contracts, collaborative Git workflows, and thorough testing. With different team members working on interconnected parts of the project, communication and integration became just as important as the individual components we developed.

What's next for Hold Short

Looking ahead, we want to expand Hold Short into a more sophisticated and realistic air traffic control training environment. One of our primary goals is to further develop our AI-assisted routing capabilities using historical aircraft movement data, allowing the system to make increasingly informed predictions about taxi times, congestion, and potential conflicts.

We also want to expand the simulator's interactive features, including more detailed vehicle controls, runway-incursion challenges, and scoring systems that compare human controller decisions against automated routing. Improving conflict alerts with natural-language explanations, voice notifications, and predicted time-to-conflict information would make the experience more immersive and educational.

Other potential improvements include integrating speech recognition for spoken ATC clearances, expanding fatigue detection and controller monitoring, and supporting additional airports and traffic scenarios.

Ultimately, we envision Hold Short as more than a hackathon demonstration. We want it to serve as a foundation for exploring how artificial intelligence, human-centered design, and interactive simulations can work together to make aviation operations safer and more efficient.

CrowdSense

CrowdSense uses two cameras, one on you and one on the room, and tells you mid-talk when you're starting to lose people. Afterward, you get a replay and tips on what to work on next time.

Like

Comment

Homepage

Description

Video Analysis

Video Report

Audience Reaction

Inspiration

Presenters can't see themselves, and they can't watch the whole room while they talk. Feedback usually comes too late (a survey a week later) and is too vague to act on ("it felt a bit long"). By the time you find out you lost the back row, the talk is over.

This hits hardest for students rehearsing class talks and pitches alone, for lecturers who don't notice one side of the hall drifting, and for non-native or anxious speakers who speed up, say "um" and stare at their notes. We wanted feedback that arrives during the talk, based on measurements, with a clear reason for each nudge and privacy built in.

What it does

CrowdSense coaches you live using two cameras: one points at you and one points at your audience.

Presenter camera: tracks your posture, swaying, fidgeting, eye contact, volume, speaking pace and filler words. It compares each one to your own baseline, which it records in a 15-second calibration.
Audience camera: turns every face into an anonymous dot on a room map. It estimates engagement from head pose and spots when one side of the room is drifting or people are looking down.
Audience phones: people scan a QR code to tap Lost me, Too fast, Love this or Question without giving their name.
Confidence Monitor: shows one quiet nudge at a time, with the reason behind it, for example "The right side is drifting. Look over there.", "Speak up." or "You've been looking at your screen for 40s."
After the talk: you get a report with a delivery score, "lost moments" on a timeline showing what you were saying at the time, AI coaching tied to exact timestamps, a comparison with your last session, and a replay where both videos and the transcript stay in sync.
Practice Mode: a virtual audience that reacts to your delivery, so you can rehearse alone.
All video analysis runs in the browser. Only anonymous numbers leave the device, and recording is off unless you turn it on.

How we built it

Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite. Each device (presenter camera, audience camera, dashboard, monitor, phone) is just a browser page connected by WebSockets.
Computer vision in the browser:
MediaPipe Pose and Face Landmarker for the presenter.
For the audience, OpenCV's YuNet face detector (from Hugging Face) running on ONNX Runtime Web, followed by Face Landmarker on each face crop to get head pose and facial movement.
Speech: Whisper runs on our server through Hugging Face Transformers.js. Hugging Face Inference Providers (Whisper Large v3) can be used instead, with local Whisper as the fallback.
Backend: Node, Express and ws. Each live session runs as a room that updates once per second. It merges the signals, runs a shared nudge engine and a lost-moment detector, and scores the delivery. The browser and the server use the same TypeScript code for thresholds and scoring.
Data:
Neon Postgres stores sessions, metrics, transcripts, reactions and coaching tips.
Opt-in recordings upload straight from each camera to AWS S3 in parts, using presigned links. ffmpeg then fixes the files so the replay can skip around.
AI: Gemini writes the coaching report from the metrics, lost moments, transcript and past sessions. Gemini can also review a lost moment using a frame of the presenter (never the audience). An earlier version used Claude on Amazon Bedrock.
Accounts and hosting: Amazon Cognito sign-in with a private video library. The app is deployed on AWS Lightsail behind CloudFront.
No keys needed: every integration falls back to something that works without setup, such as local JSON storage, local disk, browser speech or rule-based coaching. That means npm run dev works out of the box.

Challenges we ran into

Faces in a real room are small. MediaPipe's face detector found only 3 of 29 people in a group photo. YuNet found all 29.
Whisper cleans up speech too well. It strips out "um" and "uh", which are exactly what we needed to count. We had to prompt the decoder with filler-heavy text so it keeps them.
Phone cameras need HTTPS. Browsers only allow camera access on secure pages, so getting phones on a local network, WSL and tunnels working took real effort.
Keeping devices in sync. Clock sync between nodes, and replaying two recordings next to a transcript without drift, needed careful timing.
Browser recordings couldn't skip. WebM files from MediaRecorder don't support seeking until ffmpeg reprocesses them.
Too many nudges. A coach that talks constantly is worse than no coach. We added cooldowns, a gap between nudges and a priority order, so only one nudge shows at a time.
AI reliability. We switched AI providers more than once, and had to handle timeouts and failed regenerations without wiping a report that was already fine.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

All video analysis runs on the user's device. There's no face recognition, no stored identities, and the audience preview is blurred by default.
Every nudge shows the measurement that triggered it, so the coaching never feels like a black box.
Small faces across a room actually get detected, and filler words actually get counted.
The whole app runs with zero API keys, and turns on more features as you add them.
It's built end to end and deployed: live session, report, synced replay, practice mode and accounts.
What we learned
Calibrating to each person beats fixed thresholds. "Slouching" means something different for everyone.
A small, well-timed nudge helps more than a dashboard full of numbers while you're speaking.
Head pose tells you about room-level engagement trends, not what one person is feeling. We learned to say so clearly.
Designing for privacy from the start (consent screens, recording indicators, anonymous metrics) shaped the architecture for the better.
Having a fallback for every external service made the project much easier to demo and to work on as a team.

What's next for CrowdSense

Better engagement estimates in large or poorly lit rooms, and tracking that survives people changing seats.
Lower-latency transcription, and support for more languages and accents.
Practice Mode audiences tuned to specific settings: a lecture, a pitch, a thesis defense.
Progress tracking across many sessions, plus drills aimed at each person's weakest skill.
Sharing a session with a teacher or mentor so they can comment on the replay.
A mobile-first setup that needs just one phone on a stand.

title: Accessibility Audit
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Accessibility Audit

A quick and easy way to ensure your website is accessible.

Like

Comment

Shows empty homepage

Shows the process of entering a website and processing

shows the empty results panel

shows the empty AI chat box

shows highlighted problems on mobile

shows highlighted problems on desktop

shows no problems on mobile

shows no problems on desktop

shows no problems on desktop

Shows formatted chat response

Inspiration

Most developers know WCAG exists, but it’s often hard to tell what a rule means for their own code. We wanted to close that gap with an accessibility auditor that helps developers understand these standards and apply them to make their sites more accessible. We also wanted developers to be able to learn from other websites by seeing how they handle accessibility, both the good and the bad.

What it does

Accessibility Audit scans any public website against WCAG 2.2 A/AA standards on both desktop and mobile layouts. It shows what’s broken directly on screenshots of the site, with numbered, color-coded highlights by severity. A built-in AI assistant, powered by Hugging Face, explains each issue in plain language and suggests fixes.

How we built it

Frontend: React and Vite, with a results panel, a screenshot viewer, and a chat panel.
Backend: FastAPI, which runs the scan and serves the screenshots.
Scanning: Playwright opens each site in a headless browser at desktop and mobile sizes. The open-source axe-core engine then checks the page against WCAG rules.
Visual highlights: we find where each problem element sits on the page and draw numbered outlines on a screenshot, colored by severity.
AI assistant: a FastAPI endpoint sends a scan summary to a model via Hugging Face Inference, so users can ask questions about their results.

Challenges we ran into

At the very beginning, we struggled to come up with a concept for our project that could be reasonably done within the short time-frame of the hackathon event. Additionally, it had to fit our capabilities as a mostly new developer team. So we had to keep things manageable. Following our decision on what our project was going to be, we ran into multiple issues using git. Most of these from our branches not getting updated from main properly when doing merges. We landed on using the GitHub desktop application to have a cleaner interface to work through our problems which helped us greatly. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud to have a working end-to-end flow: paste a URL, then get visual, annotated results for desktop and mobile. We are also proud to have found a way to turn abstract WCAG rules into something you can see on the page, and to include an AI assistant that makes accessibility approachable for developers who aren’t experts. Learning responsive sizing in front-end development, so the tool itself works across screen sizes, was also a highlight of this project.

What we learned

We learned how to connect a FastAPI backend to a Hugging Face AI chatbot and how React manages frontend components and state. We also learned a lot about WCAG, including that automated tools only catch part of the problems. A clean scan doesn’t mean a site is fully accessible, which is why we include a disclaimer on every report.

What's next for Accessibility Audit

Authenticated pages: scanning sites that require a login, such as Canvas for UCF students or a Facebook feed.
Scan history: saving scans so teams can track fixes and catch accessibility regressions over time.
Full-site crawling: auditing every page of a site, not just one.
Accessibility scores and dashboards: showing progress at a glance.
Site comparison: comparing two sites side by side to learn from how others handle accessibility.

title: KnightMaps
text:
Notifications

Loading...

KnightMaps

KnightMaps brings navigation indoors, using Wi-Fi signals to locate you and guide you to classrooms and campus resources—so you spend less time lost and more time where you need to be.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Navigating campus buildings and finding specific classrooms on time has always been a frustrating challenge for the incoming freshmen. Standard map applications completely lack indoor floor plans, turning a simple walk to class into a guessing game. Trying to locate a room like ENG 107 becomes an uphill battle when rooms 105 and 106 are mysteriously located on the complete opposite side of the building. We built KnightMaps to solve this campus navigation problem once and for all.

What it does

KnightMaps is an advanced indoor and outdoor hybrid navigation system designed to help students seamlessly navigate campus buildings and classrooms. It tracks the user's real-time position across both environments, providing turn-by-turn indoor routing, room search, voice guidance, and different localization systems depending on if you are inside or outside a building.

How we built it

We engineered a robust hybrid architecture combining backend intelligence with a custom mobile application:

Localization via Nearest Router (LVNR): We captured and stored RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator) and BSSID data points across key building nodes. Using a k-nearest neighbors (KNN) algorithm with a weighted average of the top three matches, boosted by device accelerometer data for dead reckoning, we achieve smooth, accurate indoor tracking.
Visual Place Recognition (VPR): Powered by computer vision and a VLAD (Arandjelović et al., Keetha et al.) aggregator (vpr/ network.py), the system recognizes locations to assist with exterior and hybrid positioning.
Backend & Frontend Stack: Built with a Flask backend (app.py) for localization and routing logic, paired with an Android app built using Capacitor, Vite, and custom native Java plugins (WifiScanPlugin.java) to handle Wi-Fi scanning, step-counting, compass tracking, and GPS.

Challenges we ran into

Distorted Floor Plans: The floor plan section we chose was unfortunately not drawn to scale and featured significant spatial distortions. This led to initial localization errors where the model miscalculated the user's relative position inside the building.
Server Latency: Relying on a local server for computation initially hampered our ability to process and stream locational data quickly. We had to optimize our data structures and scanning logic to ensure smooth performance.
Domain Gap: Our initial dataset for VPR consisted of google maps street view, however the cameras used were extremely different from the camera of a regular phone which caused lots of errors. We solved this by going outside and collecting our own data.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Successfully designing and executing a functional hybrid indoor/outdoor localization pipeline (LVNR + VPR) from scratch.
Building a working proof-of-concept Android app that bridges native hardware sensors (Wi-Fi, accelerometer, compass) with a clean, interactive floor plan interface.

What we learned

Deep practical knowledge of how Wi-Fi fingerprinting and RSSI datasets can be leveraged for indoor positioning.
Real-world experience integrating hardware sensor data with software algorithms for dead reckoning.
Valuable troubleshooting skills in handling spatial assumption errors and optimizing local computation latency.

What's next for KnightMaps

We are working on scaling the architecture, getting rid of errors in localization, optimizing server performance and cloud integration, with the ultimate goal of allowing universities and communities worldwide to deploy KnightMaps for their own local campuses.

title: OmniBelt
text:
Notifications

Loading...

OmniBelt

What if seeing for the blind is as easy as feeling it?

Like

Comment

Omni Belt is a wearable guide for blind and low-vision people: a belt that buzzes you toward where to walk, a ring that guides your hand to what you're reaching for, and a memory that knows where you left your things.

Say "Belt, find my keys." The belt turns you toward them and steers you around anything in the way. At arm's length, a ring on your finger takes over and pulses faster as your hand closes in. Set them down, walk away, and later ask "Belt, where did I leave my keys?" It tells you where they are, then offers to take you there.

Inspiration

A white cane is great at the ground right in front of you. It tells you nothing about the table edge at hip height, the open cabinet door at head height, or the chair someone pushed out two meters ahead. And once a blind person sets down their keys or wallet, finding them again means sweeping their hands across every nearby surface.

We split the problem the way the body already does: the belt tells you where to walk; the ring tells you where to reach. Seven vibration motors around the waist steer you like a compass you can feel. One motor on your finger guides your hand the last half meter to the object.

Our guiding rule: the AI decides where; the reflexes decide how. A cloud model may choose the goal, but it never touches a motor. Everything safety-critical runs locally, on the belt.

What it does

Say
What happens

"Belt, find my wallet."
Finds it, walks you there around obstacles, then hands over to the ring at arm's length. The ring pulses faster as your hand gets closer and gives a solid buzz when you're on it.

"Belt, where did I leave my keys?"
Answers from memory ("on the table behind you, to your right, about 2 meters away"), then asks "Want me to take you there?"

"This is my wallet."
Hold it up and the belt learns your wallet, not just any wallet.

"Belt, find me a seat."
Finds a chair nobody is sitting in and walks you to it.

"Belt, take me to the door."
Walks you to the nearest door and buzzes when you arrive.

"Belt, what's in front of me?"
A short spoken description, obstacles first.

Walk mode
Dodges obstacles from ankle to head height in real time, fully offline.

"Stop."
Stops everything, any time.

How we built it

iPhone 17 (eyes + ears) ──WebSocket──▶ Jetson Orin Nano Super (reflexes) ──USB serial──▶ ESP32 + ULN2803 (muscles) ──▶ 7 belt motors + ring
│
▼
Gemini (understand · find · describe) · ElevenLabs (voice)

Phone: eyes and ears. An iPhone 17 at the wearer's navel streams camera frames, the ARKit camera pose and intrinsics, ARKit feature points, and Apple Vision hand keypoints over a WebSocket. It listens for the wake word "Belt" and speaks every reply in an ElevenLabs voice.

Jetson Orin Nano Super: reflexes. Every model runs on the belt, each in its own thread:

YOLO11n (TensorRT) with ByteTrack for people and everyday objects
Depth Anything V2 Small (metric, indoor) for per-pixel distance. We have no LiDAR.
YOLO-World (small), an open-vocabulary detector, for finding things by name. Gemini steps in when it misses something, and for unusual descriptions like "the green dino on the desk".

ESP32: muscles. A small line protocol (M 3 70 P4, SWEEP, ARRIVE) drives a ULN2803 low-side driver. The firmware enforces its own safety limits: at most 3 motors at once, and everything stops if the Orin goes quiet for 500 ms.

Hardware. We designed the 3D-printed motor pods, Orin tray, hub, phone cradle and a swappable-size ring in code with manifold3d, so changing a part is one parameter and a re-export.

From depth to obstacles

For a pixel at row \( v \) with metric depth \( d \), camera pitch \( p \), focal length \( f_y \), principal point \( c_y \) and lens height \( h_{cam} \), exact pinhole geometry gives that point's height above the floor and its level distance ahead:

$$h = h_{cam} + d\left(\sin p + \frac{c_y - v}{f_y}\cos p\right), \qquad x = d\left(\cos p - \frac{c_y - v}{f_y}\sin p\right)$$

A point only counts as an obstacle if \( 0.15\,\text{m} < h < 1.9\,\text{m} \), so the floor never becomes a wall. We split the view into 16 sectors and take a low percentile of \( x \) in each. A sector is blocked if anything in it is closer than 1 m. Because monocular depth drifts in scale, we re-scale it every frame against ARKit feature points, or against the known floor height.

Mapping and planning

Depth rays plus the ARKit pose feed a 12 m × 12 m occupancy grid with 15 cm cells. Old evidence decays, so things that move away fade from the map. A* plans around everything on the map, including obstacles that have left the camera's view. Each step costs extra near walls, which keeps routes centred:

$$c(\text{step}) = w \cdot \bigl(1 + 3\max(0,\; 0.8 - \text{clearance})\bigr), \qquad w \in {1, \sqrt{2}}$$

Steering follows the route toward a point 0.8 m ahead. A reactive dodge layer still checks every frame, picks the open sector closest to that heading, and buzzes the nearest motor. Pulses speed up from 2 Hz to 7 Hz as things get closer.

Finding, remembering, reaching

One fixed vocabulary. Our demo items plus look-alikes ("phone", "credit card", "remote"). If something is more confidently a phone, it isn't your wallet.
3-of-5 agreement. A new location needs 3 of the last 5 sightings to agree, checked in world space so it still holds while you walk.
Small items. When nothing is found, the belt takes a zoomed second look at the lower frame and the horizon band.
Your things. "This is my wallet" saves image embeddings (CLIP) of your item. Later finds are ranked by how much they look like it.
Memory. Every sighting is stored in world coordinates. Each item keeps a weighted-median track, so one bad detection can't move your keys across the room, and a real move is detected after two sightings.
Reach. Within arm's length, or when your hand appears next to the item, the belt hands over to the ring.

Challenges we ran into

Frame rate on an 8 GB edge device. Profiling showed the Hugging Face depth pipeline took 110 ms per call, because it quietly upscaled our 320×240 input to 518 px. Calling the model directly in fp16 took 33 ms. YOLO-World spent 215 ms re-encoding text every time we switched between "find the target" and "scan for memory". The fix was one fixed vocabulary, a separate thread for each model, and TensorRT for YOLO11n.
"Wallet" kept turning into "phone." Open-vocabulary detectors confuse look-alikes, so we put the look-alikes into the vocabulary on purpose, and require several sightings to agree before trusting a new location.
Reach only triggered when you were standing on top of the item. Scale drift in monocular depth made everything look farther away. Per-frame re-scaling and measuring to the item's near surface fixed it.
Memory limits. Loading a bigger detector next to depth, tracking and CLIP ran the 8 GB board out of memory. We kept the small YOLO-World, load models one at a time, and guard every optional model with a free-memory check.
A motor right behind the camera. The navel motor sits in the phone cradle, so it can shake ARKit tracking. We watch fps and the map while it buzzes, and have a foam-pad fallback ready.
Free-tier API quotas. We split Gemini into a smart tier for what the user asks and a light tier for background work, with per-minute budgets, so the demo can't die halfway through.
Physical layout. Checking the CAD widths showed the battery and Orin trays overlap on any waist under about 110 cm at our planned spacing, so we moved the electronics to sit together along the spine.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A complete wearable built in one weekend: custom firmware, code-generated CAD, an iOS app, an edge-AI server and a live judge dashboard.
Navigation that keeps working with the Wi-Fi off. The cloud only adds understanding and voice.
A ring that solves the "last meter", and a memory that answers "where did I leave it?"

What we learned

Profile before you optimize. Our biggest bottleneck was a library default we never asked for.
Geometry beats guessing. Exact pinhole maths and ARKit's pose made the difference between a belt that buzzes at the floor and one that buzzes at the table.
Keep the LLM out of the control loop. Gemini chooses goals; local code owns every motor command. That kept the system safe, fast, and working offline.
Haptics need to be unmistakable, not subtle. Small steering corrections felt like noise. Exaggerating dodges into a clear 45° side cue made them readable.
Edge AI is a systems problem. Threads, memory, power modes, quotas, serial resets and thermal limits mattered as much as the models did.

What's next

Testing with blind and low-vision users, a lighter belt with fewer separate parts, stair and curb detection, and running the language model on-device so the whole system works offline.

title: StormBox
text:
Notifications

Loading...

StormBox

When cell towers fail, StormBox stays alert. This offline hurricane safety box detects home hazards, tracks NOAA storm data, and guides you through emergencies without internet or cell service.

Like
3

Comment

StormBox: an offline hurricane safety box. It watches your home and tells you what to do, with no internet needed.

The phone screen a family sees during a storm. One clear status and the most important instruction first.

Ask the box any safety question. A small AI runs fully offline and answers from trusted safety guides.

Replaying a real hurricane through the system. The risk score rises and alarms fire just like a live storm.

Tested on Hurricane Nicole, a storm the model never saw. The risk score warned hours before the storm’s closest point.

Our storm risk model, trained on NOAA hurricane data. You can see exactly why it makes each prediction.

The sensors and ESP32 inside the box. Alarms come from fixed rules, never from the AI.

Our wind speed sensor. It warns at 39 mph and alarms at hurricane force (74 mph).

Inspiration

Every Floridian knows the moment: the lights go out, the phone drops to one bar, then zero. After a major hurricane, power and cell service can be gone for days, exactly when families need information most. Is this calm the end of the storm, or the eye? Is water coming in while we sleep? Is it too hot to stay inside?

Every smart-home device and AI assistant goes silent the moment the internet does. We wanted the opposite: a device that gets more useful when everything else fails.

What it does

StormBox has three jobs: warn, guide, and help you last.

Senses the home: air pressure, wind speed (from an anemometer we built ourselves), indoor temperature and humidity, and floor water.
Sounds the alarm on its own: flood and heat alarms run on the microcontroller with a buzzer. If the hub dies, the box still alarms. The AI never decides an alarm.
Predicts the storm: a model trained on 20 years of real NOAA hurricane data gives an early-warning risk score. With pressure and wind, it caught every unseen test hurricane about 22 hours before closest approach.
Reads the storm's phase: falling pressure, a possible eye ("the calm is temporary, stay inside"), and recovery.
Talks you through it: an offline AI agent explains alarms out loud and answers questions by voice or chat from vetted guides (Ready.gov, CDC, NWS, EPA, FDA, Red Cross), always citing its source.
Knows what "hot" really means: the NWS heat index ("feels like 112°F, danger level") from indoor readings, which matters when the AC is out.
Replays real hurricanes: recorded NOAA data from Ian, Nicole, Idalia, Helene and Milton, with a live risk curve, a timeline you can speed up or rewind, and the decision path behind every score.

How we built it

Sense → Understand → Explain → Show. A self-contained sensor node keeps the house safe; an edge AI hub makes it smart.

The hardware node

An ESP32 reads a barometer, temperature/humidity sensor, floor-water sensor, and our homemade anemometer, which counts rotations with a Hall-effect sensor.
Alarm rules (with hysteresis so they don't flicker) and the buzzer run on the microcontroller, so safety never depends on anything else.
The node talks to the hub over Wi-Fi with MQTT (Mosquitto, with a "last will" so the hub knows instantly if the box dies), with USB serial as a fallback.

The edge hub

A Python service keeps the live box state, logs to SQLite, runs the storm logic and replay, and serves a FastAPI + WebSocket dashboard (family and engineer views). Every AI model runs locally, with no network calls.

Storm risk model on real NOAA data

Data: hourly pressure and wind from ~20 NOAA buoys and coastal stations around Florida (2005–2025), labeled with NOAA's HURDAT2 storm tracks: "a storm center passes within 150 km in the next 12 hours."
Honest testing: trained on 2005–2018, threshold tuned on 2019–2021 (at most one false alarm per week), tested on 2022–2025 hurricanes it never saw.
Explainable: we compared logistic regression with decision trees and shipped small depth-3 trees. They had far fewer false alarms, and the dashboard highlights the exact path behind every score.
Sensor failover: three trees (pressure, wind, both). The hub uses whichever matches the sensors still working.

Model

Pressure-only is our original model on all hours; the other two are compared on hours where both sensors had data. Each tree is ~3 KB and runs in microseconds.

The offline agent and RAG

Knowledge pack: 15 emergency guides written from Ready.gov, CDC, NWS, EPA, FDA, FoodSafety.gov, Florida Emergency Management and the Red Cross, with exact numbers kept (6 inches of moving water can knock you down; 8 drops of bleach per gallon). 71 sourced chunks.
Fastest path first: instant alarm explanations, then canned answers, then live sensor and storm tools, and only then RAG: the top guide passages (nomic-embed-text + ChromaDB) plus live readings go to a small local LLM (Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen3 0.6B fallback, via Ollama).
Guardrails: code routes questions, not the LLM. If no guide matches, it says "I'm not sure" instead of guessing. Every answer cites its source and every step is logged to a trace panel.

Voice

Speech recognition with Whisper (faster-whisper) and speech output with Piper, both fully offline. Every model on the box is an open-weight model from the Hugging Face Hub.

Challenges we ran into

Our Raspberry Pi died mid-build. We redesigned overnight into a distributed system: a wireless ESP32 sensor node plus an edge AI hub over MQTT. Because the AI layer was modular, almost none of it had to change.
**Our esp32 was faulty from the start - We replaced the the esp32 with an another model and redesign our pin layouts as well as features based on the capabilities of this new model.
A sensor went down, so we made the model survive it. When the barometer failed, we trained wind-based and combined models from the NOAA data and built automatic failover.
Barometers don't read what NOAA reports. NOAA uses sea-level pressure; a box on a table reads lower. Without calibration, the model would show storm risk on a sunny day.
Small models, real stakes. A 1B model

title: Spot-MIA
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Spot-MIA

An operator console for Boston Dynamics Spot that replays every inspection, surfaces hidden failures, and writes a checked plain-English brief.

Like
2

Comment

Inspiration

Boston Dynamics Spot robots walk inspection routes and report each mission as completed or failed. When we looked inside the data, 26 of 27 missions said completed, yet 21 of those had at least one failed inspection hidden inside. A status light that says "done" while a third of the checks failed doesn't earn an operator's trust. We wanted a tool that tells an operator what actually happened, where, and what to do next, without reading a log.

The name says it: things go MIA inside "completed" missions. Spot-MIA (Mission Intelligence Analysis) finds them.

What it does

Spot-MIA is an operator console for robot inspection missions.

Mission control: replay any mission on the facility map. The robot walks its route, each stop turns green or red, the battery drains toward a 30% danger line, and alerts stack up as failures and anomalies arrive.
Mission report: a headline ("7 of 10 actions succeeded") next to the robot's own COMPLETED stamp, a plain-English shift-log brief, one clear next step, and a ranked list of what needs a human.
Fleet trends: why missions fail, and whether performance is improving.

What we found in the data:

Completed doesn't mean it worked. 21 of 26 completed missions hid a failed action.
Battery is the biggest driver of failure. Below 30% battery only 49% of actions succeed, against 87% above it.
Low battery breaks sensors, not walking. 16 of 19 low-battery failures were sensor timeouts or unreliable readings. Navigation failures don't track battery at all.
V2's improvement is mostly battery. V2 raised success from 77% to 91%, but it also used half the battery per mission. At the same battery level, V1 and V2 perform about the same.
Problems hide behind successes. 8 anomalies sat on actions that reported success, including a critical abnormal temperature.

How we built it

Data pipeline: Python and pandas join missions, actions, readings, anomalies, locations and assets into one findings file. The dashboard only reads that file, and every number on screen has a note saying how it was computed.
Anomaly flags: each reading is compared against the normal range for its measurement type.
AI mission briefs: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, an open-weight model from Hugging Face, runs locally with transformers. Code builds a fact sheet for each mission, and the model only turns those facts into plain sentences.
Guardrails: about 20 checks in code reject any draft that adds a number or asset not in the facts, puts an asset in the wrong place, guesses a cause, adds an opinion, or flips above and below normal. Rejected drafts get one retry, then fall back to a template. 14 of 27 passed. The model never picks the next step and never grades its own work.
Front end: Streamlit and Plotly for the dashboard, plus an HTML and SVG reference console with an animated map replay.

Challenges we ran into

The small model made things up. It called a 52.9 dB reading "above normal" when normal is 72, and said the battery was "still sufficient". Instead of trusting it, we wrote checks for each kind of mistake and show the rejection count on screen.
Separating battery from configuration. V2 looked far better, but it also ran on fuller batteries and shorter missions. Comparing V1 and V2 at the same battery level showed the real story.
Incomplete event stream. The supplied replay file stops partway through mission M023, so we rebuilt the stream from the CSVs and checked it event by event against the original.
Running a model on a laptop CPU: version conflicts, a failed 3 GB download, and a nearly full disk, all solved in time for the briefs.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Finding that V2's gain is mostly a battery effect, instead of reporting the headline number.
An AI feature that can't show an operator a made-up fact.
A console where an operator learns what failed, where, and what to check next in under 20 seconds.

What we learned

Small language models are good at wording, not facts. Code should decide what's true and check every sentence.
The first comparison is usually confounded. Always ask what else changed at the same time.
A mission status is a receipt, not an inspection.

What's next for Spot-MIA

Ask SPOT: operators type a question like "what keeps going wrong at Turbine Hall?" and get an answer drawn only from mission records, with the records shown.
Launch alerts: warn before a mission starts below 70% battery.
Live data: connect to Spot's API in place of the synthetic files.

title: Farsight
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Farsight

Explore a building through a rescue rover: live camera and person detection, LiDAR-guided indoor autonomy, and a dense room you can walk through in VR.

Like

Comment

Demo video

Inspiration

A responder should be able to inspect an unfamiliar room before entering it.
We wanted more than remote steering on a small screen: a live view of the
rover's surroundings, help finding people, and spatial context that stays
available as the rover moves. VR telepresence and a measured room map bring
those views together. Our demonstration is a controlled indoor rescue scenario.

What it does

Farsight lets a responder explore a room from a Meta Quest instead of entering
it first. An ELEGOO rover carries a LiDAR iPhone and an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.
The headset shows the live camera: move the right joystick to drive, press A
for autonomous Explore, and press B to stop and return to MANUAL. In AUTO,
the joysticks move your viewpoint through the map while Nav2 navigates the rover.

YOLO11n-pose finds people and derives face boxes from head keypoints. The
mission report keeps encounter snapshots and draft SBAR notes. A responder can type on the laptop, or hold the left trigger in VR, to ask about the live view. Local
Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct answers, Whisper base.en transcribes, and Piper speaks
replies or preset survivor phrases in English and Spanish. The models run
locally; remote driving still needs the cellular link.

After the run, the Mac pulls the posed photos and measured LiDAR seed, then
trains a Gaussian-splat reconstruction with Brush on Metal. Walk the room in a
browser, replay the rover's route, or open the splat in the Quest. Dechante's
face-enabled browser walkthrough puts red dots on the minimap; clicking a face
jumps to its recorded viewpoint and opens the real camera frame with the face
boxed. These are observed face locations, so a moving person may leave more
than one spot.

How we built it

Swift and ARKit on the iPhone supply synchronized RGB, measured depth, camera
intrinsics, and poses. The Jetson runs the Python/FastAPI rover server,
YOLO11n-pose through TensorRT, Nav2 integration, and serial commands to the
Arduino Uno. Two phone bridges carry the cellular/Tailscale connection. The
Mac operator relay serves the TypeScript/Three.js/WebXR app to the Quest over
USB using ADB reverse.

Our local assistant uses Hugging Face model artifacts: Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct
GGUF with its vision projector through llama.cpp, Whisper base.en through
whisper.cpp, and Piper voices. The same vision-language service drafts SBAR
notes from encounter crops and metadata.

The post-run pipeline selects a continuous drive, preserves its posed photos,
seeds Brush with measured LiDAR points, trains on the Mac GPU, and prunes the
output for Quest. A watcher waits for captures to stop changing before a
SSH pull. Face processing runs on the CPU alongside GPU training.
The browser walk combines the reconstructed room, recorded route, and face-pin
evidence. The immersive Quest splat page provides
stick walking and snap turns.

Challenges

We had to make camera streaming, perception, navigation, and motor control
share a small computer and an uneven cellular link. Mapping and reconstruction
also belong on different schedules: a detailed post-run room should not delay
the live camera or control path.

A convincing reconstruction needs coherent camera poses and useful views.
Parked stretches repeat images; malformed JPEGs can stop Brush; an oversized
LiDAR seed can make a short training budget much slower. Reducing splat count
for a headset can also introduce visible streaks even when the original
training score looks good.

We kept measured LiDAR, learned reconstruction, simulation, and replay distinct.
A face location is evidence of a sighting, not proof of a unique person, and a
model-generated note still needs a responder's judgment.

Accomplishments

Connected headset driving, live onboard perception, autonomous navigation,
and mission evidence in one search-and-rescue prototype.
Built a local vision/voice assistant with spoken answers and bilingual
survivor phrases on the rover's Jetson.
Turned real rover captures into walkable Gaussian-splat rooms with a Mac
pipeline based on Dechante's LiDAR-seeded Brush method.
Built a room and its face evidence in 114 seconds locally on an M5 Pro
from a saved 60-second / 119-photo capture sample. Brush took 112 seconds at
5,000 steps, with 62 seconds of CPU face processing in parallel. A 10-second
idle allowance and local-copy stand-in bring that to 124 seconds, excluding
real Jetson transfer and browser loading. The sample reuses a longer run's
LiDAR seed; it is not a live short-drive end-to-end timing.
Added a browser walkthrough that connects face pins to the original boxed
camera frames, making the room useful for reviewing what the rover saw.

What we learned

Give each device the work that fits it: the phone captures depth and pose,
the Jetson handles perception and navigation beside the motors, and the Mac
trains the post-run room. Capture quality and seed size matter as much as
training steps. Measure the final pruned viewer result as well as the training
score, and compare settings on the same held-out photos.

A useful search record connects a location to the actual observation. A red
pin becomes much more informative when it opens the camera frame that created
it. Keeping those links also makes it easier to spot duplicate sightings and
model mistakes.

What's next

Improve room quality within a predictable end-to-end build budget, including
transfer, face processing, and publication. Bring the browser's face-evidence
interaction into the immersive Quest viewer. Evaluate localization, detection,
and operator performance across repeated physical search-training runs, and
make multi-room review easier.

Sponsor tracks

Hugging Face — Best Use of Open Source AI: local vision, speech recognition,
and synthesis use Hugging Face-distributed models for a responder's workflow.
NVIDIA — Best Use of Jetson Nano: the Orin Nano runs onboard perception,
local AI, navigation integration, camera streaming, and motor control.
Encompass — Data Capturing Hardware: a rover-mounted LiDAR iPhone turns
synchronized real-world observations into encounter records and a 3D room.
Full Sail — Pathways & Perception: pathfinding, face detection, timed rescue
drill scoring, and room walkthroughs support a search-training scenario.

Team: Aziz Umarov, Saicharan Ramineni, Dechante (Chang), Mehdi Chraibi.

title: SocietySim
text:
Notifications

Loading...

SocietySim

AI models play Werewolf, a game of hidden roles and bluffing. We replay their moves and measure which models deceive others, and which ones spot the lies.

Like

Comment

Home Screen

Mode Selection Screen

Gameplay

Leaderboards

Research Data

Research Data

Inspiration

AI models increasingly talk to one another. We wanted to see when one model could mislead another, and how the listener reacted. Werewolf gives us a clear test: a few players know they are wolves, while everyone else has to work out whom to trust.

What it does

SocietySim puts language models from different providers in the same Werewolf game. A deterministic Python engine keeps the true game state and enforces the rules. Each model writes a private note with suspicion scores for the other players, then makes a public move. We record every event, label lies, and measure which models mislead others and which ones spot the wolves. The labels sit beside the original logs, which stay unchanged.

How to use it

Visit society-sim.us on a desktop. Watch a game replay and step through the votes, accusations, and labeled lies. Take a seat to play against the AI models. The global leaderboard shows the best liars and wolf detectors. The research page lets you explore the results across games.

How we built it

The Python engine runs the game and checks each model's structured replies. LiteLLM connects players served by Hugging Face, Google, and OpenAI. We also ran a self-hosted gpt-oss-20b player on AMD hardware. Neon stores game events, and Databricks holds the data and recomputes the metrics. A React and TypeScript viewer shows replays and results. A Render play server runs visitor games.

Results

We finished a batch of 100 ten-player games. Villagers won 62 games and wolves won 38. Across 4,702 statements, the models marked 1,129 as lies in their private notes, or 24%. Gemini Flash had the highest lie success rate by our suspicion-shift measure: 45% of 943 comparisons moved the way the liar wanted. It also had the highest wolf-detection score among village seats, with an AUC of 0.77. These lie results show an association, not proof that a lie caused a change of mind.

Challenges we ran into

We had to keep each role's private information separate. Wolves can see their own channel, while villagers cannot. We also had to handle invalid replies from different providers without letting a model change the rules. Measuring a lie was another challenge: a false claim and a vote that follows it are different observations.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We built the full path from a model's move to a replay, a lie label, and a comparison across games. The viewer lets people see what a player said beside what it privately wrote. The same system supports games between models and games with a human at the table.

What we learned

Private notes make deception easier to study, but only if each player sees the information its role allows. We also learned to read vote and suspicion changes carefully. A vote after a lie does not prove the lie caused it.

What's next

We want to use the site to compare human and model play, run more games, and test whether these patterns hold with other groups of models. The code is open for anyone who wants to inspect the rules and analysis.

title: ThirdEye
text:
Notifications

Loading...

ThirdEye

ThirdEye is an edge AI security system that tracks people, objects, and events over time, remembers what happened, detects meaningful activity, and records only important incidents.

Like
4

Comment

ThirdEye detecting and tracking people and objects in real time on-device.

Multiple active incidents shown at once, including restricted-zone activity and an unattended object.

Backpack 1 linked to Person 2 with last-seen details, event history, and the object-moved alert.

NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with the Arducam CSI camera powering ThirdEye’s local computer vision pipeline.

ThirdEye’s end-to-end pipeline from camera capture and detection to memory, event reasoning, incident recording, and the live dashboard.

Inspiration

Most security cameras are good at recording video, but not at understanding what actually happened.

They can tell you that motion occurred or that a person was detected, but they usually do not maintain context over time. If someone leaves a backpack behind, another person picks it up, or an object disappears from where it was last seen, a traditional camera often leaves the human operator to manually review footage and connect the dots.

We wanted to build a system that could do more than detect objects frame by frame. Our goal with ThirdEye was to create an edge AI system that maintains memory of a scene, tracks relationships between people and objects, understands meaningful events, and only records footage when something important happens.

We also wanted the system to work locally on dedicated hardware instead of depending on cloud inference, making it faster, more private, and more resilient to unreliable internet connections.

What it does

ThirdEye is a real-time edge AI security and event-intelligence platform running on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.

A live camera feed is processed locally to detect and track people and portable objects such as backpacks. Instead of treating every frame independently, ThirdEye builds a persistent world state that remembers what entities have been seen and how they relate to one another.

ThirdEye can currently detect and reason about events such as:

people entering and leaving the scene
restricted-zone entry
dwelling in a monitored area
occupancy and crowding
backpacks and other portable objects
associations between people and objects
unattended objects
objects moving from their previous location
objects leaving the scene with a person
last-seen locations and event history

ThirdEye also includes event-triggered incident recording. Rather than continuously storing hours of footage, the system keeps a short rolling buffer and automatically saves video from before and after a meaningful event occurs.

This allows the system to preserve the context surrounding an incident without requiring constant recording.

How we built it

ThirdEye runs locally on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano using a CSI camera and a real-time computer vision pipeline.

The core architecture is:

Camera
→ YOLO object detection
→ tracking
→ persistent identity/world state
→ spatial and relationship reasoning
→ event engine
→ SQLite event history
→ incident recorder
→ live dashboard

We use Ultralytics YOLO for real-time object detection and built our own tracking, identity, world-state, event, relationship, memory, and recording layers around it.

A major design decision was separating raw tracker IDs from logical identities. Tracker IDs can change when an object briefly disappears, so ThirdEye maintains its own persistent entity layer that allows logical people and objects to survive short detection gaps and maintain their history.

For portable objects, the system also maintains last-known state so an object is not immediately forgotten just because the detector temporarily loses it.

Events are stored locally in SQLite, including timestamps, entity relationships, last-seen information, and incident metadata.

For incident recording, ThirdEye keeps a rolling pre-event buffer in memory. When an important event occurs, it saves footage from several seconds before the event and continues recording afterward, creating a compact incident clip instead of continuously storing video.

The system also includes two interfaces:

a simplified judge/demo dashboard for real-time monitoring
a debug view with deeper tracking, timing, and event information

Everything required for the core demo runs locally on the Jetson.

Challenges we ran into

One of the biggest challenges was realizing that object detection alone was not enough.

YOLO could detect people and backpacks, but real-world detections are imperfect. A person might disappear for a few frames, a backpack could temporarily be classified as a handbag or suitcase, or an object could stop being detected entirely depending on lighting, angle, or occlusion.

That meant we had to build logic above the detector to create continuity over time.

We ran into issues such as:

one real person being assigned multiple IDs
temporary duplicate detections creating ghost people
one backpack being classified as multiple different objects
a backpack disappearing from detection even while still physically visible
associations between people and objects breaking when detections were missed
tracker IDs changing when someone left and returned to the scene

We addressed these problems by adding duplicate filtering, object-family normalization, persistent logical identities, archived entity states, last-seen memory, relationship recovery, and more conservative event reasoning.

We also had hardware-specific challenges on the Jetson, including CSI camera configuration, JetPack compatibility, CUDA/PyTorch setup, OpenCV with GStreamer support, power limits, and over-current throttling during heavier model experiments.

Another major challenge was presentation. Our early dashboard exposed too much technical information at once, so we redesigned it to focus on the events a user actually cares about while keeping a separate debug view for development.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are especially proud that ThirdEye evolved from a basic real-time detector into a stateful event-intelligence system.

Instead of only answering:

"What is in this frame?"

ThirdEye can begin answering questions like:

"Who was this backpack previously associated with?"

"Where was this object last seen?"

"Did this object move after the original person left?"

"What happened immediately before this incident?"

We also achieved real-time performance directly on the Jetson. During testing, the full pipeline ran at roughly 20–24 FPS while performing detection, tracking, event reasoning, dashboard rendering, and incident recording.

Our event-triggered recorder was able to save footage from approximately five seconds before an event and continue recording afterward without creating a measurable FPS penalty in our testing.

We are also proud that the core system does not depend on cloud inference. ThirdEye continues processing locally even if internet connectivity is unavailable.

What we learned

The biggest thing we learned is that building useful computer vision systems requires much more than choosing a good detection model.

A detector gives you observations. A useful product needs memory, state, relationships, uncertainty handling, and logic across time.

We learned a lot about:

edge AI development on NVIDIA Jetson
JetPack and CUDA
real-time video pipelines with GStreamer and OpenCV
GPU inference
object tracking and identity persistence
managing imperfect detections
designing event-driven systems
balancing performance with model complexity
local data storage and incident recording
building user interfaces that communicate complex AI behavior clearly

We also learned the importance of being conservative with AI conclusions. ThirdEye intentionally distinguishes between detecting an association and claiming ownership, and it avoids making strong claims when the evidence is ambiguous.

What's next for ThirdEye

The next step is improving long-term identity and object persistence.

We are experimenting with lightweight visual re-identification so ThirdEye can recognize when the same person or object leaves the scene and later returns, while keeping the system anonymous and avoiding facial recognition.

We also want to improve portable-object tracking when objects become partially occluded or difficult for the detector to see.

Beyond that, we envision ThirdEye supporting multiple cameras, configurable security policies, better incident search, and natural-language queries such as:

"Where was Backpack #1 last seen?"

"Who was near it before it moved?"

"Show me the incident where it left the room."

The long-term goal is to move security systems from passive video recording toward local, privacy-conscious systems that understand and remember what is happening in the physical world.

title: Lumen
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Lumen

Lumen turns spare devices into extra ears for your home: with real-time captions, visual alerts, and family updates. From a doorbell to a smoke alarm, see what matters as it happens.

Like
1

Comment

Dashboard

Inspiration

About 1 in 3 adults between 65 and 74, and nearly half of those older than 75, have hearing loss. Most of the house still assumes you can hear a beep.

A smoke alarm, a doorbell, someone calling your name from the kitchen: if you cannot hear it, or you are asleep in another room, that sound has to become a light on a phone you can actually read. Lumen is that light. Full access to the sounds of your own home is not a privilege. The tools should not only work one way.

What it does

Lumen turns spare phones into a home safety system for deaf, hard-of-hearing, and older people. Each phone is its own page. Together they turn sound and pose into captions and alerts you can see.

Four jobs, each on its own page:

Room nodes (/node). A spare phone listens and watches. It sends audio, body pose, and one still every few seconds. No live video leaves the phone.

Captions (/captions). Hold your phone up like a window. Speech appears in large, high-contrast type on the face whose mouth was moving, or at the bottom if the match is unsure. A line is tagged TO YOU when someone is facing you. Name calls, doorbells, glass, timers, and possible falls stay on screen until you tap them. Small gray text is how an alert gets missed, so the type stays big.

Bedside strobe (/strobe). When the kitchen hears a smoke alarm, the nightstand flashes and vibrates until someone taps it. You arm it on purpose. Nothing else on Lumen flashes fast.

Caregiver dashboard (/dashboard). The floor plan lights up the room an alert came from. Ask Lumen can answer “Where are my keys?” or “What happened while I was asleep?” It only reads memory. It never decides an alert.

Every alert and every tap is logged. A Databricks pipeline compares this week with last week for the same person. If she is slower to notice, or she misses more, the family gets a note that says worth a call. It never says diagnosis.

How we built it

Each page talks to one FastAPI brain over WebSockets. Face, pose, and object detection run on the phone with MediaPipe. On the demo rig, AST (sounds), Whisper (speech), and OWLv2 (what is in a still) run on an AMD Radeon cloud GPU. A Mac bridge plus cloudflared gives the phones HTTPS.

Sound direction

Three mics on the person, not one shared clock. The headset is the origin, the chest phone is about 30 cm away, the back camera about 28 cm behind. Training delays are calculated, not downloaded.

Sound travel time in seconds = distance in meters / 343.

At 343 m/s that chest gap is about 0.9 ms, roughly 14 samples at 16 kHz. A small model keeps a pick only if it is at least 55% sure. Otherwise we keep whichever mic heard the bump first. Direction never fires an alert.

Distance from the camera

A box is not a range. We use the camera’s focal length and a known object height: 1.7 m for a person, 1.5 m for a car.

Estimated distance = (focal length × known object height) / bounding box height.

Good to about plus or minus 30%. Enough for “car close, on your left.” A box cut off by the frame is treated as already inside 2.5 m.

Falls

Torso past 60 degrees from vertical, hips down more than 40% of standing height within 1 second, then 8 seconds of stillness. Leaving the frame means unknown, not fallen.

Smoke alarm

No model. Energy between 2.8 and 3.6 kHz. Three beeps in about 3 seconds fires the strobe.

History pipeline

Live alerts go out on the socket and do not wait on the warehouse. The same events are JSON lines, one file per hour. The Mac uploads new files. Auto Loader reads each file once.

Bronze keeps every raw line.

Silver drops bad rows: no alert kind, a timestamp before 2024, a test-button alert, blank captions, item sightings under 30% confidence.

Gold joins each alert to the first tap.

Time to notice = time of first tap minus time of alert.

No tap within 5 minutes counts as missed.

Worth a call only if the week before has at least 20 real alerts, and either median time to notice grew by more than 25% or misses at least doubled. One slow day does not page the family. The generated household is maria. The live one is home. They are never on the same chart.

Challenges we ran into

A strobe that waits on Databricks is a failed fire alarm, and a week-over-week number inside the alert loop is a lie until you have a week. The warehouse stays off the live path.

The three phones do not share a clock, so each half-second is lined up with the headset before we use the sound travel-time calculation. Distance from a box assumes you see the whole object, so we clamp it and we say plus or minus 30%. Free Edition has no personal access tokens, so the Mac sync uses an OAuth login. Test-button alerts are dropped in Silver so a demo click cannot look like a missed alarm.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Live alerts and a caregiver history that share one log and do not share a latency budget.

A smoke-alarm path with no AI in it: a band check and a beep count.

Captions and alerts large enough to read at arm’s length at night. The Eclipse logo is the only color.

A family note that stays quiet until there are 20 real alerts in the week before.

Automated tests in CI on every pull request.

On generated maria data, misses go from 5 to 15 (2 to 7 at night) and the note says worth a call. That slowdown was planted to show the feature. It is not a real person. Real home logs can say what happened this afternoon. They are not long enough yet for a week-over-week percent.

What we learned

The hard part is not hearing the tone. It is who is asleep, who is in another room, and how big the words have to be.

One missed tap means little. A week of slower taps is a phone call.

The sound travel-time calculation is only as good as the mic positions, and the camera distance calculation gives only a rough range. We publish both limits.

What's next for Lumen

Ask “how’s she doing this week?” out loud, and still refuse to call a short log a trend. Test the walking view on real phones. Replace maria with a real household once the family agrees and the log is long enough for the 20-alert baseline.

FastAPI, React, Python, MediaPipe, Whisper, PyTorch, Databricks, WebSockets.
