TrueView

TrueView: on-device AI deepfake detection for iPhone. Spot AI-generated photos and voice clips. No uploads and no cloud. Bloom-Blessed or Blight-Touched verdicts with confidence. Private by design.

Like
1

Comment

Banner

Main Screen

Ai Generated photo/audio results

Figma

Human photo/audio results

Inspiration

AI-generated photos and cloned voices get harder to spot every day. I wanted a detector that's always with you, your phone, and doesn't upload your private media to a server to do its job.

What it does

TrueView is an iPhone app that detects AI-generated photos and 4-second voice clips, entirely on-device. Snap or upload a photo, record a voice clip, and get a clear verdict, Bloom-Blessed (real) or Blight-Touched (AI-generated), with a confidence score. Your media never leaves your phone.

How I built it

Swift/SwiftUI app with AVFoundation for audio recording and PHPicker for photo selection. I converted Hugging Face transformer models to CoreML with coremltools, verifying that the on-device model matches the original PyTorch version. Custom preprocessing pipelines replicate each model's exact training preprocessing, resize method, normalization values, all of it.

Challenges we ran into

Model selection was brutal. My first model flagged everything as fake; the second couldn't spot AI images at all.  I learned to verify empirically, testing in Google Colab, checking confidence scores, curating test sets and got guidance from the Hugging Face team right here at Knight Hacks. I also discovered that re-compressed images can flip a verdict, and that the iPhone's preprocessing must match the model's training pipeline exactly or accuracy silently breaks.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Fully on-device inference, no server, no API calls, works in airplane mode. Photo AND voice detection in one app. A verdict UX (Bloom-Blessed / Blight-Touched) that makes deepfake detection feel approachable instead of intimidating.

What we learned

How to convert PyTorch models to CoreML and prove the conversion is faithful. That deepfake detection is as much about the data pipeline as the model itself. And to evaluate models empirically instead of trusting download counts.

What's next for TrueView

Compression-robust detection for screenshots and forwarded images, real-time video deepfake detection, and voice detection in more languages.

Knight's Eye

Security guards lose focus on long night shifts. Our game watches the watcher.

Inspiration

After hearing about the category "Serious Game", I came up with this project idea with our team after remembering about the psychology principle of sustained attention. Combining the elements of computer vision, job training, and the job at the pinnacle of paying attention, we chose to do a game that is a Night Shift Security Camera Training Simulator. - Lilly

Why?

"Psychologists discovered the human attention span lasts roughly 20 minutes. After these 20 minutes, security guards will miss up to 95% of occurrences. " Citation

CCTV operator training is straight forward, but maintaining peak operational performance isn’t. 
What if CCTV teams could assess and train their observation concentration through a game?

Many ways to play:

This game can be used as a rapid scanning and crisis trainer like demonstrated in the video or a slow endurance concentration game. 

Ex) rapid paced game = short time (<10 minutes), many events, fast reaction time required.

Ex) slow endurance game = long time (1 hour+), few infrequent events, paying attention consistently required.

What it does

Knight's Eye is a browser game where you're the night operator at a security desk. There are anomalies that you must let your dispatcher know to alert knights to investigate. This is a "Serious Game" that can serve as a job trainer or skills practicer.

Watch the feeds: 2,4, or 6 live camera feeds show a building full of indiscernible NPCs. Most are ordinary. A few are suspicious: loitering, revisiting doors, entering restricted rooms, or avoiding the cameras. Either track them by their movement patterns, or by observing suspicious behavior (green glows).

Gaze tracking: A 13-point calibration maps your webcam gaze to the screen, so the game always knows which feed you're watching. You can also use your mouse to stand in as a camera.

Report and radio: Report a sighting on a feed, or hold Space and say "Camera 3, sighting." A simulated (AI) dispatcher answers over the radio in a realistic or robotic voice and sends a knight through the building to investigate. Your speed in scanning and reporting determines if the suspect runs free.

Distractions: Pop-ups cover your feeds, feeds glitch, and dispatch checks in with questions like "How many people are on camera 2?" that you answer by voice.

Debrief: When the shift ends, you get a grade, your catches and false reports, a heatmap of where your attention went on each feed, a per-camera timeline, and coaching. The dispatcher reads a summary aloud.

How we built it:

Frontend: TypeScript and Vite

Gaze Tracking: MediaPipe: runs in the browser calculating eye tracking from your iris position, eyelid opening, head yaw, pitch and position, which is then fit on a ridge regression on a 13-point calibration, and a One Euro filter to smooth the output.

World Simulation: A tile-based building with rooms, doors, and six cameras. The office is larger than what the cameras can see creating blinds spots. NPCS follow scripted plans and move with A*path finding. 

Simulated (AI) Dispatcher: Google Gemma via Hugging Face Inference Providers. The game is brought to life by a dispatch team that follows your command, investigates your dispatches, and requests your understanding of the scene. Choose either from dynamic or preset lines generated by Gemma or templates, and realistic and robotic voices made with Eleven Labs or Web Speech API. The dispatch system still works even after support for Hugging Face and Eleven Labs run out of credits. Every line has a template fallback if the AI takes more than 2 seconds.

Voice: ElevenLabs text-to speech create pre-generated MP3s to save credits and Web Speech API as a fallback.

Architecture: We split up the project into 4 parts: (vision, world, game, analytics), each part was owned by one teammate letting us work in parallel. Together we shared design decisions about gameplay and interactions!

Design: The concept of this project was inspired from Windows 98. The design was first drawn on paper, formed as bare boxes, and then remade in Figma Design and Figma Make.

Hosting: The game is hosted on Github Pages at a custom domain: ([knightseye.us]. This was registered through GoDaddy, and the API keys to connect to ElevenLabs and Google Gemma via Hugging Face were hosted through Netlify which connected back to GitHub.

Challenges we ran into

Team of first-time hackers and having to start with teaching what is git, and how to use it, how to set up a project to everyone being able to contribute to the project and have an impressive result!
Getting accurate calibrated eye tracking that was intuitive to use. Needed to consider camera placement, head moving for scanning, posture, head tilt. 
Hosting the game site. Our setup up to host was quite complicated since we needed to integrated our API keys!

Making sure the game is reactive and interactable with NPC pathfinding techniques (A*)

Eye tracking actually working and being properly calibrated.
Integrated an AI system into our Simulated Dispatcher that will work even after we stop having the free trials.

Properly hosting a website with a custom Domain (first time for everyone!)
Game User interface style and aesthetics!

title: diarockets
text:
Notifications

diarockets

Trained on human society's flaws and virtues, how well can AI simulate the world that shaped it? We built our project, GEarth, to find out: recreating governance, trade, and conflict to watch it live.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

As humans, we experience both the flaws and virtues of society: how we cooperate, compete, govern, and build our lives together. AI is trained on accounts of those same human experiences, the good and the bad. That made us wonder: how well could it simulate the world that shaped it?

To find out, we built GEarth. With an abundance of computing power, our project sets out to recreate the core systems of society (citizens, governments, economies, trade, diplomacy, and conflict) and watch how AI agents navigate life together.

What it does

GEarth is a generated/simulated Earth where AI agents represent countries, institutions, and citizens. Our default world contains 1000+ agents across ten fictional countries
.

Citizens work, buy necessities, seek healthcare, and start businesses.
Governments, banks, and businesses make policy decisions, provide loans, and produce and trade goods.
Countries navigate diplomacy, resource shortages, and conflict.
and much more... 

These decisions interact: a shortage can affect production, production can affect employment, and unemployment can affect an entire country's economy.

Through our browser dashboard, viewers can watch the simulation unfold, explore countries, and inspect individual agents' decisions and explanations. GEarth makes it possible to follow both a society's overall development and the choices of the individuals living within it.

How we built it

Simulation Engine: We built the simulation engine in C# and .NET, giving it responsibility for time, resources, transactions, and the consequences of every action. AI agents receive observations about their circumstances and choose from actions the engine allows.
Distributed AI Inference: Our Python inference workers connect those agents to Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B, running across two NVIDIA DGX Spark systems and an AMD GPU. We use the larger model for institutional and entrepreneur decisions and the smaller model for resident decisions. Scheduling and batching help coordinate requests across the hardware.
Cloud, Data & Analytics: We use Neon PostgreSQL to preserve simulation checkpoints and event history, and Google Cloud to keep the shared world running independently of our laptops. A browser dashboard makes the simulation observable, while our Databricks analytics pipeline processes completed runs to help us investigate their outcomes.

Challenges we ran into

Balancing a Functioning Economy: Making a society function was harder than giving agents personalities. Early simulations exposed businesses hoarding money, high unemployment, and declining citizen health. We had to revisit how wages, production, healthcare, public services, and spending connected to one another.
Coordinating Distributed Inference: Different machines had different capacities and response times, and model requests could time out or arrive after the world had changed. We worked on bounded scheduling, batching, validation, and fallback behavior to keep the simulation progressing.
Enforcing Reliable Accounting: Every decision had to respect available money, goods, and authority. Recording events and distinguishing model decisions from rule-based fallbacks helped us understand what actually happened.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Building a connected AI society where individual choices have consequences beyond a single conversation, with citizens, businesses, banks, and governments participating in the same economic system.
Bringing NVIDIA and AMD inference into one shared simulation, preserving worlds for later inspection, and building a dashboard that makes complex interactions easier to explore.
Designing a full-year rule-based calibration test that checks economic consistency over time, giving us a repeatable foundation alongside our live AI experiments.

What we learned

We learned that believable agent behavior depends on the world around it. A model needs meaningful choices, useful information, and consistent consequences.

Building GEarth also taught us how interconnected society's systems are. Healthcare affects people's ability to work. Employment affects spending. Spending supports businesses, and businesses help fund governments. Small implementation choices can ripple through the entire simulation.

We learned to inspect those connections carefully and separate problems in the economic rules from problems in model behavior or infrastructure.

What's next for GEarth

We want to expand our what-if experiments so viewers can change a policy or a citizen's circumstances and compare how alternate timelines develop. Our initial experiment system uses rule-based decisions; extending it to live AI decisions is a next step.

We also want richer visual replay, more scenarios, and longer experiments with matched starting conditions. As we scale the population, we'll measure sustained inference performance and decision coverage.

Ultimately, we want GEarth to become a place where people can explore how individual decisions shape a society, and discover outcomes we didn't anticipate.

title: Permanence
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Permanence

Intelligent Spatial Awareness & Object Permanence

Like
6

Comment

Hydrogen Astra vs. Coughing Baby

Permanence Dashboard & Telemetry

Permanence X-ray view (left) through a solid wall (right)

Hydrogen bomb (Astra, Fable) vs. coughing baby: who understands object permanence?

Inspiration

Frontier models like Fable seem more intelligent in almost every way. They write software, explain advanced mathematics, and work through hard problems. But on one fundamental concept, a roughly one-year-old baby has something to teach them: object permanence.

Object permanence is understanding that things keep existing when we can't see them. It lets us remember what's behind an obstacle, follow where it went, and look for it again. Babies show it long before they can explain it.

This isn't a claim that babies beat AI on a benchmark. It's the gap that interested us. A model can explain object permanence, but a robot still needs a way to keep it in a changing physical world. A detector losing sight of something shouldn't mean the robot forgets it exists.

We built Permanence to turn "I detected it" into "I still know where it is."

What it does

Permanence gives a robot a persistent 3D memory of objects. The rover scans the table by itself, identifies the objects, and keeps track of where they are as they get hidden or leave the camera's view.

Our clearest demonstration is a shell game. Show the robot colored balls, cover them with cups, shuffle the cups, then reveal. Permanence tracks which cup holds each hidden ball and checks its answer against the real reveal. It called the right cup in 7 of 7 recorded games and 3 of 3 live.

You can also:

Talk to it. "Hey rover, the cup next to the green ball": a 3D vision-language model picks the object from the scan and shows how confident it is.
See its memory. A live 3D dashboard and an x-ray display on XREAL glasses show hidden objects through the cups covering them.
See what's seen versus remembered, including how long each object has been out of sight.
Send it to a remembered target. "Hey rover, drive": the rover plans around the other cups and goes to its target, even when nothing on camera shows where the ball is.

The cups are a demonstration, not the whole idea. The goal is a robot that acts on what it knows, not just on what's in frame.

How we built it

Two brains, one Jetson. Everything runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB). An iPhone on the rover is only the sensor: it streams color, LiDAR depth and its own position over USB through Record3D.

The reasoning: Qwen-3D, a 3-billion-parameter 3D vision-language model. It reads 18 views of the scan and turns language like "the cup next to the box" into a specific object, in about 4.5 s. Three identical cups have no names; only a model that understands language and space can tell them apart.
The fast reflexes: YOLOE. It's prompted with words (no training on our props) and compiled to a 22 MB TensorRT FP16 engine that keeps up with the camera's 15 fps.
The memory between them: a 3D tracker we wrote. It matches detections across frames, follows each object through occlusion, and knows that a ball under a cup moves with the cup.

Fitting it in 8 GB. CPU and GPU share the Jetson's 8 GB, and Qwen-3D alone was 7.1 GB. We wrote our own 8-bit quantization in plain PyTorch, loading the model one tensor at a time so the full-size version never exists in memory: 4.5 GB. The pipeline allows one memory peak at a time. Qwen-3D picks the target, hands it to the tracker, and its process exits to free its memory before tracking starts. A full run peaks at about 6.1 of 7.4 GB.

Interfaces. A Three.js dashboard shows the robot's calibrated view, a top-down memory map, the camera feed, the confidence behind each pick, and live Jetson memory. A web HUD on XREAL glasses brings the x-ray view and key state to a wearable display. Voice commands use Chrome's speech recognition.

Movement. The Jetson drives an Arduino Uno and L298N motor driver and steers from the phone's position. The rover scans by stop-and-shoot: turn, stop, take a sharp view, roll, repeat. It learns how much power its cheap motors need to start moving, and stops on its own if commands stop arriving. We also built a separate head-steering interface with a Pico W and GY-521 motion sensor.

Challenges we ran into

8 GB is small for two models. Loading both crashed the board, and an earlier run left behind can eat the room. We added the handoff, our own quantization, and cleanup of leftover processes.
A wobbly camera. With the phone mounted high on the rover, scanning while moving gave blurred frames. Stopping for each shot fixed it.
Cheap motors. They stall when started too gently and hum instead of turning, so the rover measures its own speed and adjusts power. When its left and right turned out to be swapped, it detects that and corrects it in software.
Disappearing isn't the same as hidden. A missed detection doesn't mean the ball went into a cup. We needed geometry, motion and containment checks, and matching in 3D so identical cups don't swap identities when they cross.
Freshness over completeness. An overlay that shows where the world was seconds ago is useless, so every stage takes only the newest frame.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The full loop on a palm-sized edge board: perception, memory, language, visualization and physical action, with a 3B vision-language model and a real-time tracker together in 8 GB.
The reveal. The robot commits to where the hidden ball is, and we lift the cup to check. Nobody has to take our word for it.

What we learned

Recognizing an object is only the beginning. Useful intelligence needs continuity: what was there, what changed, and what should still be there when you can't see it.
Memory is a design constraint, not an afterthought. Deciding what runs when mattered as much as which models we picked.
The strongest demo is a claim you can check: show it, hide it, move it, reveal it.

What's next for Permanence

Prediction: a learned world model that guesses what happened out of view, instead of only remembering what it saw.
Bigger hardware: Jetson Thor, so the language model can stay loaded and answer at any time.
Better hardware and integration: wheel encoders, and ROS 2 / Isaac ROS.
Beyond the tabletop, with clearer uncertainty when memory gets old.
Longer term: assistive robots and glasses that help people find misplaced things.

The coughing baby had this figured out in its first year. Now our robot does too.

Out of sight should not mean out of memory.

Built with: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, TensorRT, CUDA, PyTorch, Qwen-3D, YOLOE, Record3D, iPhone LiDAR, Python, Three.js, JavaScript, Web Speech API, XREAL, Arduino, L298N, Raspberry Pi Pico W.

title: Campus Time Machine
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Campus Time Machine

Turn familiar UCF locations into a world-model powered video time machine. See snow across Engineering II, a rocket flying above Memory Mall, or drones and flying cars around the Student Union.

Like
1

Comment

Inspiration

We (Diego and Broc) were inspired by the challenges presented by AMD (Best Use of AMD Technologies) and Hugging Face (Best Use of Open Source AI) tracks. Before the hackathon even started, we had a vision for making AI video generation something people could explore and interact with.

What it does

Campus Time Machine turns familiar University of Central Florida locations into imagined video moments. Choose a waypoint on the campus map, pick a photo and a moment, and generate a short video with synchronized audio. See snow in Orlando, a rocket beyond campus, or black-and-gold balloons drifting through a plaza; then compare the arrival with the original photo and explore the shared Journey Wall.

How we built it

Our generation worker runs Kandinsky 6.0 Video Lite, an open-weight world model available on Hugging Face. We run the model on an AMD Radeon Pro W7900D with 48 GB VRAM, using PyTorch with ROCm on AMD Radeon Cloud. The model is on the GPU and serves jobs from a file queue through the Jupyter notebook gateway. Once the jobs are finished, they are uploaded to a Hugging Face bucket for remote storage.

Challenges we ran into

We had a number of issues on the backend:

After LTX-2.5 exceeded the instance's host-memory budget, we switched to Kandinsky Lite (an easy transition thanks to Hugging Face) and kept the pipeline on the GPU, avoiding repeated model loads and CPU-offload copies.
We pinned masked attention in the text encoder and video VAE to PyTorch's math SDPA backend after getting NaNs on the ROCm stack. Transformer attention keeps its native path.
Tiled VAE decoding and a source-image size limit control peak memory; failed jobs report an error while the worker continues serving the queue.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Building a complete experience from campus selection and photo input to live generation, playback, comparison, and download.
Running an open AI video model with synchronized audio on AMD Radeon hardware using ROCm.
Connecting Hugging Face storage to a shared Journey Wall so finished videos remain accessible beyond the generation session.
Recovering from memory and attention issues while keeping the frontend and backend connected throughout development.

What we learned

We learned that running a large generative model requires understanding more than its VRAM requirements. Host memory, attention implementations, image dimensions, and video decoding all affected whether our pipeline produced usable results.
We also learned how much prompt design matters for image-to-video generation. Describing something moving through an existing scene worked better than asking the model to completely restyle a location within a short clip.

What's next for Campus Time Machine

The video generation, due to being compute and time-limited for the presentations, only renders at a maximum resolution of 864x480. We would like to expand the resolution by taking advantage of the in-built Super-Resolution of the world model, which we did not have time to test.

We would like to transfer the backend away from a Jupyter notebook based solution to a proper server, running the worker Python file and using a normal server and API-based solution.

title: Kairos
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Kairos

Catch the puddle. Clear the storm. A weather and water plugin for Orbit: Spot gets RECALL when a storm turns mid-round and HOLD when its camera sees water in the path.

Like
2

Comment

Dashboard: Kairos calls RECALL as rain passes Spot's IP54 limit, with fleet KPIs and the next round on HOLD

Our fine-tuned water model finds a spill in Spot's path at WP02; Spot holds until the operator confirms

The storm hits 2.8 mm/h mid-round; Kairos recalls Spot to the dock

The water model runs in the browser, with calibrated 'water 90%' and honest held-out numbers

Plant map with water pins and the weather-gated outdoor stop, next to live radar

Every detection and operator label is stored in Neon, and model versions are scored on a frozen branch

The same dashboard on a phone

Catch the puddle. Clear the storm. A weather and water dashboard for Boston Dynamics Spot, built as a plugin for Orbit, for the NextEra Energy "SPOT Management Dashboard" challenge.

Live: https://kairos.boston

Inspiration

NextEra runs Boston Dynamics Spot robots on inspection rounds at its plants. I talked with NextEra's Spot team at the Knight Hacks career fair and at their workshop, and they named two problems. Weather on the route is not caught as early as they want, and a storm that builds mid-round is the hard case. Small puddles and spills on the route are also hard to catch.

Spot is rated IP54: light rain and splashes are fine, harsh rain and storms are not. Orbit, Spot's fleet software, can block a launch on a rain forecast. The gap is after launch. Kairos keeps checking rain, thunder, gusts and heat against Spot's limits while the round runs, and calls a recall when they cross. No forecast can see a puddle in Spot's path, so Kairos also watches the floor.

What it does

Kairos watches the weather and the floor on every round. When the weather turns mid-round, it says RECALL. When Spot's camera sees water in its path, it says HOLD until an operator confirms. Every call is logged.

Dashboard: the call for a Spot on route right now (RECALL / HOLD / GO), the rain rate against Spot's IP54 limit, thunder, gusts and heat, a 12-hour rain chart with the next safe launch, live radar around the plant, the latest water Spot's camera found (Confirm / Reject), and the next round's call.
Live round: one simulated round. Spot walks its route, its camera checks every waypoint, a spill in the path holds Spot until the operator answers, and the recorded storm recalls Spot to the dock.
Storm drill: a real pop-up storm at St. Lucie (May 19, 2024), replayed minute by minute with no hindsight. The recall fires before the NWS warning (first on my thunder rule, which is labeled as my assumption).
Water model: try my model on your own photo, in the browser, with honest held-out numbers and what each confidence % means.
Evidence and Incident review: every water detection and operator label, stored in Neon; each model version scored on a frozen Neon branch; saved moments read back from Neon snapshot branches.

A scenario switch in the top bar replays a real St. Lucie storm I captured Sat Oct 10, 5:56 PM ET (NWS + Open-Meteo + 50 minutes of radar), so the demo works whatever the sky does. Live uses the feeds right now. The demo site is NextEra's St. Lucie plant; Kairos works for any plant from its coordinates.

How it fits Orbit: Kairos is a layer on top of Orbit, not a replacement. A HOLD maps to pausing the schedule and a RECALL to sending Spot to the dock (Orbit API v0 endpoint names, simulated in this demo). The water model runs wherever Spot's camera frames are: in the browser today, on Spot's CORE I/O as a Network Compute Bridge worker in a real deployment.

Rules (all in lib/verdict.ts, cited in the UI)

Rain above 2.5 mm/h before Spot can dock (beyond IP54's "light rain") → HOLD before launch, RECALL during a round.
NWS warning → HOLD / RECALL. NWS watch or advisory → HOLD.
Thunder chance ≥ 30%, gusts ≥ 50 km/h → HOLD / RECALL (my assumptions: the Spot guide is silent).
Air temperature within 5 °C of Spot's -20 / 55 °C limits → HOLD / RECALL.
Water in Spot's path → HOLD at that waypoint until an operator confirms or rejects. An unknown floor (model loading or failed) also holds.
Missing or stale weather never shows GO.

How I built it

Next.js 16 on Vercel, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui. Rules are pure, tested functions (lib/verdict.ts, npm test), so the live dashboard, the storm drill and the backtest run the same code.
Hugging Face: my water detector is fine-tuned from RT-DETRv2-R18 (Apache 2.0) on Hugging Face Jobs (one L4 GPU, 18 epochs, about $1 of credits), published on the Hub with an honest model card, and run in the browser with transformers.js (WebGPU fp32, WASM int8 fallback). Without it, Kairos can see the sky but not the floor.
Neon: Neon Postgres is the evidence log (every detection and label), a frozen branch scores each model version, every visitor and every storm drill writes to its own copy-on-write branch so nobody's clicks touch production, and snapshot branches power Incident review. Without it there is no audit trail, no model scoring, and a public demo anyone could break.
NextEra (the challenge): the problem came from their Spot engineer, and the robot data is NextEra's synthetic SPOT challenge kit (labeled synthetic in the UI).
Weather: National Weather Service (api.weather.gov) alerts and forecast grid, Open-Meteo 15-minute rain, NEXRAD radar tiles via the Iowa Environmental Mesonet, map tiles © OpenStreetMap contributors.
Data for the model: split by source and scene, never by single image. Test photos come from a puddle source the model never trained on, plus whole recordings from a camera on a real Spot (UT Austin SCAND). The threshold was picked on a separate calibration split, never on test.
Domain: kairos.boston, a GoDaddy Registry TLD.

The numbers (all on public photos; no NextEra camera frames exist)

Water model, held out (never trained on), fp32 (the WebGPU file): flags 85% of wet photos from a puddle source it never saw (463 of 543); 1.2 false alarms per 100 frames from a camera on a real Spot (2 of 172). Known gap: tiny puddles under 1% of the frame, 6 of 57.
Confidence that means something: "water 90%" means 9 in 10 boxes at that score were real water, measured on a calibration split (315 boxes) and checked on test (680 boxes).
Plant-like floors (int8 file): on the industrial-like test slice (indoor hard floors and spills), it flags 86% of wet frames (245 of 284) with 2.4 false alarms per 100 indoor Spot frames (4 of 165).
Speed: about 70 to 100 ms per frame on WebGPU in Chrome (two measurements: 67 ms p50, and 101 ms median of 10 runs).
Weather backtest: at the kit's 27 round times, on archive weather for the plant (Open-Meteo ERA5, Sep 1-10), Kairos would hold 1 round for weather. It does not cry wolf. The archive has no thunder data, so this does not test the thunder rule.

Full tables, splits and 95% intervals: docs/model/water-v2/RESULTS.md and CONFIDENCE.md in the repo.

Challenges I ran into

No weather and no real camera frames in the kit. NextEra's kit is synthetic and indoor, with no weather fields. Every weather assumption (outdoor leg, dock, walking speed, my thresholds) is labeled on screen, and every camera frame is a public photo with its license.
A score that was too good. My first water model (a ConvNeXt classifier) scored 99.6%, because wet and dry images came from different datasets. The honest single-source number was 92.7%. That is why v2 splits by source and scene and picks its threshold on a separate calibration split.
Tiny puddles are hard. Under 1% of the frame, v2 finds 6 of 57. I tried a second fine-tune (v3) with bigger inputs, copy-paste of tiny water and mosaic; it lost to v2 on every recall metric, so v2 stays and I say so.
A rain-at-the-door camera model that learned "gray sky". After deduplicating its splits it was near chance on cameras it never saw, so it gates nothing. Weather data decides.
Browser inference. The transformers.js object-detection pipeline drops every box of a one-class model, so I decode the raw outputs myself. The int8 file ran at 1.3 s per frame on WebGPU (no int8 matrix kernel); fp32 on WebGPU runs at about 70 to 100 ms. I also patched two float64 casts in the exported graph that browsers cannot run (outputs identical).

Accomplishments that I'm proud of

NextEra's Spot engineer gave me the two problems at the workshop, liked the idea, and asked to hear back as I build it.
A replay of a real storm at the real plant where Kairos recalls Spot before the NWS warning, with no hindsight.
An honest model card: the number that is not flattering (tiny puddles) is in the headline, and a confidence % that is measured, not a raw score.
A public demo that cannot be broken: every visitor writes to their own Neon branch.

What I learned

How Spot actually runs: Autowalk missions can keep going when the link drops, so a recall must be sent while Spot is still in coverage; the radio range drops behind concrete; operators return Spot to charge around 20% battery.
A clean benchmark score can come from the dataset, not the model. Split by source and scene.
Shipping a model in the browser means owning the decode, the precision and the export, not just the weights.

What's next for Kairos

I want to take Kairos past Knight Hacks. NextEra's Spot engineer asked to hear back as I build it, so the next steps are the ones that need a real plant:

Train and test on NextEra's real Spot footage and the operator labels Kairos already stores in Neon, to close the tiny-puddle gap on plant floors.
Run the water model on Spot's CORE I/O as a Network Compute Bridge worker, next to NextEra's own models.
Wire HOLD and RECALL to the real Orbit API instead of the simulated calls, and pilot it on one site's outdoor rounds.
Add a dock-door camera check, so Kairos sees rain at the door, not only in the forecast.

Disclosure (Knight Hacks rules)

All project code, both fine-tuned models and the data pipelines were made during the event (hacking began Fri 2026-10-09, 11 PM EDT). The repo's first commit (Fri 7:54 PM) is GitHub's empty repo setup only (a title line and .gitattributes).

AI tools: Claude Code (Anthropic Claude models) wrote most of the code under my direction; OpenAI Codex reviewed facts and evaluations. I chose the problem, the rules and every product decision, and reviewed and tested the output. The intro narration is an ElevenLabs voice ("Misa").
Base models: PekingU/rtdetr_v2_r18vd (Apache 2.0), fine-tuned by me into builtbyd3v/kairos-water-rtdetr. Earlier experiments: facebook/convnext-tiny-224 (Apache 2.0) into builtbyd3v/spot-wetfloor-convnext-tiny and builtbyd3v/kairos-door-rain.
Datasets: Bhutad and Patil (2021), Dataset of Stagnant Water and Wet Surface with Annotations, Mendeley Data V4, doi:10.17632/y6zyrnxbfm.4 (CC BY 4.0); Roboflow Universe slipp/spill_detection, hk-hsse/puddle-qrpyh and projects-pwwbs/water-puddle-joyj6 (CC BY 4.0); Kaggle muftirestumahesa obstacles in public spaces (CC0); UT Austin SCAND, Karnan et al., doi:10.18738/T8/0PRYRH (CC0); for the door-rain experiment, Kaggle Weather Image Recognition (CC0), Multi-class Weather Dataset (CC BY 4.0) and Weather-Time (CC0).

Fireline

Satellites see a wildfire once it is big. Fireline sees the first smoke.

Like
1

Comment

Cover

How It Works

Console Smoke Alert

What's in the box

What the crew sees

Weather-gated wake up

Is it really Smoke?

What's Next

Fireline

Tagline: Satellites see a wildfire once it is big. Fireline sees the first smoke.

Inspiration

From January 1 to April 13, 2025, the Florida Forest Service counted 1,300 wildfires and 57,025 acres burned (FOX 35). Much of that land is remote: no power lines, no cell signal, nobody watching.

Satellites can't close that gap on their own. The ones sharp enough to see a small fire pass over a few times a day: VIIRS has about 375 m pixels and 3 to 4 looks a day at mid-latitudes (NASA Earthdata). Ground cameras see smoke sooner, but they need a tower, grid power and an internet connection.

We wanted a camera box you can strap to a tree in the middle of nowhere that decides on its own whether it is seeing smoke, and that sends only what matters.

What it does

Fireline is a flock of tree-mounted camera units and a live console for the crew that manages them. Each unit runs a smoke detection model on its own NVIDIA Jetson, wakes up only when the weather says fire is likely, and sends a single alert packet of 340 bytes or less over a satellite link. The console puts every unit on a map and sounds the alarm the moment one of them confirms smoke.

Smoke detection on the device: Pyronear's open YOLO smoke model runs on the Jetson's GPU. Smoke must appear in at least 4 of the last 6 frames, which filters out clouds, fog and dust.
Weather-gated wake-up: a cheap humidity sensor on an ESP32 sets a fire-risk tier. The Jetson scans every 30 minutes when it's humid, every 5 minutes when it's drying out, and continuously in critical fire weather.
Satellite-sized alerts: every message fits the 340-byte limit of an Iridium short burst data message. In our tests a smoke event is 178 bytes. Images never cross the satellite link.
A live console: a fleet map with markers colored by state, an alarm and desktop notification that fly the map to the unit, weather charts for each unit, and a link log showing each packet's size and satellite delay.
Plain-language write-ups: each incident gets an instant summary ("Smoke seen by gw-14 in 5 of 6 frames during critical fire weather (34 °C, 22 % humidity). Likely early wildfire."), which Gemma 3 then rewrites for the crew. Gemma also gives a second opinion on the smoke crop.

The demo: we point a hair dryer at the sensor. Humidity drops, the status LED goes from green to orange, and the Jetson starts scanning. We hold a smoke video up to the camera. A few seconds later the console sounds an alarm, the map flies to the unit, and the alert card shows the packet that crossed the simulated satellite link.

How we built it

DHT11 → ESP32 sets the fire-risk tier → MQTT wakes the Jetson → smoke model + 4-of-6 frame check → interest score → 340-byte packet over the simulated satellite link → FastAPI on Azure → WebSocket → every open console

Field unit (hardware)

NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano runs the smoke model on its GPU with TensorRT, through Ultralytics. It idles with the model loaded until the ESP32 asks for a scan.
ESP32 (Arduino) is the always-on sentry. It reads a DHT11, averages 3 readings, changes tier only after 3 agreeing readings, and drives the status LED and buzzer.
MQTT with a Mosquitto broker on the Jetson connects the two inside the box.

AI/ML

Pyronear's YOLO wildfire smoke model from Hugging Face (Apache 2.0), trained on Pyro-SDIS, a dataset of labelled smoke images from fixed ground cameras. No training needed.
An interest score: average confidence × (frames with smoke / 6) × fire-weather weight. Smoke in critical weather outranks a faint blob on a humid day. An alert fires at 0.5.
Gemma 3 (4B) served by Ollama writes each incident up and checks the smoke crop.

Backend and infrastructure

FastAPI + SQLite ground station: a satellite simulator (340-byte limit, 5–20 s delay, optional drops), incident grouping, offline detection, and a WebSocket for live updates.
Azure VM running Docker Compose: the app, Gemma on Ollama, and Caddy for automatic HTTPS (browsers only allow notifications on secure sites).

Frontend

React, TypeScript and Vite, with Leaflet for the map on Esri satellite imagery.

Challenges we ran into

A satellite link delivers out of order. With a 5–20 s random delay, an older heartbeat can land after a newer one. The ground station only lets the newest packet set a unit's state. It treats a packet as a duplicate only when the unit, counter and timestamp all match, because a rebooted unit restarts its counter.
340 bytes is a tight budget. We used short keys and rounded numbers, and kept images off the satellite link entirely. The unit refuses to send anything over the limit.
A Jetson is slow to boot. Power-cycling it for every scan wasn't practical, so the cheap ESP32 does the always-on watching and the Jetson stays idle with the model loaded until it's needed.
AI write-ups on a CPU-only server. Gemma on a CPU VM can take a while. The console shows a template summary instantly, and Gemma's version replaces it when it arrives. If Gemma never answers, the alert still works.
We changed the architecture mid-build. We started with a Raspberry Pi ground station and an installed desktop app, and merged them into one hosted website. That meant fewer devices at the judging table, and anyone on the crew can open the console.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Detection never leaves the forest. The decision "is this smoke?" happens on the box. Only a small verdict crosses the satellite link, which answers the reason ground cameras need towers and internet today.
The whole chain, end to end: weather sensor, wake-up, on-device detection, satellite-sized uplink, live alert on the map.
A console built for the crew, not the demo. Alerts group into incidents, units that go quiet turn grey, and every packet's size and delay is on screen.
Honest about what's real. The satellite link and most of the fleet are simulated, and the console labels every simulated unit on screen.

What we learned

How to deploy a YOLO model to a Jetson and export it to TensorRT
How to design a message format around a hard 340-byte limit
How to keep state consistent when messages arrive late, out of order or twice
How to split work across embedded, ML, backend and frontend lanes by agreeing on a packet contract in the first hour

What's next for Fireline

Tap to place: an NFC tag on each tree holds its name and coordinates, so a crew sets a unit's location with one tap.
Locate the fire: two units seeing the same smoke from different angles can triangulate where it is.
One modem per flock: units relay to each other over LoRa radio, so only one carries the satellite modem.
Field-ready power: cut the Jetson's power completely between scans, with solar and a LiFePO4 battery.
Test on Florida scenery: Pyronear's model was trained on other regions' landscapes, so it needs testing against local false alarms like dust and prescribed burns. We haven't measured our false-alarm rate or detection range yet; that is what a pilot is for.

Ecoforest

Our project utilizes AI to identify different objects and tell the user how to properly dispose of them in an eco-friendly way, all from an interactive task list website made for staying green!

Healed Forest

Waste Scanner

Corrupt Forest

Inspiration

Ecoforest was inspired by our desire to make recycling more accessible, intuitive, and environmentally friendly. We recognized a common problem in everyday waste management: many people unknowingly place contaminated or non-recyclable items into recycling bins, potentially compromising the recycling process. We wanted to address this issue by creating an AI-powered web application that helps users identify waste and understand how to dispose of it properly. Our goal is to make sustainable habits easier to adopt and encourage environmentally conscious decisions.

What it does

Ecoforest is an interactive web application that uses computer vision to identify everyday objects and provide guidance on how to dispose of them responsibly. Using a YOLOv8 object detection model, the application identifies items through a camera feed and classifies them into appropriate waste categories, helping users determine whether an item should be recycled or discarded.

Beyond waste classification, Ecoforest incorporates a gamified sustainability experience. Users can complete eco-friendly tasks and check them off on their dashboard, gradually transforming a virtual forest into a greener, healthier environment. This feature encourages users to build sustainable habits while visualizing the impact of their actions.

How we built it

We developed Ecoforest using a combination of modern web development technologies and machine learning frameworks.

Frontend: React and Next.js for building an interactive, user-friendly interface.
Backend: FastAPI for handling communication between the frontend and the machine learning model.
Computer Vision: Ultralytics YOLOv8 for real-time object detection and waste classification.
Dashboard Design: We used Claude to assist with generating and refining the dashboard interface.

Challenges we ran into

Lack of knowledge about web development and the implementation of AI into software
Issues with teammate availability throughout the hackathon
Hardware availability
Transferring HTML to React 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are especially proud of developing a functional web application that combines computer vision with an interactive sustainability dashboard.

Our biggest accomplishment was successfully integrating a YOLOv8 object detection model with a FastAPI backend and React/Next.js frontend, allowing users to identify waste items through a live camera feed.

We are also proud of creating a visually engaging dashboard that makes sustainability more interactive through task completion and virtual forest growth. Bringing these components together during a time-constrained hackathon was a significant achievement for our team.

What we learned

Building Ecoforest gave us valuable hands-on experience in both software engineering and applied artificial intelligence.

Integrating a FastAPI backend with a computer vision model.
Connecting a React/Next.js frontend to backend APIs.
Working with HTML, React, and other web development technologies.
Designing interactive and responsive user interfaces.
Collaborating effectively under tight deadlines and adapting to unexpected technical challenges.

What's next for Ecoforest

We envision Ecoforest evolving into a more comprehensive smart waste management platform.

One of our next goals is to support remote camera integration, allowing users to monitor and classify waste from different locations throughout their homes. We also want to expand our computer vision capabilities to detect and classify multiple waste items simultaneously, providing users with a complete breakdown of how to sort a larger collection of trash.

In the future, we hope to improve classification accuracy, expand the range of supported waste categories, and provide more detailed disposal recommendations based on local recycling guidelines.

Ultimately, our vision is to make Ecoforest an accessible, intelligent tool that helps people make more sustainable decisions in their everyday lives.

R3AI - AI-Powered Robotic Cleanup Simulation

Inspiration

R3AI was inspired by two goals: exploring how robotics and AI can work together in simulation software and addressing a local community problem: waste buildup and environmental cleanliness. We wanted to build something technically innovative and socially meaningful.

Our solution simulates an autonomous cleanup robot that scans an area, identifies trash, determines what it can carry, and plans an efficient waste collection route.

What We Built

R3AI is a simulation-based cleanup platform that integrates AI-powered object detection, optimization algorithms, route planning, and an interactive web interface.

The project combines three main ideas:

Recognize -> identify trash in a target area using computer vision.
Recover -> plan and simulate robot collection runs subject to storage, size, and weight constraints.
Restore -> show the environmental impact and operational performance of cleanup missions.

Furthermore, the project focuses on four main concepts:

AI-Powered Trash Detection: Integrated Hugging Face's YOLO26n model to identify common waste objects, such as water bottles.
Intelligent Collection Planning: Implemented multidimensional tabulation-based knapsack logic to prioritize trash collection while respecting the robot's storage capacity.
Route Optimization: Integrated OSRM to retrieve optimized routes for navigating the cleanup area.
Interactive Simulation: Developed a web-based interface that visualizes scanning phases, route planning, collection runs, and overall cleanup progress.

What We Learned

One of our biggest takeaways was understanding the complexity of integrating AI perception, optimization algorithms, and robotics-style simulation into a unified workflow.

We also explored the trade-offs between simplified optimization models and more physically realistic approaches, particularly when accounting for storage constraints in two-dimensional space. Additionally, we learned how important clear data visualization and thoughtful frontend design are to making complex simulation processes understandable.

Challenges

AI Detection Accuracy: Improving the quality and reliability of trash detection.
Storage Optimization: Adapting knapsack-based selection logic to a robot with two-dimensional storage constraints.
Simulation Realism: Balancing realistic behavior with implementation complexity, particularly when considering a full 2D rectangular-packing heuristic.
Frontend Complexity: Designing a clean, intuitive interface to communicate simulation data and robot behavior effectively.

Impact

R3AI allowed us to explore how AI-powered perception, algorithmic optimization, and robotics simulation can work together to address environmental challenges. By combining these technologies in an interactive platform, we demonstrated a potential approach to making autonomous waste collection smarter, more efficient, and more accessible to simulate and evaluate.

Atlas

Your cameras record. Atlas remembers. A private AI assistant that runs locally, connects to devices, replies with evidence, and continuously learns.

Like
2

Comment

recursive model training

housing model

camera vision

model explosion

Inspiration

AI assistants live in someone else's cloud and only know what you type into them. Your life is spread across devices and apps: a camera at the door, a calendar, Canvas, group chats, a browser, a watch. We wanted one personal AI computer that lives in your home, connects to all of them, remembers what happens across them, helps with your actual week, and keeps that memory on the box while constantly improving. 

What it does

Atlas is one everyday tool: a personal AI computer (an NVIDIA Jetson) that connects to your devices and apps, remembers what happens across them, and helps with your day.

Plugs into anything. Every device or app is a connector: reads sync into Atlas's memory, and anything that writes to the outside world waits for your tap. Today: a camera, the web (search and Reddit through a real browser), Canvas, your Outlook calendar, GroupMe, the campus site, your watch's health data, and voice on your phone. Smart lights, a gate or a car plug in the same way.
Remembers. Everything it hears about becomes events in an append-only log: its memory. The camera is one source: detection, tracking and zones run on the Jetson, and faces are blurred before anything is stored.
Answers in plain English, with evidence. "What happened at our table overnight?" "Where did I leave my keys?" "What's due this week?" Every answer cites the episode, keyframe, message or link it came from. If Atlas doesn't know, it says so.
Alerts and acts, with consent. A package left at the door buzzes your phone. Anything with an outside effect (a message, a calendar invite, a data export) is an approval card on your phone first.
Plans across all of it. Before an exam, Atlas writes a short plan from the course site, Reddit, your group chat and your free slots, and offers study blocks as calendar invites to approve.
Runs your day. Each morning it plans from your calendar, sleep and habits, re-plans when the day slips, and reviews it at night. Day Run lets you play tomorrow on a campus map before you live it. Voice in and out on the phone.
Friends' Atlases plan together. Atlases in a Circle agree on a time through Neon Postgres; each box only answers free, busy or a counter-offer, so nobody's schedule leaves their box.
Waste Watch. Atlas counts single-use items at the table, sees which bin they end up in, and reports the measured diversion rate before and after nudges.
Learns new tasks. Teach a task on the phone, approve the export of blurred keyframes, and a Qwen3.8-27B teacher on an AMD Strix Halo labels them while a LoRA fine-tune of the Jetson's small Qwen runs on a second one.
Pull the plug. Remembering, alerting and answering keep working with no internet; your memory never leaves the box.

How we built it

Jetson (all runtime inference): a Python 3.11 FastAPI modular monolith; an in-process event bus with a durable JSONL log as the source of truth (state rebuilds by replay); SQLite; ultralytics + TensorRT for detection and tracking; llama.cpp (CUDA) serving Qwen3.5-4B Q4_K_M with its vision projector; OpenCV YuNet for face blur; Whisper and Piper for voice. One Runtime interface hides every model.
Agent: common questions are pre-fetched in code and answered from one short prompt, which suits a small quantized model; open questions use a tool loop capped at 3 calls. Rules are YAML or plain English turned into validated JSON and evaluated on event time, so alerts work offline.
Connectors: each source is an MCP server; reads sync on a timer, writes become approval cards. The browser connector uses patchright in a visible, persistent profile.
Learning lab (AMD): two AMD Strix Halo pods (Radeon 8060S, gfx1151, 64 GB shared memory) on AMD's AUP Learning Cloud. The teacher is vLLM built from source for gfx1151 with our patch, serving Qwen3.8-27B; the trainer is PyTorch + PEFT/TRL LoRA. amd-smi and tegrastats give watts, so every answer and training run has a joule count.
Circle: Neon Postgres for shared state (agent messages, RSVPs, leaderboards), with a local outbox so the box works offline.
Phone: a web app served by the Jetson, a WebSocket event stream, and self-hosted ntfy for alerts and approval buttons.
Team process: four people, each with a coding agent, coordinating through Notion task locks, Q&A pages and an overnight status board.

Challenges we ran into

Making a 4B model reliable. Multi-step tool calling is shaky on a small quantized model, so the most common questions skip the tool loop. We wrote 48 ways a judge might ask our 8 demo questions: 35/42 at first, 48/48 after the fixes, answers in 0.6s.
Losing our GPUs mid-hackathon. The hub with our two Radeon AI PRO R9700s went down on Saturday, so we moved the lab to two Strix Halo pods and rebuilt vLLM for a new chip.
Fine-tuning on AMD. A 27B model is ~54 GB in bf16, too big to train on one device, which is why we went teacher-student.
Bot checks. Headless browsers get CAPTCHAs; a visible, persistent profile gets through for the sites a person would visit anyway.
Replay safety. Rebuilding state from the log must never resend a message or repeat an approved action, so handlers opt in to replay explicitly.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Everything at runtime happens on the Jetson: one box for memory, answers and actions across every connected device; the GPUs are only where Atlas learns.
Every answer cites its evidence, and every outside action needs a tap.
From the box's own log on Saturday: ~10,700 frames seen, 9,738 objects and people observed, 19 episodes remembered, 55 cited answers, 725 calendar/Canvas/chat items read. 
YOLO11n TensorRT FP16 at 41 FPS; a 30-minute soak at 15 fps with 0 errors; Qwen3.5-4B at 13–14 tok/s on the Orin Nano.

What we learned

Pre-fetching beats tool loops for small models.
An append-only event log makes a system safe to change while it runs.
Consent is a product feature: approval cards made the agent feel trustworthy, not risky.

What's next for Atlas

More connectors: smart lights, a garage gate, the car, so Atlas can see more of your life and (with a tap) act on it.
More learned skills (food, drink and recyclable recognition).
Replays of real footage: frame interpolation on AMD turns approved, blurred keyframes into a short video.
More campus connectors and place packs, so Day Run works on any campus.

Understory

Scout for invasive species with a VR field-survey robot!

Like
9

Comment

Look at our set up

Utilize the Meta Quest to control the robot

Dashboard and look from the Meta Quest

Powered by the Jetson-Nano

Inspiration

Central Florida's conservation land is being overrun by invasive plants such as Brazilian pepper, air potato, and cogongrass.
Crews remove them by hand, but checking whether a removal worked means scouting the land through thick brush, heat, and mud, so most of it is never re-surveyed.
Our goal: a robot that drives through a habitat, maps it, identifies the plants with on-device AI, and turns the survey into a place you can walk through in VR.
Understory is named after the layer of a forest below the canopy, where these plants spread and where people rarely look.

What it does

Maps as it drives: a 2D lidar builds a floor plan live with SLAM, and the robot plans its own survey points on that map.
Captures 360° "bubbles": at each survey point the robot spins in place, stopping every 30° to take 12 photos, each tagged with its heading.
Finds and names plants: an open-vocabulary detector finds plant-like objects, and a biology model names the species and flags it as invasive or native.
Pins each plant on the map: the plant's position in the image plus the lidar range in that direction places it on the floor plan, with a cropped photo saved for each pin.
VR walkthrough: a Meta Quest app shows a tabletop miniature of the map with the robot, bubbles, and pins. Pick a bubble and you are standing inside it, with the plants marked around you.
Before and after: survey once, remove the invasives, survey again, and the app shows which plants are gone and which remain ("7 invasive → 1 remaining").
Voice commands: hold a button on the Quest controller and say "start survey", "take a picture", or "come back home". Speech is transcribed on the robot's own network.
Manual driving: the Quest thumbsticks drive and strafe the robot, and one button is an emergency stop that overrides everything else.
Web dashboard: a live lidar view of the robot and the saved map with its pins, open to any laptop on the robot's network.
Mission logging: every mission is saved to a folder (bubbles, pins, photos, map) that the dashboard and cloud steps read.
Works offline: every model in the live demo runs on our own hardware.

How we built it

Compute: Raspberry Pi 5 on the robot (lidar, camera, mapping, navigation); NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano at the table (AI and dashboard); ESP32 for motor control
Sensing: Slamtec RPLIDAR C1 and a Logitech Brio 101 camera
Motion: mecanum chassis powered by 6× AA cells (7.2 V)
Perception: OWL-ViT for detection, BioCLIP for species ID, Whisper for speech, and OpenCV for panorama stitching, all through PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers
Acceleration: NanoOWL-style TensorRT engine on the Jetson for detection
Robotics: ROS 2 Jazzy in Docker with slam_toolbox, Nav2, twist_mux, and our own mission manager and survey planner
VR: Unity 6 with the Meta XR SDK and OpenXR on a Meta Quest, talking to ROS through ROS-TCP-Connector
Dashboard: Streamlit, with a WebSocket relay for the live lidar and headset view
Data: mission folders handed off through a private Hugging Face dataset
3D reconstruction: MASt3R and gsplat on an AMD Radeon PRO W7900, with Depth Anything V2 as a fallback
Tooling: Foxglove for debugging; pytest for the geometry, voice, and mission logic

Technical details

Two-stage plant ID

OWL-ViT only answers "is this a plant?" using general prompts like "a plant" or "a leaf".
Each box is cropped from the exact frame it came from and passed to BioCLIP, which picks from a fixed list of five species by scientific name.
The list also contains non-plants (a wall, a hand, a laptop). If one of those wins, the crop is dropped instead of being forced into a species.

Rejecting things that are not our plants

The list also holds 20 other living things by scientific name (people, pets, house plants). If one of those wins, the crop is dropped.

TensorRT on the Jetson

The detector runs as a TensorRT engine: 19 ms per frame vs. 62 ms in PyTorch, enough to keep up with the camera at 15 frames per second.

Putting a plant on the map

The box's horizontal position becomes an angle using the camera's field of view; added to the robot's heading, that gives a direction in the map.
The lidar range in that direction gives the distance.
Sightings of the same species within 0.5 m merge into one pin, and a pin is only published after 3 sightings.

360° bubbles

The mission manager rotates the robot in 30° steps using the SLAM heading, waits for it to settle, and asks for a frame.
The 12 frames are sent to the headset as a ring of curved panels at their recorded headings, so the bubble works even when stitching fails.
A stitched panorama follows as an extra when OpenCV can build one.

Who controls the wheels

Three sources can send drive commands, and twist_mux picks one by priority: e-stop, then Quest thumbsticks, then autonomy.
The ESP32 stops the motors if it hears nothing for 300 ms.

Built against fake data first

We agreed on topic names and JSON shapes on Friday night and wrote them down in one file.
Every part was built against a fake mission generator and a mock ROS endpoint, so the Quest app, navigation, and perception could each be tested without the robot.

Challenges we ran into

Heat: running both models on the Pi 5 pushed it to 83 °C in five minutes and throttled the CPU, so the AI moved to the Jetson.
Speed: OWL-ViT takes about 3 seconds per frame on the Pi's CPU, so the detector drops frames and the species step matches each box to its original frame by timestamp.
Lookalike plants: in photos, cogongrass looks like grass and wild coffee looks like leaves. Both scored so low that we dropped the detector threshold to 0.05 and relied on BioCLIP to reject the junk.
False positives: a ceiling decoration was confidently named cogongrass until we added the "not a plant" list.
Faces and decorations: the first live pins were a face named Brazilian pepper and an artificial flower garland named air potato. Adding other species by scientific name fixed it.
Pi power and clock: the Pi rebooted several times and has no clock battery; it once came back almost six hours slow, which breaks ROS transforms between machines.
USB power: on a power bank the Pi 5 limits its USB ports, so the lidar kept dropping out with over-current errors until we raised the limit in the bootloader.
Hotspot: on 2.4 GHz the phone hotspot could not carry the camera stream. Moving to 5 GHz took ping from over a second to 5 ms.
Two of everything: more than once both computers started mapping at the same time, with two mission managers driving the same wheels, until we added a check to the start scripts.
Motor shield: loose I2C wiring made the wheels keep turning after a stop, so the firmware now re-sends stop while idle and recovers the bus.
Humble vs. Jazzy: our navigation code was written for ROS 2 Humble. On Jazzy, slam_toolbox needs lifecycle activation, twist_mux expects a different message type, and Nav2 plugin names changed.
Panoramas with no start angle: OpenCV's stitcher crops its output, so the headset couldn't place pins on it. We switched to always sending the 12 raw frames with their headings.
Boxes off the frame: our detector scaled box heights by the image width, so boxes ran off the bottom of the picture.
Quest build: the first headset build took 13 minutes, and a shader that worked in the editor failed on Android.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A full chain from camera frame to named, mapped plant, built only from open-source models and running offline
Detection at camera speed (15 frames per second) on an 8 GB Jetson, alongside the species model
A VR view where you can stand inside a spot the robot photographed and see what it found there
A before/after comparison that turns two surveys into one number
Two computers, a headset, and a microcontroller sharing one map over a phone hotspot
Four people building in parallel against a shared contract, with a fallback for every fragile part

What we learned

How to split a robot's work across a Pi, a Jetson, and a microcontroller with ROS 2
Chaining a general detector with a specialist classifier, and why a "none of the above" option matters
How much sensor fusion depends on timestamps, clocks, and measured offsets
Building a Unity app against a robot that doesn't exist yet
Thermal and power limits decide where code runs as much as software does

What's next for Understory

An outdoor chassis that can handle real understory terrain
A real before-and-after survey of a habitat, to replace our staged data
A larger species list, including animals
Soil moisture, light, and air quality readings shown as heat maps on the map
Before/after reports and similar-plant search in the dashboard for land managers
Full 3D Gaussian splat reconstructions of each survey site
GPS so surveys line up across weeks and seasons

3D CADASTRAL SYSTEM

A 3D Cadastral System that transforms LiDAR and survey data into an interactive digital twin, enabling accurate property mapping, ownership visualization, and smarter urban land management.

Like
2

Comment
2

Inspiration

Traditional cadastral maps are primarily 2D, making it difficult to represent complex urban properties such as multi-storey buildings, apartments, and vertically divided ownership. We wanted to build a system that brings land records into the 3D era by combining geospatial data, LiDAR, cadastral information, and digital twins.

What it does

Our 3D Cadastral System converts geospatial and LiDAR data into an interactive 3D representation of urban properties. It enables visualization of buildings, floors, and individual property units while associating them with cadastral and land-record information such as ULPIN and LADM concepts. The system provides different visualization modes for elevation, cadastral boundaries, structural information, and urban density.

How we built it

We developed a geospatial processing pipeline that combines LiDAR/elevation data, cadastral boundaries, building footprints, and property information. The processed data is converted into structured 3D building representations and visualized through an interactive web-based interface using Cesium. The architecture is designed to support LADM-based property relationships and future integration with government land-record systems.

Challenges we ran into

The biggest challenges were integrating heterogeneous geospatial datasets, handling differences in coordinate systems and data formats, and converting 2D cadastral information into meaningful 3D property structures. We also had to balance visualization quality and computational performance while working with large spatial datasets.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We successfully created a working prototype that demonstrates the transition from conventional 2D cadastral mapping to an interactive 3D cadastral digital twin. Our system can represent buildings and their spatial hierarchy while providing multiple visualization modes for understanding urban land and property data.

What we learned

We learned how challenging real-world geospatial data integration can be and how important coordinate systems, data preprocessing, spatial relationships, and efficient visualization are. We also gained practical experience with LiDAR processing, 3D GIS, digital twins, cadastral concepts, LADM, and web-based geospatial visualization.

What's next for 3D CADASTRAL SYSTEM

The next step is to move from prototype to a scalable platform by integrating real cadastral and survey datasets, automated building/floor/property-unit extraction, ULPIN linking, LADM-compliant data models, and cloud infrastructure. We also plan to add automated change detection, ownership/tenancy visualization, spatial queries, and APIs for integration with existing land-record systems.

title: PenUmbra SOC Auditor™️
text:
Notifications

Loading...

PenUmbra SOC Auditor™️

Security logs tell a story, but finding it is hard. PenUmbra analyzes simulated logs to provide users with interactive attack graphs, event timelines, and AI-generated event reports. 

Like
1

Comment

Inspiration

All three of us are passionate about cybersecurity, so we wanted to build a tool a security professional could actually use. We’re relatively new to the field, and we wanted a project that was both practical and a way to learn how logs and threat-intelligence dashboards work in real environments.

As beginners, many professional tools felt intimidating. Some have complex UIs because of age, like Windows Defender, and others have to be complex so professionals can find exactly what they need, like Wireshark. PenUmbra instead relies on visual language to convey important information, like suspicious activity and the order events happened in. That became our threat graph, the feature that makes PenUmbra unique.

What it does

Ingests a .log file line-by-line in order to simulate events happening in real time.
As new events come in, the program grabs key info like timestamps, IP addresses, and alerts before moving forward. 
Creates a live graph through a visual map of nodes and lines, turning IPs and accounts into connected dots that light up and show you how an attack spread across the timeline. 
Using Hugging Face, the program sends each node data over to a Gemma AI to read, interpret, and generate an individual node report summary, then sends it back to the program for. It can also send all nodes to create a full report.

How we built it

Front End

Built using React , TypeScript, and Vite to provide a live header, event feed, threat graph, inspector, reports, and detection timeline, all updating together as the replay runs.
Zustand keeps all of the app's live data in one shared place. The app checks the backend twice per second and updates that shared data for every panel. 
Cytoscape.js renders the threat graph using the positions assigned by the backend. Entity types are distinguished by shape and node size.
Inspector shows the selected entity's risk score, detections, and connections, and its per-node report with live status.
Tailwind CSS handles all styling throughout the front end, with a slowly drifting animated background behind rounded panels.

Back End

Flask (Python) is the core of the backend. It exposes the API, the front end polls twice a second, serves the reports, and accepts live log lines.
Python threading runs a background replay of the log file with its original timing, and a separate worker that generates reports without blocking the API.
NetworkX models the graph of users, hosts, IPs, processes, and files, and its spring layout assigns the node positions that the front end draws.
A rule-based detection engine written in plain Python raises alerts and risk scores for brute force logins, path traversal, scanning, and suspicious processes.
The report manager keeps one report per node and queues them for Gemma, with risky nodes first. A node that changes while waiting is merged into a single request with the latest data.
The requests library sends each prompt to the Gemma server, and the program adds the exact risk score, detections, and connections under the model's explanation. If the server can't be reached, a rules-based report is shown instead.

VPN and Local Model

Hugging Face was used to download the gemma-2-2b-it model, which was used to process information that could be sent back to the program to populate the graph and generate the reports. This allowed for immediate understanding and action in case of a major security issue. The Gemma AI allowed for constant data processing without dealing with usage bottlenecks that could lead to major security vulnerabilities.
Tailscale is a VPN that allows multiple machines to access the same server from any distance, so that we could generate reports and catch security breaches as they were occurring. Tailscale was useful for seamless integration of new computers so that they could detect and help resolve breaches as they occurred.

Project Structure

│                        Frontend (React + Vite)                         │
│ ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
│ │ React        │  │ Cytoscape.js │  │ TypeScript   │  │ Tailwind CSS │ │
│ │ Components   │  │ Threat graph │  │ + Zustand    │  │ + shadcn/ui  │ │
│ └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          Backend API (Python)                          │
│ ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
│ │ Flask        │  │ Converter    │  │ NetworkX     │  │ Report queue │ │
│ │ REST API     │  │ convert.py   │  │ Graph, rules │  │ 1 per node   │ │
│ └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          AI & Services Layer                           │
│ ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
│ │ Gemma 2B     │  │ Tailscale    │  │ Rules backup │  │ Token auth   │ │
│ │ Node reports │  │ VPN link     │  │ Offline mode │  │ Access guard │ │
│ └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Challenges we ran into

After running into some issues with usage limits on the Gemini AI, we decided to run an AI  locally on a PC so that we could circumvent these issues. After implementing Gemma, we used Tailscale so we could connect multiple computers to the same VPN. This allowed us to run the web app on multiple machines, so we could process multiple logs at once and do it at any distance away from the main server. 
Combining different elements was also a challenge, as everyone was focused on different tasks (front-end, API set-up and log management, AI-report). We ended up with different implementations and had to make sure that features could work on the API.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Setting up a local AI model with a VPN to use it remotely for the first time. None of us had done anything like this before and now that we know how it's something we can implement into future projects.
Making such a useful tool for cyber analysts. We are all interested in cybersecurity, but before today, we had never made any cybersecurity projects or applied the concepts that we had learned. Being able to successfully complete this project has made the idea of a career in cybersecurity into an actual possibility.

What we learned

How to run a model locally. This is the first time any of the 3 of us downloaded a model from HuggingFace and got it running locally. Now that we know how to do this we won’t have to worry about AI usage limits for future projects.
How to connect to a remote server running on a local PC using a VPN. We did this using Tailscale. This is another useful thing to know as a developer as we can utilize the resources of a much more powerful PC while developing on laptops remotely.
How to build a graph on a React Web App. To do this we used the Cytoscape.js library to render graphs, and then also relied on styling to have different events be represented by different node shapes, color effects, and connecting lines to make an attack path easy to follow visually. 

What's next for PenUmbra SOC Auditor™️

We would like to make it work with logs that are currently being generated. So in real-time attacks, a response with our program could become immediate.
Moving the model onto a dedicated server. Right now the AI runs on a single local PC, which limits how many logs it can process at once. A dedicated server would give us the power to run more AI generation, so PenUmbra can keep up with larger and busier environments. 
Real-time AI responses. We want the AI to generate its analysis and reports as events arrive, instead of after the fact, so analysts get explanations and recommended actions the moment suspicious activity appears on the threat graph.
