title: Waymaker
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Waymaker

Fully offline AI backpack for the blind with haptic obstacle warning and voice assistant

Like

Comment

Inspiration

A white cane is great at finding curbs, steps, and anything on the ground, but it can't warn you about a branch at head height, a bike closing in from the side, or tell you what a sign says. The AI tools that can, like smart glasses and phone apps, mostly depend on the cloud, which disappears in subways, tunnels, and rural areas. We wanted to build something that fills the gaps a cane leaves and never needs a signal to keep someone safe.

What it does

Waymaker is a backpack wearable for blind and low-vision people that runs fully offline on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.

Feel obstacles: two ultrasonic sensors and a chest camera drive vibration motors under the left and right backpack straps. Pulses speed up as obstacles get closer, and turn steady when it's time to stop.
Understand the street: an on-device YOLO11n model tracks people, bikes, poles, and other obstacles, and predicts whether each one is actually on a collision course. A second model reads pedestrian crossing signals and announces when they change.
Ask about the view: hold the button on the strap, ask "What does that sign say?", and Waymaker answers through your AirPods using a local vision-language model.
Safety first: crossing-signal alerts interrupt the assistant mid-sentence, and the motors never wait on the AI. If the camera fails, the ultrasonic sensors keep working.

How we built it

Hardware: Jetson Orin Nano 8GB, a 130° USB camera on the backpack strap, two Grove ultrasonic sensors, two PWM vibration motors, a Grove button, and AirPods Pro over Bluetooth, all wired directly to the Jetson.
Obstacle detection: YOLO11n, exported to TensorRT, runs on the Jetson's GPU. Because a chest camera sways with every step, we measure that rotation from the background and remove it before tracking.
Collision prediction: we estimate time to collision from how fast an object's bounding box grows,
$$\text{TTC} \approx \frac{1}{\frac{d}{dt}\ln s(t)}$$
then project where the object will be when it reaches the user. Both motors fire only if it will cross the walking path.
Sensor fusion: a 100 Hz haptics thread takes whichever source is more urgent per side. Ultrasonic gives true distance up close and catches glass and plain walls; the camera sees farther and knows what's coming.
Voice assistant: pressing the button grabs the sharpest recent frame and starts encoding it in Qwen3-VL-2B (via llama.cpp) while the user is still talking. Whisper transcribes the question, the VLM streams its answer, and Piper speaks each sentence as soon as it's ready.
Demo view: a live MJPEG stream with bounding boxes, motor states, and Q&A timings, served to a laptop over a local hotspot.

Challenges we ran into

Memory: the CPU and GPU share 8 GB, so every model competes for space.
False alarms: early versions buzzed at people just walking past.
A dead board: our first Jetson wouldn't boot, and it took us a while to realize the board was broken.
New to hardware: it was our first time with circuits, so we learned by trial and error.
Wiring: at 11 p.m. Saturday we realized we needed Grove cables. We asked other teams for spares, then made our own with tape.
Loose wires: our chained jumper wires kept disconnecting and were hard to track.
Scarce data: we couldn't find enough labeled data, so we annotated images by hand.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A complete pipeline, from sensors to vibration to spoken answers, that works with zero internet.
Warnings that can tell the difference between someone walking toward you and someone walking past.
A custom 3D-printed case for the Jetson Orin Nano.
Training our own classification model on data we labeled by hand.

What we learned

Safety alerts must be instant while answers can take a few seconds.
Two cheap sensors that cover each other's blind spots can beat one expensive one.
On edge devices, memory runs out before compute does.
Test the hardware first.
Plan and label your wiring before building.

What's next for Waymaker

Testing with blind users and orientation and mobility instructors.
A lighter enclosure and longer battery life.
A better case to integrate Jetson Orin Nano and Arduino

title: Tattle
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Tattle

Your phone is tattling on you. Tattle shows every company your apps secretly contact, live, and explains it in plain English. It sees hostnames only and stores nothing.

Like
2

Comment

Tattle’s AI explains in plain English which companies an app is contacting.

User Interface

Tattle: who is your phone talking to?

Hand someone a phone, they open an app, and a screen fills with every company that app quietly contacts: live, in plain English, with one click to block one.

Inspiration

We come from a cybersecurity background, so we know how big a problem it is when companies quietly collect your data. Most people have no idea how much their phone shares. Privacy policies are long and vague, and the traffic itself is invisible. We wanted to make it visible. Tattle shows, live, exactly which third-party companies your apps are talking to, so anyone can see it for themselves in seconds.

What it does

Tattle is a laptop that acts as a Wi-Fi hotspot. A phone joins it, with nothing installed on the phone. Before an app can connect to a server it has to ask "where is this server?" (a DNS lookup), and on our Wi-Fi we are the one it asks. So we see the name of every server the phone looks up, and never what is sent afterwards.

The screen shows the phone in the middle and one bubble per company around it, coloured and tagged by what the company does: advertising, analytics, social, fingerprinting, content delivery, or the app's own servers. A click on a bubble opens a panel that says who the company is and lists every server name the phone asked for. One more click blocks the company: we answer "that name does not exist", the app cannot reach it, and a counter shows the app trying again and again while it keeps working.

Who it helps

Anyone who wants to know what an app really does and has no time for packet captures. The tools that show this today are buried in settings, show raw server names, or need installing and configuring. Tattle takes a minute and reads like a sentence. From our simulated test session: "In 58 seconds, Demo Game contacted 14 companies: 9 advertising, 1 analytics, 1 social, and 3 others."

How we built it

Tech stack:

Hotspot: Linux, NetworkManager, a virtual access-point interface on the laptop's one Wi-Fi card, iptables for the DNS redirect.
Resolver ("sensor"): Python, one file, one dependency (dnslib).
Backend: Python, FastAPI, WebSocket, state in memory. Optional Postgres for the history of our own test phones.
Screen: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. No framework, no build step, nothing loaded from the internet.
Tracker data: Disconnect's tracking-protection list (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), about 4,400 domains, plus 65 hand-written entries.
AI: an open-source model served by Ollama on an AMD Radeon PRO W7900 through ROCm, reached over an SSH tunnel. 
Tests: 101 backend tests, 35 resolver tests, and a 21-step end-to-end check that runs without Wi-Fi.
In the product: Ollama (open source, on the AMD GPU) names the servers no list knows, writes the session summary and explains each company in the detail panel. The screen never waits for it and labels its answers as guesses.

AI tools we used:

AI coding assistants: Claude Code, used for help writing the hotspot scripts. All code was reviewed by the team.

Challenges we ran into

The hotspot took three tries on real hardware. The network manager refused our virtual interface until it had a hardware address of its own, then moved the laptop's own Wi-Fi onto it. We stopped forcing a layout and let the script use whichever interface was left free.
The phone avoided us twice. First it quietly used its cellular connection, then it sent its lookups to a leftover VPN server. Turning cellular data off fixed the first; redirecting all DNS traffic, whatever its destination, fixed the second.
Blocking looked broken. We blocked an app's server and a message still went through. DNS blocking only acts when the phone asks for a name; it had the answer already and kept a connection open. Shortening every answer's lifetime to 10 seconds made blocks take hold at the app's next connection.
The tracker list is written for websites. Phone-only advertising servers and the phone maker's own servers were missing, and one social network's servers showed up under its parent company. We found these by reading live lookups, not by tests.
A looked-up name is untrusted input. A phone can ask for a name made of markup. We resolve and show plain host names only; anything else is refused and counted.
The screen was built in the last three hours before feature lock, as a plain page instead of the planned framework app: no build to forget before the demo.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A working end-to-end demo: connect a real phone, open an app, and watch the trackers appear live
Turning raw network metadata into something a non-technical person understands instantly
A tracker database built on the open-source Disconnect list, so categorization is grounded in real data rather  than guesses
Plain-language explanations from an open-source model running on AMD cloud hardware
A design that makes privacy feel tangible instead of scary or technical

What we learned

How much a single app can reveal about you through DNS lookups alone, even when the content is encrypted [add a surprising example you saw while testing]
How DNS and hostname metadata really work in practice, including limits like encrypted DNS that hides lookups
How to turn technical data into explanations people actually care about
How to split a project cleanly between frontend, backend, and AI work with a shared contract between us

What's next for Tattle

One-tap blocking of trackers, so you can see a tracker and shut it down
Handling encrypted DNS and newer TLS features so more traffic stays visible
A privacy score per app, so you can compare apps before installing them
A standalone box (for example a Jetson or Raspberry Pi) that anyone can plug in at home
Explanations that work offline with a smaller on-device model

More Screens

Inspiration

Many children and teens with motor differences spend hours on fine motor exercises in therapy, and the exercises often feel like chores. Meanwhile, almost every kid already fidgets with something in their hands. We wanted a fidget toy that also works as practice, so the time a child spends interacting with it, clicking, sliding and spinning, builds the skills they use every day. Jimmy and his games are made for their user to feel success, not judgement by how well their hands cooperate.

What it does

JimmyIt is a handheld fidget toy with buttons, a slider, a rotary knob and a spinner, plus a small OLED screen and haptic feedback. It pairs with an Android app over Bluetooth Low Energy, and the app has minigames that turn the toy into a controller. In Button Hero, you press, strum and spin along to notes. In Knob Quest, you steer Jimmy through a level using two controls at once. There are also stylus games for tapping, tracing and drawing shapes. The toy plays its own games without a phone, stores up to 200 sessions, and syncs those scores to the app the next time it connects. Every game rewards effort with stars, milestones and gentle celebrations!

How we built it

We designed all app screens in Figma, taking inspiration from children’s platforms like PBS Kids, Papumba, and Animal Jam. We used Figma Make to explore initial layouts, then refined the screens through several iterations to establish a consistent visual direction. Accessibility guided our choices around readable text, clear navigation, generous touch targets, and encouraging feedback. We carried a playful, bubbly style throughout the interface to make practice feel welcoming. These Figma screens became the reference for implementing the frontend in React Native, while we designed the toy’s physical enclosure in CAD alongside the software.

The toy runs on a Seeed XIAO nRF52840 with C++ firmware for the Arduino nRF52 core. It reads its inputs through an MCP23017 port expander and an AS5600 magnetic sensor, and drives a DRV2605L haptic motor and an OLED. The app is built with Expo and React Native on a TypeScript monorepo. That monorepo holds a shared BLE protocol, a scoring and sync core, a game SDK, and an app-kit layer, so screens only render. We wrote a simulated "virtual toy" that speaks the real protocol, so the frontend and game authors could build and test without hardware. Golden byte vectors, generated independently in Python, keep the firmware and the TypeScript code agreeing on every byte. We designed the physical enclosure in CAD alongside the software.

Challenges we ran into

Fitting rich toy state into 20-byte Bluetooth packets, and keeping the C++ firmware and the TypeScript codec in perfect agreement, took careful protocol design and lots of tests. Designing for kids with motor differences changed how we think about games. We slowed Button Hero down a lot, widened the timing windows and removed every penalty, so a miss only resets a combo. The hardware also changed as we went: we cut the squeeze sensor and the shirt-button flap, and added a push switch on the knob, which meant updating the protocol on both sides. We also removed AI level generation late in the project, because we decided children's data should never leave the device.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We built a complete loop from designing pages to hardware to app. A child can play on the toy alone, and their scores show up in the app later without being lost or duplicated. The toy approves each phone before connecting, celebrates score moments with animations and haptics, and ends games gently instead of with a "game over."  We shipped six minigames that practice different skills: timing, two-handed coordination, tracing and shape drawing. We're also proud of the architecture, which let firmware, backend, frontend and game work happen in parallel without anyone blocking anyone else. We are also proud of translating our Figma designs into a working frontend with a consistent, fun visual identity, bringing accessibility and playfulness into the same experience.

What we learned

We learned that designing for children with motor differences means considering both how an interface looks and how it responds when a movement takes longer or doesn’t go as planned. Adjusting timing windows, removing penalties, and celebrating small achievements helped us put encouragement at the center of our games. Moving from Figma to React Native taught us to think beyond individual screens and build consistent components, navigation, and feedback. Connecting the hardware, firmware, and app also taught us the value of clear shared contracts and a virtual toy that let us develop without waiting for physical hardware. Above all, we learned to treat accessibility as a starting point for both the physical toy and the digital experience.

What's next for JimmyIt

For Jimmy 2.0, we want to add diagonally arranged buttons that users can press with individual fingers, similar to playing a piano. We also plan to add a physical shirt button and fabric loop so users can practice an everyday task alongside the toy’s games.

title: Knightro Tracker
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Knightro Tracker

Easily track Knightro across campus through an interactive radar. Snap a photo, drop an instant sighting pin on the live map, and tackle daily bounties to earn points and climb up the leaderboard!

Like
4

Comment

Overview of the entire map

Sighting details panel to browse a specific pin when it has been clicked

Recent sightings panel to browse active Knightro sightings with photos, locations, and timestamps

Toggleable navigation menu to switch campuses, check events, leaderboard, and past reports

Panel for uploading a picture to report a sighting

Panel to confirm location of a sighting

Inspiration

After our team realized that we had only seen Knightro a few times and almost always at football games, we wondered: why can't we find him and where is he on campus? After watching Spider-Man, we were inspired by its own Spidey Tracker website. We wanted to bring that same excitement to UCF, giving students a fun way to find our mascot, share sightings, and connect with one another. We understand the importance behind being the face of UCF, and that is why we brought this tracker to life to promote student spirit and social interactions in a fun and friendly competitive manner.

What it does

Knightro Tracker turns rare, lucky encounters with Knightro into a student-powered campus adventure. Students report sightings, discover possible appearances, earn points, and compete through an interactive video-game styled radar interface.

Report a Knightro Sighting

Sign in: Sign in with a UCF email 
Choose the location: Allow location access so the app can retrieve your current coordinates and automatically identify the campus building or nearby area for your sighting.
Snap a live photo: Take a picture directly inside the app, keeping sightings tied to the moment rather than old gallery photos.
Check for Knightro: Our trained Hugging Face recognition model evaluates the photo to determine whether Knightro is present.
Publish and earn points: A successful report drops an instant sighting pin on the live map, appears in recent sightings, and normally awards 1 point.

Other students can follow recent reports to find out where Knightro was last spotted. Pins fade and eventually expire so the map emphasizes recent activity.

Daily Bounties

Each day, a randomly selected campus section is highlighted as a bounty area. Eligible successful sightings inside the highlighted area earn 2x points instead of 1. Everyone can participate, and the bounty remains active for the entire day. A fresh random selection happens at midnight, giving students a new reason to explore.

Campus Events

Our event pipeline collects public listings from KnightConnect, stores their details, and filters for events where Knightro may appear. Instead of filling the map with ordinary club meetings, the tracker looks for appearance-related information and recognizable campus locations. Students can browse likely appearances and open the original event listing for more information. These are potential appearances, helping students plan their search without presenting an event listing as a confirmed sighting.

Leaderboard

The leaderboard ranks students by the points they earn from successful sightings. It adds a friendly competitive element: find Knightro, contribute useful reports, and climb the rankings.

Knight-Sense

Inspired by Spidey-Sense, Knight-Sense looks for signals that Knightro might be nearby. When several participating users open the app near the same building within a short period, the system can trigger an unconfirmed location hint. An upcoming event with a likely mascot appearance can also trigger an alert. Messages such as “My Knight-Sense is tingling near Memory Mall…” give students a place to investigate.

My Photo Reports

My Photo Reports gives each user a personal history of their submitted Knightro sightings. Students can revisit their report records, check their status, and see the locations and points associated with their contributions even after the sightings disappear from the live map.

How we built it

Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript power the responsive interface, inline camera flow, pixel artwork, and retro styling.
Interactive map: Leaflet and OpenStreetMap provide campus navigation, sighting pins, marker clustering, building locations, and highlighted bounty areas.
Backend: Python APIs handle accounts, photo reports, building identification, points, bounties, and Knight-Sense activity.
Databases: SQLite supports the application’s local storage. Our event pipeline uses SQLAlchemy and supports SQLite or PostgreSQL.
Event collection: A Python scraper uses Playwright to collect public KnightConnect listings, Requests to retrieve calendar files, and iCalendar parsing to extract structured event information.
AI recognition: We trained a model with over 150 photos of Knightro and 100 negative samples. The model is stored on Hugging Face and called through Python scripts hosted on Vercel.
Hosting: We used Vercel for frontend deployment and the Python scripts supporting recognition. We also prepared deployment support for the application backend to run on AWS.
Development tools: Claude and Codex helped us implement features, debug problems, and refine the interface. We reviewed and tested the resulting code as a team.

Challenges we ran into

Switching backend approaches meant keeping our API calls, authentication, data storage, and frontend behavior consistent while the architecture evolved.

Automating the event database presented another challenge. Collecting listings was only part of the job: we also needed to parse locations and times, avoid duplicate records, and keep the published feed reliable.

We worked around free-tier limits and restricted resources, which pushed us to prioritize essential features and simplify our deployment choices.

We also had to balance the retro design with usability. The interface needed to feel playful while keeping the map readable, the camera flow simple, and the controls usable on mobile devices.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of turning a simple question like “Where is Knightro?”, into a working project through teamwork and communication.

Seeing the pixel artwork, animated assets, map, and frontend come together into a retro looking experience was also very rewarding.

We are also proud of training a recognition model that successfully identifies Knightro in our test photos. Combining that work with live reporting, campus events, and rewards made the project feel like a complete experience that we're proud to have worked on.

What we learned

We learned how training examples and negative samples affect an AI recognition model, and why testing across different photos matters as much as getting an initial prediction to work. We gained experience deploying frontend applications and Python scripts through Vercel, connecting frontend features to backend APIs, and managing configuration across environments. We also learned more about web scraping, database storage, and keeping automated event feeds consistent. And of course, we learned how to divide responsibilities, communicate through changing requirements, and test the full user experience as a team.

What's next for Knightro Tracker

We want to expand the training dataset with more photos of Knightro across different lighting conditions, poses, distances, and backgrounds. Our goal is to reduce both false positives and missed sightings. We also plan to complete and validate the AWS backend deployment, improve reliability as more students participate, and continue refining the mobile experience. Future interactive features could include new campus challenges, community milestones, and additional rewards for participation. Our goal is to grow Knightro Tracker into a campus tradition that encourages school spirit, exploration, and real-world social connections.

title: ContextLens
text:
Notifications

ContextLens

See the full story behind viral videos. ContextLens fact-checks Instagram Reels and reveals missing context in short clips using AI-powered analysis and evidence.

Like

Comment

ContextLens — Homepage and Features

Instagram Fact-Checking — Evidence Review

Video Comparison — Matching Clips and Timestamps

Inspiration

Short clips and social posts often remove the context that changes how a statement should be understood. Viewers rarely have time to find the original recording, locate the matching moment, or verify factual claims. We built ContextLens to make that process fast, transparent, and accessible.

What it does

ContextLens supports two complementary workflows:

Video context recovery — Upload a short clip and its original video. ContextLens transcribes both, finds the matching passage, shows the precise timestamps, and presents what was said before, during, and after the clip. Optional Gemini insights highlight evidence-based context flags without changing the deterministic match result.
Instagram Reel fact-checking — Paste a public Reel URL. ContextLens retrieves and transcribes the Reel, identifies factual claims with timestamps, and reviews selected claims using grounded evidence and citations. Predictions, opinions, financial advice, guaranteed-return language, and unreviewed claims remain clearly separated.

Results are shareable through stable URLs, and the interface is responsive for desktop and mobile.

A high transcript similarity score does not mean the short clip accurately represents the speaker's message. ContextLens separates word matching from contextual interpretation, helping users recognize when real words may create a misleading impression.

How we built it

The frontend is a React + Vite application deployed on Vercel. The backend uses AWS API Gateway, Lambda container workers, S3 presigned uploads, DynamoDB, SQS, CloudWatch, FFmpeg, and Faster-Whisper running with CPU int8. Gemini provides optional contextual insights and grounded claim reviews, while the API key remains server-side in AWS Secrets Manager.

The asynchronous architecture lets uploads finish quickly while workers perform transcription and analysis in the background. The frontend polls job status and renders completed results using backward-compatible API contracts.

Challenges we ran into

Our biggest challenges were packaging FFmpeg and Faster-Whisper for an AMD64 Lambda container from an Apple Silicon Mac, keeping processing reliable within Lambda limits, securely configuring Gemini, handling CORS across Vercel, API Gateway, and S3, and making uploaded videos playable from shared result pages.

Instagram retrieval also required careful error handling because public Reels can still be restricted by availability, rate limits, or platform changes. We kept manual video comparison as a reliable core workflow and designed AI analysis to be non-blocking.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Deployed two functioning AWS analysis pipelines end to end.
Preserved a deterministic video-matching algorithm while adding optional AI context.
Produced timestamped, citation-backed Reel claim reviews.
Made comparison results and their videos shareable.
Built a polished responsive experience with clear loading, failure, partial-review, and evidence states.
Kept secrets out of the frontend, repository, logs, and API responses.

What we learned

We learned how to design asynchronous media-processing systems on AWS, package ML workloads in Lambda containers, combine deterministic analysis with generative AI safely, and communicate uncertainty rather than presenting AI output as unquestionable truth.

What's next for ContextLens

Next, we would improve retrieval reliability, expand evidence-source ranking, add richer media provenance signals, optimize transcription latency, and support more social platforms while preserving clear citations and human-readable limitations.

HearthWatch

An Edge-AI platform for simulating and monitoring at-risk nursing home and dementia patients in real-time.

Like
7

Comment

GIF

Simulated Room with Real People

GIF

Live Feed

GIF

Resolving an Issue

Opt-in Resident Recognition

GIF

Live on a Jetson Nano: ResNet-18 poseNet finds & Labels 5 People

Jetson Nano & Camera

ResNet-18 skeletons + our Posture Model

Inspiration

Nursing home staff currently have to balance daily care, scheduling appointments, and unexpected requests for assistance. When staffing is limited, it becomes harder to notice when a resident needs help. HearthWatch came from the idea that timely alerts could help staff respond sooner to possible falls, requests for assistance, and missed appointment check-ins. Our goal is to make those needs easier to notice and coordinate, giving staff more time to focus on residents.

What it does

HearthWatch connects local camera observations and care check-ins to a nurse response workflow:

Possible Fall Detection: Our own posture model, trained by us (using timed labels from Hugging Face's OmniFall) and running on an NVIDIA Jetson Nano, labels everyone in view as upright, sitting, or on the floor. Prolonged floor tagging notifies a nurse to check in.
Gesture Help Requests: Recognize a held fist as a request for assistance, with a manual help button as another option.
Nurse Subscriptions: Let nurses select rooms and alert categories, receive updates, and accept responsibility for a response.
Appointment Reminders: Notify the care team when a patient's arrival is not confirmed within 15 minutes of a scheduled appointment.
Camera Health: Flag disconnected sources, stale observations, and missing visibility.
Simulation and Replay: Explore resident activities and staged incidents in a 3D environment where residents and staff navigate with pathfinding. Real people seen by the Jetson appear as live avatars beside clearly labelled simulated residents.

How we built it

Dashboard: Built with React, TypeScript, and Three.js for interactive room visualization and simulation controls, alongside a nurse dashboard that receives WebSocket alerts and supports room subscriptions, response acceptance, and resolution.
Edge Perception: On the NVIDIA Jetson Nano, jetson-inference poseNet (TensorRT) finds every person's keypoints. When someone may be lying down, it adds rotated inference passes, because poseNet sees lying bodies far better when the frame is turned 90°. Our posture model then judges each person in 0.56 ms, alongside res10 face detection, all at about 13 FPS on a 2 GB board. Only structured observations leave the device, never video.
Our Own Posture Model: Written and trained in PyTorch on an RTX 3060 Ti. Using timed labels from Hugging Face's OmniFall, we built about 100,000 training frames from five public fall datasets (including AI-generated elderly residents), extracting body keypoints with YOLO11-pose. The network is a small neural network (7,683 weights), exported to plain numpy for the Jetson.
Monitoring: Implemented in Python and FastAPI, using Pydantic to validate observations and temporal state machines to generate alerts from sustained issues. SQLite preserves appointment schedules and overdue reminders, while WebSockets deliver updates to subscribed nurses.
Simulation and Evaluation: Built a seeded simulation with autonomous resident ing, configurable rooms, and controllable incidents. Synthetic observations passthrough the real monitor and are compared against separate ground-truth timelines to measure detection delay, missed events, and false alerts.

Challenges we ran into

Camera Placement: Height-based floor rules depended heavily on camera position. Our trained model judges body shape instead of position in the frame, so it only needs the whole body in
view.
Incomplete Body Detection: Lying bodies were difficult for poseNet to capture. Rotated inference passes improved keypoint coverage, and we extended them to everyone in view, not just the
tracked person.
Unstable Predictions: Brief gestures, low-confidence classifications, and missing frames could interrupt detection. We added hold times, confidence thresholds, release conditions, and
cooldowns.
Live and Simulated Clocks: Accelerated playback needed to preserve posture timing while camera health reflected actual arrival times. We separated the clocks and isolated replay runs with
unique identifiers.
Identity Without Overclaiming: Face detection establishes presence, not identity. Appointment check-in uses an explicit token. Recognition (YuNet + SFace) is a separate, opt-in demo with fictional profiles.

Accomplishments

Training our own posture model that, on a locked test of 10,333 frames from pemacro F1 of 97.0% (weighted 97.5%):

Floor: precision 97.9%, recall 96.1%, specificity 99.3% (a 0.67% false positive rate)
Upright: precision 98.4%, recall 98.6%
Sitting: precision 95.5%, recall 95.7%
On our own camera it catches 96% of floor frames.

Running it live on a 2 GB Jetson Nano for every person in view, with the panel warning when anyone is on the floor.
Connecting observations to a complete alert -> nurse acceptance -> resolution workflow
Bringing the live Jetson feed into the 3D simulation, so real and simulated residents share one room.
Supporting fist help requests even when the posture model cannot detect a body
Adding persistent appointment reminders and a clearly labelled 15-second demonstration mode.
Evaluating the real monitor without giving it access to simulator ground truth

What we learned

Temporal Reasoning: Useful alerts depends on evidence over time.
Honest Metrics: Splitting by person and locking a test set matters. Validation that shares rooms and cameras with training will overstate accuracy.
Shared Contracts: Pydantic models and generated TypeScript types helped indepeagree on their inputs and outputs.
Uncertainty Handling: Camera silence, occlusion, and weak detections must remain visible rather than imply safety.
Evaluation Design: Repeatable scenarios make failures easier to investigate, iat can still trigger a possible-fall alert.

What's next for HearthWatch

Motion-Aware Model: A model that reads several frames at once, to tell falling to handle close-ups and partial views.
Broader Testing: Evaluate more camera positions, lighting conditions, mobility aids, and real older adults rather than young actors staging falls.
Appointment Interface: Add a calendar and accessible resident check-in control
Resident Feedback: Make it clearer when a help request is received and a nurse is responding.
Access and Retention: Add authentication, protected room access, and configuraing real resident records.
Expanded Evaluation: Report detection delays, missed events, and false alerts across a larger set of scenarios.

title: Cookie Crumbs
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Cookie Crumbs

Analyze cookies, spot hidden trackers, and visualize your digital footprint, one crumb at a time. Open up the cookie jar to learn more about the cookies that follow you around.

Like
6

Comment
1

Cookie Jar (Overview)

Crumb Trail (All Cookies Tracker)

Crumb Test (Website Comparer)

Behind the Crumbs (FAQ)

Settings Page

Inspiration

While brainstorming ideas, we always knew we wanted to create a product that we would use ourselves, one we could confidently say helps improve our everyday life. As computer science students, we know how important it is to keep our data safe and how easy it is to simply give it away. Hence, we created Cookie Crumbs to help educate people on their data and the places it goes.

What it does

Cookie Crumbs is both an extension and website. You can access it through Google Extension or simply go to cookiecrumbs.club to join the Cookie Club. To use the application via extension, simply click on it while on the website you want to investigate. The pop up window will then display the number of known trackers, 3rd party requests, pages accessible and 3rd party domains while giving you the option to be directed to the website. On the website, you will see your cookie jar, a dashboard that shows you a detailed overview of the cookies on the website you last used the extension on. Additionally, you can see the categories of trackers, review the other websites you've used Cookie Crumbs on and their scores, compare websites and learn more about cookies through our Behind the Crumbs FAQ on our website as well.

How we built it

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS, with every illustration designed in Canva and Adobe first. The Crumb Trail is an interactive Cytoscape.js graph where each tracker is a color coded crumb you can click to learn about and Crumb Test compares two sites as cookies dunked in milk. “Open The Cookie Jar” in the extension sends the real scan straight to the dashboard.  We also integrated Neon Auth to support user sign-up, login, logout, and session management, allowing us to build a personalized dashboard experience with protected routes and user-specific scan history.

Extension: We built a Chrome extension using TypeScript and the Chrome Extensions API to analyze the websites users visit. It collects information about trackers, third-party requests, and external domains, then displays a quick privacy overview in a popup. Through our “Open the Cookie Jar” feature, users can transfer their scan results directly into the website dashboard. We implemented communication between the extension's background service worker, content scripts, and web application to make this handoff possible.

Backend: We built our backend using Python and FastAPI to process website scan data, classify trackers, and power the dashboard's privacy features. We used SQLAlchemy to interact with our database and organized API endpoints for scan analysis, history, user preferences, and AI-generated explanations. Our backend also supports consent-based data handling so users can control whether their scans are stored.

Database: We used Neon PostgreSQL as our cloud-hosted relational database, connected to FastAPI through SQLAlchemy and psycopg. We structured our database around websites, scans, trackers, scan-to-tracker relationships, and user preferences. This gives Cookie Crumbs a foundation for organizing scan results, maintaining privacy histories, and associating data with individual users.

AI: We used an open-source model from Hugging Face called "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct". The model never decides who is tracking you. Our classifier and tracker list provide the facts, a small trusted knowledge base describes what each tracker category does, and the model only turns that into readable language. If the model is slow or unavailable, a built-in explanation built from the same knowledge takes over.

Challenges we ran into

Keeping the AI honest. An LLM will happily say a domain is “spying” on you. We solved it with facts-first prompts, hedged language (“can” and “may”), and verified/unverified labels with confidence scores.
Model availability. The open model we first chose wasn’t served by any inference provider, and everything quietly fell back to the built-in answers. We added debug output and a script that tests candidate models, then switched to one that was live.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

An AI feature that can say “I don’t know” and tells users when a label is only an estimate.
Consent enforced on the server so that nothing is saved without opt-in, users can only see their own scans, and AI features can be turned off.  Another feature we're proud of is how our application is able to keep track of all the websites it was used on, building users a history that they can review and reflect on. We're also proud that Cookie Crumbs became more than just a prototype running on our laptops. We connected a working Chrome extension to a full-stack web application, integrated a cloud-hosted PostgreSQL database, and deployed everything to our own domain using Docker and Vultr. Seeing our extension and website communicate successfully in production was one of the most rewarding parts of the project.

What we learned

Grounding an LLM in trusted data makes it far more useful and far safer than letting it improvise. As users, we also learned how much our data is being tracked as some websites contain hundreds of disclosed and hidden cookies alike.

What's next for Cookie Crumbs

Fine-tuning a small open model on labeled tracker domains to improve the classifier, and publishing it on Hugging Face. We also want Cookie Crumbs to be the one stop cookie shop for all things cookies, so in the future we plan on adding an AI chatbot to out Behind the Crumbs FAQ, so users can ask questions and learn more about cookies at their own pace.

TrueFan

TrueFan turns any franchise into an interactive constellation. See where to start, watch in order, unlock entries as you go, and ask AI about confusing lore. Never watch out of order again.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Have you ever tried to get into a show everyone is talking about, only to find out it has four seasons, two movies, a prequel, three OVAs, and a spin-off that takes place between season 2 and season 3?

So you search "what order should I watch it in?" and land on a forum thread with five conflicting answers, a wiki page the length of a novel, and a Reddit comment that spoils the ending in the first line.

Now scale that up to franchises like Gundam, Fate, Star Wars, Doctor Who, or the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Some have dozens of entries across decades, multiple timelines, and characters who show up in the middle of one series and only make sense if you watched another. New fans give up before they start, and longtime fans still argue about the "right" order.

We asked a simple question: what if figuring out a franchise felt like exploring its universe, instead of reading its homework?

What it does

TrueFan is an interactive visual guide that turns an anime franchise into a constellation of connected nodes. Every season, movie, OVA, and spin-off becomes a star you can explore, instead of a line in a boring list.

What a fan wants
What TrueFan does

"I want to get into this show"
Search any anime or franchise and explore its connected universe

"Where do I even start?"
A clear, highlighted starting point for new fans

"What do I watch next?"
A guided viewing path, one connected node at a time

"Don't spoil anything"
Entries unlock as you mark them complete, so you only see what you've reached

"Who is this character again?"
An episode-aware character relationship view showing how characters connect

"Wait, how does this connect to that?"
AI-assisted character graphs that reveal relationships based on your viewing progress

The result: you can go from "I've never seen this" to "I know exactly what to watch tonight" in under a minute, without opening a wiki.

Beyond the watch order

Progress that feels like a game. Completing an entry lights up its node and reveals what's newly unlocked, so working through a franchise feels like charting a map.
Spoiler-safe by design. Locked nodes stay hidden or blurred, and character information is filtered based on your episode progress to avoid revealing future events.
Characters, not just episodes. Fans can explore characters and their relationships within an anime, revealing new information as they progress.
AI-assisted connections, not AI spoilers. Our system uses AI to extract character relationships from episode descriptions, then filters those connections according to what the user has watched.

TrueFan turns a confusing pile of titles into one connected story: for new fans who don't know where to start, and longtime fans who want to see it all fit together.

How we built it

Franchise data. We pull titles, release dates, and relationships for each franchise from the AniList GraphQL API. Each entry becomes a node, and each "sequel," "prequel," "side story," or "spin-off" relationship becomes an edge. For example, searching Fate reveals a connected universe containing Fate/Zero, Fate/stay night, Unlimited Blade Works, Heaven's Feel, and related entries.

Building the watch order. We treat a franchise as a directed graph. We use relationship metadata and release dates to organize the main storyline and related works, while acknowledging that there isn't always one definitive viewing order. Unlocking follows progression rules: an entry becomes available once its prerequisites are completed, with manual unlocking available when needed.

The galaxy view. The universe is drawn using React Flow, ELK.js, and Motion for React. Main-story entries form the core, and spin-offs and side stories branch away from the entries they connect to, so the shape of the galaxy shows the shape of the franchise. Users can navigate between worlds, view the overall constellation, and enter an anime to explore its characters.

Character relationships. Characters are linked to each other through relationships such as allies, rivals, and family. We retrieve episode descriptions through Kitsu and TVmaze where available, use Hugging Face inference to extract character information, and cache the results in Neon PostgreSQL. Character profile pictures come from AniList. Fans can switch from the watch view to a character view that reveals information based on their episode progress.

The AI guide. Our current AI functionality focuses on automatically extracting character information and relationships from episode descriptions. Each extracted fact is associated with the episode where it was revealed, allowing the backend to filter out information beyond the user's progress. We're also interested in expanding this into a conversational AI guide that can answer lore and relationship questions without revealing future events.

Stack: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Flow, ELK.js, Motion for React, Python, FastAPI, Hugging Face Inference, AniList GraphQL, Kitsu, TVmaze, Neon PostgreSQL, and Neon Auth. Frontend deployed on Vercel, backend deployed on Railway.

Challenges we ran into

There is no single "correct" order. Release order, chronological order, and fan-recommended order often disagree. We had to decide which to recommend by default and how to show connected stories without implying that one order is universally correct.
Franchise data is messy. Titles change between regions, OVAs and specials are listed inconsistently, and some relationships ("takes place between episodes 12 and 13") aren't captured in any database.
Making a big universe readable. A franchise with 50+ entries turns into a hairball fast. We iterated on layout, clustering, and zoom levels until the galaxy stayed clear.
Keeping AI spoiler-free. An AI that knows everything will happily spoil everything. We had to filter extracted character information based on each user's progress and make sure advancing or rewinding episodes updated the visible graph correctly.
Deployment and API reliability. We ran into issues with deployment configuration, custom-domain updates, and networks blocking our Railway API hostname. We addressed this by routing production API requests through Vercel and improving our deployment setup.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Turning a franchise's tangled history into a constellation you can understand at a glance.
An unlock system that makes watching through a franchise feel like progress, not homework.
AI-assisted character relationship graphs that reveal information as viewers progress, instead of exposing the entire story at once.
Mapping complex franchises like Fate, with 28 connected anime entries appearing in our demo constellation.
Building researched early-story graphs covering 7 series, 37 story units, 86 character nodes, and 132 directed relationships during the hackathon.

What we learned

Data visualization is about decisions, not just drawing. Choosing what to hide matters as much as what to show.
Fans care deeply about spoilers, so trust is a feature.
AI is most helpful when it's grounded in structured data instead of answering from memory.

What's next for TrueFan

Add more franchises, and let fans suggest and vote on viewing orders.
Switch between release, chronological, and "essentials only" paths.
Sync progress with watch-tracking services like AniList, Trakt, and Letterboxd.
Show where to stream each entry.
Build a conversational AI guide that explains lore and relationships using only information the user has unlocked.
Expand beyond TV and film to games, manga, and books that share the same universe.

Tagline: Always feel like a TrueFan.

title: VIGIL
text:

VIGIL

Low-cost thermal person detection and geolocation for search-and-rescue (SAR) drones.

Like
7

Comment

Drones! : )

GIF

Outside viewpoint of drone

GIF

Man hiding in bush in a midnight environment

GIF

Person exiting thick brush

RedStart - Our custom flight board

3D CAD model of our custom quadcopter

Inspiration

Search-and-rescue operations are often limited by time, manpower, and the cost of specialized equipment. Commercial thermal drones cost thousands of dollars, so many volunteer teams and small departments have one at most, or none. We wanted to find out how far cheap hardware plus AI could close that gap. Our target was a thermal search drone for under $500 that could do real search work, so a team could afford several instead of hoping one is enough.

What it does

VIGIL is a low cost thermal search-and-rescue drone prototype designed to help operators locate people when visibility is limited. The drone cost under $500 to build, which is nearly 1/10th the price of the nearest competitor.

It combines a thermal camera, person-detection AI, and a ground-station dashboard. Operators can watch live thermal footage with tracked person detection, review each suspected person using the exact image that triggered the detection, and see estimated locations when enough telemetry is available.

Operators can also add or remove person markers manually and create search routes. Locally saved maps and terrain elevation data allow prepared mission areas to remain available without internet access.

How we built it
Lepton 3.5 → ESP32-S3 (Wi-Fi) → ground computer (YOLO26 detection + tracking) → Socket.IO → web dashboard
Flight controller (INAV) → ExpressLRS → radio → telemetry bridge → web dashboard

We built VIGIL as four connected systems: flight control, thermal capture, AI processing, and the operator interface.

The drone uses a custom carrier PCB flight board built around a STM32 Black Pill running a fork of INAV which we modified to work with our chosen sensors. We added support for the ISM330DHCX IMU, a BMP581 barometer, and the LIS3MDL magnetometer. Additionally, we added NMEA GPS support as well as a flight data recorder. ExpressLRS was used to communicate with the drone remotely from the controller, while a Python bridge decodes flight telemetry from the serial output of the controller.

A FLIR Lepton 3.5 thermal camera connects to a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 running C++ firmware. The ESP32-S3 captures the 160 x 120 frames from the camera and streams them over Wi-Fi through its own access point. 

The ground computer connects to the hosted access point then pulls the stream in Python.  On that computer two YOLO26 detectors with an extra high-resolution detection layer for small targets run on every frame:

a far-range model, trained on drone thermal footage
a close-range model, fine-tuned on close-up thermal images degraded to look like real Lepton output (motion smear, sensor noise, auto-contrast)

Their detections are merged per frame and tracked with ByteTrack, so people keep a consistent ID. A track is only shown once it has been seen in several frames. Because every pixel carries a real temperature, we also reject "people" too hot to be human, such as lamps and electronics. Our training pipeline uses whole-video validation splits and data-leakage checks.

The dashboard uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, and Socket.IO to bring together thermal review, mapping, telemetry, manual markers, and route planning.

Challenges we ran into

Low-resolution thermal detection was a major challenge. Distant people can occupy only a few pixels, and the Lepton's slow sensor smears anyone who moves. Models trained on clean datasets lost confidence as soon as someone walked, so we fine-tuned on synthetically blurred, noisy frames. Hot objects were the next problem: a shorted circuit board was once detected as a person, which led to the temperature check. Overlapping boxes followed, with one person detected as separate head and body boxes; we fixed that with custom merging rules.

Reliable camera capture required careful handling of packet synchronization, memory buffers, and network delays. We patched the camera library and separated frame acquisition from streaming.

Getting a 7 inch drone to hover stably. Our first takeoff flipped instantly. This added a 12 hour delay to our progress right in the middle of the event. We traced it to a gyroscope high-pass filter in INAV's driver for our IMU that removed the bias a second time after calibration, leaving a constant false roll. Later flights were better, but still oscillated and crashed. We set up proper logging, which due to RAM constraints could only record the last 16 seconds of flight. That logging allowed us to find that our motors had a slight later lag time (40-60 ms) to inputs than most drones which caused the drone to always respond to the current state too late. After that breakthrough we adjusted our gains and were able to achieve a stable hover.

Mapping detections required combining each image with the drone's position, attitude, heading, camera geometry, and terrain. Small convention mismatches matter. INAV reports pitch with nose-down as positive and altitude relative to home, which was not what the CRSF convention implies. We found both by reading the firmware source, and either would have misplaced every pin. Missing or stale information must prevent an estimate rather than produce a misleading pin.

Offline operation required saving both map imagery and numerical elevation data.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud of connecting custom hardware, thermal AI, and a practical operator interface.

Our documented camera bench testing achieved approximately 8.8 unique thermal frames per second at native resolution. We developed a custom INAV target and achieved a stable hover, with roll and pitch held within about 1 degree. The drone streams attitude, barometric altitude, GPS position, and a calibrated compass heading to our dashboard over ExpressLRS.

On live Lepton footage, our blur-trained model detected the person in 94% of frames of an indoor test session, at an average confidence of 0.78. Every live session is recorded, so we can replay it offline and tune detection without the camera attached.

The dashboard provides a human-review workflow that preserves the matching thermal image and bounding box for each detected person. Manual markers let operators supplement the model's observations.

We also built automated tests for critical interfaces, and offline map and terrain support.

What we learned

We learned that reliable detection depends heavily on data quality and evaluation design. Neighboring video frames can make results appear stronger than they are, so separating entire sequences and checking training ancestry matters. Training data also has to look like the real sensor: clean thermal datasets did not prepare the model for the Lepton's blur and noise.

We learned that integration is as important as detection: a correct detection paired with the wrong image, stale telemetry, or a flipped sign convention still produces an incorrect result.

Hardware testing exposed issues that documentation alone could not resolve, including sensor filtering and board orientation.

Finally, we learned that human review belongs in the design from the beginning. Source images, confidence scores, and clear indications of unavailable information help operators judge what the system actually knows.

What's next for VIGIL

Our next priority is completing hardware bring-up and controlled flight validation, progressing from stable manual flight to altitude hold, GPS navigation, and waypoint missions.

We need to calibrate camera mounting, heading, and image-to-telemetry latency, then measure location error against known ground targets.

For the AI, our live testing so far has been at close range. Next we want in-flight Lepton footage across different altitudes, backgrounds, and motion conditions. We'll measure missed detections, false-alert episodes, and detection delay alongside conventional accuracy metrics.

We also want systematic area-coverage routes, persistent review records, easier offline mission preparation, and feedback from search-and-rescue operators to guide the next version.

title: Spore Protocol
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Spore Protocol

An endless horde and zero bullets. Survive the Spore Protocol by freezing the infected to secure your extraction.

Like

Comment

GIF

Checklist complete, the player reaches the truck and escapes the outbreak.

GIF

Scavenge the quarantine zone. Glowing pickups mark weapons and CDC emergency supplies on your checklist.

GIF

The extraction truck’s lights cut through the fog. Get all six supplies before you make a run for it.

GIF

A cured zombie stands frozen and tinted green: one vaccine dart takes it out of the horde for good.

GIF

Chokepoints matter: a narrow, lit corridor funnels the horde straight toward you.

GIF

Non-lethal only: cure zombies with vaccine darts and keep moving. Two hits and you’re infected.

Inspiration

The core idea for Spore Protocol was born from wanting to flip traditional survival horror and round-based zombie mechanics completely upside down. Instead of giving the player an arsenal to mow down the horde, we wanted to create a tense, non-lethal loop where the infected are both the threat and the tool. The inspiration was to use a "cure" mechanic—firing the pistol doesn't kill the zombies; it freezes them in place. This transforms enemies into physical roadblocks, allowing players to manipulate the horde's pathing, plug up choke points, and carve out safe traversal routes through the fog to scavenge supplies.

How We Built It

We built Spore Protocol entirely in Unreal Engine 5 using Blueprint visual scripting. The level was designed with spatial readability in mind, utilizing dense terrain and impassable tree clusters to create looping trench pathways. Because the AI relies on constant AI MoveTo logic without complex sight/sound perception, these narrow pathways naturally funnel the horde, maximizing the utility of the freeze mechanic.

The game loop centers on a HUD bound to the player's inventory state, tracking six specific CDC items (Water, Food, First Aid, Radio, Flashlight, Documents) via direct casting for optimal performance. The extraction sequence is governed by a unified boolean logic check acting as an AND gate when the player enters the extraction trigger volume:

$$W = \bigwedge_{i=1}^{6} I_i$$

Where $W$ is the win state and $I$ represents the collection of the six required supplies. Once validated, the blueprint immediately hides the player character and uses a Set View Target with Blend node to snap the perspective to a CineCamera positioned directly behind the Humvee. It then instantly deploys the final Win Screen UI to the viewport to lock in the victory.

Challenges We Faced

The biggest hurdle was engineering the extraction sequence within the strict time limits of the hackathon. Initially, we wanted to build a complex timeline animation with a full cinematic drive-off for the vehicle. However, managing the player controller, camera transitions, and potential mesh clipping proved too costly for our remaining time. To solve this, we had to aggressively scope down the sequence. We realized that a sudden, clean camera cut to a static shot of the Humvee, paired with hiding the player mesh and popping up the Win Screen, delivered the exact same sense of finality without risking game-breaking animation bugs right before submission.

What We Learned

This project reinforced the absolute necessity of scoping and the power of "smoke and mirrors" in rapid game development. We learned that a clean, simple transition is always better than a broken, complex one. We also deepened our understanding of UE5's camera blending systems, specifically how to properly pass Actor references to cleanly hijack the player's screen using CineCameras. Finally, we learned that level design—specifically using negative space and terrain to funnel AI—can be just as effective as programming complex enemy perception behaviors when racing against the clock.

title: Market Maps
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Market Maps

Lower the physical and mental cost of your grocery trip! A simulation demo that takes your shopping list and calculates the shortest route to every item and the checkout.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

An average able-bodied person's grocery trip can take up to 45 minutes. For shoppers with disabilities, chronic pain, or limited stamina, walking for that long takes a mental and physical toll. Most people wander a grocery store, double back for forgotten items, and cross the store more than once. I wanted a tool that takes a grocery list and gives the shortest possible walk through the store, with clear guidance the whole way.

Core loop

Type your list. Enter items in plain words. The app understands typos ("bannana"), plurals, and common names ("oj" for juice, "tp" for toilet paper), and tells you when the store doesn't carry something.
Get the best route. The app finds the order to visit the aisles that keeps your total walking distance as short as possible, then draws a glowing line on the floor with an arrow pointing the way.
Follow and shop. When you reach an aisle, a prompt asks if you want to pick up each item. Picked-up items are checked off your list and appear in your cart.
Stay on track. If you wander off the line, the route recalculates from where you are. You can also pick items up in any order, and the route adjusts.

How I built it

Engine: Unity, with the A* Pathfinding Project for walking paths, Feel for feedback effects, and Synty's POLYGON Shops assets for the store.
Item data: I used the Instacart grocery dataset from Hugging Face, about 50,000 products across 134 categories. I mapped those categories to the demo store's 12 aisles and built a table of about 30,000 searchable item names, plus a list of common generic items and nicknames.
Real walking distances: The app finds the walking path around the shelves between every pair of stops and records its length.
Finding the best order: Choosing the order of stops is the traveling salesman problem, which I realized halfway through the project. Checking every possible order has a time complexity of O(n!). I used the Held-Karp algorithm, which is O(2ⁿ · n²). It records the shortest way to reach every combination of visited aisles and current position, so for 12 aisles it finds the guaranteed shortest route in about 600,000 steps instead of checking 479 million orders. For lists above 16 aisles, the app switches to the nearest neighbor method to build a good route quickly, then improves it with 2-opt and Or-opt.
Smooth guidance: A* paths are made of straight lines and sharp corners, which look rigid for a person walking, so I replaced each corner with a curve to make the route feel natural. The sim tracks your progress along the route every frame, and the arrow always points along the path ahead of you, up to your next stop.

Challenges I ran into

The arrow got confused. Walking diagonally to the line made the arrow jump and point backward. I fixed it by using a dot product to project your position onto the route and measure progress as a distance that only moves forward, and by keeping the arrow from pointing past your next stop.
Higher difficulty than expected. Although I practice LeetCode whenever I can, I didn't realize this was the traveling salesman problem until I started writing out the logic.

Accomplishments that I'm proud of

The route is mathematically guaranteed to be the shortest for any list in the demo store, and it recalculates instantly.
The number of different products you can type in and get results for.
The sim is polished and feels good to play.

What I learned

Dynamic programming.
How much work real-world data needs before it's usable.

What's next for Market Maps

Accessibility-aware routes: Avoid narrow aisles, high shelves, and crowded areas based on each shopper's needs, using cameras in partner stores to detect crowds.
Audio-only guidance: Spatial sound that guides shoppers with low vision along the route.
Voice input for building the list hands-free.
Real store layouts, so the route works in actual grocery stores.

Built with

Unity, C#, A* Pathfinding Project, Feel, Synty POLYGON Shops, Python, Hugging Face (Instacart dataset)

alien in interrogation

Inspiration

It's easy to feel like an alien when you don't understand what face to make and when.
Alien Interrogation took inspiration from the nuances of social interaction, and how some people, especially those with neurodivergence, struggle to understand them. 

What it does

Alien Interrogation involves a simple gameplay loop, using facial recognition as an input for gameplay. You are being interrogated and shown photo stimuli. Your job is to make the right face and blend in as a human.

How we built it

We utilized OpenCV and GameMaker to detect live facial recognition from the user. First, we utilized Copilot within Visual Studio Code to create a python program and set up a webserver. Using the OpenCV webserver and MediaPipe, we were able to return the shape of the user's face as a JSON. In GameMaker, we requested the webserver for the result, and this allowed us to create an interactive facial recognition experience in Alien Interrogation.

Challenges we ran into

We persevered through conflicting GitHub commits, being abandoned by a team member mid-hackathon, and installing dependency after decency for OpenCV. The process to create Alien Interrogation was difficult yet rewarding. A major challenge we overcame during development was handling facial recognition and understanding different emotions. We switched detection models after prioritizing facial geometry over machine learning.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Alien Interrogation boasts quick, consistent facial recognition, a vibrant atmosphere, and lots of love put into its development. We are very proud of the project we have created.

What we learned

We became comfortable using GameMaker and requesting live responses from a webserver. 

What's next for Alien Interrogation

We hope to detect more emotions, specifically anger and disgust. We also hope to flesh out the story more and explore the vibrant atmosphere.

Trapped in a fantasy world, you have 36 minutes to solve four coding challenges and escape. With Bao Bao, your AI-powered panda companion, turn programming practice into an adventure!

Like
3

Comment

Inspiration

What if your dream job depended on your ability to escape another world?

As computer science students, we're familiar with the pressure of technical interviews, coding challenges, and the constant pursuit of becoming better programmers. We wanted to transform that pressure into something more exciting: a fantasy adventure where your programming skills determine your fate.

Inspired by our love for gaming, storytelling, and computer science, we created The Last Commit, an immersive experience that combines coding challenges, artificial intelligence, and an enchanted world.

Our goal was simple: make practicing programming feel less like studying and more like an adventure worth surviving.

What it does

Welcome to Knight Hacks, a world you were never meant to enter.

You awaken in a mysterious amber-crimson forest, surrounded by ancient ruins and an unfamiliar world. You have just 36 minutes to find your way home or become part of this world forever.

Fortunately, you're not entirely alone.

Meet Bao Bao, a friendly, AI-powered panda who becomes your companion throughout your journey. With the wisdom passed down through Grand Bao Bao's book, Bao Bao is ready to offer guidance when you need it most.

Deep within the ruins stand four broken pillars, each inscribed with mysterious ancient text. As an otherworldly computer scientist, you discover that these inscriptions conceal programming challenges.

Interacting with a pillar opens an in-game coding editor, where players must complete partially written programs, execute their solutions, and pass predefined test cases.

Each successfully completed challenge restores its broken pillar. Restore all four, and a magical portal appears, granting you passage back to your world and another chance to pursue your dream job.

But the clock never stops.

If the 36 minutes expire before you complete the trials, your journey ends, and you become one with the world of Knight Hacks.

And Bao Bao does more than offer coding hints. Through facial-expression analysis, our game explores how an AI companion can recognize visible signs of difficulty and respond with encouragement, reminding players that help is always available.

The Last Commit turns algorithmic problem-solving into an immersive, time-sensitive adventure, making coding practice more interactive, engaging, and rewarding.

How we built it

We developed The Last Commit using Unity 6 as our game engine, with C# for game logic and Python for supporting functionality.

Our development process combined game development, artificial intelligence, computer vision, and 3D environment design.

Game Development & Environment

Using Unity 6 and Blender, we created an atmospheric fantasy environment featuring a crimson forest, ancient ruins, interactive pillars, and a portal that represents the player's escape.

We also used Aholo to generate high-quality 3D assets, helping us bring our fantasy world to life within the limited timeframe of the hackathon.

Interactive Programming Challenges

We implemented an in-game coding interface using HTML alongside our other development technologies. Players interact with partially completed programs, fill in missing code, execute their solutions, and receive feedback based on predefined test cases.

AI-Powered Companion

Bao Bao is powered by the OpenAI API, allowing him to assist players as they work through programming challenges.

Instead of leaving players to struggle alone, Bao Bao acts as a supportive companion who can provide hints and encouragement throughout the experience.

Facial-Expression Recognition

We incorporated MediaPipe and OpenCV to analyze players' facial expressions and explore more responsive AI interactions.

This allows Bao Bao to offer encouragement when the player's expressions suggest they may be experiencing difficulty, creating a more supportive learning environment.

Development Tools & Collaboration

Throughout development, we also used ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and GitHub Copilot to support brainstorming, debugging, research, and implementation.

We collaborated using Git and GitHub to manage our Unity project, scripts, and shared assets.

Challenges we ran into

Our biggest challenge was building an entire 3D game under hackathon time constraints, especially because most of our team had never developed a game before.

We were learning unfamiliar tools and workflows while simultaneously trying to build a playable experience.

Integrating multiple technologies was another major challenge. Our project combines Unity gameplay, an interactive coding environment, AI-generated hints, and computer vision, each with its own technical requirements.

We also encountered difficulties with 3D asset compatibility, materials, shaders, and rendering in Unity. Importing assets from different sources sometimes resulted in missing textures or incompatible shaders, requiring troubleshooting and adjustments.

Version control introduced additional complexity. Large 3D assets, Unity scene files, and simultaneous contributions made GitHub collaboration more challenging than we initially expected.

Finally, designing a game that was both educational and entertaining required us to think carefully about the balance between challenge and accessibility. We wanted players to feel the urgency of the countdown without losing the enjoyment of learning.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're incredibly proud that we took an ambitious idea and turned it into an interactive game during a single hackathon.

For most of our team, this was our first experience developing a game, making the entire process a significant learning experience.

One of our favorite accomplishments was creating Bao Bao, an AI-powered panda companion who doesn't just provide programming hints but also encourages players through facial-expression-based interactions.

We're also proud of combining programming education with immersive fantasy gameplay. Rather than presenting coding exercises as isolated questions, we made them part of the world's progression, where every solved challenge physically restores a piece of the environment.

From the crimson forest and ancient ruins to the interactive coding editor and AI companion, each part of the project represents something new we challenged ourselves to learn and build.

Most importantly, we're proud of what we accomplished together.

What we learned

The Last Commit taught us far more than how to develop a game.

We gained hands-on experience with Unity 6, C#, Python, Blender, OpenAI API integration, MediaPipe, OpenCV, and interactive coding interfaces.

We learned how different technologies can work together to create a unified player experience, and how important it is to design around both technical functionality and user interaction.

We also learned how challenging collaborative game development can be, especially when multiple people are contributing scenes, scripts, and assets to the same project.

Beyond the technical lessons, we discovered how educational experiences can become more engaging through storytelling, visual progression, and supportive feedback.

Above all, we learned that being unfamiliar with a technology shouldn't stop us from trying to build something ambitious.

What's next for The Last Commit

We hope to continue developing The Last Commit beyond Knight Hacks.

Our next steps include expanding the variety and difficulty of programming challenges, improving Bao Bao's AI interactions, and refining how facial-expression feedback contributes to the player's experience.

We would also love to introduce additional environments, more interactive characters, and new puzzles that test different computer science concepts.

Eventually, we envision The Last Commit becoming a more complete educational adventure where players can strengthen their programming skills, prepare for technical interviews, and explore imaginative worlds along the way.

Because sometimes, the most important commit isn't the one you push to GitHub. It's the one you make to keep learning.
