Swarm

Cheap attack drones are now one of the biggest threats to bases and infrastructure. Operators practice against scripted enemies. We built a trainer where the enemy learned to attack

Like
4

Comment

Drone attack

Drone attack

Visual Neural Network

Training Explained

SWARM

A counter-drone defense trainer where the enemy swarm taught itself to attack, trained on an AMD Radeon GPU.

Inspiration

Cheap attack drones have become one of the biggest threats to bases and critical infrastructure. Yet the people who
plan air defenses usually practice against scripted enemies that do the same thing every time.

So we asked: what if the enemy in the training sim had to figure out how to beat you? A red team that probes your
defense, finds the radar shadow behind the ridge or the gap between two sensors, and makes you pay for it, the way a
real one would.

What it does

SWARM is a 3D training simulation with three phases:

Defend. Spend a fixed budget on radars (line-of-sight detection, blocked by terrain), jammers (scramble drone
navigation) and interceptor pads. Hover with the radar tool to see exactly what it would cover from that spot.
Attack. Choose an enemy: a classic Scripted A* planner, or a swarm trained with reinforcement learning
at three difficulties (Recruit, Regular, Veteran). SWARM simulates 64 attacks against your defense and
replays a representative one on a sand-table map.
Review. An after-action report shows your breach rate across all 64 attacks, the corridors the drones used, an
automatic blind-spot diagnosis with a suggested fix, the A* planner's view of your defense, and how you compare
to an AI-optimized layout.

What sets it apart from other defense simulations:

Tactics the swarm found. We never programmed tactics. The swarm was only rewarded for getting through. SWARM
mines every attack and names what emerged: wait-and-dash runs, valley runs, radar-shadow corridors, saturation,
pincers, decoys, multi-axis probing. You can draw each one on the map or watch an example. Against the same defense,
A* takes the radar-shadow route; the learned swarm holds position and then dashes.
See inside its head. During a replay, a "What it's thinking" panel shows the selected drone's live move
probabilities and the network's own forecast of whether it will get through. Press N and you get the full
neural network: the drone's actual inputs, all 7 hidden layers firing, the 10 outputs, the neurons that pushed
for or against its move, and an attention map projected onto the terrain. The server re-runs the exact battle
from its seed, so every number shown is what the network actually computed.
Watch it learn. Replay your defense against five snapshots from the swarm's own training run, from random
flight to Veteran, and watch the breach rate climb.
Two theaters. A north-axis mode, and a 360° mode where the base sits mid-map and drones can come from any edge.

Who it helps: air-defense planners and trainees, and anyone teaching how sensor coverage, terrain and layered
defense interact. It works as an automated red team: you find your defense's weaknesses before someone else does.

How we built it

Where
Algorithm

Interceptors
All-pairs Dijkstra next-hop tables per map, so 4,096 parallel battles route every interceptor with one GPU tensor lookup. Targets are picked by threat evaluation (closest to the base, weighed against flight distance) and aimed with lead pursuit

Scripted enemy
Threat-aware A*: distance plus penalties for radar, jammer and interceptor zones, replanning when jamming knocks a drone off course

Learned swarm's senses
The same threat-aware cost field, solved for every cell of every battle at once by parallel Bellman-Ford relaxation on the GPU

Learned swarm's reward
Progress along the plain shortest-path distance to the base

A unit test checks that A* and the Dijkstra tables produce identical routes.

The simulation (redcell/env.py) is written entirely as PyTorch tensor operations: movement, line-of-sight
detection, jamming drift, interceptor assignment and pursuit, kill rolls. The same code runs 4,096 battles on the GPU
for training and one battle on a CPU for the live simulation, so training and what you see on screen can never disagree.

The swarm is one neural network shared by all six drones, trained with PPO. Each drone sees an 11×11 local
view (terrain, radar coverage, jammers, interceptors, other drones, the threat field), a 16×16 map summary and a
few status values. It can move in 8 directions, hover, or "follow the pathfinder". It started from completely random
flight.

An arms race: every 10 training updates, a genetic search over defense layouts finds the defenses that just
barely beat the current swarm, and the swarm trains against those. The same search produces the "AI-optimized"
defense shown in the report.

AMD hardware: we trained on an AMD Radeon Pro W7900D with ROCm. Each theater trained from scratch in about
17 minutes: 252 million drone decisions at roughly 250K per second.

Stack: Python, PyTorch (ROCm), FastAPI, Three.js, procedural Web Audio for sound, and Playwright for end-to-end UI
tests. The UI follows military documents rather than a generic dashboard: an operation order, an after-action
report, MIL-STD-2525-style unit symbols and date-time groups. The simulation runs fully offline.

Results

Measured on held-out strong defenses: layouts the A* attacker mostly fails against, never used in training or
for picking checkpoints. 24 battles each.

Scripted A*
Learned Veteran

North theater (205 defenses)
21.4% breach
29.2% (+36%)

360° theater (252 defenses)
25.0% breach
61.7% (2.5×)

How it beats A*: it spends 4% of its flight detected vs. 11%, waits for openings (taking 70 steps to break
through vs. 30), spreads its attacks over nearly twice as many cells, and follows the pathfinder on only 43% of its
moves, improvising the rest.

When we upgraded the interceptors with threat-based targeting and lead pursuit, A* lost ground. We retrained the
swarm against the new interceptors and it gained: the learned enemy adapts to a smarter defense, and the fixed
pathfinder can't.

Challenges we ran into

The swarm that refused to attack. Our first Veteran posted the best numbers, but against the strongest defenses
it never attacked at all: it loitered outside radar range until time ran out. Two causes: timing out cost the
same as being shot down, and the blue-team search threw away every defense the swarm couldn't beat, including the
ones where it hid. Then the AI-layout search found that habit and exploited it. We made timing out 3× as costly,
kept the stall-inducing defenses in training, and now reject any checkpoint that stalls on more than 10% of drones.
That cost us a few points of headline breach rate, and we report the honest number.
ROCm performance. Small convolutions were 30–60× slower than the equivalent matrix multiplies, and fp32 matmuls
were about 40× slower than bf16. Switching to a bf16 MLP made training 13× faster.
An arms race that stalled. The blue team first kept only unbeatable defenses, which give no learning signal.
The fix was to keep the frontier: defenses the swarm beats about 20% of the time.
Reward hacking. A penalty for being detected made the swarm hide and time out instead of attacking, so we
removed it.
A comparison bug. CPU and GPU random generators with the same seed produce different defenses, so our first
A*-vs-swarm comparison wasn't apples to apples. We now evaluate both on identical layouts.
The cloud box. No internet and roughly 17 KB/s upload meant shipping slim tarballs. Running two GPU jobs at
once crashed the driver, so jobs ran one at a time.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A learned enemy that beats a classic pathfinder on defenses it has never seen, trained from scratch in minutes.
Tactics nobody programmed, detected and named automatically.
A neural network view that shows the real computation behind each move, not an illustration.
Being honest about the numbers: held-out benchmarks, a stall rate on every simulation, and a lower score we chose
over a better-looking broken one.
A polished, end-to-end simulation that runs offline, with unit tests and an automated UI test across both theaters.

What we learned

RL agents will exploit any gap in the reward, and an arms race will find the exploit before you do.
Writing the simulation as batched tensor operations turns the simulation itself into a training environment for free.
Profile on the hardware you actually train on: what's fast on one GPU stack can be 60× slower on another.
Pathfinding and learning complement each other. Give the agent a pathfinding field as a sense and it starts at A*
level, then learns what A* can't: timing, spreading out and dodging.

What's next

Let the player's own defenses feed the blue-team pool, so the swarm keeps adapting to how people actually defend.
Heterogeneous swarms (decoys, fast scouts, heavy strikers) and moving or pop-up air defenses.
Real elevation data (DEM tiles) so planners can train on terrain they actually defend.

Presence

Cameras record known threats but don’t recognize them. Presence alerts security within seconds when a flagged person appears on any camera. A human confirms every alert. It finds missing people too.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Taking attendance manually interrupts class, while scattered check-in records make it difficult to understand participation over time. We built Presence to explore how face recognition and data analytics can simplify check-in and turn attendance records into useful insights.

What it does

Presence is a prototype for automated attendance, designed to reduce manual work and support identity-verification workflows that help staff create a safer environment.

The camera can recognize multiple registered individuals, displaying names, face boxes, and match scores. Participants can be removed from the demo gallery while guests can be temporarily registered and identified on site and then deleted afterward. Unmatched faces in the database appear as “Unknown.”

The attendance system manages course rosters, sessions, and saved check-ins. Our Databricks integration calculates attendance rates, late-arrival rates, and daily trends, then displays the exported results in Presence.

How we built it

We built the frontend with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, featuring UCF and Full Sail themes. A Node.js backend manages PostgreSQL-based attendance workflows, with PGlite supporting our local demo.
Our Python recognition pipeline uses OpenCV, YuNet face detection, and SFace embeddings. A Databricks PySpark notebook validates attendance records, removes exact duplicates, rejects conflicting records, and calculates aggregate metrics. We manually export its JSON report and import it into the app.

Challenges we ran into

We also needed to handle uncertain matches, avoid duplicate check-ins, and preserve existing attendance functionality as we added features.
Presenting results accurately was another challenge: face similarity scores are not accuracy percentages, and synthetic attendance data must be clearly distinguished from real records.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Saving attendance against classes and sessions, with history and corrections.
Analyzing 1,080 fictional attendance records in Databricks and displaying the results in Presence.
Demonstrating how recognition-assisted check-in can support staff verification by making unmatched participants visible, while keeping decisions with staff.

What we learned

Computer vision becomes useful when it supports a clear workflow. We also realized that simply recognizing a person wouldn't solve our problem. As a result, we had to handle uncertainty, preserve accurate records, and give users understandable feedback.

What's next for Presence

We want to connect recognition and classroom attendance into a smoother check-in experience, automate the Databricks report transfer, and measure recognition errors under different lighting conditions and camera positions.
The main purpose of Presence is to automate identity verification and attendance to help staff create a safer environment, whether in a classroom, airport, concert, or a doctor’s office.

ParaEditor

ParaEditor is a perspective based parallax video and photo editor, which also allows you to create visual effects and filters using math.

Like
1

Comment

GIF

Visual effects made using Para Editor

Inspiration

The Nintendo 3DS made me want photos I could look into.

ParaEditor started with that fascination.
I wanted to take an ordinary photo, give it depth, and make its perspective respond to the person looking at it.
Phones and tablets already have cameras and motion sensors.
I wanted to use them to make images that feel alive.

Then I wanted an editor built around that idea.

What it does

ParaEditor turns ordinary photos into interactive scenes with depth and perspective.
Head tracking or device tilt changes the view as you move.
You can edit the image, apply mathematical treatments, draw your own marks, and turn the composition into a moving piece.

The effect system is where things get interesting.
Effects are built from mathematical blocks.
You can rearrange those blocks, open the functions inside them, and get down to the executable source that draws the image.

That makes the effects themselves part of the creative process.
A texture can become a photo treatment or the basis of a custom brush.
You can experiment with the math, see what happens, and keep the result as something you made.

Radeon Cloud GPUs handle the heavier AI preparation while your device handles the creative interaction and rendering.
The iPad becomes the place where you take the photo, work on it, and explore the result.
A public gallery gives those pieces somewhere to go.

How we built it

I built ParaEditor with Claude Code coordinating Codex agents for implementation and review.

The editor uses Preact and a custom WebGL2 renderer, with hand-written shaders for the mathematical effects and perspective rendering.
Cloudflare Pages and Workers host the application and its APIs.
Radeon Cloud provides GPU processing for depth and background preparation.
Neon Postgres stores project records, while Cloudflare R2 stores image assets and published gallery pieces.
Figma was used for user experience planning.

Challenges we ran into

The biggest challenge was building an entire editor in 36 hours.

A parallax effect sounds like a contained project.
Once you want people to create something with it, you need selection tools, layers, drawing, history, saving, and export.
Each feature has to work with the others.
As a solo developer, choosing where to spend that time was difficult.

Mobile memory was another major obstacle.
Running the larger models in the browser pushed my phone and iPad beyond their limits.
Radeon Cloud gave me a way to move that preparation onto GPUs and keep the editor usable on those devices.

That changed how I thought about the project.
The cloud could make more demanding creative tools available on the hardware people already have.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

I’m proud of making something I wanted to exist.

Taking a flat photo and seeing its perspective respond to movement is still my favorite part.
Opening an effect, changing how it works, and carrying that texture into a brush gives the editor another kind of possibility.

I like visuals with some crunch and imperfection.
I wanted a tool that leaves room for people to make those choices themselves, and to make things I would never have thought of.

What we learned

I learned how much of an image’s character comes from math.
A few functions, their parameters, and the order they run in can produce very different results.

Cloud GPUs were my favorite discovery.
Being able to connect a browser editor to remote compute opened up possibilities I had ruled out after hitting mobile memory limits.

I also learned a lot about working with coding agents.
They helped me build far more than I could have written alone in the time available.
Choosing the scope, coordinating the pieces, and testing the actual experience still took attention.

What's next for ParaEditor

I’m keeping ParaEditor open source so people can explore the rendering, take apart the effects, and build on the ideas.

There’s plenty left to polish.
I want to make it easier to create and share effects and brushes, and keep exploring what depth and perspective can bring to an image editor.

The Radeon Cloud GPU service will shut down after the hackathon.
I plan to keep the website online for as long as I can afford it, with desktop hardware running the models locally.
Keeping the same cloud assisted iPad experience available will depend on future GPU hosting.

title: RAWRchery
text:
Notifications

RAWRchery

Draw a real bow with your real muscles. A VR survival game where an EMG armband turns your arm’s strength into arrows against dinosaurs, meteors and a boss.

Like
2

Comment

Inspiration

VR archery usually comes down to pulling a trigger. We wanted the bow to feel like a real bow, where how hard you pull is how hard you shoot. MyoWare EMG sensor on your forearm reads how hard you squeeze, and that squeeze draws the string. We put that idea in the most dramatic setting we could think of: a prehistoric valley full of dinosaurs, a meteor strike, and a final boss. When a dinosaur gets its teeth into you, a vest on your torso buzzes on the side it came from, so you feel where the next threat is before you turn your head.

What it does

The bow lives in your left hand. To shoot, you grab the string with your right hand and squeeze your fist: the MyoWare 2.0 sensor on your forearm turns that squeeze into draw strength, and the arrow flies when you let go. A short calibration at the start (relax, then squeeze as hard as you can) maps your own range onto the bow, so a strong player and a weak player both get a full draw. 

A vest with three vibration motors (left, right, back) tells you where a hit came from. The game works out the attacker's direction relative to your head: a bite from the left buzzes the left motor, from the right the right one, and a bite straight to the face fires all three at once. Harder hits buzz longer.

Calibrate: the game learns your resting and full-strength muscle signal.
Act 1, Survive: dinosaurs spawn outside your view and close in from every side.

Maip is fast and attacks up close.
Gorgosaurus is slower and tougher, and spits acid from range.
Aim matters: a head shot kills instantly, a body shot takes 3 hits, and hitting the legs slows them down.

Act 2, Meteors and the Boss: survive the timer and the sky goes dark. Meteors wipe out the dinosaurs, a box crashes down, and a boss breaks out. His face comes from a photo uploaded from a phone. Defeat him before time runs out, or he snaps his fingers and you lose.
The haptic vest buzzes on the side you get hit, so you feel where the danger came from.

There's a fast mode (30 s survive) for demos and a regular mode (180 s) for the full experience.

How we built it

•One ESP32 on the player's body runs both the armband and the vest, and talks to the game over Wi-Fi. Everything else is Unity.

• Wearable hardware. An ESP32 (LilyGO T-Display) powered from a USB power bank. The MyoWare 2.0's envelope output goes to pin 32; a three-channel relay board on pins 25, 26 and 27 switches the left, right and back vibration motors from their own battery.
• Firmware (Arduino C++). Samples the EMG 8 times per reading, smooths it and streams it to the game 50 times a second over UDP. It listens for hit messages like L,200 and turns strength into buzz length (120 to 400 ms), with non-blocking timers so overlapping hits extend a buzz instead of stacking. Motors are forced off if Wi-Fi drops.
• Networking. Plain UDP in both directions (port 5005 muscle data, 5006 hits). The game sends a silent heartbeat every second so the ESP32 learns the laptop's address immediately, instead of relying on broadcasts that phone hotspots often drop.
• EMG in the game. The armband sends its raw level; the game does the calibration. During "relax" it averages your resting level, during "squeeze" it records your peak, and it maps that range to a 0 to 1 draw (topping out at 85% of your peak, so a full draw doesn't need a full-strength squeeze).
• VR and the bow. Unity 6 with URP and the XR Interaction Toolkit on a Meta Quest Pro over Link. The bow is two-handed: draw strength sets arrow speed, and arrows are simulated with gravity and raycasts so fast shots never pass through a dinosaur.
• Dinosaurs. Two CC BY models from Sketchfab, reduced from about 151k to 29k triangles. On top of the model animations we wrote procedural leg, neck and tail motion that follows the NavMesh agent's real velocity (walking backwards plays the legs in reverse), sidestep and strafe behaviour, several death variations, hit zones (head, body, legs), and per-dinosaur size and colour variation.
• Game flow. A single state machine runs the whole act: tutorial, calibration, practice targets, facing check, countdown, survival timer, cutscene and restart. Every tuning number (round length, health, spawn arc, music volumes) lives in one config asset, so we tuned the game without touching code.
• The world. We rendered the full terrain map plus 25 close-up sheets, walked the best candidates in the headset, and picked a clearing that looks out over a valley. We baked a NavMesh for just the arena.
• Face-scan boss. MediaPipe Face Mesh (ONNX) runs locally through Unity's Inference Engine, finds 468 landmarks in three passes, and builds a 3D face mesh fitted to a generic head. Hair style and colour are read from the photo. Consent comes first, and the photo lives in memory only.
• Audio and video. The battle music was generated by our team with Suno; the meteor cutscene plays through Unity's VideoPlayer on a world-anchored screen while the rest of the world fades to black.
• Teamwork. Four people on four Git branches with Git LFS, a shared contracts file (events, hit zones, haptics and EMG interfaces) so nobody had to touch anyone else's scripts, and test scenes for every part.

Challenges we ran into

_An alpha that could not die. Our big opening dinosaur shared hitboxes with a lighter model whose bones had different names, so arrows passed straight through it. Instead of patching hitboxes one by one, we gave it a whole-body fallback hitbox and turned the bug into a mechanic: it ignores arrows until it has bitten you twice, then one arrow kills it.

Turning a noisy muscle signal into a bowstring. EMG data is jittery and different for every person, so per-player calibration and smoothing were essential.
Missing animations. The dinosaur models only had idle or run cycles, so we built procedural animation ourselves instead of swapping to simpler models.
VR performance. Smoke, fire, foliage and several dinosaurs on screen all compete for frame time, and low frame rates in VR make people sick.
Merge conflicts. Two of us edited the same dinosaur script at once and had to coordinate which branch merged first.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A bow that responds to how hard you actually pull.
A full two-act game loop, from the first dinosaur to the boss fight, built in one hackathon.
Dinosaurs that feel alive despite having almost no original animations.

What we learned

How EMG signals work and how much calibration matters for body-based input.
NavMesh AI, hitbox design and procedural bone animation in Unity.
How to keep a VR scene beautiful and fast.
How to split one Unity project across four people without breaking each other's work.

What's next for EMG Bow

title: Sprouts of Safety
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Sprouts of Safety

Defend Lenny's forest with your eyes: blink Morse code to summon allies in a hands-free tower defense game that teaches you SOS and beyond.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

The theme for this hackathon centered on the enchanted forest that both Lenny and T.K. found themselves in. We wanted to use this to our full advantage when creating the lore for our game and the theming. Since the hackathon features two opposing factions: Blight and Bloom, we wanted to incorporate that into the enemies and allies of our game. This resulted in a game akin to a tower defense, with Morse code as our main objective: SOS is the most famous call for help, so we made a game about answering it. Lenny is nearing the heart of the forest, creatures are creeping in to reach him, and the only way to defend him is to call for help in Morse code.

We also wanted the controls to be unique, fun, and educational. The game is played hands-free, by blinking. A short blink is a dot and a long blink is a dash. That makes it a game you can play without a keyboard or mouse, and it teaches you Morse code while you play.

Features

SOS: Sprouts of Safety is a tower defense game controlled by your eyes.

Enemies walk toward Lenny from the edges of the forest, each carrying a letter and its Morse code.
You blink that letter in Morse. Your webcam reads the blinks, and a forest ally sprouts from Lenny and hunts down the enemy with that letter.
Score and combo: every kill scores points. Chaining correct letters builds a combo up to ×5, and a wrong or wasted letter resets it.
Word waves: every 10th kill, a whole word walks in, spelled left to right across the entrances (SOS, HAT, HELP…), so you practise real beginner Morse words.
An online leaderboard to compete for the top score.
Accessibility options: a calibration screen, adjustable dot and dash timing, and a keyboard-only mode.

How we built it

Engine: Godot 4 with GDScript.
Eye tracking: a Python helper using MediaPipe's Face Landmarker and OpenCV measures how open each eye is. It reports blinks and their length to Godot, and a Morse parser turns those lengths into dots, dashes and letters. The helper is packaged as a standalone executable with PyInstaller.
Gameplay: tile maps with navigation built from the walls, so enemies and allies pathfind to their targets. Spawns rotate fairly across the entrances, and word waves place letters in reading order.
Leaderboard: a small API on Supabase edge functions, with a local fallback when offline.
Art: every sprite, icon, button and background is hand-drawn by our team, from the SOS logo and the wisteria forest to Lenny himself.

Pathfinding

Using Godot's built in nodes for Navigation, we were able to build logic for 2 agents: Enemies and Allies. Enemies seek out the player, while the allies seek out enemies. The nodes allowed us to easily make a navmesh tile set, and search using A*.

Challenges we ran into

Blinks are slow input. A letter takes a few seconds to blink, so the maps had to give enough time to react without feeling empty. We designed switchback lanes and measured how long each enemy takes to reach Lenny until it felt fair.
Telling a blink from a dash. Everyone's eyes and lighting are different, so we added calibration and adjustable thresholds instead of fixed values.
Fighting through walls. Large sprites meant allies and enemies "touched" through bushes and fought across walls. We changed combat so units only meet along the actual walking path.
Getting the camera running on every Windows machine. Getting the plugin for Mediapipe to work with every Windows machine took a lot of debugging due to issues with gitignore.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A full game you can play without touching anything, just by blinking.
It actually teaches Morse code: after a few rounds, you start remembering letters.
All of the art is our own, and it gives the game a warm, storybook feel. 

What we learned

How to run computer vision alongside a game in real time and turn noisy signals into reliable input.
Godot's navigation system, tile maps and scene workflow, and how much level layout shapes the feel of a game.
How to split a game across four people working in parallel on vision, pathfinding, art, and UI, and merge it all together with Git.

What's next

More maps, and difficulty that ramps up over a run.
Tougher enemies that need several allies to take down.
A practice mode for learning the alphabet before playing.
Numbers and punctuation, longer words, and full phrases.
One-click setup, so anyone can download the game and play with their webcam right away.
An art gallery featuring the assets created by the team
A special illustration for reaching a certain high score

title: GestureLab
text:
Notifications

Loading...

GestureLab

With the implementation of an AI assistant, we are able to directly manipulate objects within a 3D workspace directly with our hands.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Having navigated through 3D modeling software, we noticed that the user experience is very clunky and unfriendly, with a steep learning curve to use efficiently, due to the software doing its best to turn 2D mouse movements combined with keyboard shortcuts into 3D movement. 

What if, instead of using the mouse and keyboard to interact with objects in the workspace, we could use our hands and directly manipulate the entities? This would not only completely bypass the challenge of maneuvering a 3D space with 2D inputs, but it could also prove to be more accessible to people with disabilities, especially with our addition of voice recognition.

What it does

Gesture Lab is a browser-based 3D modeling tool that relies on input from your hands and voice, using nothing but a webcam. Workspaces are able to be saved and loaded as .json files on the device.

Hand Gestures
Pinch to grab: pinch an object with your thumb and pointer finger to pick it up and move it. 
Thumb + index will snap the object to the grid or flush with other objects. 
Thumb + middle will allow you to move the object freely.
Push and pull for depth: move your hand closer to the camera to move an object deeper into the space and pull it away from the camera to bring it closer.
Two-hand scale: pinch both hands and bring them apart or together to resize.
Two-hand rotate: twist both hands like a steering wheel to turn an object, or move both hands up or down to tilt it.
Move the camera: pinch empty space and move to rotate the view. Push or pull to zoom in or out.
Press buttons: hover over a button and pinch to press it. The entire app can be run without a mouse.

AI Assistant
Using the microphone button, you are able to voice out commands, with Claude turning those requests into actions on the screen. Using this, you are able to add objects to the workspace and adjust their orientations.

How we built it

Gesture Lab is composed of 3 different services working together in real time:

Computer vision backend (Python): OpenCV captures the webcam, and MediaPipe Hand Landmarker tracks 21 landmarks on each of up to two hands. We detect pinches with hysteresis to avoid flicker, smooth hand positions, detect two-hand scaling, and stream everything to the browser over Flask-SocketIO.

AI backend (Node.js / Express): Claude (Anthropic API) runs as a tool-using agent with tools for creating, moving, rotating, scaling, recoloring and deleting objects, plus generating models. It receives the current scene each turn (including which object you have selected), so it can resolve “it” and “that sphere”. Model generation calls Fal’s Hyper3D Rodin text-to-3D and returns a .glb.

Frontend (React + TypeScript + Vite): Three.js through React Three Fiber and drei renders the scene, and Zustand holds the shared scene state, so gestures, the AI, the gizmo and the Inspector all edit the same objects. All gesture interpretation happens in the frontend from raw landmarks: raycasting from the hand cursor into the scene, camera-facing drag planes, depth from apparent hand size, snapping, collision push-out, and the scale/rotate mode lock. Voice uses the browser’s built-in Web Speech API.

Challenges we ran into

Telling a twist from a stretch. Our first iteration of the two-hand rotation mostly resized objects instead. The cause: the webcam image is 4:3, and distance measured in normalized coordinates grows when hands rotate toward vertical, so a twist looked like a 33% stretch. Correcting for the aspect ratio, plus “first clear movement wins” mode locking, fixed it.

Noisy, ambiguous hand data. Raw landmarks jitter, hands disappear from frame, and MediaPipe’s left/right labels can swap. We added pinch hysteresis, smoothing, deadzones, release safeguards (letting go when a hand vanishes or the connection drops), and tracking by position rather than by label.

Depth from a 2D webcam. A single camera has no real depth, so we used the hand’s apparent size as a proxy: reaching toward the screen makes your hand look bigger, which pushes the object deeper, and vice versa.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A multimodal interface: hands, voice, text, and mouse all edit the same scene, allowing you to switch between them at any time.

Text to 3D in the scene: being able to describe an object, see it be created, and then "physically" pick it up feels like magic.

Being able to create an entire scene without a mouse: create with your voice, and manipulate objects with your hands and voice, no mouse needed.

What we learned

Gesture design is more about what to ignore, rather than detection. Through deadzones, hysteresis, and mode locks, we were able to prevent sensor noise and consequently unwanted gestures/inputs.

Small geometry details, such as aspect ratios, coordinate spaces, and which plane you drag on can make or break how a gesture unfolds.

What's next for Gesture Lab

More gestures: 3D sculpting, drawing custom shapes mid air, duplicating with gestures.

Smarter AI: multi-step building (such as the command, "build a small house"), and better awareness of the user's goals.

Multi-user collaboration: allow users to build together and see each other's hands.

title: CrowdClear
text:
Notifications

Loading...

CrowdClear

A Web & Immersive VR emergency evacuation training simulation: spot crowd jams, open exits, unblock obstacles, redirect the flow, and calm evacuators.

Like
1

Comment

VR View

Action Log

Side By Side Simulation

Review

Results

Score Draft

Figma Tutorial 1

Figma Tutorial 2

Figma Tutorial 3

Inspiration

When a stadium lobby is full and the exit everyone walked in through gets blocked, a staff member has seconds to decide where the crowd goes. Full evacuation drills are expensive and disruptive, so chances to practice that decision are limited, and staff almost never get to see what would have happened if they had acted differently.

We built CrowdClear so staff can run that emergency again and again, hear it the way a real one sounds, and then watch their run play back next to their best one. We also wanted to measure the person in charge, not just the crowd. With Presage, the laptop webcam shows how calm you stayed.

What it does

CrowdClear is an evacuation training game that runs in a laptop browser or in VR through WebXR. You manage a stadium lobby with 60 people and three exits during a 60-second drill.

Guided practice first. Two untimed tasks teach you to open an exit and send people to it. Each step advances only after you actually do it.
A drill that escalates. Two or three blockages hit during the drill. The first lands 10 to 20 seconds in, and each one strikes the exit most people are heading for at that moment. Blocked exits stay blocked until you deal with them: clearing takes four seconds, one exit at a time, and reopening the door is a separate step. Sending people to another exit has a five-second cooldown, so timing matters.
Panic you have to manage. At each incident, about one in five guests panics. They wander, ignore redirects and won't queue until someone calms them. On a laptop, press Reassure and an ElevenLabs voice tells the crowd "You are safe. Follow staff to the open exit. Stay calm." while two or three panicking guests settle. In browsers with speech recognition you can also just say "calm" into the microphone. In VR, that's how you calm people.
Act in the scene. Click a door or blockage with the mouse, or point a controller and pull the trigger in VR. In VR, select a blocked door twice within 450 ms to start clearing it, and the controller pulses when an action goes through.
ElevenLabs voices the incident. A PA announcer opens the drill, calls out each blocked exit ("Attention. Exit B is blocked. Staff, respond now.") and directs the crowd after every redirect, over an evacuation alarm and looping crowd ambience.
Presage measures the trainee. With the Presage SmartSpectra helper running, the HUD shows your breathing rate and pulse from the laptop webcam. After the drill, the results card turns those readings into a 1 to 10 calm score (Steady, Tense or Panicky) and tells you whether this was your calmest run yet.
Review against your best. The review puts people out, time left, guests calmed, guests still panicking and your score next to your best run, along with the longest line and a timestamped log of every action. Drag a 0 to 60 second slider or press Play to watch your best run as wireframe figures alongside this run as solid ones. In VR, −5 s / +5 s buttons and Play do the same.
Shareable runs. Finished drills save to Neon Postgres, and the page link reopens that run's review.

How we built it

Drafting the flow to determine its function. Figma was used to help develop a vague idea of how we wished to develop the application, and how certain elements could look. It was the start of the creative process, to understand color schemes and the layout of different elements.

One deterministic simulation drives everything. The simulation is plain JavaScript with no dependencies and no clock. It advances in fixed 0.1-second ticks, and the live drill, the best-run replay, saved-run reopening and the server's save check all call the same function. A run is just its scenario seed plus a list of timestamped commands (clear, open, redirect, calm), so any run can be rebuilt exactly without recording every person's position.

The crowd model is simple on purpose. People walk at seeded speeds from 1.8 to 3 m/s toward their assigned exit, queue in three columns and keep 0.55 m of personal space. Each exit lets one person out every 1.2 seconds, and every person beyond ten in line adds 0.05 seconds, so a crowded exit gets slower. The Reassure button picks which panicking guests to calm with a seeded shuffle, so calming replays exactly too.

ElevenLabs makes every sound the trainee hears. A Node script (npm run audio) calls the ElevenLabs Text-to-Speech API with the eleven_multilingual_v2 model to voice eight lines: the drill start, a blocked-exit call and a redirect call for each of the three exits, and the Reassure line. It calls the ElevenLabs Sound Effects API (eleven_text_to_sound_v2) for a three-second two-tone evacuation alarm and a 12-second crowd murmur generated to loop.

The spoken text lives in one file that both the game and the generator read, so the audio always matches the on-screen copy. We generate the clips ahead of time and serve them as static MP3s. That means no waiting on audio mid-drill, and the API key never reaches the browser. The alarm plays at 45% volume and the ambience at 25%, so the announcer stays clear over both. If the alarm clip is missing, the game falls back to a synthesized Web Audio siren.

Presage SmartSpectra reads the trainee's vitals. A small Node helper (npm run sensor) uses the Presage SmartSpectra Node.js SDK to read breathing rate, breathing amplitude, pulse and heart-rate variability (Baevsky stress index) from the laptop webcam. It posts the latest reading to the game server about once a second. The page polls it, shows breathing and pulse on the HUD once Presage reports at least 50% confidence, and logs samples for the review from 40%.

At the end of the drill we average the samples and combine breathing, pulse and stress into our own 1 to 10 calm score, compared against the calmest run stored in that browser. It's a training signal, not a medical measurement. Readings stay in server memory and are never written to the database. The endpoint only talks to the same machine unless remote posting is switched on for a deployed demo, optionally protected by a shared token.

A-Frame, Three.js and WebXR bring the lobby into the browser and VR. A-Frame 1.8.0 (built on Three.js) renders the lobby, and WebXR provides the headset session and tracked controllers. Mouse clicks and controller triggers press the same page buttons, so both ways of playing share one set of rules. In VR you stand on a raised command post with world-fixed instruction, analysis and replay panels. Kenney's CC0 Mini Characters make up the animated crowd, with colored foot rings showing each person's exit.

Higgsfield helped create the concourse art. We generated the floor, wall and exterior textures with Higgsfield (GPT Image Flare): three generations for 0.75 credits, compressed to local WebP files totaling about 156 KB. Doors, EXIT signs, equipment cases, smoke and flames are lightweight A-Frame geometry and SVG sprites.

Node.js, Express and Neon Postgres make runs shareable and verifiable. Express 5 on Node.js serves the game and its API. Before saving a run to Neon, the server replays the submitted commands with the shared simulation and rejects any run whose result it can't reproduce. The client picks the run ID, so a retried save never creates a duplicate.

Meta's Immersive Web Emulator let us test VR without a headset. The Immersive Web Emulator browser extension, built on the Immersive Web Emulation Runtime (IWER), emulates a Meta Quest 3 headset and controllers in desktop Chrome. We used it to check VR entry, panel placement, controller-trigger actions and the return to the laptop view.

Automated tests and strategy sweeps. Our 110 automated tests cover the simulation, tutorial gating, panic and calming, multiple blockages, saving and reopening, audio, Presage readings and the VR layout. GitHub Actions runs them on every push to main and every pull request.

We also ran scripted strategies against all 202 drill scenarios (101 first-incident times, each with two or three blockages):

Doing nothing: 12 to 19 of 60 people get out.
Clearing, reopening and redirecting only after each blockage, while calming guests: 34 to 45 get out.
Keeping the lines balanced from the start and clearing right away, but never calming anyone: 48 to 58 get out.
The same, plus calming two guests every 1.2 seconds: all 60 get out, in 34.2 to 49.3 seconds.

These come from scripted bots in our simulation, not human players or real evacuations.

Challenges we ran into

Keeping replays exact as the game grew. Every new mechanic (timed clearing, multiple blockages, panic, calming) had to stay deterministic or replays would drift. Input at a tick is now applied before that tick's incident, calming goes through recorded commands, and even the Reassure button chooses guests with a seeded shuffle. Testing caught replayed redirects losing their target exit. When the rules change, we bump the simulation version (now 9), so older saved runs say they can't be replayed instead of replaying wrong.

Making decisions matter. Early versions cleared themselves without help, and spamming redirects beat thinking. Blocking the busiest exit, a redirect cooldown, slower crowded lines, repeat blockages and panicking guests turned it into a real tradeoff. In the sweeps above, only the bot that spread the crowd early, cleared right away and calmed guests got everyone out.

Calming by voice. Our first microphone version calmed guests whenever it heard moderately loud sound held for a fraction of a second. We switched to the browser's speech recognition, so it only reacts when the trainee actually says "please stay calm", with a 1.2-second cooldown between reassurances.

Running Presage on our hardware. The SmartSpectra Node SDK ships a Windows x64 runtime but not a Windows ARM one, and our laptop is a Snapdragon. We run the helper under x64 Node emulation, where the camera drops below 25 frames per second and readings take longer to become confident; we saw 52 to 54% confidence. A webcam also can't see your face inside a headset, so Presage is a laptop feature for now.

Testing VR without a headset. The Immersive Web Emulator found bugs that laptop testing missed. Controller rays reached only 4 m when the doors are about 25 m away. The panel sat 0.9 m from your face. And because the emulator installs its XR runtime after the page loads, VR wouldn't start at all until we rechecked for a headset when practice begins. Pointing accuracy, comfort and performance still need a physical Quest.

Network limits. Our network blocked outbound Postgres connections on port 5432, so we verified real Neon saves through Neon's serverless driver over port 443.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

A best-run replay that shows, in the same scene, how two runs played out differently.
Runs that rebuild exactly from a seed and a command list, checked by the server before saving.
ElevenLabs audio wired to game events, generated ahead of time with no key in the browser.
Presage webcam vitals turned into a calm score the trainee can try to beat.
One set of door controls shared by mouse and VR controllers.
Game balance backed by strategy sweeps over every scenario.

What we learned

Build determinism in from the start. It gave us replay, server-side checks and testable balance, and every later feature had to respect it.
Measure strategies before tuning by feel. The sweeps showed that a strong strategy without calming tops out at 58 of 60 people. Adding calming gets everyone out.
Pre-generating ElevenLabs audio suits a timed drill: no delay when an incident hits, no key in the browser, and one source file for every spoken line.
Presage gave us a second outcome besides people out: how calm the person in charge stayed while making those calls.
The review deserves as much attention as the drill. Watching your run next to your best is where a score turns into a lesson.

What's next for CrowdClear

CrowdClear is a prototype with a deliberately simple crowd model. Its results are simulation outputs, not predictions of real evacuations. Next, we want to:

Test pointing accuracy, panel placement, comfort and performance on a physical Quest.
Run Presage on hardware it supports natively, and find a way to measure trainees in VR, where the headset hides the face.
Replace the single "calm" keyword with real conversations with panicking guests.
Add navigable obstacles and more floor plans with proper pathfinding.
Add people with mobility needs and coordination between several staff members.
Give trainers tools to assign drills and track progress.
Compare the crowd model with published evacuation research and get feedback from venue staff.

Enchanted Defense

Enchanted Defense: A game where the Bloom fights the Blight, and two first-timers fight GitHub and DevPost!

Like

Comment

Game cover

the banner for the Application

the Icon 

The start of the camera system and its boundry

The map layout and development

The code for the camera movement using InputSystem_Actions

Future game preview #1

Inspiration

It all started with a mix of Celsius Energy Drink, ambition, and a bit of nerves. As a team entering our very first hackathon, we wanted to create something that wasn’t just fun to play, but visually and mechanically driven by the theme. The eternal struggle between Blight and Bloom sparked our imagination. We wanted to give players a choice: do you nurture the resilient, numerous forces of nature, or do you command the heavy-hitting, destructive power of the corruption? That spark became Enchanted Defense.

What it does

What it does...in the future..?!? Enchanted Defense is a top-down tower defense game showcasing a battle between two different sides: the natural Bloom and the toxic Blight. The main goal is to strategically place defensive towers to protect your central power crystal from waves of oncoming enemies.

-The Bloom Faction: Focuses on strength in numbers, rapid fire rates, and map-spreading synergy.

-The Blight Faction: Relies on slow, hard-hitting, high-damage single-target strikes and area-of-effect corruption.

Players strategically place towers, manage their resource pools, and try to survive increasingly difficult waves as the map dynamically reflects the balance of power between the beautiful Bloom and the decaying Blight.

How we built it

For this hackathon, we focused on establishing the visual identity and structural layout of the game. Instead of building the entire game from scratch, we implemented the basic functions of the layout and lighting to showcase our theme's atmosphere. We built using the Unity game engine and C# scripting.

To turn this prototype into a fully complete project post-hackathon, we plan on using:

The Unity Game Engine: To tie our graphics, level layouts, and visual scenes into an interactive application interface.
Pathfinding: Implemented dynamic waypoint navigation for enemy AI to traverse the map.
C# Scripting Layout Structures: To program our grid-placement logic for tower installations, wave-spawning mechanics, and custom enemy tracking loops.
Lighting & Art Assets: To expand on our high-contrast layout, contrasting vibrant greens and pinks for the Bloom with deep purples and sickly greens for the Blight.

Challenges we ran into

First Hackathon Hurdles: Being our very first hackathon, figuring out how to manage our limited time and set up team roles was a huge learning curve.
Brainstorming Overload: It took us a lot of time just to agree on the final project concept and figure out what features we could actually build.
Learning C# on the Fly: LaDonna had to scramble to learn C# coding language basics live during the event to help with documentation and code logic.
Building vs. Workshops: It was tough balancing active development time with taking breaks to attend the educational event workshops to build our skills.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Our biggest accomplishment is simply crossing the finish line and submitting our very first hackathon concept project! Stepping into the competitive hackathon world was challenging, but pushed a basic foundation, and future design and concept artwork for the game to Devpost before the buzzer.

What we learned

As first-time hackathon attendees working as a duo, it was tough but incredibly rewarding. While we only completed the basic foundation, future gaming concepts, and design art work, we gained great hands-on experience with:

Basic prototyping: Building early systems and troubleshooting baseline bugs directly inside Unity.
Team workflow sync: Managing smooth communication channels and navigating live version control together.
Submission cycle: Understanding how to bundle, document, and submit a project for formal judging.
Acquiring new code: Stepping up to learn entirely new programming language logic on the fly.

What's next for Enchanted Defense: Blight vs. Bloom

Our core focus moving forward is on refining and finalizing Enchanted Defense by expanding upon the initial universe we established this weekend. Our development roadmap features: 

Dual-Campaign Mode: Introducing a campaign progression system where level choices dynamically reshape the following terrain.
More Tower Variants: Adding extra tower options for both factions.
Polished Soundtrack: LaDonna will be taking charge of creating a fully polished soundtrack to truly immerse players in the battle.

Dronautics

Revolutionizing drone control with wireless local detection and GPS tracking at a very low cost

Like

Comment

Project Logo

Project Icon

General Hardware device made

The Tello Drone itself

Inspiration

Most drones are limited by a simple factor: the fact that you have to control them. Furthermore, the drones that have built-in sensing, I feel, are too expensive for regular consumers, and also not very practical for day-to-day usage.

I really wanted to make a system that treats the drone as a supporting actor on everything that you perform. Furthermore, I wanted to make it easily affordable, and implementable across any programmable drone line. The "Leash" drone system that I came up with, alongside some built hardware accessories, can help in achieving the accuracy required to transform this into a real product that can aid many different people in different professions, such as construction workers, firefighters, policemen or general consumers. 

What it does

Dronautics is a wearable brace that flies a drone based on body language.
Follow: the drone holds a set distance from you as you walk.
Radius by button: Closer (White button) and Farther (Black button) on the brace move the leash 0.4 m per press, with a haptic buzz to confirm the action took place.
Orbit: the drone circles you while its camera stays locked on you. Done by making the drone move around you in an arc while the camera locks the person in the center.
Target lock: with several people in view, it follows only you. 
Lost and found: if you leave the frame, it looks where you were heading instead of freezing. If fully lost, the drone will start looking in a 360-degree radius, 
Phone control center: a live map with drone support, the camera view, modes, simulators, the radius, and an emergency stop, all on a nicely designed GUI. 

How I built it

This project consists of four technological layers, each one talking to the next: the brace measures your location and angle, a base station relays this information with 30-byte packets, the laptop decides what to do with those packets, and the drone flies.

The brace: an ESP32 reads a BNO085 compass (heading, otherwise the degrees that a person is facing, initialized by the button "a"), two buttons (radius controllers), a DRV2605L haptic driver (feedback by using a vibration motor), and a u-blox MAX-M10S GPS. It broadcasts a 30-byte packet 20 times a second over ESP-NOW.
The base station: an ESP32 on the laptop's USB turns each packet into a JSON line. Did this to prioritize safe, controlled handling over drones on general public areas. 
The brain (Python): YOLO on the GPU finds and locks onto you. Your box gives a bearing and a distance, the brace gives your facing, and the leash calculator places a target point beside you. The YOLO tracker makes sure to scan over your shirt color for further locking of your identity. 
The app: Expo + React Native + TypeScript, linked to the laptop over WebSocket's, designed in Figma first. The app hosts a simulation mode, specifically made for judges that want to utilize the drone in an educational, no-risk manner. 
AMD Cloud RIFE, an open-source frame-interpolation model, runs in PyTorch on ROCm on an AMD Radeon Pro W7900D. It turns the drone's ~15 fps into ~30 fps for the human watching. The drone's AI only ever sees real frames, to not confuse the data tracking. Two streams are visible to the person, to compare and contrast the given interpolated footage. 

Challenges I ran into

I failed in reverse-engineering a toy drone. I originally wanted to make the drone in this project from an old model Snaptain. As I started to program inside of it, I realized that the streaming server for the drone was inaccessible, even if you sent tiny "heartbeats" inside of the drone. Because of this, I decided to go for a really simplistic model for this project and try my best to make the model as advanced as possible, even with a strict budget. Because of this, I landed on a TJI Tello Drone, with a 720p camera, 10 to 2-minute battery span, and no sensor usage.
I also did some rewrites that made the project worse. After the hackathon started, I had a version stacked on separate mathematical rules, each assuming something unchecked about the drone. I rebuilt it around one geometric idea, the target point, plus calibration steps that turn assumptions into measured numbers. Furthermore, every single tool in the brace is used. All of the calibrations and stability aides, alongside pathfinding data present in the drone, is due to usage of every single tool present in the brace.
The insane video lag also was a hard challenge. With the Tello drone, the video frames would arrive considerably late, so the drone always overshot or undershot. The fix was remembering where it pointed when each frame was taken and turning toward where the person is now. The drone, essentially, predicts where the person will be in the future in order to find its way to the person, and recalibrates constantly to center the person in its camera, making this extension perfect for video-recordings.
I had insane difficulty getting into the AMD Cloud. No open ports, SSH blocked, and the platform's tunnel failing with a 403 from a network proxy. I was consistently going over to the AMD Team's office hours, who were graceful enough to help me in generating my own SSH key and also creating my own instance. In the end, starting the tunnel (URL) with the proxy settings removed finally connected the instance to my local base.

What I learned

I learnt the value of consistency. Staying up, late at night, constantly trying to calibrate a drone that lasts a maximum of 2 minutes in the air, was exhausting. However, it was even more gratifying once I saw that the project worked, and that it flew on its own. 
I was also made aware of AMD Radeon technology. I was not actuated with the AMD Cloud, but when I saw that you could interpolate streams to almost double effective fps, I decided to make it a key factor of my project. It was a good call, as I learned many different instance integration techniques and got many different tips from the AMD team. I also made certain to know the limitations of interpolation technology by keeping real data from real streams separate from the interpolated stream, for greater pools of accuracy. 
I also really liked to work on the hardware of this project! Utilizing and wiring different pieces of hardware for this project was generally the most fun part for me. I have many different pages of written blueprints made for this project, which all got put to good use.

What's next

A GPS drone for long-range following outdoors, the hand-tilt gauntlet (firmware's already in production, I just need to design the blueprint...), obstacle avoidance on the real drone model, and moving the general brain of the project from the laptop onto the phone.
Also producing a custom PCB utilizing KiCad, it's almost done!

ReefRoute

ReefRoute is an application that boaters can use to help them saflty navigate around reefs to reach their desired location.

Like

complex reef navigation

Florida map with collapsed menu

Simple-reef-navigation

path with stops

The first path finding prototype.

What inspired us

The Inspiration for ReefRoute is to help prevent damage to our local coral reefs by helping boaters safely navigate these unseen, but delicate ecosystems. We wanted to make a project where the idea could make an impact in the real world and help boaters better plan their routes and traverse them to their desired locations.

What it does

ReefRoute allows the user to select a starting point and a desired destination. The application then plots the shortest path to the destination that avoids land, restricted/protected waters, and of course, coral reefs. The user can then simulate their boat traversing the path.
The biggest goal of the application is to provide boaters with a tool for better planning and raise awareness of our beautiful Florida coral reefs.

How we built it

This application was built using Node.JS and Javascript.
Gemini was a tool that was heavy used to assist in code generation and debugging.
We implemented many parts of the react-leaflet library for building the maps in out application.
The application then uses a grid system and longitude and latitude coordinates to collect a start and end location from the user.
We then implemented an A-star algorithm (treating the map like a grid) to efficiently preform the path finding from point A to point B while avoiding obstacles. Which uses Dijkstra's algorithm to look at the distance that has been traveled at any given point and a Greedy-best-first-search to estimate how much distance is left to reach the goal.
The path is then displayed over the map to the user, where the user can then choose to play the simulation of the boat traversing the route.
Everything was written in JavaScript in order to keep the tech stack simple.

Challenges we ran into

A challenge we faced was getting the animation to work properly as well as balancing the grid square size for accuracy and computational efficiency. If each grid was too small too many calculations would be preformed during the A-star algorithm and the application would be very slow, but if they were too big we would loose accuracy and the path would clip through the edges of obstacles go around them by a large margin them and choose a less efficient path than was possible.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are very proud of what we were able to accomplish with the time we were given. We are also particularly proud of our implementation of the A-star algorithm in JavaScript.
Most of all we are proud of ourselves for working together to lean new things and build a cool project.

What we learned

We learned how to use the react-leaflet library in JavaScript to generate and place polygons on the map to designate obstacles. This was a tool that no one on the team had any experience with.
We also all learned more about Node.JS and JavaScript development best practices, such as: npm can be very dangerous since it has a lot of compromised and malware containing packages. So, we learned to containerize Node.JS in a docker Dev-container to protect our computers from potential infection, and provide a consistent development environment across all of our computers.

What's next for ReefRoute

The next features we would like to add to ReefRoute would be to add full deployment that would allow users to accsses it online. We would alos like to expand our map data to be able to assist with boat navigation on a global scale instead of just for Florida.
We would also like to allow users to uploal information to a ReefRoute server where the update information could be considered to be added to tha application. We could then add the user data to the set to further map and enhance our application. This could possibly even allow more up to date maps and markers then using an automated system that relies on stored data to be updated. It would allow every user to interact with the application and contribute to it and breath life into it allowing it to adapt and grow as fast as our beautiful Earth does.

Inspiration

The inspiration behind Syntax Error is a combination of everything we as computer scientists love and hate: video games, development, bugs, and the idea of our technology breaking. As developers, we can spend endless hours programming only to watch it get ruined by bugs, with some experiences leading to hardware issues and hacks. We wanted to take that experience, and transform it into a thrilling game where everyone can find the love, anxiety, and joy that comes from development, all within a coding based tower defense game.

What it does

Syntax error is an arcade-style tower defense game infused with a coding twist. Built with Python and Pygame, the game combines foundational computer science ideas into real-time strategy. You'll need to defend your CPU, deploying Debuggers, Firewalls, and Antiviruses to combat against Bugs, Memory Leaks, Zero-Day vulnerabilities, and Injection payloads that follow dynamic path finding in order to ruin your code and CPU. 

How we built it

We built Syntax Error in Pygame, as a way to learn a new way to develop video games and expand our experience with Python. Additionally, we incorporated Claude and Antigravity into our programming development to speed up development. For designs, we used a mixture of hand-drawn images and images generated by Adobe FireFly, where we used the hand-drawn images as the references to guide the other art pieces used. 

Challenges we ran into

The key challenges we ran into, and overcame, were integrating a live "Compiler" that can execute and be held back by code, combining and using all of the most appropriate path finding algorithms, and creating an engaging and thematically appropriate UI and gameplay. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Our accomplishments are high and vast, starting with the fact that Knight Hacks IX was the first hackathon that both of us attended. Building a complete project in 36 hours was an achievement in it of itself, but on top of it we learned how best to work with agents in order to build develop code in a healthy relationship with them and develop video games with little footprint in Pygame. 

What we learned

The takeaways we got from this experience was how powerful a sidekick AI agents can be, the ways to incorporate different path finding techniques dynamically, the , and Pygame's ability to create fully fleshed out 2D video games with charming art.

What's next for Syntax Error

In the future, Syntax Error will have a more user-friendly and introductory-friendly compilers, potentially with unlock paths, a universal database to see what the high-score is across every player, the ability to save in the middle of games, incorporating more path-finding for actions executed by players, and more custom sprites or art to further the creativity and theme.

Guiding Hands

Projection meets physical therapy.

Like

Inspiration

Strokes are currently the second leading cause of death worldwide, causing 44% of deaths worldwide, and of the very few who survive, the path to recovery is brutal. This project aims to help those who have had their fine motor skills impacted by a stroke, or other related conditions. By presenting these therapeutic exercises as a way to control a game, we can engage the patient, and ensure a path towards their recovery.

What it does

Guiding Hands is an interactive top down game projected on a board, that uses specific fine motor exercises as a way to engage post-stroke individuals with their rehabilitation of their fine motor skills and improve consistency in their physical therapy.

How we built it

Hardware Acceleration: We utilized a Jetson Nano provided by Nvidia, using the Google Media pipeline model with Linux native hardware acceleration to improve model efficiency. The Nano also runs the game on a locally hosted web app to make the project more accessible.

Gesture Tracking: In conjunction with the Jetson Nano, we were able to use cameras in the project to track the gestures made by the patient's hands to ensure they are properly doing the exercises intended, as well as to let these gestures control the game.

Game Projection: With a projector mounted on top of the main board, we were able to project the game onto the surface of the board, which provides immersion to the patient.

Programmable Robot: One of our goals is bring the game beyond the screen, and unto the physical world, using a programmable mBot combined with an onboard esp32. The Jetson Nano would send executables to the esp32, then the mBot, based on the position of the mBot as seen from a camera on the robot.

Challenges we ran into

There was a challenge when it came to running the Google Media pipeline model on the Nano, which didn't run as fast as we wanted to at first. We resolved this issue by implementing a form of hardware acceleration onto the Nano, being able to run the model over 900% faster.

We also had difficulty in the scalability of the hardware when it came to using the esp32 and the MBot boards, where we encountered many problems, such as the lack of appropriate components, and difficulties in communication between the boards and the Nano. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of the engineering process the team took when it came to resolving issues like the hardware acceleration issue for the Google Media pipeline, being able to work through the problem, and resolve it quickly.
But we are most proud of the fact that we could actually create a system that helps with a real world problem like post-stroke therapy.

What we learned

Through this project, we were able to learn about the uses of hardware acceleration in models, hardware integration and wiring, serial communication with microcontrollers, as well as the issues that come with hardware compatibility.

What's next for Guiding Hands

We hope to be able to be able to more seamlessly introduce the iteration of our design with a sleeker finish, a full robotic integration, and more user-friendly interface.

title: WaveBoard
text:
Notifications

WaveBoard

Education at the flick of your wrist.

Like
1

Comment

GIF

💡 Inspiration

In high school, our classrooms had smart boards that cost a fortune and still got in the way. When one froze or needed an update, the lesson stopped while someone tried to debug it. Every board needed its own mix of software, and most schools can't afford one in every room, or at all.

So we asked: what if the interactive part didn't need a special screen? A projector, a small computer and a webcam can turn any wall into an interactive board. We wanted it to feel like Tony Stark's holographic workbench with JARVIS: reach out and move the lesson with your hands. Teachers get one device for everything they present. Students get 3D models and video, not just notes on a board.

🕹️ What it does

WaveBoard is an all-in-one teaching projector. A Jetson Orin Nano, a USB webcam and any projector become a workspace you control with your hands, with no touch screen, pen or headset.

Your hands are the mouse. The camera tracks your hand and draws its skeleton over the projection, with a cursor between your thumb and index finger. A quick pinch taps a button. Pinch and move to draw, drag or scroll. Swipe an open palm to change slides. Every menu, dialog and setting works by hand, and there's an on-screen keyboard for search.
Draw: a whiteboard with pens, highlighter, eraser and undo, saved as an image.
3D: open GLB, glTF, OBJ and STL models and turn them with your hand.
Slides: present PowerPoint and PDF files.
Video: play, pause and scrub through videos.
Files: open lessons from the device or a USB stick.
Projector mode: lines up your hand with what's on the wall. Point at four targets to calibrate, or let the camera find markers in the corners of the projection.

It's made for real classrooms. Text and buttons stay readable on cheap 480p projectors. It runs fully offline, with no internet, account or subscription. Camera images never leave the device and are never recorded.

💻 How we built it

Hand tracking (Python, OpenCV, NumPy, MediaPipe): MediaPipe's hand landmarker finds 21 points on each hand. Our gesture layer turns them into finger states, pinches and swipes, smooths every joint with a One Euro filter, and maps the camera view onto the projected screen. Camera capture and AI inference run on separate threads and keep only the newest frame, so lag never piles up. Between AI frames, sparse optical flow keeps the hand moving smoothly.
The workspace (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js): a touch-first interface designed for projectors. It runs inside a PyQt5 / Qt WebEngine desktop window, so there's no web hosting, browser or server. The interface calls Python directly through Qt's WebChannel. The hand tracker sends its data to the app through a process pipe, so no network port is ever opened. LibreOffice and Poppler turn PowerPoint and PDF files into slides.
Setup: one install script prepares everything on JetPack 6 and adds WaveBoard to the Applications menu.

‼️ Challenges we ran into

Speed. Our first version read the camera, ran the AI and drew the screen in one loop, and it crawled at about 6 FPS. We split capture from inference, kept only the newest frame, filled the gaps with optical flow, and stopped searching for a second hand when only one presenter is there.
Jitter vs. lag. Raw hand points shake, and heavy smoothing feels sluggish. A One Euro filter, plus pinch thresholds with hysteresis and debouncing, made taps land where you aim without flickering.
Reading real hands. Our first finger-detection rules failed on real hands. We rebuilt them and checked them against real MediaPipe hand photos.
Matching the camera to the projection. The camera sees everything mirrored, at an angle and at a different scale than the screen. That's why we built Projector mode, with hand calibration and corner markers.
The browser got in the way. Browsers ignored hand input for some actions, snap browsers failed to start on JetPack 6, and local servers fought over ports. In the end we moved everything into one offline desktop app with no servers at all.
Teamwork at speed. We built the workspace and the hand tracker in parallel, then merged them into one product.

🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of

You can run a whole lesson with just your hands: open slides, draw, spin a 3D model and play a video.
It's built from parts that cost a fraction of a smart board, and it turns any wall into an interactive surface.
It installs with one command and works completely offline and privately.
Over 120 automated Python tests, plus browser tests, cover the gestures, tracking and interface.

🦾 What we learned

Real-time computer vision on edge hardware, and how much of "accuracy" is really filtering and timing. We also learned calibration and perspective mapping, how to design for hands and projectors instead of a mouse, and how to package a desktop app for NVIDIA's ARM-based JetPack.

🤖 What's next for WaveBoard

Testing in real classrooms, and tuning speed and accuracy on the Jetson at presenting distance
GPU (TensorRT) acceleration for the hand model
Two-hand gestures to zoom and rotate 3D models
Letting students take turns at the board
One enclosure with the projector, Jetson and camera that a school can just plug in

We were inspired by both Pablo's dad, who works in construction, and the popularity of warehouse robots. We wondered why safety inspection has not yet been heavily connected to the construction space. Market research gave us these conclusions: 1. connectivity 2. price 3. environment adaptability. Talking to Pablo's dad also taught us there is much more room for automation and assistance in construction than we initially thought - pre-shift inspection can be incredibly hazardous due to unknown dangers (such as poisonous gas), and mid-shift supervision is often hectic and very limited for the shift supervisor to be able to carry out by himself (no eyes on the back of his head)!  Our goal was to create an MVP for a construction pre-shift and mid-shift inspection & monitoring robot that is able to autonomously drive and use ML for hazard detection and object identification.

What it does

B.O.B (Building-Site Observation Bot) is  a construction safety robot made to reduce injuries and save lives through automating pre-shift inspection and aid the shift supervisor in during-shift monitoring. 
It has 3 areas of focus: 

Providing Offline AI Safety and Inspection - This is where the Jetson Orin Nano Dev Kit came into play. 
Lower Cost - We used easy-to-find, cheap, OTS components such as ESP32 compatible sensors from Amazon, 3D printing, & RC supplies. 
Providing Environmental Adaptability - Using tools such hazardous gas modules for detecting site hazards as radar for detecting humans through dust.
## How we built it
We were able to localize our robot controls and storage by keeping the Jetson fully on our robot, connected to a battery source and our ESP32. Our project utilizes the Jetson Orin Nano Dev Kit with aid from ML tools such as OpenCV data, SH17 weighting, and YOLO, and hardware tools such as ESP32, RC supplies, an iPhone camera, & more.
## Challenges we ran into
Localization was an anticipated and definitely experienced challenge. In addition, many sensors we were aiming to use in construction site conditions were not able to be tested in such due to lack of accessibility during this timeframe. 
## What's next for BOB
Achieve autonomous driving, fully wire and test all environmental and hazard sensors, increase model accuracies, improve product design and durability.

text:
