Sophro Shoppers

Make shopping easier through the art of accessibility

Like

Comment

Computer Vision using ultralytics Yolov8nano

Tablet Display

Items in Cart. Scanned by computer vision software

Shopping UI

Allergy Warning Display

Inspiration

Coming into the hackathon with the idea of a shopping software, we wanted to make a project that is helpful in ways people would never expect. During brainstorming and setup, one of our teammates told us a story that involved one of his middle school friends who was hospitalized after eating stir-fry that unknowingly had peanut oil as one of its ingredients. That’s when we realized that we, as buyers, need to be considerate about the things we buy, because we never know what they contain.

The main problem when it comes to shopping is that not only do buyers spend to the point where they accidentally go over budget, but they also unknowingly buy items that have ingredients that are restricted by their diet. Labels do show the ingredients, but oftentimes buyers would overlook them because of their smaller font size, complex terminology, or the sheer rush of grocery shopping, leaving them unknowingly exposed to health risks.

We decided that for this year's KnightHacks, we would build a user-friendly software that can help make shopping easier through budgeting, macro goals, and dietary restrictions. Want to keep track of your items in the cart? Let our Sophro Shoppers help you practice moderation.

What it does

Sophro Shoppers allows shoppers to get a more in-depth analysis of the items in their cart, while keeping track of needs catered to them. The user will have a tablet and webcam attached to their shopping cart that scans items and informs the user of the macro compositions, the total and subtotal of the items, and whether or not there are dietary restrictions that would restrict items. The user would input their budget and dietary restrictions, change their macro goals, and the software does it for you.

How we built it

React, Vite, Python, and TypeScript are the backbones of our frontend and API. Object scanning runs on Jetson Nano using Computer Vision and YOLOv8 Nano to establish the boundaries for the cart. That way, we can keep track of items coming in and out of it. We also easyOCR to be able to read labels on the items in the cart and classify the brand of the object to give to Gemini for added accuracy. 

Finally, the results are transferred into Google Gemini. The API would scour the database and grab the price, macro composition, and dietary restrictions that come with it and return a validated JSON to display in the UI for the user to see. It will also flag the user if an item is found to have an ingrediant that violates a dietary restriction a user has input.

Challenges we ran into

Computer Vision was the biggest hurdle we needed to overcome because it's the glue that held the project together, since it's the one thing that can help us identify the objects placed inside the cart and ensure proper data can be transferred to the Backend and showcased on the Frontend.

We had issues moving from Windows to Linux, especially with how different each of our laptops is in terms of OS.

Finally, starting up the Jetson Nano took way longer than we expected and, as a result, took a majority of our time that could be spent working on other utilities.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We got the computer vision model to reliably detect the objects we placed in the shopping cart and track their status by adding and removing them, communicating those changes to the Tablet UI screen.

We worked hard on the tablet UI because we wanted users to feel at ease and not overwhelmed. From element coordination to simple color palettes and logos, we aimed to make the backend data as easy to digest as possible.

What we learned

We learned how to use Jetson Nano to empower our project using computer vision, which is another thing we used for the first time. We have also gained experience with using Google Gemini and learned how to prompt it correctly in order to scrape the data we need to properly inform the user about the items they buy.

What's next for Sophro Shoppers

Calorie Counter: We plan to incorporate a calorie counter that would inform the user how many individual and total calories the items in their shopping cart consist of.

Text-to-Speech: Since our project aims to improve accessibility for our users, a text-to-speech option would be essential for those that hae a hard time reading or seeing our UI.

Upgraded Recipe System: While the recipe system is nice to have, we could upgrade it a little more and have Google Gemini scour the internet for recipe links and other items they can buy in order to make those appetizing meals.

Better Mounting Process: Having a Jetson Nano display alongside the mounted tablet and camera would make it so we can use it to roam around in shopping districts and scan more items.

title: KnightScribe
text:
Notifications

Loading...

KnightScribe

A Raspberry Pi in the back of the classroom that records the lecture and the whiteboard, plus a chatbot that knows the whole course and only the course material.

Like
6

Comment
2

Inspiration

Every one of us has sat in a lecture copying what's on the board and missed what the professor was saying while we wrote. Or we listened instead, and the board got erased before we copied the one equation we needed.

Lecture recordings exist, but they're usually a wide shot of the room with muddy audio, and nobody wants to scrub through 75 minutes of video at 1 AM to find a single explanation.

We wanted something a professor could quickly set up and that a student could easily ask questions to afterward. It should know what was said and what was written, and answer like a classmate who never missed a day. It should also only reference material allowed by the professor, not the internet.

What it does

KnightScribe has three main parts.

1. The Capture Device

It's a Raspberry Pi 4 with a camera and a wireless mic. The teacher selects the teaching area and hits record.

From there, the Pi:

Records video and audio on the same clock so they stay in sync.
Transcribes speech live, with captions showing up within a few seconds.
Watches the board and saves a cleaned-up, higher-contrast snapshot once the teacher stops writing.
Checks whether a person is standing in front of the board and holds off on the snapshot if the board is blocked.
Runs snapshots, transcription, and detection only while a recording is active.

2. The Website

Teachers get a lecture library, course materials, and settings for how the chatbot behaves. Students can see board snapshots alongside a timestamped transcript.

3. The "Class Peer" Chatbot

The chatbot doesn't answer from only one lecture at a time. It can search across lectures in the course, including transcripts and board snapshots, so a student can ask about something that was explained earlier and get relevant context.

Teachers can also set limits on what the chatbot is allowed to help with.

How we built it

We split the project across the team, with Jack working on the hardware, Gustavo on the backend, Larry on the frontend, and Yoni on the AI integration.

On the Pi, video and audio capture is written in C/C++, while transcription and board processing are handled in Python. Video goes through the Pi's hardware H.264 encoder at 720p30, and audio is saved as FLAC. For live captions, we show instant streaming drafts and then correct them with Whisper on short pieces of audio. OpenCV handles the board cleanup and person detection.

Gustavo built the FastAPI backend that connects the Raspberry Pi, website, database, and AI features. It handles lecture data, transcripts, whiteboard events, search, quizzes, course settings, and the context used for features like "What Did I Miss?" and the chatbot.

We originally used Render and Neon for the backend and database, but near the end of the hackathon we wanted to get the most complete version of the project working together. We moved the demo to a local database so the Pi, frontend, backend, and AI could all run on the same network and be easier to test and connect.

Challenges we ran into

The Pi only has 4 GB of RAM, and we asked a lot of it. We started at 1080p so board writing would be easy to read, but the Pi couldn't keep that up while also transcribing, so we dropped to 720p30 and moved some of the heavier transcription work off the device.

Early on, the snapshot code would happily photograph the professor's back. Getting the board check and person detection to agree that the board was clear and finished took a lot of testing.

Whisper by itself was too slow to feel live, which is why we ended up using streaming drafts that Whisper corrects afterward.

3D modeling was another challenge. We initially tried using Meshy AI to create our models, but our first print was estimated to take around 22 hours. We had to scale down the design significantly to fit our time constraints. We also had to work around the limits of the 3D printer, which changed how our hardware fit into the final enclosure.

Having four people build different parts of the system also meant we had several pieces that worked well individually before they worked well together. Getting the hardware, backend, frontend, database, and AI onto one network at the event became its own challenge, and in the end we ran the demo locally to reduce extra dependencies and network hops.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Recording, live transcription, and clean board snapshots all running on a Raspberry Pi 4.
Snapshots that skip themselves when someone is blocking the board.
Captions that show up within a few seconds of speech.
A chatbot that can answer using material from across the course.
Hardware, backend, frontend, and AI connected together over one weekend.

What we learned

A real-time pipeline gets tight fast when everything shares one small processor. A lot of the hardware work turned out to be deciding what not to run.

We also learned how important integration is when several people are building different parts of the same system. Something can work perfectly on its own and still need a lot of work once it has to communicate with everything else.

Most importantly, you should build the demo for the network and environment you'll actually be using.

What's next for KnightScribe

A proper mount so the camera stays still and upright in a real classroom.
Testing on real whiteboards and projectors during actual lectures.
Starting automatically on boot, with the Pi creating its own Wi-Fi network so setup is as simple as plugging it in.
A physical record button and status light.
More storage, since an hour of lecture can take a few gigabytes.
Better reading of board text and more teacher controls for the chatbot.

title: Cue
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Cue

Cue: a longevity coach on Meta glasses. AI vision auto-logs healthy habits, suggests swaps the moment you slip, and a clip-on sensor coaches reps, tempo and form. One Longevity Score, zero logging.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

A long, healthy life isn’t built in big decisions. It’s built in small daily moments: the energy drink at 11 PM, the reels in bed, the rushed rep at the gym. Those moments add up. Most health apps only work if you log everything, and most people stop logging. Personal coaching works, but trainers and longevity programs cost more than most people can pay.

I wanted a coach that is simply there in the moment. Cue runs on smart glasses. It sees what you see, speaks up before the bad choice instead of after, and needs nothing typed in. It logs for you: late caffeine, screen time before bed, and every rep with its form. But glasses can’t see how your own body moves, so I built a clip-on sensor that tracks your movement and coaches workouts rep by rep.

No manual logging. No expensive coach. Just the right cue at the right moment.

What it does

Cue has three parts that all feed one Longevity Score.

Gym spotter

Cue Clip: counts curls, times each rep (“Slow down on the way down”), catches half reps (“All the way up and down”) and buzzes when form slips.
Glasses camera: counts squats.
No hardware? The web app counts squats and curls from a laptop camera and scores each rep out of 100.

2.Longevity coach
The glasses log good habits straight from what they see: water, morning sunlight, fruit and veg, brushing, sunscreen, vitamins, stairs and time outside.

Habit breaker
Cue catches late caffeine, doomscrolling, screens at night, vaping and nicotine pouches, sugary drinks, betting apps, late meals and evening alcohol. Then it speaks a short swap in your ear.

Advice depends on the time of day. Coffee at 8 AM gets logged; coffee at 11 PM gets “Put it back.” For nicotine, Cue coaches you through the craving and offers the free quitline, 1-800-QUIT-NOW.

Longevity Score and companion app
Everything rolls into one score with plain reasons. The app shows a Today checklist from morning to night, a Break column for bad habits, streaks and a weekly view. It updates live from the glasses and clip. A demo clock lets you jump through the day to see how the advice changes.

Cue is wellness coaching, not medical advice.

How we built it

I built Cue solo in 36 hours, with Claude as an AI coding assistant. The pipeline runs in six steps:

See: The Meta glasses stream first-person video over a WhatsApp video call to a Windows laptop, where the Cue app screen-captures the call window.
Understand: Every 3 to 6 seconds, one frame goes to a vision model through an OpenAI-compatible API. The live demo uses Google Gemini Flash-Lite. I also served the open-source Qwen2.5-VL-7B on AMD Radeon Cloud with ROCm and vLLM; because the API is the same, the code runs on either model. One prompt asks which of about 20 habits are happening, and whether you are outdoors, in daylight or in the dark.
Decide: A rules engine turns that answer into logs and nudges. It uses the time of day, cooldowns, and two-frame confirmation for things like vaping, so one bad frame never triggers a warning.
Coach: Windows text-to-speech plays into a virtual audio cable that WhatsApp uses as its microphone, so Cue speaks through the glasses’ open-ear speakers.
Feel: The Cue Clip is an Arduino Uno with a Grove accelerometer and a servo that buzzes for haptic alerts, in a 3D-printed case. It streams tilt 50 times a second over USB. My rep counter learns the resting position, so it counts curls however the clip is mounted, and it times both halves of every rep.
Track: The laptop app keeps the day’s score and serves it locally; the companion web app polls it every 2 seconds. The web app also runs MediaPipe Pose in the browser for camera rep counting, all on the device.

Quality: 27 automated tests, including a simulation of 20 random clip mountings that must each count exactly 6 curls.

Challenges we ran into

Getting video off the glasses. I didn’t have direct camera access, so I streamed through a WhatsApp video call and screen-captured the call window.
Getting a voice back in. It was the same problem in reverse. I routed text-to-speech through a virtual audio cable that WhatsApp uses as its microphone.
False alarms. One blurry frame could make Cue think you were vaping. Two-frame confirmation and cooldowns fixed it.
The clip never sits the same way twice. Each mounting gives a different angle, so the rep counter learns the resting position before it counts.
Doing it all solo in 36 hours: hardware, vision, voice and the app at the same time.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Real hardware, built solo this weekend. The Cue Clip counts real curls and buzzes in your hand. In a live set, it counted 10 of 10 curls and flagged the rushed ones.
A rep counter that works however you clip it on. It learns the resting position, and it passed a simulation of 20 random mountings, counting exactly 6 curls every time. It’s backed by 27 automated tests.
Coaching that knows the clock. The same coffee gets logged at 8 AM and gets “Put it back” at 11 PM.
No warnings from one bad frame. Serious nudges, like vaping, need two frames in a row before Cue speaks up.
A real voice in your ear. I routed text-to-speech through a virtual audio cable into the WhatsApp call, so Cue speaks through the glasses’ own speakers.
An app that fills itself in. The companion app updates live from the glasses and clip, with nothing typed.
Runs on open-source models too. The same pipeline works with Qwen2.5-VL-7B, which I served myself on AMD Radeon Cloud.
A demo anyone can try. Put on the glasses, pick up a drink, do a curl. No glasses? The web app counts reps from a laptop camera.

What we learned

Simple beats fancy for reps. A clean tilt angle, good thresholds and learning the resting position counted reps better than anything complex.
Coaching is about timing. The same advice is useful at 11 PM and just noise at 8 AM.
Vision models see well, but not perfectly. They name objects well in a messy first-person view, but every warning needs a second look to avoid false alarms.
Design for swapping models. Using an OpenAI-compatible API let me move between Gemini and my self-hosted Qwen without rewriting code.
Honest labels build trust. The app marks what is live and what is sample data.

What's next for Cue

Cue Band: Turn the clip into a wireless wristband: an ESP32 with Bluetooth and a battery. The Bluetooth code is already in the project. A band stays on all day, so Cue can buzz you anywhere, not just in the gym.
Direct camera access: Use the glasses’ camera directly instead of a video call, for all-day use.
Privacy: Cue never saves frames. Today, each frame is sent to Google’s Gemini API to be read. Next, the open-source model runs on hardware we control, so frames never leave it.
More of the day: Add sleep and steps from the Cue Band or wearables people already own, protein from meal photos, and coaching that adapts to each person’s goals.

title: R2 Hope
text:
Notifications

Loading...

R2 Hope

It’s an autonomous triage-support droid. It finds the patient in a room on its own, drives to them, and monitors their eyes for fatigue — so nobody gets overlooked when staff are stretched

Like

Comment

Inspiration

I've wanted to build an R2 unit since I was a kid.

Not a replica — a working one. Something that rolls into a room on its own, figures out what's going on, and does something about it. That's the part of R2 that always got me: he was never the hero. He was the one who showed up, assessed the situation, and handled it while everyone else was panicking.

The medical angle came later, and it came from a simple observation. In a hospital at 3 AM, or a field tent after a bus crash, the thing that's short isn't medicine or equipment. It's attention. Somebody has to walk the room and notice which patient is going quiet. When there are twelve patients and two nurses, somebody doesn't get noticed — and that's not a failure of skill, it's a failure of arithmetic.

That's a problem a droid is actually good at. Not diagnosing. Not treating. Just going to every patient, every time, and taking a reading. Being the thing that doesn't get tired and doesn't skip anyone.

That's where the name came from. R2 Hope — the droid that shows up.

What it does

R2 Hope is an autonomous triage-support robot. It automates the part of triage a person currently has to do on foot: finding the patient, getting to them, and taking a reading.

In autonomous mode it sweeps the room looking for a patient — not just any person, but specifically someone in a medical gown, identified by combining YOLO person detection with a calibrated color signature. A person alone isn't enough and the gown color alone isn't enough; both have to pass before it commits. Once it has a lock, it drives toward them, steering around obstacles with lidar and slowing as it closes, then holds position on arrival.

From there it switches from navigating to monitoring. Using facial landmarks it tracks eye closure against a baseline it calibrates on the spot for that specific person, and reports PERCLOS — the share of a rolling 60-second window the patient's eyes were closed. PERCLOS is the standard clinical measure of drowsiness, and it's the earliest honest signal you can get from a camera that a patient is fading.

It also has a complete manual mode: mixed throttle-and-steering keyboard teleop over UART, so an operator can take over at any moment.

What it deliberately does not do is make the call. It gathers the data. The clinical judgment stays with the human.

How we built it

Split the brain

Before we cut a single wire we spent a long time arguing about architecture, and almost every decision from those conversations is why the robot works at all.

The big one: a Raspberry Pi 5 is the navigator, an ESP32 is the driver.

The Pi runs the camera, the lidar, and the vision models, making maybe 5–10 decisions per second. The ESP32 does nothing clever — it runs motor control at a hard 100 Hz, forever.

Those two jobs have incompatible requirements. The Pi runs Linux and Python; it can stall for 200 ms because an inference ran long or the scheduler felt like it. That's fine for deciding where to go. It is not fine for holding a PWM signal. So we gave the motors a processor that cannot be interrupted by a YOLO frame.

They talk over UART with a line protocol we specified ourselves — plain ASCII, one reply per command:
M <left> <right>    per-wheel PWM          -> OK <l> <r> <heading>
R <degrees>         closed-loop gyro turn  -> TURN ... DONE
S                   stop                   -> OK 0 0
P                   ping                   -> PONG
G                   orientation            -> H <z> PITCH <x> RATE <r>

And the single most important feature in the project lives on the ESP32: a watchdog. If no motor command arrives for 500 ms, the motors stop. The Pi sends a heartbeat at 10 Hz to keep it fed. So if Python crashes, if SSH drops, if I close the laptop — the robot stops. It does not keep driving. We designed the failure mode before we designed the feature.

Finding the patient

A person is not a patient. That distinction is the entire detection problem.

We run YOLOv11n for person detection, then check an HSV color mask inside each box. The patient is the intersection, and it has to clear two independent gates:

$$
\text{patient} \iff \left( N_{\text{px}} > N_{\min} \right) \;\wedge\; \left( \frac{N_{\text{px}}}{A_{\text{box}}} > f_{\min} \right)
$$

where \( N_{\text{px}} \) is the matching pixel count and \( A_{\text{box}} \) the bounding box area, with \( N_{\min} = 800 \) and \( f_{\min} = 0.04 \).

Why two gates? Because a count alone fails in both directions. A patient far away is small and fails a fixed threshold. A bystander standing close fills the frame, and a few hundred stray pixels from a lanyard sail right past it. The fraction gate kills the bystander; the count gate kills sensor noise. Together, a close-up person with 1,200 stray pixels in an 80,000 px box (\( 1.5\% \)) is correctly rejected, while a real gown passes at \( 25\% \) whether near or far.

Monitoring fatigue

Parked at the patient, we compute eye aspect ratio from facial landmarks — eye height over eye width:

$$
\text{EAR} = \frac{\lVert p_2 - p_6 \rVert + \lVert p_3 - p_5 \rVert}{2\,\lVert p_1 - p_4 \rVert}
$$

Every face has a different resting EAR, so an absolute threshold is useless. We calibrate a per-person baseline \( \text{EAR}_0 \) during the first seconds of eyes-open and count a frame as closed when \( \text{EAR} < 0.75\,\text{EAR}_0 \).

PERCLOS is then the proportion of closure over a rolling window:

$$
\text{PERCLOS} = \frac{1}{T}\int_{t-T}^{t} \mathbb{1}!\left[\text{EAR}(\tau) < \kappa\,\text{EAR}_0\right] d\tau, \qquad T = 60\text{s}
$$

We chose this deliberately over the flashier option. We could have tried to read pain or distress from facial expression. We decided not to, because it doesn't work reliably and we weren't willing to demo something we couldn't defend.

Not hitting things

The lidar gives ~210 scattered \( (\theta, r) \) points per revolution, which is awkward to reason about. We bin them into 36 sectors of \( 10° \) and keep the nearest return in each:

$$
d_i = \min {\, r_k : \theta_k \in S_i,\; r_k > r_{\min} \,}
$$

Nearest, not average, on purpose — for not crashing, the chair leg at 40 cm matters and the wall 4 m behind it does not.

On top we built a cut-down Vector Field Histogram, the approach used in F1TENTH autonomous racing. Score every candidate bearing, steer toward the best:

$$
\text{score}(i) = c_i - \beta\,\lvert \alpha_i \rvert, \qquad c_i = \min_{|k| \le w} d_{i+k}
$$

Two details matter. \( c_i \) is the corridor width, not the distance at \( i \) alone — the robot has physical width, so the sectors beside a gap must be clear too, or it aims at an opening it can't fit through and clips the edge. And \( \beta \) is a straight-ahead bias costing score per degree off center; without it the robot drifts sideways forever just because the room is marginally roomier that way.

That becomes a steering correction mixed into the wheels via standard differential drive kinematics:

$$
v = \frac{v_R + v_L}{2}, \qquad \omega = \frac{v_R - v_L}{L}
$$

In practice: left = speed + turn, right = speed - turn. Smooth arcs, no pivoting.

The body

Chassis, head, legs and caster mounts designed in Fusion 360 and 3D printed. We also built a Webots simulation world so we could break the navigation logic in software before breaking it on hardware.

Challenges we ran into

Honestly? Everything broke. Hardware, soldering, firmware, software, and the laptop running the IDE — in roughly that order of pain.

The robot kept falling over backwards

This was the big one, and the fix taught me the most.

My instinct was to solve it with the gyro. It's an orientation sensor, the robot has an orientation problem, done. That instinct was wrong, and understanding why was the most valuable thing I learned all weekend.

R2 Hope rolls on two driven wheels plus a caster. It's statically stable — not an inverted pendulum, so there's no balancing to be done. By the time the gyro says "you are tilting," you are already falling. A gyro cannot save a statically stable robot. It can only file a report.

The actual cause was torque reaction: commanding full PWM instantly makes the wheels shove hard against a chassis with a high center of mass, and the body pitches backward. The fix was a slew-rate limiter in firmware — PWM can only change a few counts per 20 ms tick:

$$
u_{t+1} = u_t + \text{clamp}\big(u^{*} - u_t,\; -\Delta_{\text{down}},\; +\Delta_{\text{up}}\big)
$$

with \( \Delta_{\text{up}} = 4 \) and \( \Delta_{\text{down}} = 12 \) at 50 Hz — about 200 PWM/sec up, and faster to stop than to go. The robot now accelerates instead of lurching. That's what stopped the falling. Not the gyro.

The gyro then became a genuinely useful last-resort guard, but we had to trigger on rate, not angle. Our IMU is mounted high and off-center, and an accelerometer fundamentally cannot distinguish gravity from linear acceleration — so its tilt estimate is corrupted at exactly the moment you're accelerating, which is exactly when you need it. Angular rate is immune. We cut the motors at \( 90\,°/\text{s} \) of pitch rate.

Soldering and wiring

Hours went into connections that looked fine and weren't. Motors that ran one direction only. A motor that ran backwards — fixed by swapping IN3 and IN4 in firmware rather than redoing wiring at 2 AM. Joints that passed a continuity check on the bench and failed under vibration once the robot was actually moving.

One bad sensor bricked the whole robot

After one fall, R2 Hope went completely dead. No PONG, no motor response, nothing. We traced it to the MPU6050 being knocked loose on impact, which made mpu.begin() fail, which hit this:
if (mpu.begin() != 0) {
Serial2.println("MPU FAILED");
while (1) delay(1000);     // halts forever - kills ALL commands
}

An optional sensor took down the entire control loop, including everything that had nothing to do with it. We rewrote it to degrade gracefully: flag the gyro unavailable, skip the features needing it, keep driving. Never let an optional sensor take down the control loop.

We had a quarter of the control authority we thought

We assumed 0–255 of PWM to work with. We put the robot on the floor and ramped it by hand to check. The wheels don't move at all below 20, and 30 is already medium speed.

The real usable band is roughly \( 20 \)–\( 70 \), not \( 20 \)–\( 255 \). Every gain in the system — steering, turning, cruise — had to be resized for a band a quarter of what we'd assumed. Otherwise we'd have shipped a robot that only knew how to go full speed.

A Raspberry Pi tried to install CUDA

pip install ultralytics cheerfully began downloading 2.5 GB of NVIDIA CUDA libraries — cuDNN alone was 651 MB — onto a Raspberry Pi with no GPU and no room, and killed the SSH session mid-download. Installing CPU-only torch wheels explicitly first, then ultralytics, fixed it and freed 2.7 GB of wasted cache.

Smaller ones that still cost real hours

Bracketed paste. Pasting a command into a serial terminal wraps it in invisible escape codes (ESC[200~), silently corrupting every parse. Every command returned ERR bad. Fixed by filtering to printable ASCII and writing the parser by hand instead of trusting sscanf.
A race on the serial port. Our ping kept returning OK 0 0 instead of PONG — the background heartbeat thread was also reading the port and swallowing replies. Fixed by making the heartbeat the sole reader.
The heartbeat cancelling our own turns. The ESP32 runs a gyro turn to completion, but any incoming M aborts it — so our own 10 Hz heartbeat killed every turn ~100 ms in. Fixed with a pause flag.
A black video stream. Hours debugging a camera that was working perfectly. The real cause: a stale file. Our deploy silently kept an old copy, so we were debugging code that wasn't running. We now md5sum both ends before debugging anything.
Python buffering. tail -f showing nothing, because Python buffers stdout when redirected. python3 -u.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

It doesn't fall over anymore. Going from a robot that tipped on every start to one that accelerates smoothly — by understanding the physics instead of adding more sensor — is the thing I'm proudest of.

The safety architecture. The watchdog, the slew limiter, and a panic stop that ignores direction entirely all sit below anything clever. Nothing in the Python can override them. If the brain dies, the body stops. That's a property we designed in from the first hour, not patched in after a crash.

Detection that actually discriminates. Getting from "anyone standing nearby is the patient" to a two-gate test that rejects a bystander at 1.5% coverage while accepting a real gown at 25% near or far — with the math to explain why — felt like real engineering rather than threshold-fiddling.

We shipped continuous steering, not stop-and-turn. Most hackathon obstacle avoidance is: see wall, stop, spin, go. Ours scores every bearing and arcs around things while still moving. It looks like a vehicle, not a Roomba.

We tested instead of assuming, once, and it saved us. The lidar started returning points at 0.11 m and I was certain it was seeing its own mounting bracket — ready to filter out everything under 25 cm. A teammate pushed back: he thought it was just his hand near the sensor during the test.

So we looked at the data instead of arguing. Across 618 scans, the close returns were smeared across \( +165° \), \( +95° \), \( +175° \), \( -15° \), \( -5° \) — everywhere. Fixed structure would appear at a fixed bearing. It was a moving hand.

Had I applied that filter, I'd have permanently blinded R2 Hope to anything within 25 cm, to fix a problem that didn't exist. Best 20 minutes we spent all weekend.

What we learned

Safety in robotics is architectural, not reactive. The watchdog, the ramp, and the panic stop work because they're the lowest layer, underneath everything clever.

Measure, don't assume. The deadband, the lidar artifact, the dead camera stream — every one of them was an assumption that cost us hours and a measurement that cost us minutes.

Know where your system stops. The most important thing we built might be the thing we chose not to claim. We don't diagnose. We don't read pain. We take one honest measurement and hand it to a human.

And the one I keep coming back to: the right answer to "can the gyro stop it falling over?" was no. The ramp stops it falling. The gyro just notices. Getting that wrong first — and then understanding why — was worth more than if it had worked on the first try.

What's next for R2 Hope

Multi-patient triage. Right now it finds a patient. Logging each one with location, timestamp and PERCLOS, then ranking worst-first, turns a single monitoring pass into an actual prioritized queue — real triage.
LLM-generated handoff reports from the monitoring data, used as a reporter and dispatcher — deliberately not in the control loop, where its latency has no business.
A rotating head, so tracking a patient doesn't require turning the whole robot.
Lower the center of mass. The slew limiter solved the symptom honestly, but the LiPo and power bank belong at the floor of the chassis. No amount of firmware beats that.
A web dashboard for remote monitoring and voice dispatch.

ARCHER Program

The ARCHER program coordinates drone fleets for reconnaissance and surveillance, helping responders locate missing people and monitor emergencies before rescue teams can reach the scene.

Project Story — ARCHER

About the Project

ARCHER (Autonomous Robotic Coordination for Hazard Evasion & Reconnaissance) is an AI-powered autonomous drone system designed to make drone operations smarter, safer, and more accessible.

Our goal was to go beyond traditional remote-controlled drones by developing a system capable of understanding natural-language commands, planning missions, navigating around obstacles, and monitoring flight operations in real time.

ARCHER combines artificial intelligence, autonomous navigation, computer vision, and drone hardware into one integrated platform. Using a Pixhawk-based flight controller and MAVLink communication, the system connects drone hardware to a Python-based autonomy framework and a custom-built ground-control dashboard.

One of ARCHER's core features is its AI mission-planning architecture, which uses Claude to interpret mission objectives and translate them into structured flight actions. Its navigation system incorporates geofencing, waypoint planning, obstacle avoidance, and autonomous flight patterns such as surveying, patrolling, and orbiting.

We also developed a ground-control interface that brings together live drone telemetry, GPS tracking, 3D mapping, camera feeds, and AI-assisted flight monitoring. This allows operators to visualize drone activity, inspect flight data, and manage missions from a centralized dashboard.

Throughout development, we used PX4 SITL and Gazebo simulation to test autonomous behaviors before moving toward real-world hardware integration.

ARCHER represents our vision of a future where drones are more than remotely operated machines — they are intelligent robotic systems capable of assisting humans with complex tasks.

Our long-term vision is to expand ARCHER into a scalable multi-drone platform for applications such as search and rescue, environmental monitoring, infrastructure inspection, and autonomous reconnaissance.

Clairvoyance

Clairvoyance is a wearable camera necklace for visually impaired users, paired with a voice assistant.

Like
1

Comment

Wearable Asset

Website UI

Website UI

Inspiration

We initially considered building a device that could help people find objects around their homes. While exploring that idea, we thought about the game Hot and Cold, where someone is guided toward an object through verbal feedback. That led us to ask: what if we applied that same concept to a real-world accessibility challenge?

From there, Clairvoyance was born. Our goal is to create a wearable, portable, and simple-to-use tool that works with a smartphone to help visually impaired individuals better understand and navigate their surroundings. By combining a camera, voice interaction, and AI-powered scene analysis, Clairvoyance acts as an assistive aid that helps users perceive what they may not be able to see.

What it does

Clairvoyance is a wearable camera necklace for visually impaired users, paired with a voice assistant.:

Uses an ESP32 camera module as a necklace-mounted vision source
Captures a snapshot or live frame from the camera
Lets the user ask a spoken or typed question about the scene
Sends the image and question to a server-side analysis route
Uses a vision model to describe obstacles or scene layout
Speaks the result back to the user via browser TTS

The system is designed around a simple loop:
listenOnce() → getSnapshot() → analyzeScene() → speak()

Challenges we ran into

Some of the biggest challenges we ran into are pretty clear, and they include things along the lines of:
Hardware reliability: connecting the ESP32 camera to Wi‑Fi and getting a stable stream
CORS and proxy issues when accessing the ESP32 camera from the phone app, while also having issues of things like weak USB power bricks, board power problems, and needing 2.4 GHz Wi‑Fi.

Real-world device variability: different camera modules, power issues, and Wi‑Fi configuration

Maintaining a demo-ready experience without blocking feature work, trying to balancing accessibility UX with a practical camera-and-AI workflow.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Inspiration

Clairvoyance was inspired by the idea of helping blind or visually impaired people better understand their surroundings in real time using a lightweight wearable camera and voice-first interaction. The repo frames the product as a “voice-first Next.js phone client for the ESP32 necklace camera,” with the core goal of answering simple questions like “What’s ahead?” or “Any obstacles?” using a camera feed and AI analysis.

The project also seems inspired by accessibility and real-world demo constraints: the app is designed to work end-to-end with stubs by default, while still being ready for real camera + AI integration later.
What it does

Clairvoyance is a wearable AI perception app that:
Uses an ESP32 camera module as a necklace-mounted vision source
Captures a snapshot or live frame from the camera
Lets the user ask a spoken or typed question about the scene
Sends the image and question to a server-side analysis route
Uses a vision model to describe obstacles or scene layout
Speaks the result back to the user via browser TTS

The system is designed around a simple loop:
listenOnce() → getSnapshot() → analyzeScene() → speak()

The repo’s docs emphasize concise visual guidance for a blind user, specifically returning answers like left/center/right obstacle awareness, without markdown, in a natural voice.
How we built it

The project is split into clear engineering lanes:
Lane A: app shell / UX in client-web-app/src/components and src/app/page.tsx
Lane B: camera access in src/lib/camera.ts
Lane C: speech / STT / TTS in src/lib/speech.ts
Lane D: AI vision analysis in src/lib/analyze.ts and src/app/api/analyze/route.ts

The app is built in Next.js and includes a server route at:
client-web-app/src/app/api/analyze/route.ts

This route expects multipart form data with:
A question and an image

It validates the request, checks for required env keys, and then calls a Gemini model using Google’s generative API. The repo intentionally keeps model keys on the server with .env.local / hosting environment variables instead of exposing them in the client.

The hardware side is handled by an ESP32 camera project under:
esp32-cam/src/main.cpp

This firmware initializes the camera, connects to Wi-Fi, and serves a stream for the camera, with config tuned for the ELEGOO ESP32-WROVER module and M5STACK_WIDE pin mapping.

The repo also includes a “stub” mode for local demos:
NEXT_PUBLIC_STUB_MIC=1
NEXT_PUBLIC_STUB_CAMERA=1
NEXT_PUBLIC_STUB_ANALYZE=1

That allows the app to run without hardware or API keys in a demo environment.

What we learned

Through this project, we learned how to integrate hardware and software into one cohesive system. We worked with an ESP32 camera, a web-based phone client, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and AI-powered image analysis.

We also learned how important it is to design a project modularly. By separating the camera, voice, AI, and user interface into independent components, we were able to develop and test each part more easily.

Another major lesson was how to adapt to hardware limitations. We had to work around constraints involving camera capabilities, processing power, Wi-Fi connectivity, and available resources. These limitations taught us to design flexible solutions, use stubs for testing, and create fallback paths when the full hardware setup was unavailable.

Finally, we gained experience implementing speech-to-text and building a voice-first experience with accessibility as a central design goal.

What's next for Clairvoyance

Replace stubs with real microphone capture and transcript handling
Integrate a reliable ESP32 camera stream from the necklace hardware
Finish real end-to-end vision analysis with a model such as Gemini
Tune the prompt so the AI provides short, actionable scene descriptions
Improve UX for accessibility, especially error states and voice feedback
Trial the full system on actual hardware and in the target walking/demo environment
Iterate on latency and reliability so the app works in a hallway or real-world mobility use case

Pulse 

We made a radar that can be used to help find people that are trapped due to natural disasters or other crises, it uses frequencies to find people through walls, and can read also their heart rate.

Like
3

Comment

Final state of our prototype

Our radar UI running on the Raspberry Pi

Soldering of the hlk-ld2450 sensor

UI demonstrating bpm and range sensors

Inspiration

Pulse began with an idea from Rainbow Six Siege, where the character Pulse uses a device to sense people through barriers. We wanted to explore whether a real version of that idea could serve a more practical purpose.

We built a prototype around the idea of helping responders locate people during an emergency, such as after a natural disaster. Our goal was to combine location tracking with close range vital sign sensing in a handheld device.

What it does

Pulse combines two radar sensors to give responders a clearer picture of who may be nearby. The 24 GHz HLK-LD2450 tracks up to three moving targets and plots their positions relative to the device as dots on a radar screen. When someone is within the 60 GHz DFRobot C1001’s sensing range, it can provide breathing and heart rate readings. An operator can tap a dot to view available readings and on-screen guidance for aiming the sensor toward that person. Together, the location and vital sign information can help responders save lives in emergency situations.

How we built it

We built Pulse from the hardware up in 36 hours, including its sensor drivers, fusion engine, and radar interface.

Hardware: A Raspberry Pi 4 with 2 GB of memory runs the system and connects to a 7 inch Hosyond DSI capacitive touchscreen with an 800 × 480 resolution. The HLK LD2450 tracks targets using 24 GHz radar. The DFRobot C1001 uses 60 GHz radar for close range breathing and heart rate readings. Both sensors connect directly to separate hardware UARTs on the Pi. The LD2450 uses UART0 at 256000 baud, and the C1001 uses UART3 at 115200 baud. A USB power bank makes the unit portable.

Software: A Python and FastAPI backend streams radar data to a JavaScript canvas interface over WebSocket at 10 Hz. We wrote Python parsers for both sensors using their documentation and DFRobot’s Arduino library as references. The parsers handle split frames, resynchronization, protocol checks, and reconnection.

The fusion engine uses an alpha beta tracking filter, one to one target association, and range hysteresis to reduce flicker and help maintain target IDs when people cross paths. Since the C1001 does not report a target’s location, the interface pairs its readings with a dot only when the operator aims at a nearby target and the reading is in range.

The touchscreen interface runs full screen in kiosk mode. It includes a radar sweep, touch range controls, a contact history drawer, and a tap activated card with available vital readings and direction guidance. We also built a simulator that runs scripted scenarios through the same fusion code, along with 187 automated tests. Setup scripts, SSH deployment tools, a system service, and serial debugging tools helped us develop and test the system on the Pi.

Challenges we ran into

We changed our idea late in the process, which left us searching for parts that could arrive in time. Overnight shipping helped us get started, but our limited options meant making compromises in the hardware we could use.

The LD2450’s small, closely spaced pins did not match the jumper wires available to us. We had to cut, strip, and solder wires directly to the sensor. Keeping the joints separate was difficult, and we had to be careful to avoid shorting neighboring pins.

Neither sensor came with a ready to use Raspberry Pi driver for our setup. We built Python parsers from the sensor documentation and the available DFRobot Arduino library, then worked through serial communication issues on the Pi.

Our first readings also made the displayed dots jump around instead of following people smoothly. We traced this to sensor noise and adjusted the movement threshold so the interface responded to more significant movement. That made the display steadier, while also making it less responsive to small movements.

Accomplishments that we’re proud of

• Built a handheld prototype with a Raspberry Pi, touchscreen, and two radar sensors in 36 hours.

• Connected the Hosyond display to the Pi, configured it to launch Pulse full screen, and used SSH to make changes during development.

• Displayed up to three HLK LD2450 targets as dots, using the sensor’s X and Y position readings.

• Built a touch interface for selecting targets and viewing available readings.

• Wrote sensor parsers and a fusion engine, then developed a simulator and ran 187 automated tests through the fusion code.

• Soldered connections to the LD2450 despite its small, closely spaced pins.

What we learned

Radar fusion takes more than combining data. The LD2450 gives us target positions, while the C1001 provides close range vital readings without a target location. Each sensor has different strengths and limits, so the software has to be careful about when it associates a reading with a dot.

Serial communication needs careful setup. Getting two sensors working on separate UARTs meant configuring the Pi’s hardware serial ports and writing parsers that could recover when data arrived in partial frames or contained invalid values.

Soldering small connections takes patience. We learned to prepare and position wires carefully, control how much solder we use, and inspect close pins for accidental bridges before powering the hardware.

Clear displays matter more than effects. We chose a high contrast interface that could be read at a glance on the 800 × 480 screen. The amber and green states are prototype cues, not medical assessments.

Radar has physical limits. Signals may pass through some materials, but performance changes with the material and environment. Solid concrete and water soaked debris can block or weaken them. We learned to be precise about what our prototype has demonstrated and what still needs testing.

A shared data contract helps teams work in parallel. Defining the information exchanged by the Python backend and JavaScript interface let us develop both sides alongside a deterministic simulator and test suite.

What’s next for Pulse

Our first prototype was built with the sensors we could obtain in time. Next, we want to evaluate higher quality radar options that could improve positional accuracy, extend useful range, and track more than three people. We also want to test how different walls and debris affect detection, improve calibration and target association, and make the hardware more durable and portable.

With stronger sensing and extensive testing, Pulse could grow into a more capable tool for search and rescue teams. Our long term goal is to help responders find useful information about people who may be difficult to see.

title: Echo
text:
Notifications

Echo

Nobody left behind

Like
2

Comment

Inspiration

Since 1998, 1,070 children in the U.S. have died of heatstroke in parked cars, an average of 37 a year (NoHeatStroke.org, updated September 28, 2026). 35 died in 2025, and 25 more have died so far in 2026. More than half were under 2. Florida is second only to Texas. 118 Florida children died in hot cars from 1990 to 2023, against 155 in Texas, and 7 died in Florida in 2023 alone, the most since 2017 (Kids and Car Safety, via FOX 13). This July, a 17-month-old in Fort Myers became Florida's fifth hot-car death of 2026 (WFTV). By early July, every Florida child lost was three or younger (FOX 13). Most of these deaths are not neglect. From 1998 to 2025, 52.9% of the children were forgotten by a caregiver, 23.8% climbed into a car on their own, and 21.9% were knowingly left (NoHeatStroke.org). A memory lapse can't be fixed with a reminder sticker. It needs something in the car that notices. Florida leaves almost no time to notice. A closed car warms about 19°F in its first 10 minutes, and cracking the windows changes that by less than 3°F (Null, San Jose State; McLaren, Null & Quinn, Pediatrics 2005). On an ordinary 91°F Orlando afternoon, that puts the cabin past 104°F, where heatstroke sets in, within about 7 minutes. Echo's Warning fires at 95°F, a few minutes before the cabin reaches danger.

What it does

Echo turns a forgotten child into a siren within seconds and a phone call within minutes, and it keeps working with no internet.

Detects. When the ignition turns off, the box watches the car seat with an ultrasonic sensor and reads cabin temperature every 2 seconds.
Predicts. It fits a line through the last 2 minutes of readings and computes minutes until the cabin reaches 104°F. That number comes from real sensor data, never from AI.
Alarms. Alert levels climb from Armed to Occupant to Warning (95°F, or 10 minutes to danger) to Emergency (104°F, or 5 minutes). An RGB LED changes color and a siren sweeps. Only a person pressing the button on the box, or turning the car back on, can stop it.
Dispatches. At Emergency, plain code starts a backup call ladder: call Contact #1, call again at 2 minutes, call Contact #2 at 3 minutes, alert everyone at 5. An AI voice agent rides on top: it tells the parent how hot the car is and how long is left, hears "I'm 20 minutes away," and calls someone closer.
Shows. A mobile app gives the parent a red full-screen alert with a minutes-to-danger countdown, the live heat curve, "I'm on my way" and "Call 911" buttons, and a feed of every call the agent makes and why.
Forecasts Florida risk. A Databricks notebook pulls the next 24 hours of weather for six Florida cities and estimates how fast a parked car would reach danger each hour, so the app can say "On a 91°F afternoon in Orlando, a parked car hits danger in 7 minutes."

The AI may act earlier than the ladder, never later. Nothing received over Wi-Fi can silence or lower an alarm.

How we built it

We split Echo into layers so that each one can fail without taking down the one below it.

The box (Arduino Mega 2560). An HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor aimed at the car seat, an LM35 temperature sensor, an RGB LED, a passive buzzer for the siren sweep, an ignition jumper, and a cancel button, on a 9V AA pack. The alert levels and minutes-to-danger math live in a plain C++ header that compiles for the Arduino and on a laptop, so we unit-test the life-safety logic before it touches hardware.
The Wi-Fi modem (ESP8266 NodeMCU). It only forwards the Mega's JSON status line every 2 seconds over a phone hotspot. Pull it out and the siren keeps going.
The server (Node.js, built-ins only). It receives the status, runs the backup call ladder, marks the box offline after 10 seconds of silence, and serves a live dashboard. Real calls only happen when an explicit live flag is set, so tests can never dial a phone.
The calling agent. Twilio places the calls. The ladder's first call tries an ElevenLabs voice agent and falls back to a plain Twilio call on any error or timeout. Gemini reads live car data and picks one tool at a time: get the car's status, place a call, or log a reason.
The app (Expo / React Native). Home, Live alert, Activity, Contacts, and Heat insights screens, with a rotating 3D car rendered locally with three.js.
The data (Databricks). One notebook logs every heat test from the box. A second pulls hourly Florida weather from the Google Maps Platform Weather API into Delta tables and applies the published cabin-heating curve to rank each hour from Watch to Extreme.
The Challenger. During development, Gemini invented tricky scenarios (a bag on the seat, a cooling cabin, a flickering sensor), and plain code graded the box's response. AI writes the tests; it never decides who passed.

Challenges we ran into

Aiming the seat sensor. An empty seat closer than 40 cm read as occupied forever. We learned to aim so the empty seat reads 55 to 60 cm, which gives a clear gap when a child is in it.
The silent Wi-Fi link. With its own USB plugged in, the ESP8266's USB chip held the receive line high, so the Mega's messages never arrived. Powering it from the Mega fixed it.
Siren vs. color. The siren's tone() borrows the timer behind pins 9 and 10, which broke color mixing. We moved the RGB LED to pins 44 to 46.
Texts don't get through. U.S. carriers block texts from unregistered numbers, and registration takes weeks. We made voice calls the alert channel, which also helps a saved emergency contact break through.
Cutting scope. Mid-hackathon we removed the humidity sensor, LCD, motion sensor, and joystick to keep the box simple and the demo reliable.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The alarm can't be talked out of it. Pull the Wi-Fi modem mid-emergency and the siren keeps sweeping. Nothing from the server, app, or AI can silence or lower an alarm; only a person at the car can.
AI on a leash. The call ladder runs in plain code on a fixed schedule. If the AI crashes or stalls, the calls still go out.
Real numbers, not guesses. Every temperature and countdown the agent speaks comes straight from the box's sensors.
Tested like it matters. 283 server tests, 49 app tests, and 98,374 checks on the alert logic all pass, including 15 tricky Challenger scenarios.
A Florida-specific forecast. Echo turns tomorrow's weather in six Florida cities into minutes-to-danger for a parked car, hour by hour.

What we learned

A car becomes dangerous much faster than most people think. Most of the heating happens in the first half hour, and cracked windows barely help.
Most victims weren't left on purpose. Designing for a tired, distracted parent changed our app: one action per screen, big text, plain words.
Safety systems need a floor that doesn't depend on the clever part. Writing the rule first ("AI may act earlier, never later") made every later design choice easier.

-Hardware debugging is mostly power and grounding.

What's next?

Breathing, not just presence. Our ultrasonic sensor can't tell a bag from a baby. A production box adds mmWave radar to detect breathing.
Works anywhere. An LTE module so the box can call without a phone hotspot, and GPS so callers know where the car is.
A better cabin sensor. A BME280 for steadier readings in direct sun.
Florida first. Pilot with Florida daycare centers and pediatric offices, and push the hourly risk forecast to parents on the state's hottest days.

Sources
NoHeatStroke.org, Jan Null, San Jose State University: national totals, 2025 and 2026 counts, circumstances, ages (updated September 28, 2026)
FOX 13, May 22, 2024: Kids and Car Safety report, Florida and Texas totals 1990 to 2023

WFTV, July 22, 2026: Florida's fifth hot-car death of 2026

Inspiration

Beginning to plan our project, we knew one thing from the very start- we wanted to make more than just something on the screen. Specifically, we wanted to implement some sort of AR/VR to be able to really help give effect. With some influence from a team member who had a recently rough time with training due to a lacking professional, we came up with the idea of ghost hands- a software that allows you to receive the training of a professional wherever you are. 

What it does

Ghost hands takes in video input and scans the hand input along with the objects they touch. Using this data, the Meta Quest 3S our project uses generates a set of translucent ghost-like hands that mimic the actions of the inputted video. It then gives training steps overlayed over a real world environment on top of the headset, showing the user how to perform the task, and giving them a rating linked to how close there movements where with the designated task. 

How we built it

Our Project is split into two main facets- half of it being a build of mediapipe to scan videos for hand movements, along with a database connection connected to a frontend webpage that allows for video storage to be transitioned and scanned to allow for training. The other half is the fun part- it consists of the Meta Quest 3S, which takes the inputted data that's stored after going through media pipe, and uses it to make the Ghost Hands. We then used the Meta Quests hand tracking capabilities to get data of the users hands, and compare that to the training data. 

Challenges we ran into

For challenges well.... we ran into quite a few. One of the big ones was getting our initial pipeline set up between the database and media pipe. Though it went smoothly getting our endpoints set up along with getting the video to go through the initial steps, tuning it to properly take in the hand movements was a fairly large challenge at times. Additionally, we ran into a lot of issues setting up our initial environment with the headset, as though some of our members had experience with unity, setting it up to work with the headset was quite difficult at times.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Really, I'd say what we are proud of the most is being able to set up and have our full pipeline working along with the VR. It was extremely rewarding to be able to see our idea come to life.

Additionally, we had a sub 5 second analyzation time for the mediapipe scanning of the hands, which took a lot of work when it came to honing the process.

What we learned

Really, we all learned a lot- though it boils to experiencing more how to properly set up a dev environment within our team. Additionally, working with the VR headset allowed us to pick up a lot more on how unity works, along with connecting it to outside services via a database.

What's next for Ghost Hands

Quite a lot really- next up, we have plans to extend ghost hands into more visualizing the video through generated images of the objects being touched, rather than basic matching. Additionally, we want to further help learners by giving more detailed descriptions, hoping to be able to further develop the learning process while going through a ghost hands tutorial.

handoff

We gave AI a hand. Handoff is a wearable exoskeleton designed to help people with paralysis regain independence in everyday life and empower anyone to learn physical skills through AI-guided movement.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

We gave AI a hand. Literally.

Artificial intelligence can see, listen, reason, and communicate. But what if it could physically interact with the world?

That question inspired Handoff, an AI-powered wearable exoskeleton designed to bridge the gap between artificial intelligence and human movement.

Our biggest motivation was accessibility. Millions of people experience paralysis or limited hand mobility, making everyday activities significantly more difficult. We envisioned a future where AI could provide physical assistance, helping people regain independence.

But we wanted to go beyond accessibility. Imagine learning piano, practicing a new skill, or completing an unfamiliar task with an AI that doesn't just explain what to do, but can help guide your movements.

We wanted to take AI beyond the screen and into the physical world.

What It Does

Handoff combines a wearable robotic hand exoskeleton with AI-powered smart glasses to create an interactive system connecting human movement with artificial intelligence.

The system is designed around three main capabilities:

Physical Assistance: A tendon-driven exoskeleton designed to assist individual finger and thumb movements, with the long-term goal of supporting people with limited mobility.
AI-Powered Learning: A system intended to provide real-time explanations and guided movements, helping users develop physical skills through hands-on learning.
Multimodal Interaction: Smart glasses equipped with a camera, microphone, and speaker, allowing the system to capture visual information, receive voice input, and communicate through speech.

Our goal is to allow users to ask questions, receive intelligent guidance, and eventually translate approved AI actions into physical movement.

How We Built It

We approached Handoff as two interconnected systems: an intelligent perception interface and a physical actuation system.

For the wearable interface, we used an ESP32-S3 Sense with an integrated camera and microphone, alongside an external audio amplifier and speaker. We developed firmware supporting simultaneous live camera streaming, microphone capture, and text-to-speech playback.

For physical movement, we designed a wearable exoskeleton using six ST3215 serial bus servos, custom 3D-printed components, tendon-driven mechanisms, and PTFE tubing. Each actuator is assigned to a finger or thumb movement, allowing us to work toward independent hand control.

We also incorporated a Waveshare servo interface and designed the architecture around a central AI application responsible for interpreting user requests and coordinating the hardware.

Our software and hardware were developed together, with an emphasis on modularity so that individual components could be tested, improved, and integrated independently.

Challenges We Faced

One of our biggest challenges was translating rotational servo movement into natural finger motion. Unlike a conventional robotic hand, our exoskeleton must accommodate the complex mechanics of actual human joints. We experimented with tendon tension, spool geometry, routing, and mechanical alignment to make movement more predictable.

Another major challenge was working with hardware we had never used before. This was our team's first time soldering, and we had to learn how to properly solder header pins onto our ESP32-S3 microcontroller. We learned about soldering techniques, electrical connections, and how to avoid damaging sensitive components. What initially seemed like a simple task became an important hands-on learning experience that helped us better understand embedded hardware development.

We also faced difficulties getting our camera, microphone, and speaker to operate simultaneously on a single ESP32-S3. This required troubleshooting I²S communication, audio output, memory allocation, camera orientation, and live video streaming.

Beyond the electronics, we had to consider wearable comfort, cable management, power distribution, and safe servo operation. Integrating so many different technologies into one wearable system challenged us to constantly troubleshoot, adapt, and improve our design.

Each obstacle pushed us to learn something new, turning our first experiences with unfamiliar hardware into a working foundation for Handoff.

Accomplishments We're Proud Of

We're proud of bringing Handoff from an ambitious idea to a working prototype.

We successfully configured and controlled six ST3215 servos, integrating them with custom 3D-printed components and tendon mechanisms to enable finger and thumb movement.

We also achieved simultaneous camera streaming, microphone input, and text-to-speech output on a single ESP32-S3.

Beyond the technical achievements, we designed and assembled our wearable exoskeleton, learned to solder for the first time, and gained valuable hands-on experience in robotics and embedded systems.

Most importantly, we established the foundation for connecting AI perception and communication with a wearable physical interface.

What We Learned

Handoff challenged us across robotics, embedded systems, computer vision, mechanical design, and software integration.

We learned that creating physical AI involves much more than generating intelligent responses. It requires translating software decisions into precise, reliable physical actions while accounting for mechanical limitations and human safety.

We also gained experience combining multiple hardware systems into a single architecture and learned the importance of iterative prototyping.

What's Next for Handoff

Our vision extends far beyond this hackathon.

We want to develop reliable, individualized finger control, expand AI-driven movement assistance, and support increasingly natural interactions between humans and intelligent systems.

Future development includes more advanced movement calibration, more precise real-time visual understanding, personalized learning assistance, and collaboration with accessibility specialists to evaluate potential assistive applications.

Ultimately, we envision Handoff as a step toward a future where AI doesn't just tell people what they can do.

It gives them a hand.

AquaWave

AquaWave makes water monitoring smarter with real-time wireless sensor telemetry, custom software-defined radio decoding, and cloud analytics to detect environmental changes.

Like
2

Comment

Water Quality Real Time Dashboard

Hardware

GIF

Lenny Approves

Inspiration

Water quality is essential for healthy ecosystems and communities, but monitoring environmental conditions can require expensive equipment and complex infrastructure. We wanted to create a wireless monitoring system that could collect sensor data and make it accessible through cloud technology.

This inspired AquaWave, a project combining embedded systems, software-defined radio, and cloud analytics to explore a more accessible approach to environmental monitoring.

What it does

AquaWave collects water-quality data using a temperature, pH, and turbidity sensor to predict the chance of an algae bloom. An Arduino transmits the readings wirelessly through a CC1101 radio module, while an ADALM-Pluto software-defined radio receives and decodes the signals.

The decoded measurements are published through MQTT and uploaded to Amazon S3 as JSON batches. Databricks provides a foundation for analyzing historical sensor data, while our dashboard is designed to visualize readings and environmental changes.

How we built it

We started with an Arduino UNO R4 WiFi connected to our sensor inputs and a CC1101 radio operating at 433 MHz. The Arduino collects measurements and transmits them wirelessly.

On the receiving side, we used an ADALM-Pluto SDR and developed custom Python digital signal-processing code to recover the transmitted data. Our decoder processes frequency-shift-keyed signals, synchronizes with packets, and reconstructs the sensor readings.

We then connected the decoded telemetry to MQTT and built a Python pipeline that uploads JSON batches to Amazon S3. We configured a Databricks external location to support cloud-based analysis and worked on a dashboard for visualizing the data.

Challenges we ran into

Our biggest challenge was the pH sensor. We spent approximately eight hours troubleshooting inconsistent readings before deciding to replace it with a potentiometer. This allowed us to simulate pH changes while keeping the rest of our system functional and avoiding inaccurate measurements.

Another major challenge was decoding wireless transmissions using the Pluto SDR. Recovering digital packets from raw radio signals required debugging frequency offsets, timing, synchronization, and signal processing.

Connecting the embedded hardware, radio receiver, MQTT, and cloud services also required careful coordination to keep the data flowing consistently.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Our proudest accomplishment was successfully transmitting sensor data over radio and decoding it with our own software-defined radio receiver. Instead of relying on a conventional receiver, we implemented the signal-processing pipeline ourselves.

We also established live MQTT telemetry and successfully uploaded JSON batches to Amazon S3. Bringing together embedded hardware, wireless communication, Python, and cloud infrastructure into one system was a major achievement for our team.

What we learned

AquaWave gave us hands-on experience with embedded programming, RF communication, digital signal processing, MQTT, and cloud infrastructure.

We learned how software can recover information from raw radio signals and how sensor measurements can move from physical hardware into cloud storage and analytics.

Most importantly, we learned how to adapt when hardware does not behave as expected. Our pH sensor difficulties reinforced the importance of reliable measurements, honest reporting, and making practical engineering decisions under time constraints.

What's next for AquaWave

We plan to integrate a properly calibrated pH sensor, improve wireless reliability, expand our Databricks analytics, and develop more advanced environmental alerts.

In the future, AquaWave could support multiple wireless sensor nodes and provide a more comprehensive platform for monitoring water conditions.

title: Jolteon
text:

Jolteon

Every data center runs hot. We made that heat pay back.

Like
12

Comment
1

Basic dashboard

System Architecture

Jolteon end-to-end

TEG's

Jolteon Hardware

Seebeck Effect 

Circuit Design

Inspiration

This summer’s heat wave in New York showed us a problem we couldn’t ignore. During the hottest time in the year residents needed electricity most to stay cool, however data centers were placing significant strain on the city’s power grid. That strain feeds a vicious cycle: data centers consume huge amounts of energy, a large amount of the energy ends up as waste heat, and that heat makes the city even harder to live in.

This made us ask: why are we letting that heat go to waste? After all, heat is still energy. Instead of letting data centers push the grid and the people who depend on it to their limits, we wanted to capture that waste heat and put it to use. Our project does this with the Seebeck effect, which generates electricity from a temperature difference, turning a byproduct into a resource and reducing the burden on the city’s power supply.

What it does

Jolteon captures waste heat, turns it into stored electricity, and shows you exactly how much it has collected, live.

Step
What happens

🔥 Heat
A hot plate stands in for a server and heats one side of the generators

❄️ Cold
An ice bath keeps the other side cold

⚡ Generate
Four thermoelectric generators turn that temperature difference into electricity

🔋 Store
The current flows straight into a battery pack, no charging chip needed

📈 Track
Every reading streams to a public dashboard anyone can open on their phone

We picked the battery so its own voltage keeps the generators near their most efficient point. The physics does the regulating for us, which keeps the circuit simple enough to explain in one sentence.

How we built it

We agreed on one shared JSON format first, so the hardware, firmware, bridge and dashboard could all be built at the same time without stepping on each other.
┌──────────────── HARDWARE ────────────────┐
│  Hot plate ─► [ 4 × TEG ] ─► Ice bath     │
│         Schottky diode ─► NiMH battery    │
│   INA219 × 2 · DS18B20 × 2 ─► ESP32       │
└───────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
│  USB serial · 1 JSON line every 10 s
▼
┌──────────── MACBOOK (PYTHON BRIDGE) ──────┐
│  validate ─► timestamp ─► SQLite backup   │
│                          ─► uploader      │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────┘
│  HTTPS · JSON
▼
┌──────────────── SUPABASE ─────────────────┐
│          Postgres · readings table        │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────┘
▼
┌──────────────── VERCEL ───────────────────┐
│   FastAPI  ─── JSON ───►  React dashboard │
└──────────────────────────────┬────────────┘
▼
Any phone or laptop

Layer
What it does
Built with

🔥 Hardware
Turns heat into current and stores it
4 × SP1848-27145 TEGs, aluminum plates, Schottky diode, NiMH cells

🔧 Firmware
Samples sensors every second, keeps running energy totals that survive resets
ESP32, Arduino, INA219, DS18B20

🐍 Bridge
Validates every reading, saves it locally first, then syncs to the cloud
Python, pyserial, SQLite, supabase-py

🗄️ Database
Stores the full run
Supabase (Postgres)

🌐 Web
Serves and charts the data live
FastAPI, React, Vite, Recharts, Tailwind, Vercel

Saving every reading locally before uploading was the key decision. If the Wi-Fi drops, readings just wait their turn. If the USB cable gets bumped, the bridge finds the ESP32 again on its own.

Challenges we ran into

Our first database couldn't handle the venue Wi-Fi. We started on a different cloud database, but the connection kept failing on the hackathon's network, and a run that lasts all night can't depend on that. Around 5 a.m. we moved everything to Supabase, which talks over plain HTTPS and went through on the first try.

The ESP32 resets every time you open its port. Every time the bridge connected, the board rebooted, its packet counter started back at 1, and the database quietly threw away new readings as duplicates. Nothing crashed, the data just vanished. We fixed it by saving the counter to flash and jumping it ahead on every boot, so a number can never be reused.

The laptop wasn't hot enough. This was the big one. A laptop's underside is designed to stay cool, and after the heat passes through a thermal pad and two aluminum plates, our generators barely saw a temperature difference, not enough to push a single milliamp into the battery. [We switched to a hot water loop, which turned out to be closer to how modern liquid-cooled data centers actually carry heat away from servers.]

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We tried hard to break our own pipeline, and it held up:

Test
Result

Simulated network outages
0 readings lost, 0 duplicates

Bridge killed 20 times mid-stream
0 missing, 0 duplicates

1,000 corrupted lines
All rejected, 0 crashes

Sensor reading to visible in the API
~200 ms

Chart data with downsampling
83% smaller

Over 3 hours, Jolteon collected 1.2 Wh from heat that would have been thrown away. Every one of those watt-hours is a real measurement, and anyone can scan our QR code and watch the number tick up on their own phone.

What we learned

Heat is easy to make and hard to move. We assumed "hot laptop" meant "lots of usable heat." It doesn't. Thermal contact, a few degrees here and there, and even which side of a module faces up mattered far more than we expected.

Plan for things to break. Saving locally first felt like overkill at the start. Then the Wi-Fi died, the ESP32 kept rebooting, and the cable got bumped, and not one of those cost us a reading thanks to our safety-net data base.

Agree on the data before writing code. Settling the JSON format on day one let four parts get built in parallel, and when something changed, there was exactly one place to change it first.

What's next for Jolteon

The biggest step is moving onto real heat. Server racks and liquid-cooling loops run hotter and steadier than anything we could set up in a weekend, and that's where these generators start to make sense. After that: a proper energy-harvesting chip that works at smaller temperature differences, an estimate of what a full rack or data center could recover, and cost and carbon numbers on the dashboard so the energy we capture means something to the people who would pay for it.
