TrailBuddy

TrailBuddy is a Raspberry Pi hiking companion featuring a pixel-art animal companion, GPS tracking, and friend location sharing.

Like
4

Comment

Active walk display mockup

Start walk display mockup (closed eyes)

Start walk display mockup (open eyes)

Start walk display mockup (tongue sticking out)

Web application mockup

Figma Mockup

🌲 Inspiration

TrailBuddy started with a simple question:

What if you always had a friend to walk with?

We wanted to combine the nostalgia of caring for a virtual pet with something that encourages people to explore outside. Instead of leaving your buddy at home, TrailBuddy joins your adventure, tracks your walk, and gives you another reason to keep moving. 🐾

🐱 What it does

TrailBuddy is a Raspberry Pi-powered virtual pet and GPS trail tracker.

Our working hardware prototype allows users to:

🥕 Feed their virtual pet
💚 Pet it and manage its happiness
🍽️ Monitor its hunger
🛰️ Record a real walk using GPS
📺 View the pet, distance, time, and GPS status on an OLED screen
💾 Save walks locally on the Raspberry Pi
📤 Upload a completed walk to the laptop after reconnecting

When the user selects Send, the Pi creates a walk through our API, uploads its recorded GPS points, and marks the walk as completed. The backend then stores the walk persistently in SQLite.

Our React frontend includes an interactive Leaflet and OpenStreetMap interface that demonstrates how users and their friends’ routes can be visualized.

🛠️ How we built it

TrailBuddy combines physical hardware with a complete software stack:

Hardware: Raspberry Pi, GPS module, OLED screen, and physical button
Hardware software: Python, GPIO controls, GPS parsing, Pillow, and local SQLite storage
Backend: FastAPI and SQLite
Frontend: React and Vite
Maps: Leaflet and OpenStreetMap
Design: Figma

The Raspberry Pi stores GPS coordinates locally throughout a walk. Once the walk ends, it sends the route to a FastAPI server running on a laptop connected to the same hotspot.

The backend supports:

Persistent walks and GPS points
Retry-safe batches of GPS points
Walk distance, duration, pace, and point-count summaries
Four demo user profiles
Friend requests and friendships
Private, friends-only, and public walk visibility
Timed GPS data for future route replay
Safety-event storage
Location-sharing permissions and Last Ping information

We also wrote automated backend tests covering the walk lifecycle, persistence, friendships, visibility, GPS validation, walk summaries, safety events, location sharing, database migrations, and connection cleanup.

😅 Challenges we ran into

Our hardest challenge was connecting the Raspberry Pi to the FastAPI backend and ensuring it sent the correct information.

The Pi originally stored walks using local numeric IDs and Unix timestamps, while the backend expected UUIDs, ISO timestamps, and a different GPS point structure. We had to transform and validate the data before uploading it.

Networking added another challenge. The Pi and laptop needed to be connected to the same hotspot, FastAPI had to listen on 0.0.0.0, and Windows Firewall had to allow the connection.

We also encountered:

GPS fixes and inaccurate coordinates
OLED and physical-button reliability issues
SQLite connection handling
Frontend build and Node.js setup
Git branches, merge conflicts, and teammates updating main
Learning several unfamiliar frameworks during one hackathon

There were many moments when one part worked independently but did not yet communicate with the others. Seeing the Pi finally upload a complete GPS walk successfully was one of the most rewarding moments of the project. 🚀

🎉 Accomplishments that we’re proud of

We are especially proud that:

This was our first hardware project
Our physical pet has animations, hunger, and happiness
The Pi records real GPS coordinates
The Pi successfully uploads completed walks to our FastAPI backend
Walks and GPS points are stored persistently in SQLite
Walks remain available after restarting the server
The backend validates GPS coordinates and timestamps
GPS batches can avoid storing duplicate points
FastAPI serves both the API and the built React application
We created the foundation for social, racing, location-sharing, and safety features
Four team members combined hardware, backend, frontend, and design work into one project

⏳ What we couldn’t finish

We built more backend functionality than we had time to connect to the user interface. Some features remain prototypes or foundations for future work:

Real route integration: The React map currently displays sample routes instead of GPS points retrieved from the backend.
Real friend data: The friends sidebar currently uses mock profiles and locations.
Walk selection: Users cannot yet select between their uploaded walks from the interface.
Ghost racing: The backend stores timed GPS points and a follow/race permission, but the animated ghost and time comparison were not completed.
Public trail discovery: Visibility rules exist in the backend, but there is no public trail browser in the frontend.
Live location: The backend stores Last Ping information, but the Pi currently uploads its route only after a walk ends.
Safety check-ins: The backend can store check-in and SOS events, but the complete physical check-in and emergency-contact notification flow was not finished.
Authentication: The demo uses four seeded users and an X-Demo-User-Id header instead of real accounts.
Additional pets: Cat, capybara, dog, and bear profiles exist in the database, but only the cat has complete visual assets.
Automatic synchronization: Failed uploads can be retried manually, but a complete automatic background synchronization queue was not finished.

Even though we could not complete every feature, we designed the backend so these ideas can be added without rebuilding the entire project.

🧠 What we learned

We learned that hardware and software integration depends heavily on agreeing on data formats and responsibilities early.

We gained experience with:

Raspberry Pi hardware and GPIO
Reading and validating GPS information
Designing APIs for physical devices
FastAPI and SQLite
React, Vite, Leaflet, and OpenStreetMap
Offline-first data collection
Testing and debugging across multiple devices
Git collaboration and resolving merge conflicts
Dividing a large idea into smaller team responsibilities

Most importantly, we learned how to keep adapting when our original plan met real hardware limitations.

👋 About us

Team Hackattack was formed in July 2026 at BloomKnights, the first hackathon for all four of us.

Inspired by the projects and people we met there, we decided to reunite for KnightHacks and challenge ourselves to build our first hardware project: TrailBuddy.

Our team consists of Sam, Xavian, Pablo, and Laeh. Each person contributed their own ideas and skills across hardware, backend development, frontend development, and design.

Combining a Raspberry Pi, GPS hardware, an API, a database, and a React frontend pushed each of us outside our comfort zones. TrailBuddy was a major learning experience, and we hope to carry everything we learned about teamwork and hardware-software integration into future hackathons. 💚

🔮 What’s next for TrailBuddy

Our first priority is replacing the frontend’s sample routes with real uploaded GPS data.

After that, we would like to add:

🗺️ A completed-walk selector
👻 Ghost racing against a friend’s recorded trail
🌐 Public and friends-only trail discovery
📍 Optional live location and Last Ping display
✅ Physical safety check-ins
🆘 Emergency-contact notifications
🔐 Real accounts and authentication
🐻 Additional pets and customization
📶 Reliable automatic offline synchronization
🏆 Achievements, challenges, and walk statistics

Our long-term goal is to make exploring outside feel safer, more social, and more playful.

CardioView

A 3D heart that beats with your real time ECG. A Polar H10 streams your heartbeat into the browser, every beat moves the heart, and Gemini turns any patient you describe into a rhythm.

Like
8

Comment
1

Inspiration

An ECG strip is one of the most important pictures in medicine and one of the least intuitive. I wanted to put a strap on and watch my own heart, chamber by chamber, do exactly what the trace says it is doing, right now in real time.

What it does

CardioView turns a Polar H10 chest strap into a live 3D heart in the browser. You connect your own strap over Web Bluetooth, the server finds every beat, and an anatomical heart model squeezes in sync: P wave for the atria, QRS for the ventricles. Next to it sit the live trace, heart rate and a chamber timeline. Exercise mode runs a guided session with voice prompts and prints a report on real ECG paper with a QR code. Gemini heart takes a sentence like "a 40 year old on cocaine" and turns it into a rhythm recipe the simulator plays on the same heart.

How we built it

Python and FastAPI, one pipeline per viewer, so any number of straps work at once. NeuroKit2 finds beats on a rolling 8 second window at the strap's native 130 Hz, stamped in stream time so the heart squeezes when the R wave crosses the now line. The heart is Three.js with a vertex shader that weights every vertex by its distance to each chamber. Gemini runs in JSON mode against a fixed schema with every value clamped. 160 tests, and a public copy on Render.

Challenges

The first 30 seconds off the strap are junk, so a signal monitor separates lost, pads and streaming, and the heart stops instead of lying. Chrome lists the strap twice. A WebSocket reconnect after a deploy produced a false "Not connected" until the page learned to re-send its state. And I tore the design down twice before landing on one dark surface where the heart is the only bold thing.

I learned about how Computer Vision yesterday from the guys at #NextEraEnergy and decided try the spot challenge because at the workshop I instantly thought of a moonshot agent for good - #OneEthos

Like
1

Comment

Inspiration

America’s infrastructure is aging and underfunded, and the cost of waiting keeps rising. Bridges, roads, water systems, and the power grid continue to receive poor grades, while local governments and agencies are asked to do more with limited budgets and incomplete information. The data that could help prioritize repairs already exists in public reports and databases, but it is scattered, hard to compare, and rarely turned into clear recommendations that decision-makers can act on.

I built The AIFA because better prioritization can stretch limited infrastructure dollars further. When leaders can quickly see which problems carry the highest risk and community impact, they can focus resources where they matter most instead of reacting to whatever issue is loudest or most recent.

What it does

The AIFA is a tool that helps surface and prioritize infrastructure issues so public officials, engineers, and community groups can make clearer decisions with the information they already have.

It pulls together publicly available data on roads, bridges, weather risk, and related conditions, then highlights which problems appear most urgent based on safety, community impact, and available context. Users can ask straightforward questions such as “Which bridges in this area should we look at first after heavy rain?” or “Where should limited maintenance dollars go to reduce the biggest risks?” and receive a prioritized list with supporting details and suggested next steps.

The goal is not to replace engineers or policymakers. It is to help them spend less time hunting for information and more time acting on the highest-impact issues.

How we built it

I focused on making the tool useful for people who need answers, not on building the most complex system possible. The AIFA connects public infrastructure and weather data sources, organizes the relevant information, and uses AI to compare options and explain why certain issues rise to the top. The result is a simple interface where someone can ask a question in plain language and get a structured, prioritized response they can review and share.

The prototype concentrates on a practical loop: bring the data together, highlight what matters most, and present clear recommendations that support real decisions.

Challenges we ran into

Public infrastructure data is often incomplete, outdated, or formatted differently depending on the source, so making it comparable took more work than expected.
Ranking issues fairly is difficult. Safety risk, number of people affected, and repair urgency do not always point in the same direction, and the tool had to make those trade-offs visible.
The scope of infrastructure is huge. I deliberately narrowed the focus so the prototype could deliver useful answers instead of trying to cover every type of asset at once.
Decision-makers need to trust the output. That meant showing the key factors behind each recommendation rather than just delivering a score or a list.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

Created a working tool that turns scattered public data into prioritized recommendations decision-makers can actually use.
Designed the prioritization so users can see both the ranking and the main reasons behind it.
Built a simple interface that lets non-technical users ask questions and receive clear, structured answers.
Demonstrated the prototype on realistic scenarios such as post-storm risk and maintenance backlog prioritization.
Showed that better organization and prioritization of existing information can improve how limited infrastructure resources are allocated.

What we learned

The biggest barrier is often not a lack of data but the difficulty of turning that data into decisions that busy leaders can act on.
Clear prioritization and transparent reasoning matter as much as the underlying analysis.
Narrowing the scope early made it possible to deliver something useful instead of an incomplete general system.
Public agencies and communities already have more useful information than they can easily act on; the opportunity is in making that information easier to compare and prioritize.
Tools like this create the most value when they support existing decision processes rather than trying to replace them.

What's next for The AIFA (American Infrastructure Fixing Agent)

Expand coverage to additional infrastructure types and more geographic areas based on where the greatest need and available data exist.
Incorporate additional public sources that improve the quality of prioritization.
Allow users to adjust how different factors (safety, population impact, cost) are weighted so the tool can reflect local priorities.
Add simple ways for teams to review, comment on, and share recommendations.
Explore pilot opportunities with local governments or agencies that want better visibility into where limited funds should go first.
Continue refining the tool so it remains practical and easy for non-technical users to adopt.

ParkVision: Building a Smart Autonomous Parking Rover | UCF Hackathon 2026 🚗
For UCF Hackathon 2026, our team has been developing ParkVision, a smart RC rover project that brings together embedded systems, computer vision, autonomous navigation, and web development.
Our goal is to combine physical robotics with intelligent software to explore how a small-scale autonomous vehicle can navigate and support parking-related applications.
What We're Building
Our project brings together three major components:
🔧 Embedded Systems & Robotics
Using an ESP32-S3 microcontroller programmed in C++, we've developed a control system for our RC rover that supports Wi-Fi communication, steering and throttle control, and autonomous movement.
The rover can execute a programmed square route using calibrated motor timing and steering adjustments. We've also implemented connection recovery and navigation status feedback.
👁️ Computer Vision
Our project includes a computer vision component intended to help the system interpret its surroundings and support parking-related decision-making.
By integrating visual processing with the rover's control system, we're working toward a more intelligent approach to autonomous navigation.
💻 Frontend Development
We're developing a web-based dashboard to provide an interface for interacting with the system and viewing information from the rover.
This brings the hardware, robotics logic, and user interface together into one project.
Collaboration and Development
One of the most valuable aspects of this hackathon has been integrating multiple areas of software engineering into a single system.
Our team organized the project into separate GitHub directories for the Arduino firmware, computer vision code, and frontend application. This allowed us to work on different components while maintaining a shared codebase.
We've also encountered challenges involving sensor integration, hardware calibration, and communication between components. Troubleshooting these issues has been an important part of the engineering process.

What's Next?
We're continuing to work toward integrating the rover's embedded control system, computer vision functionality, and dashboard into a complete demonstration.

title: Sprout
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Sprout

Sprout is an AI-powered desktop companion that helps blind and low-vision people create, understand, and edit presentations and other visual work independently through natural voice conversations.

Like

Comment

Sprout — Your work, within reach
Sprout is a voice companion that helps blind and low-vision people create, understand, and revise digital work through conversation.

Inspiration
An idea might begin with a few words, but turning it into a presentation or understanding a spreadsheet often requires navigating a visual interface.

We wanted to make that process more accessible. A person should be able to describe what they want, hear what was created, question the result, and ask for changes.

The World Health Organization estimates that at least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment. That inspired us to explore how conversational tools could give people more control over everyday computer tasks. 

Sprout grew from that idea: helping users turn their intentions into work they can understand and share.

What it does
Sprout lives in a floating Windows companion. Users can speak naturally, ask follow-up questions, and interrupt a response when they want to change direction.

Its main showcase is creating and reviewing editable PowerPoint presentations. Users can request a presentation, include their own pictures, navigate to a slide, hear its content, make supported revisions, and undo changes. Explicit saving and same-laptop resume help them return to their work.

Sprout also includes workflows for:

Spreadsheet analysis: Compare supported datasets, inspect source records, and export Excel workbooks and presentation reports.
Personal finance: Explore spending changes, hypothetical budget adjustments, and fixed-rate payment estimates.
Electricity bills: Review extracted bill information, correct fields, and understand changes in usage and charges.
Computer assistance: Research online, open supported applications, locate named folders, describe captured screens, and perform bounded navigation.
Coding: Generate and run simple Python calculations and open generated code in VS Code.
Across these tasks, Sprout gives users a way to ask, inspect, correct, and continue.

How we built it
We built Sprout’s desktop interface with Electron, React, and TypeScript, supported by a local Fastify backend.

Hugging Face hosted Qwen models interpret conversational requests, describe images, and generate structured content. Typed validation checks proposed actions, while deterministic tools handle file operations and numerical calculations.

ElevenLabs Scribe provides streaming transcription, and ElevenLabs speech synthesis delivers spoken responses. Cancellation checks connect conversation to execution so interruptions can stop outdated work and playback.

PptxGenJS creates editable PowerPoint content, while ExcelJS produces workbooks with formulas and supporting records. Databricks verifies supported analyses against source data. Neon stores explicitly saved project state and revision history.

Original presentation images and folder bindings remain local, and resume verifies the original sources before restoring a project.

Challenges we ran into
The biggest challenge was keeping conversation, files, and application state consistent.

“Make it shorter” needs a clear slide target. An interruption can change a task already underway. A navigation request needs confirmation that PowerPoint selected the correct slide.

We also discovered that polished AI output can lose important meaning. A revision might fit the slide while dropping a qualification. That led us to evaluate content fidelity alongside formatting and layout.

We built stable slide identities, guarded file updates, recovery copies, cancellation handling, and verified readback to address these problems. Revision reliability remains an active development priority.

Accomplishments we’re proud of
We connected spoken requests to real, editable files and verified key workflows with actual providers, cloud storage, and installed PowerPoint.

Our latest integrated source suite passed 1,251 automated unit tests. Another 26 scoped browser cases passed with mocked providers and native interfaces. We visually inspected seven mixed-scene exported slides with no visible clipping or overlap.

Actual save-and-resume checks preserved presentation content and undo history, and export checks confirmed that original image bytes survived generation.

In a fictional revenue demonstration, changing the comparison to continuously operating locations changed reported growth from 52.2% to 11.9%. That showed why giving users a way to question an answer matters.

These results measure engineering progress. We have not yet measured time savings or independence gains with blind and low-vision participants.

What we learned
The follow-up is central to useful assistance.

Users need to understand what happened, inspect the evidence, and recover when something goes wrong. Requests such as “explain that,” “change this part,” and “undo that” shaped how we built Sprout.

We also learned that passing tests and receiving valid model output are only parts of verification. The final artifact must reflect the user’s intent, and the assistant’s feedback must accurately describe what succeeded.

What’s next for Sprout
Our immediate priorities are improving revision fidelity and completing release checks and physical voice rehearsals.

Our development build includes branching diagrams, keyboard diagram exploration, richer spatial descriptions, and integrated verified-chart workflows. These additions are awaiting release acceptance.

Next, we want to work with blind and low-vision participants and measure independent task completion, completion time, correction success, and requests for assistance.

Their feedback will guide Sprout’s growth to

title: fpga_LangModel
text:
Notifications

Loading...

fpga_LangModel

AI and the hardware it runs on are both getting expensive, so we decided to make our own.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Language models usually run on GPUs or CPUs. We wanted to see how small a model could be and still
generate sentences, and then build the hardware that runs it ourselves: no soft CPU, no DDR, no
vendor accelerator. Just a tiny neural network and a Verilog circuit made for it.

What it does

A laptop sends four word tokens over the USB-UART cable of a Digilent Arty A7-100T. The FPGA runs
the complete neural network in hardware and sends back one byte, the predicted next word. The laptop
repeats this to turn a typed prompt into a short plant-care sentence.

The network is a small feedforward model over a 64-word vocabulary:

$$x = [E_{t_0};\,E_{t_1};\,E_{t_2};\,E_{t_3}]$$

$$h = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_1 x + b_1), \qquad z = W_2 h + b_2, \qquad t_{\text{next}} = \arg\max_i z_i$$

4-word context, 64 x 8 embedding table, a 32-to-32 layer, a 32-to-64 layer, 3,680 parameters
INT8 weights and activations with INT32 accumulators
Under a thousand clock cycles per predicted word

How we built it

Model (Python). We trained the model in PyTorch on a small plant-monitoring corpus, quantized it
to integers, and wrote an integer-only Python reference that the hardware must match exactly. One
export script turns the trained model into the memory files the FPGA loads.

Hardware (Verilog). One reusable 8-lane multiply-accumulate array computes eight output neurons
at once. A single activation is broadcast to all lanes, and each lane multiplies it by its own
weight:

$$a_i \leftarrow a_i + x_j \, W_{ij}, \qquad i = 0, \dots, 7$$

The same array serves both layers. A finite-state machine sequences the embedding lookup, both
layers, the argmax and the reply, while weights, biases and embeddings sit in on-chip block RAM.
Each lane registers its product to keep the multiplier's critical path short. A small UART receiver
and transmitter connect it to the laptop: four bytes in, one byte out.

Verification. Every module has a self-checking testbench. The export script recomputes the
network from the files it wrote, in the order the hardware uses, and requires an exact match with
the Python reference. A whole-system testbench sends hundreds of reference vectors through the
design as serial bytes and compares every answer. On the board we used an oscilloscope to check the
clock and the serial timing, and Vivado's ILA and VIO cores to look inside the running chip.

Tools. Vivado, SystemVerilog, Python and PyTorch, LaTeX for the design diagrams, and Claude Code
to help research, write and debug.

Challenges

Timing. Our first build missed the 100 MHz clock target because the multiplier was built from
logic instead of a DSP slice, so we pipelined it with a product register and a drain state in the
control FSM.
Bit-exactness. Signed arithmetic, shifts and byte order are easy to get subtly wrong between
Python and hardware, so we made the export check itself against the reference.
Debugging hardware. Waveforms, a scope and the ILA each showed us a different class of bug.

Accomplishments

A full path from a text prompt to a hardware-computed prediction, a quantized model that matches an
integer reference exactly, and a design you can inspect from the outside with a scope and from the
inside with an ILA.

What we learned

Hardware and software have to be designed together: the number format, the memory layout and the
protocol all shaped both halves. Testing every layer against an independent reference caught more
mistakes than any amount of staring at waveforms.

What's next

Loading weights over the serial link instead of baking them into the bitstream, a larger vocabulary
and context, and moving the tokenizer into hardware.

Built with: Verilog, SystemVerilog, Python, PyTorch, Vivado, Digilent Arty A7-100T, LaTeX, Claude Code

text:

He Can See Us

One Virtual Reality Monster VS Many PC Goblins

Like
7

Comment
1

About Our Game

He Can See Us is a multiplayer survival game made in Unity where players must hide from a player playing as a monster using a virtual reality headset. Players on desktop run for refuge in a desperate attempt to shelter from the monster's wrath!

How we built it

This project was built using the Unity Game Engine version 6000.4.9f1. For VR support we used Unity's built in XR plugin and for online multiplayer we utilized Unity's Netcode for GameObjects alongside Unity Relay. Finally, we used Libre Fracture 2.0, an open-source plug-in for destruction simulation, to procedurally generate pre-fractured models. This meant we didn't have to calculate the destruction of meshes at runtime, which saved us a lot of performance. We modified the source code so that when the monster hit a building, only the area within a certain radius of the impact would be destroyed, rather than the entire building at once.

Challenges we ran into

A major challenge that we ran into throughout the development of the project was to allow cross platform multiplayer play between VR and PC. Further, networking was made even more complicated by several mechanics such as the destructible environment and syncing many players across both platforms. Another challenge we ran into was the performance cost of objects that could be destroyed. These objects were made up of many individual chunks that would break apart when hit, and rendering all of those chunks at once created a lot of extra draw calls. To solve this, we used the regular, solid model that were cheaper to render and only switched to the version made up of individual chunks when the monster hit it, for each building. This optimized performance during normal gameplay while still allowing objects to break apart when needed.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We're proud of how effectively we were able to work as a team and leverage each other's strengths to solve problems throughout the 36 hour event. Developing a PC/VR online multiplayer game is no easy task, especially in just 36 hours. We we're especially proud of ourselves for; syncing 6+ players, PC/VR compat, efficient usage of git, and our amazing communication and vibes.

What we learned

Through the development of He Can See Us we learned countless lessons about teamwork, cross platform compatibility, and how important every second can be during a Hackathon!

What's next for He Can See Us

The next steps for He Can See Us is adding the ability for players to join each other's lobbies through the Steamworks network, massively broadening our audience and quality of the game.

KnightSaver

Cheap Surprise Bags of leftover food from UCF dining spots. Pick up with your Knight Pass, see the food and CO2 you saved, and earn Saver Cash and rewards for every rescue.

Like

Comment

Inspiration
UCF's dining spots close every night with good food still on the counter, while many students eat on a tight budget. We wanted to connect the two on our own campus.
What it does
KnightSaver is an iOS app where UCF dining spots sell leftover food as cheap Surprise Bags.

For students

UCF students only: you sign in with your @ucf.edu email, so every account belongs to a real UCF student. The database itself refuses any other student sign-up.
Explore: Surprise Bags from 17 real UCF dining spots, with pickup time, bags left, street address, walking distance from your location and Apple Maps directions. Shelves like Pick up now, Near you, Community favorites and All on campus, plus search.
Reserve or join the waitlist: reserve with Apple Pay; when a bag is sold out, join the waitlist and get an offer if one frees up. Manage or cancel your pickup from Profile.
Knight Pass: one reusable QR pass in your profile that staff scan at the counter.
Past Surprise Reveals: after a verified pickup, rate the portion, quality and pickup and add a photo of what you got, so the next student knows what to expect.
Impact: UCF's weekly campus goal, plus your rescued bags, food saved, CO₂e avoided, a 6-week chart and your recent rescues. Only staff-verified pickups count, and a "How is CO₂e estimated?" page shows the formula and its FAO source.
Rewards: every verified order earns Saver Cash, which you spend at campus kitchens by showing a QR (the server checks the balance and never charges twice), and unlocks gifts from partner shops near campus, redeemed with a one-time code. There's also a weekly Rescue League (nicknames only), Knight of the Week and 8 badges.
App tour and dark mode: a short tour for new accounts and a dark mode switch in Profile.

For kitchen staff

Live dashboard: current Surprise Bags, reserved pickups, waitlist offers and today's verified rescues.
Scan Knight Pass: the camera reads the student's QR, finds their reservation (or lets staff pick one if there are several), and verifies the pickup, optionally with the bag's weight. A pickup can't be verified twice. The same scanner takes Saver Cash off the bill.
Manage listings: edit, pause, close or cancel a listing, mark no-shows as missed, and set a max bags per listing.
Impact report: bags collected, pickup completion, revenue recovered, average rating and CO₂e avoided, updated only after verified pickups.

AI

EcoKnight AI: a "How can I help you?" assistant for food-waste and climate questions. It can look up the student's own impact, rescues and league standing through read-only tools, and uses a sourced fact list (USDA, EPA) for general numbers.
AI listing assistant: staff just say what's left ("6 bagels and 4 croissants, pickup 7 to 7:30") and AI turns it into a ready listing: it splits the items into bags, sets the bag count, price and pickup time, and makes a Surprise Bag or a Rescue Bag that lists its contents. Staff can also edit a live listing by voice. Nothing goes live until staff approve it, and the AI never makes allergen or food-safety claims.
Both run on Google Gemini, with Apple's on-device model and offline rules as fallbacks, so they keep working without a connection.
How we built it
Swift and SwiftUI on iOS 17, with a Supabase backend (Postgres, Auth with @ucf.edu sign-up, row-level security and transactional functions for reservations and verification). Google Gemini powers the voice-to-listing assistant and EcoKnight, with Apple's on-device model and offline rules as fallbacks. We tested HTML previews of every screen with Playwright.
Challenges
Keeping impact honest (only verified pickups count), keeping AI suggestions under staff control, and syncing two people's work on the student and kitchen sides in one weekend.
What's next
Onboard real UCF dining partners and partner shops, capture Apple Pay only after a verified pickup, add a signed Apple Wallet Knight Pass, and open leagues for residence halls and student organizations.

title: Cyclops
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Cyclops

Say what you're looking for. Cyclops finds it with your phone's camera and walks you there, warning you about anything in the way. Built for blind and low-vision people, on any phone.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Finding an object is a constant problem for blind and low-vision people: an empty chair, the trash can, the door in an unfamiliar room. A cane finds what's at your feet, not what you're looking for. Most phone apps can name what's in front of you but can't walk you to it, and the distance features that do exist need a Pro iPhone with LiDAR. We wanted something that works on any phone, using only the camera.

What it does

Cyclops is a voice-first guide for finding things indoors.

Ask for anything. Press and hold anywhere and say "find the chair", "find the red backpack" or "find the exit sign". It knows 79 everyday objects, matches descriptions, and searches for anything else by name.
It locks on. Turn slowly; when it's sure, you hear a chime and feel a buzz. Then the voice guides you: "Chair, turn a little right and walk about 3 meters." and "Straight ahead." The gyro remembers where the target is, so if you turn away, you hear "Chair at 2 o'clock", with pulses that get stronger as you face it again.
It watches the way. Once you're lined up, it checks the straight line to the target: "Path to it looks open." or "Something in the way, about 2 meters. Go around it on the left." Anything close starts a detour ("Something close on your right. Step to your left."), and low things like boxes and bins are called out before they slip out of the bottom of the picture. The wall the target stands against doesn't count.
You arrive. Within reach it dings and says where to reach: "You're there. Reach forward and a little left, at waist height."
Walker runs it all by voice. A voice assistant handles setup, finding, and settings (units, warning distance, speech speed, haptics, voices) without looking at the screen.
Trusted voices. With their consent, record someone for 15 seconds and the app guides you in their voice.

Cyclops is clear about its limits: stationary obstacles, indoors, and never a replacement for a cane.

How we built it

App: Expo and React Native in TypeScript: camera frames, the gyro, haptics and audio. A tracker follows the target across frames in gyro coordinates, so the box doesn't jump between similar objects, and locks on after two confident sightings.
Backend: FastAPI on a Hugging Face Space with a T4 GPU, every model in half precision: about 0.1 to 0.3 seconds per frame on the server, with two frames in flight.
Models: Depth Anything V2 Metric for distance at every pixel, scaled against tape-measured photos from the venue; DETR for the 79 built-in objects; OWLv2 for open-vocabulary search; SigLIP for matching descriptions like "red bench".
Obstacle logic: a walking lane split into foot, waist and head height; the floor removed by comparing each pixel with the rest of its row; a 0.8 m wide corridor along the line to the target; the target and anything behind it ignored.
Voice: ElevenLabs Flash for speech, cached per voice and phrase; Scribe v2 speech-to-text with speaker separation, so it follows whoever said "find"; and instant voice cloning. The server only speaks the app's own phrases, so a cloned voice can't be made to say anything else.

Challenges we ran into

Depth from one camera is wrong up close. A box half a meter away read 1.3 m. We tuned the depth scale against tape-measured photos and use object size and the tracker for the last meter.
The floor in front of you isn't in the picture. Held up toward a target, the phone can't see roughly the last 1.5 m of floor, so a low box leaves the bottom of the frame before it ever reads as close. Low things are now warned about early, and the detour holds after they leave the frame.
False alarms next to the target. The wall behind a chair set off "something close on your left" right before arriving. Now only things clearly nearer than the target count.
Latency. The first version took over a second per frame on a CPU. A GPU in half precision, two frames in flight and timeouts for stragglers brought the server to about 0.2 seconds.
Talking too much. Directions ran into each other. The voice now stays quiet while you're on course and speaks when there's something to do; safety warnings always cut in.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

It's the first hackathon for all three of us.
It finds the thing you asked for and walks you to it, end to end, on an ordinary phone.
The whole app works without looking at the screen.
Safety comes first: warnings interrupt everything, and it only suggests stepping to a side the camera actually saw was open.
We personally prefer the accessibility settings provided by Cyclops compared to the iOS accessibility features

What we learned

How monocular depth behaves in real rooms, and how much it matters to tune against measured ground truth instead of trusting the model.
How to design for non-visual use: every state spoken or felt, short phrases, never talking over a warning.
How to serve several vision models on a GPU and measure latency from the camera to the speaker.

What's next for Cyclops

One language-model call per request to map "my MacBook" or "the thing I drink from" onto objects the app can find.
Remembering where an obstacle is from the phone's motion after it leaves the picture.
LiDAR depth on phones that have it, and a native build for faster photos.
Outdoors, once curbs and drop-offs can be detected reliably.

Spotlight

Spotlight turns robot data into actionable insights.

Like
3

Inspiration

(˶˃ ᵕ ˂˶) .ᐟ.ᐟ NextEra Energy’s SPOT Operational Intelligence Challenge asked us to turn robotic inspection data into something an operator could understand and act on. The challenge focused on connecting mission results, sensor readings, anomalies, and locations to help someone understand what happened and what needs attention.

We wanted to build Spotlight to bring those pieces together. Our goal was to make inspection data easier to explore and give operators a clearer understanding of the facility they are looking at.

What it does

Spotlight is a facility inspection dashboard built around the synthetic SPOT dataset provided for the NextEra challenge. It connects inspection history with spatial context so users can explore what happened, where it happened, and which findings need review.

◝(ᵔᵕᵔ)◜ Mission overview: Compare mission completion, action outcomes, and inspection findings

ヽ(°〇°)ﾉ Interactive digital twin: Explore a simulated facility, select waypoints, and view detected obstructions

( ˶ˆᗜˆ˵ ) Mission replay: Play back recorded mission events and follow SPOT’s simulated movement

ヾ( ˃ᴗ˂ )◞ Machine learning support: Provide backend APIs for gauge detection, corrosion classification, thermal-image classification, and experimental acoustic analysis

How we built it

We connected the challenge’s missions, actions, readings, anomalies, assets, and locations so users could explore their relationships.

React and TypeScript: Built the frontend dashboard
Django REST Framework: Built the backend APIs
PostgreSQL: Stores inspection records, replay events, and saved machine learning results
Three.js: Displays the facility and its waypoints in the interactive digital twin
LiDAR pipeline: Aligns point clouds, identifies changes, and groups those changes into possible obstructions
AMD AI compute: Used to train machine learning models during development
Vultr: Hosts the application
GoDaddy Registry: Provides the .select extension for our domain, getspotlight.select
Figma Make: Used to prototype the landing page design (https://www.figma.com/make/5Z1YxDxupKTOJfeXlDxnwi/Build-landing-page?t=TlUPTTC4zESwkR8W-1&desktop-link-click-timestamp=1791730157546&desktop-ul-exp-bucket=po)

Challenges we ran into

One of our biggest challenges was understanding what an operator would need from the inspection data. We had to translate NextEra Energy’s challenge into features that could help someone understand mission outcomes, investigate findings, and decide what needs attention.

We also had to connect different kinds of data while keeping their meaning consistent. Understanding how missions, actions, readings, and findings related to each other helped us bring that information into the dashboard.

We worked through LiDAR alignment, deployment, and merge conflicts as different parts of the project came together. Keeping everyone’s features working while maintaining a cohesive design took communication and iteration.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are proud of bringing our separate contributions into one working project. Seeing the dashboard, mission replay, and digital twin come together made the inspection data feel much easier to understand.

We also built a backend that can store and organize inspection records alongside machine learning results. Together, these features helped us address the challenge’s goal of making relationships in the data easier to explore.

What we learned

We learned how much work goes into connecting a full-stack application beyond building its individual pieces. Data relationships, API contracts, deployment, and collaboration all shaped how the final project came together.

We also learned that sleep is important. It is easy to keep pushing during a hackathon, but taking a break helps us think more clearly, catch mistakes, and work better together.  (- - )💤

What's next for spotlight

As we continue developing the project, we would like to improve our models, test them on more representative data, and keep refining the interface.

title: RiHab
text:
Notifications

Loading...

RiHab

RiHab is an Arduino-powered wearable that gamifies physical therapy. By tracking joint motion, speed, and stability, it delivers real-data-driven recovery scores to patients and providers.

Like

Comment

logo

Dashboard

Inspiration

Our team of three wanted to build a project that implemented physical hardware using low-level C algorithms, as C is the language we are most familiar with. We were inspired to combine this bare-metal hardware interaction with Python, using Python as a lightweight wrapper to handle the complex networking and logic scaffolding.

What it does

RiHab is a smart rehabilitation wearable that turns at-home physical therapy into a precise, gamified, data-driven experience. Using an Arduino, a rotary angle sensor, and a 3D-axis accelerometer, our hardware captures a patient's full range of motion, repetition speed, and "flux" (micro-instabilities). It compares the injured limb to a healthy limb to generate an objective recovery score. The platform also gamifies consistency with workout streaks and connects patients to in-network providers and recommended stretches if they experience discomfort.

How we built it

To maximize our 36-hour execution window, we completely decoupled our roles so no one was waiting on someone else's code to compile. We divided the team into three specific areas:

Low-Level Software Engineer: Focused on writing the core C data processing loops, managing memory, formatting the raw output data, and building the device.

Python Integration Lead: Focused on capturing the C outputs, feeding data into the logic models, and handling the reporting.

Hardware & Communications: Managed the wiring of breadboard components and ensured the sensors passed accurate voltages.

Instead of building the project feature-by-feature, we broke the architecture down by the data pipeline. We structured the flow into isolated stages: reading raw physical signals into C, processing the algorithms in C to output a formatted string of numbers, and bridging those numbers into a Python script. To avoid bottlenecks while the complex C math was being written, we temporarily passed hardcoded "dummy" data to the Python engineer so they could build the backend logic concurrently. Once each component was built we spent time to integrate them together seamlessly. Finally, we created binding devices to attatch the Arduino, breadboard, and sensors to a thigh plate to keep the components stable using OpenSCAD and then exported the files and fed them through a 3D-printer. We were able to cut printing time by decreasing the infill percentage and keeping the plates hallow. 

Challenges we ran into

The biggest challenge we ran into was integration AFTER building out each part in addition to learning how to use the hardware and setting up the pipeline on the fly. During a 36 hour hackathon it's not efficient to wait for other people to finish building their contribution to then build your own, so its alot of hardcoding dummy data until you're able to implement real data. We also ran into a lot of hardware issues as well one being a lock-up in the setup() phase due to the IC2 protocol waiting infinitely if the accelerometer wires were even the tiniest bit loose. I had to use jumper wires with the grove wires, we didn't have grove-to-male wires.  

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We are incredibly proud of the way we were able to implement great system design which helps streamline the process significantly. We're also impressed with our ability to adapt and learn new skills on the drop of a dime and implement aid skills effectively.

What we learned

We learned the critical importance of breaking a project down by its data pipeline rather than by final features. By isolating our inputs, logic, and outputs into stages, we kept development moving simultaneously—even passing hardcoded dummy arrays to the Python engineer so they could build the backend while the complex C math was still being written.

What's next for RiHab

title: KinematiX
text:
Notifications

Loading...

KinematiX

In the increasing world of embedded devices, researchers want to find out what a board does quick and fast. Our robot can probe pins, and we use detection algos to see what kind of data is going out.

Like

Comment

Main Robot Arm probing a board

interactive pin selection UI

Setup View 1

Setup View 2

sample report

Full robot electronics setup

Inspiration

We wanted to solve a problem while building a cool robot. Majority of our team works in the field of embedded systems research. There can be many cases where you might not know what program is running on a board, or could be an unfamiliar architecture. Our robot can help with automatically probing each pin you choose on the board, and report the most likely protocol and data.

What it does

The user will take a photo from their phone of the board
The photo is sent to OpenCV to find most if not all pins on the board, and determine which cartesian coordinates they are at from the perspective of the robot
The user will select which pins they want to probe
The robot arm will move the probe to the calculated cartesian point
Osciloscope will sample the data off of the pin for X amount of time and send the raw readings to our computer
The raw data will get sent to the backend, get cleaned and then sent to a detection algorithm to determine what protcol (UART, PWM etc) and data was being sent over the pin
A report is generated that the researcher can view

How we built it

Hardware Side:
We used 2 stepper motors to provide angular movement from 2 centers for X and Y movement, and an additional SG90 motor for Z movement so the probe can touch the contacts on the board. The main processor is a STM32 that calculates where and how to move the arm using Kinematics equations. It recieves commands from the Host PC via serial, which is the coordinates that the arm will move to the correct probe on the target board. The motors are controlled by stepper motor drivers and powered by a KORAD KD30005 power supply.

Software Side:
The backend and API were written with Python using FastAPI. The backend had 3 main components: osciloscope processing (capture, cleaning and detection), OpenCV processing to determine and show pins that the user can probe, and robot programming (over serial) in order to send commands to the robot controller.

Challenges we ran into

Some members of our team had little experience building robots, especially from scratch
Many of the existing parts that we either had or borrowed did not work well in practice for building an arm

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We learned how to operate a osciloscope and capture data off of it over USB
Built a robot entirely from scratch without pre-made kits (ex: Vex)

What we learned

Test all hardware prior to the start of the hackathon and know where to get it from
Learn the capabilities of different robotic components and any dependencies they will require (such as stepper motor controllers)

What's next for KinematiX

We would definitely like to improve the stability and accuracy of the robot. A lot of the hardware and algorithms would work significantly better if we had more time and were certain of resources to use. We would also like to add more detection capabilities to open up to more niche protocols, ideally with a properly trained ML solution

title: Resonance
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Resonance

Resonance is a gesture-controlled instrument that turns music into sound, visual notation, and vibration, letting Deaf and hard-of-hearing users create, see, and feel every layer.

Like

Comment

Home

Tutorial

Tempo set

Studio

Wristband prototype version 1

Inspiration

A lot of accessibility tools are built around helping Deaf people adapt to a world that was not designed with them in mind. With Resonance, we wanted to flip that idea around and ask: what if the experience itself adapted instead?

We chose music because it is one of the most universal forms of expression, but it is still usually designed around hearing first. Music is more than sound — it is rhythm, movement, emotion, creativity, and connection.

That led us to ask a bigger question: what would music look and feel like if hearing was not required to create it?

Resonance grew from that idea. Instead of asking Deaf and hard-of-hearing users to experience music the same way everyone else does, we wanted to explore a system where music could be created and understood through multiple senses.

What it does

Resonance is a gesture-controlled instrument that lets users create music with their hands in front of a camera.

Users can build a four-layer composition using:

Drums
Bass
Keys
Lead

The layers can be recorded in any order. Hand height controls pitch or drum selection, pinching triggers notes and hits, and movement intensity affects dynamics. Users can also use one or two hands to play the same instrument, which makes rhythmic patterns feel more natural.

Every composition is represented in three synchronized ways:

Sound through generated audio
Vision through particles and visual music notation
Touch through a two-motor haptic wristband

The wristband changes roles depending on what the performer is doing. During the count-in, both motors pulse together to establish the tempo. While recording over an existing composition, previously recorded Drums and Bass can be felt through the wristband, giving the performer a groove to play against instead of only a metronome. During playback, the left motor represents Drums and the right motor represents Bass.

Resonance also includes a Feel Only mode, where the audio is muted but the visual and tactile structure of the composition continues.

How we built it

Music and timing

We built Resonance with React, TypeScript, and Vite.

For the music system, we used Tone.js. One of the most important technical decisions was using a shared musical transport so that the recorded layers, audio, visual notation, particles, and haptic events all follow the same timeline.

Each recording begins with a full count-in and starts from the same Bar 1 of the four-bar loop so every layer stays synchronized.

Gesture control

For camera-based input, we used MediaPipe Hand Landmarker.

We track:

hand position
hand height
pinch gestures
movement intensity
multiple hands

Those gestures are then translated into musical events. Each hand keeps its own gesture state so two hands can independently play the same instrument without interfering with each other.

Visual system

The visual experience uses a custom HTML Canvas particle system.

We wanted the visuals to communicate actual musical structure rather than simply react decoratively to sound. For example:

rhythm creates waves and impacts
pitch changes vertical position
note duration creates trails and ribbons
dynamics affect size and intensity
each instrument has its own visual language

The score and particle system stay synchronized with the same musical events used by the audio engine.

Haptic wristband

For the tactile side, we built a prototype using an ESP32 and two vibration motors.

The browser sends haptic events over Bluetooth using the same timing system that drives the audio and visuals.

The current prototype uses:

left motor for Drums
right motor for Bass
both motors together for tactile timing cues

This shared event system was important because we did not want the tactile experience to feel like a separate accessibility feature added after the music was already built.

Challenges we ran into

Keeping everything synchronized

The biggest software challenge was synchronization.

Playing a sound from a gesture was straightforward at first, but once we added recording, looping, multiple instruments, visual notation, camera input, and haptics, every event had to happen at the correct musical moment.

We ran into issues like duplicate drum hits, events landing around loop boundaries, and recordings beginning at awkward points in the phrase. We eventually moved the entire experience onto one shared transport so each layer begins from the same Bar 1 and stays synchronized with the rest of the composition.

Two-hand camera tracking

Camera tracking also became more complicated once we added two-hand input.

Each hand needed its own pinch state, movement history, pitch position, and held-note state. Otherwise one hand could accidentally interfere with the other.

We had to make sure both hands could trigger notes independently while still recording into the same selected instrument layer.

Designing useful haptic feedback

The haptic system created a different kind of challenge.

With only two vibration motors, we had to decide what information was actually useful to communicate through touch instead of trying to represent every instrument at once.

Originally, the wristband behaved mostly like a tactile metronome during recording. We realized that this made layering harder for a Deaf performer because they could feel the beat but not the music they were playing over.

We changed the system so that after the count-in, previously recorded Drums and Bass can become the tactile reference during an overdub. If there is no tactile groove yet, the metronome continues instead.

Hardware problems

We also ran into physical hardware issues during testing.

After our vibration motors initially worked, one of the motor wires stopped making a reliable connection. We traced the issue back to the soldered connection on the motor, re-soldered the wire, and then had to re-test the circuit to make sure the motor, transistor, power connection, and rest of the wristband setup were still working correctly.

That was a good reminder that hardware debugging is very different from software debugging. Even when the code is correct, a loose or broken physical connection can make the whole system appear to fail.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

One of the things we are most proud of is that Resonance still communicates the composition when the audio is removed.

The visuals and haptics are not generated from the final sound output. They come from the same underlying musical events that create the sound.

That means a drum hit can simultaneously become:

an audio event
a visual event
a notation event
a tactile event

We also built:

synchronized four-layer composition
flexible instrument order
one- and two-hand gesture control
camera-based note and rhythm input
custom musical particle visualization
visual notation synchronized with playback
tactile Drums and Bass playback
groove-aware haptics while overdubbing
a Feel Only mode with no audio
a browser-to-ESP32 haptic hardware path

The moment that made the idea feel most real to us was seeing the composition continue to communicate something even after muting the sound.

What we learned

The biggest thing we learned is that accessibility can change the entire design of a product when it is considered from the beginning instead of added at the end.

Building Resonance made us think about music differently.

A beat does not have to only be heard — it can be felt.

Pitch can become position.

Duration can become a visual trail.

Rhythm can become movement.

An instrument can occupy a physical location on the wrist.

We also learned a lot technically about real-time browser audio, musical scheduling, MediaPipe, multi-hand tracking, Canvas rendering, Bluetooth communication, haptic feedback, and hardware debugging.

Most importantly, we learned how difficult — and how important — it is to make audio, visuals, and touch feel like parts of the same experience rather than separate features.

What's next for Resonance

Our current wristband uses two vibration motors, so we currently map those motors to Drums and Bass.

A future version could use more actuators positioned around the wrist or body so Keys, Lead, rhythm, and other musical information could each have their own physical location.

We would also like to explore:

richer haptic patterns and textures
accessibility preferences for visual and tactile feedback
saving and sharing compositions
collaborative performance
stronger mobile support
translating existing songs into tactile experiences
natural-language descriptions of compositions for screen-reader users
testing the experience directly with Deaf and hard-of-hearing performers

The larger idea behind Resonance is something we want to keep exploring:

Instead of asking Deaf people to adapt to music designed around hearing, what if we designed music experiences that adapted to them?

Vegi Knights

Enjoy slicing some vegetables with your friend though your camera!

Like
1

Comment

Logo Art for Vegi Knights

Inspiration

Our team wanted to build a fun interactive game that is different from usual forms of input. That meant we needed to limit the usage of keyboard, touchscreen, and trackpad. Many of us had Fruit Ninja as our childhood game, so that was what inspired us to make this game. For a novel form of playing the game, we implemented an AI camera detection system to do so.

What it does

The game primarily uses camera detection for your hands in order to track the vegetables the player is slashing. The game offers a single player and multiplayer mode for the player.

In the single player mode, they have unlimited time to get as much points as possible by slashing the vegetables, but they are limited to 3 lives. Lives are deducted either by not slashing a vegetable with their fingers or slashing a "Poison Mushroom." Users can keep playing to get the highest score possible!

Multiplayer will allow you to connect to another player and play the game with them. In this mode, they share all the vegetables, and they have to fight to slash as many vegetables/points as possible over the other player by the time limit (30 seconds). Stay vigilant! Since each player still have 3 lives, slashing Poison Mushrooms can make you lose even if you have more points! :)

How we built it

Since this a simple web game, we decided to go with a simple TypeScript/HTML/CSS approach for creating the game logic, structure, and design. We delegated tasks to one team member for making the design, UI, and assets for the game. Two members worked on the AI camera detector using Google MediaPipe Vision Task, and one person on setting up the peer-to-peer WebRTC for the multiplayer system.

Challenges we ran into

Our main concern when creating this project was the network system. Initially, we were planning to set it up so that two devices could connect to each other given that they are in the same network address and port. With further testing, it was inconsistent, and also meant that players could not play together if they were not on the same network system. With the new network system set up, the game could still be laggy at times.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We were proud of being able to set up the basic TypeScript/HTML/CSS system flawlessly. While adding in the network system and AI camera was a challenge, most of the necessary things like the app design, buttons, and score system were very well made.

What we learned

The most fun thing we learned was being able to implement audio into TypeScript using HTMLAudioElement. We all walked out of this project becoming more familiar with the TypeScript programming language.

We found that implementing an AI camera tracking system and network connection without a backend system is no easy task. We hope to research more on these technologies after this hackathon to become even more familiar with them, allowing us to apply it our personal projects in the future.

What's next for Vegi Knights

-We are interested in putting the network on a backend system to improve connectivity between the players.
-Having a queue system to allow users to choose who they want to play with would also be a great improvement we want to add.

title: Tilted
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Tilted

Tilted is a cooperative physics game where players tilt their phones to control one shared board. Team up, coordinate, and don’t get tilted.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

Tilted started from a simple question: what if multiple people could physically control the same game at the same time?

Instead of giving one player the controls, we wanted every player’s phone to contribute to one shared result. If everyone tilts in the same direction, their inputs reinforce one another. If players disagree, their inputs cancel. That turned a normal marble maze into a social coordination game where communication is part of the control system.

What it does

Tilted is a cooperative multiplayer physics game where players use the physical tilt of their phones to control one shared board.

Each phone sends a 2D motion vector representing the player’s tilt. The host combines the players’ inputs into a single team vector, and that resulting direction tilts the game board. The marble then moves naturally through the physics simulation.

The core idea is:

$$[
\mathbf{T} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{v}_i
]$$

where each $$(\mathbf{v}_i)$$ is one player’s input vector and $$(\mathbf{T})$$ is the team’s combined input.

When players coordinate, the marble moves strongly in the intended direction. When they fight each other, the board levels out and the marble slows down.

How we built it

We built Tilted as a browser-based multiplayer experience so players can join from their phones without installing an app.

The project consists of:

a mobile controller interface for each player
a host view containing the shared game board and maze
real-time communication between players and the host
phone motion/orientation input
vector aggregation to combine all player inputs
a physics-based marble and board simulation
a lobby and room system for joining a shared game

The phones act as controllers while the host displays the shared world, making it easy for everyone in the room to watch the same result.

Challenges we faced

One of the biggest challenges was translating phone motion into controls that felt natural across different devices.

We also had to decide what the players should actually control. We experimented with the idea of directly moving the marble, but controlling the tilt of the board produced a much more intuitive result: the players control the environment, while physics determines how the marble reacts.

Real-time multiplayer input introduced another challenge. Several phones can send conflicting movements at once, so we needed a consistent way to combine them while keeping the game responsive.

We also spent time refining the user experience around joining a room, calibrating phone orientation, and making the multiplayer interaction understandable without requiring a long explanation.

What we learned

We learned a lot about real-time multiplayer architecture, browser motion sensors, coordinate systems, physics simulation, and synchronizing input from several independent devices.

More importantly, we learned how much game design can emerge from a very small mathematical idea. Averaging a few vectors sounds simple, but once several people are physically contributing those vectors, it creates communication, conflict, cooperation, and chaos.

That social behavior became the most interesting part of Tilted.

title: The Speakery
text:
Notifications

Loading...

The Speakery

A cozy bakery game where kids practice their R, S, and K sounds by baking treats for Lenny the dragon, who actually listens and helps when a sound comes out wrong.

Like
5

Comment

Front screen of The Speakery

Diagram visual for tongue and mouth placement

Mirror mode, allowing the child to look at themselves while practicing mouth posture

Lenny the dragon makes a confused face when the child mispronounces a word

Shelf of completed lessons

Feed the dragon surprise minigame, unlocked when all lessons are completed

Creating assets in Figma

Creating the Cinnamon Roll in Figma

Creating the Cupcake in Figma

Creating Lenny the Dragon's model

Inspiration

Speech therapy for children can often be frustrating for everyone involved, the child, the parent, and the instructor. One of our members, Cameron, received speech therapy as a child until he was 11 years old, and had to work on critical sounds like S, and R. However, with the help of fun activities, he was able to learn these sounds and speak properly today. That experience shaped how we approached this game. We wanted to create something fun and engaging for a kid, that makes learning correct pronunciation an adventure. We also wanted to use this project to learn new skills, and adding speech mechanics into a game was something new for all of us. We loved Knight Hacks' mascot Lenny and thought he would be the perfect guide! 

Functionality

The Speakery is a fun easy-to-use speech-learning game for children guided by the Knight Hacks mascot Lenny! Children open the website, then choose a technique to master. Currently the options consist of "R" "S" and "K" sounds, as these are commonly difficult for children. "R" makes a cinnamon roll, "S" makes a s'more, and "K" makes a cupcake. After a choice is selected, the baking process begins, which goes as follows:

Lenny will place an order based off the child's choice! Example: "One cinnamon roll, please!"
The child will learn the sound in the practice menu. The practice menu is a visual demonstration as well as a step-by-step guide read out by Lenny. The child then practices with a warm-up word (Example: "key"). If they properly say it, they can begin their bake!
Our game uses speech to bake treats! Each step of the process is a new word the child must properly say based off the sound they chose at the start. For example "S" sounds might include "Snap," and "Set".  If a child can't properly say a word after two attempts, they'll return to the practice menu.
After the treat is completed, the child can hand the dessert to Lenny by tapping the screen! The treat then goes on the child's shelf to showcase their accomplishment! Hooray!

But the bake cycle was not all we incorporated, here are some other important features we added!

• We coded the R sound to be stronger, and detect when a child says something like "way" instead of "ray". Lenny will even tell you when this happens!

• Every line is read out loud by Lenny, as some children may not be able to read yet.

• A turtle button will make Lenny speak the target word slowly, which may help struggling children sound the word out.

• In the practice menu, children can enable mirror mode to view themselves and match the visual demonstration

• We added a grown-up mode that allows grown-ups to override the practice menu if a child begins to get frustrated.

• The treat shelf acts as an achievement board and if the child completes all 3 sound tracks, they unlock a hidden minigame that involves sounds from every track!

• No accounts or log in required, everything is saved to the device. 

How it was Built

The Speakery is a React + Vite web app coded in plain JavaScript, and hosted on Vercel at thespeakerygame.com. There's essentially no backend: Kids' voices are private so we didn't save or upload anything ourselves.

Listening: The browser's built-in Web Speech API turns what the kid says into words. the API uses its best guess, however we ask again when it isn't confident. Every word has a short list of "near misses" that never count as right. These are the real words the browser hears when a kid swaps a sound: "tea" for "key," "thee" for "see," "way" for "ray." Each one is tied to a specific tip, which is how the dragon knows what to say. 

Voice Lines: The dragon talks using an ElevenLabs voice. We wrote every line in one file (125 of them) and a small script records them all into mp3s ahead of time. That means no API key ever ships to the browser, and the voice works on bad Wi-Fi. The game has a back-up through the browser's built-in voice if necessary.

Art: Lenny was drawn by Altynai. We kept it exactly as drawn and only removed the face, then drew the eyes, brows, and mouth on top in code, so he can look happy, puzzled, or heart-eyed while eating. The cinnamon roll and cupcake sprites were created in Figma by Cameron. We built a script that centers each one on its plate. The bakery scene, the mouth diagrams, and the s'more are SVG. Altynai also designed animations for the baking steps

Saving: The treat shelf, the grown-up corner's numbers, and settings live in the browser's local storage. This way the child's information can be kept private.

Team: Rachel (project lead, game code and speech features), Altynai (created dragon sprites and animation) and Cam (created food sprites), and Ben (sound and audio). We also used Claude as a coding partner the whole weekend, especially for the audio math.

Challenges

One challenge we faced was that the browser kept accepting pronunciation mistakes and denying correct pronunciation . Kids who have trouble with R often say it like a W, so “brown” comes out “bwown” and “wrap” comes out “wap.” We’d say “bwown” into the mic on purpose and the game would count it as correct. Speech recognition is built to figure out what you meant, so we had to stop listening to words and start listening to sound. A real R pulls one of your voice’s resonances (called F3) way down, which adds energy in the middle pitches at the start of the word. A W leaves that range quiet. So for R words, the game keeps the kid’s try in memory for a moment, measures that sound shape with the Web Audio API, and scores it from “sounds like a W” to “sounds like an R.” If it’s clearly a W, Lenny tells you your R sounded like a W, even when the browser thought you nailed it.

Our first version looked for the F3 dip directly, and it flagged too many correct R’s, especially with background noise and on high voices (kids have high voices!). With Claude’s help we rebuilt it and tested it on hundreds of computer-generated R and W versions of our words, across different voices, pitches, and noise levels. On our five R words it now catches about 9 in 10 W-swaps in a quiet room and about 8 in 10 with noise, while flagging almost no correct R’s. Those are computer voices, not real kids, so when it isn’t sure, it trusts the browser. It’s not perfect, but it’s better than celebrating “bwown.”

Another challenge we faced was that Lenny kept getting cut off. At first the game moved to the next screen on a timer, so longer lines got chopped in half. We also noticed when the mic turns on or off, Macs (and especially AirPods) switch sound modes for a split second, and anything the dragon said in that moment came out as a glitchy noise. Our fix was to make the game wait for him to finish, and give the audio a beat to settle before he talks. This worked!

Safari proved to be a source of trouble. For example, the checkered tea towel on the counter showed up as a solid black square. Also, the mirror opened the camera but stayed blank. Both worked fine in Chrome, which is where we'd been testing. We fixed these bugs, but learned to always test in every browser.

Accomplishments

• Lenny actually listens and responds back. We said "tea" instead of "key" and he answered "Hmm? I heard 'tea'!"

• It never makes a kid feel bad. There's no "wrong," no red X, no buzzer. Missing a word leads to practice and a tip, and a grown-up can always unlock the next step.

• It's live on a real domain, works on a phone, and keeps progress without asking anyone to make an account.

• Privacy without a privacy policy wall. Everything is saved to the child's device. That means we never save voice recordings, names, and there are no servers that could be leaked!

What was Learned

• Speech recognition is built for adults who want to be understood. It's really good at guessing what you meant, but hard when it has to be exact, and kids' voices make it even harder.

• Designing for kids who can't read changes everything. Every prompt needs to be spoken, every button needs to be huge, and "try again" needs to feel like an invitation. The game has to be fun at every moment!

• Small details carry the final result. Some of our favorites were the dragon's puzzled head tilt, the turtle button, the treat landing on the shelf. Those took the least code and made the biggest difference.

• We learned to commit often, read what GitHub Desktop says before you push, and never click "Replace" on a folder.

What's Next?

Here are some things we want to add!

• A way for the API to listen to sounds, not just words. The R check proved the idea works in the browser. Next is an S check for lisps and a K check for when it slides forward into a T, ideally using a model trained on children's voices instead of adult ones.

• More sounds. L, TH, and SH are the obvious next three, and each one gets its own treat.

• Harder levels. Right now the target sound is mostly at the start of the word. Therapists move from sounds, to words, to sounds at the end of words, to whole sentences, so the dragon's orders should too: "Roll the dough!"

• A progress report a parent can share. The grown-up corner already tracks the useful stuff on the device. Letting a parent export it for their child's SLP, still without any server, would close the loop between home practice and therapy.
