title: ForkAround&FindOut
text:
Notifications

Loading...

ForkAround&FindOut

Quantum Privacy Firewall: Protecting quantum algorithms from reverse engineering through privacy-aware circuit transformations, verified correctness, and adaptive security evaluation.

Like

Comment

Inspiration

As quantum computing increasingly relies on cloud infrastructure, protecting proprietary quantum algorithms becomes an emerging cybersecurity challenge. Our project was inspired by research from Beat Buesser and Anil Kurmus at IBM Research on algorithmic intent leakage from transpiled quantum circuits. We wanted to explore whether quantum circuits could be made harder to reverse-engineer without changing their computation.

What it does

Quantum Privacy Firewall (QPF) is a privacy-aware quantum compilation and auditing framework. It analyzes structural information leaked by transpiled circuits and generates functionally equivalent alternatives through gate transformations, layout diversification, and transpiler randomization. It verifies correctness, measures hardware overhead, and evaluates privacy improvements against adaptive attackers.

How we built it

We used IBM Qiskit and FakeNighthawk to implement a benchmark covering seven algorithm classes, 47 circuit generators, and 24/48-qubit workloads. Ten normalized structural features are analyzed using Random Forest classifiers. Our defense pipeline uses MQT QCEC and other equivalence checks alongside resource-budget filtering. A FastAPI backend and React frontend provide interactive circuit analysis and visualization.

Challenges we ran into

Our biggest challenges were preserving quantum-circuit equivalence, correcting ancilla initialization and uncomputation errors, managing computationally expensive verification, and preventing dataset leakage during machine-learning evaluation. We also discovered that transformations which confuse an initial classifier may be less effective against retrained attackers.

Accomplishments that we're proud of

We built an independent algorithm-intent leakage benchmark, implemented circuit transformations with equivalence checks, and developed an adaptive security evaluation pipeline. Our reported experiments achieved 93–99% classification accuracy under matching compiler settings and demonstrated a modest reduction in adaptive attacker macro-F1 from 0.916 to 0.865 under the tested defense configuration.

What we learned

We learned that quantum security extends beyond protecting data and encryption keys to protecting the structure of quantum programs. We also discovered that circuit obfuscation requires balancing three factors: computational correctness, hardware efficiency, and resistance to informed attackers. A lower classifier score alone does not guarantee confidentiality.

What's next for ForkAround&FindOut

We plan to explore stronger privacy-preserving transformations, evaluate more sophisticated attackers, and improve equivalence verification for larger circuits. Our long-term goal is to integrate QPF into Qiskit's compilation workflow as a reusable privacy-auditing tool, with real-hardware validation when resources become available.

T.A.G: Totally Awesome Game

Inspired by the sights and sounds of Jet Set Radio, T.A.G. is a stylish, fast-paced competitive 2D online multiplayer game. Hop into a lobby with 4 friends and race to see who can tag the most turf. 

Like
5

Comment

Title Screen, the logo beats with the music!

The Main Menu! A POV street view of some signs!

A group shot featuring a familiar face!

Tech Knight as a Tag!

A tag of Bit from Drill Diver! One of our previous games!

All of the Tags made for the game!

The Settings menu. Featuring a graffitied wall!

The lobby menu, through the view of an mp3 player!

The Lobby waiting room before a match starts!

A group hanging out in the lobby!

The end of game screen!

The winner screen at the end of a game!

Inspiration

The primary inspiration for T.A.G. was Jet Set Radio, Bomb Rush Cyberfunk, and Sonic Rush. The visuals and music are all lovingly crafted by hand to pay homage to that grind-fiction style and hip-hop aesthetic. The multiplayer aspect was inspired by fast pace 2d competitive games like Speedrunners. The idea was to create a game that could create exciting competition between friends.

What it does

T.A.G is an online competitive multiplayer game. Up to four players can enter a lobby; then, when they're ready, the leader can start a match. The players will find themselves in the middle of a large city-styled arena. Scattered around the city are tag spots, turf for the taking. After a countdown, the players race across the city to tag as many spots as they can. The number of spots each player has tagged is shown on screen, along with the remaining unclaimed spots. The game ends when the last spot is tagged, but it's not that simple. If you happen upon one of your opponents' tags, you can take the chance to steal it for yourself!
The game has an emphasis on style and art. Every menu, button, and logo was intentionally designed and picked to fit our aesthetic. For each song in the game, a small screen on an MP3 player provides the song title and artist's name. This game is a love letter to the style and direction of grind-fiction games and we made sure it showed in every way it could.

How we built it

We primarily used GitHub, Godot, Firebase, and the Godot plugin GDSync to create this game. We split development between the four of us, alternating working on UI, controls, mechanics, level design, and art. This allowed us to work efficiently without burnout.

Challenges we ran into

Ensuring all members of the lobby were synced without connection problems and ensuring that a reasonable number of packets were sent between the host and clients. Designing the UI and art fast and efficiently while maintaining a consistent and strong aesthetic. 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

The style and flair of the game is by far it's greatest quality. We believe we were able to create something very pleasing to look at. It proudly represents it's influences and along side with our curated selection of music, feels right at home in the genre. We're also proud of creating a full working online multiplayer game with an addictive and fulfilling loop.

What we learned

How to better cooperate and work in parallel on a variety of tasks. We also learned how to design and create a multiplayer game, ensuring full connectivity.

What's next for T.A.G: Totally Awesome Game

Time trials, new arenas,  and more characters would bring new life to the game and allow it to grow.

title: Fobo
text:
Notifications

Loading...

Fobo

We all know FOMO, but what about the fear of burning out? Fobo helps you make room for what matters most, without spreading yourself too thin.

Like
20

Comment
2

Initial onboarding

Survey questions, energy gauger

Calendar syncing & initial weighing

Plans tab, calendar & agenda view

Edit, move, & weigh plans

People tab, add friends

You tab, profile adjustment settings

Inspiration

A calendar tells you when you're free. It doesn't tell you when you've had enough.
Most of us know someone, or are someone, who says yes by reflex. The invite sounds fun, and the week is already full. Every plan is "just dinner" or "just a few hours" until there are four of them, or until you find yourself forgetting faces from how many you've seen. Nothing overlaps on the calendar, but by Thursday you're running on fumes. Free time isn't the same as having energy, and almost every planning tool only tracks the first one.

Burnout also rarely arrives as one big moment. It builds from a dozen small yeses, which is why we wanted a tool that works at the point of decision: the moment a new invite lands and you have to answer. The name comes from that: Fobo, Fear of Burning Out. We built it for people whose weeks fit on paper but still wear them out, the workaholics, the people-pleasers, and anyone who gets socially tired.

As busy college students and workers, we know firsthand how exhausting it can be to spread yourself too thin. To say yes to too many plans. To work yourself down the bone. That's why we sought for a solution to the madness, so people like us could use it, too. 

What it does

Fobo is a personal capacity planner. It shows when you're full, not just when you're free, and helps you decide what to do about it.

It learns you, then learns alongside you. Fobo starts with a few gentle questions about how you recharge, when you like to head home, and what makes you feel like yourself again. After each event, a quick this-or-that ("Which plan cost more?", "About the same", "Can't remember") sharpens its picture of what energizes you and what drains you. Every question has a skip option, because we always offer an out. 

It shows your week as stacks. Each day is a stack of cut-paper scraps, one scrap per plan. The height of a scrap is its energy cost, and its color is the kind of plan: work, social, obligation, or enjoy. Each type has its own cut edge, so the stack reads without color alone (snipped corner, wavy cut, pinking shears, three scallops). Past plans drain to a calming grey. Instead of a percentage, you read the whole day at a glance by how tall the stack is. 

Rest is never a gap, but always a character. In Fobo, rest is never an empty slot. It's a sleeping character alongside all the others, and that's a good thing. We believe that rest is just as important as any other obligation in your day. Colorful creatures show how each day is going: bright, fine, stretched, spent, or asleep. The characters carry the emotion so the interface can stay neutral.

It helps you decide. When a new invite arrives, Fobo weighs it against your week and helps you accept, reshape, move, or decline it before the week overflows. It also helps you plan your exit with a gameplan for when to head home, so you can leave gracefully (no Irish goodbyes needed). Fobo notifies you as you approach your limit, giving you time to reallocate your time and energy. An app that helps you form boundaries, not wear them away. 

It's protective, not restrictive. Recommendations suggest a boundary. Fobo never says no for you, because the decision stays in your hands. You are the one with the ultimate power to reshape your habits, after all.

It's private by default. Just because your friends manage their burnout alongside you, doesn't mean they need to see it. Protect your peace, or don't, by sharing your weekly calendar with those on your friends list, allowing for overlap on those you care for. When energized, plans with the ones you love can mean everything. 

How we built it

In the initial stages of planning, we ran robust survey research trials, gathering precious user input as to times they've burnt themselves out, how it happened, as well as what useful features they would love to see in an app of this caliber. We recognize it's important to have an audience before we create something. After gathering our survey data, we then noticed that many sought the calendar syncing features that most calendar apps contain, but with the boundary management that little to no apps provided. That was where we started.

Design

We designed around five concepts:

Energy over time. Every plan shows its cost in plain language ("Costs 6 of 10"), not only its duration. This scale is also what lets Fobo plan your week. One of our many non-negotiables was deciding to scrap the usage of percentages, rings, or batteries as energy indicators. We wanted to work outside the box, display energy in a way that we haven't seen before.
Characters carry emotion. The creatures express state, and the UI chrome stays neutral so they can shine. Customize your profile's character based on a variety of different options. 
Black ink, warm paper. Near-black actions sit on an off-white ground, and all the color comes from the characters and scraps. A simple, yet fun UI was the ultimate choice for an app that can be as overwhelming as a management app. We wanted to leave all the visual language work to the lil' scrapbook paper guys.
Questionnaire galore. The this-or-that choices after each event keep improving the model. Quick surveys following commitments to help plan out your future weeks, all while keeping the same, quirky characters. 
One thumb. The app is mobile-first, with the primary action pinned to the bottom for quick thinkers.

The cut-paper language comes from the idea that a day is something you assemble and trim. Each scrap type has its own physical cut, and the stack changes shape as your day does. We designed the full flow in three stages: pre-onboarding (splash, start, pre-login, sign up, log in, forgot password), onboarding (how you recharge, when to head home, feel like yourself again, which plan cost more), and the main flow (your week, plans, event detail, people, people detail).

Frontend

The app is built with Expo and React Native for iOS, Android, and web from one codebase. At the bottom of the screen, is the powerhouse of our app: the navbar. Here, you can navigate between the four screens: plans, people, you, and week. Each tab allows for a narrower scope of what to do and how to plan out your week, down to who you spend it with. We wanted this purposeful simplicity to allow users to focus on what's most important. 

Backend

The backend is a TypeScript API running as a Neon Function on Neon Postgres. It:

• Syncs every Google Calendar a user connects.

• Works out each day's energy load in the user's own time zone.

• Controls what friends see, so shared views expose only what the user chooses to share.

• Uses Gemini to weigh new plans, pick when to leave, and rebalance the week. The server checks every answer Gemini gives and does the energy math itself, so the model suggests and the server decides.

Challenges we ran into

Showing energy without a gauge. We ruled out rings, batteries, and percentages, which are the usual tools for this. That meant the stacks had to do everything: show cost, show category, and signal when you're close to your limit. Getting a stack to read as "nearly full" without a number took many rounds of iteration. 

Making a model's output trustworthy. An AI that tells you how to spend your energy can be wrong in ways that matter. We handled it by keeping the math and validation on the server. Gemini proposes, and the server verifies every answer before it reaches the user.

*Protective without preachy. Fobo has to nudge you toward a boundary without guilt-tripping or deciding for you. Finding copy that's firm, brief, and kind took more drafts than any other part of the UX writing.

Coordinating four people across design and code. Especially for designing, all the designers possess very different palates in relations to what an ideal mobile app should look like. However, through compromise and thorough deliberation, we settled on a simple, yet enjoyable UI that blends all our tastes together. There were a fair bit of assets we had to scrap, screens we had to redo, and UX we had to adjust to get here, but getting here was the ultimate reward! 

Accomplishments that we're proud of

• A design language where the interface carries the idea. Height means cost, color means kind of plan, cut edges give each type its own shape, and a sleeping character means rest. It's visually distinct from a standard wellness app.

• A full product flow from first launch to your week, not just a single screen, covering onboarding, sign-in, planning, event detail, and people.

• A working backend connected to real calendars, with energy computed per user and per timezone. Sync from your Google Calendar directly after onboarding!

• AI that stays in its lane. Gemini helps with decisions, and the server validates its output and handles the math. No overstepping, no pushing, nothing.

• A consistent voice across every screen, with clear rules for how Fobo talks. This made it easy for all the designers to collaborate on very different parts of the app. 

• Treating rest as a feature. The most important design decision we made was refusing to show rest as an empty slot. A lot of people tend to negate rest as important to our psyche, especially when dealing with busier weeks. 

What we learned

Learning to work alongside development. In the design space, it's easy to get caught up in your own designs and forget that working alongside devs is important for the lifecycle of an app. 

Constraints improve design. We didn't want to opt for the usual indicators of energy, yet we also had a limited amount of time to survey, plan, design, and code. 

What's next for Fobo - Fear of Burning Out

• Personalization that deepens over time. Use each this-or-that answer to refine how Fobo scores your plans, so "Costs 6 of 10" gets closer to your own 6.

• Smarter exit plans and boundary suggestions tailored to the type of invite and the people involved.

• Richer shared rooms. Let friends and groups coordinate around each other's capacity while still seeing only room, a little, or full.

• More calendar and plan sources beyond Google Calendar.

• User testing with the people Fobo is for, to check that the cost scale, the characters, and the copy mean what we think they mean.

• Expanding the character set and mood states so more of a day's texture shows up without adding numbers.

• Stronger rest support. Help people protect rest, not just fit it in. Maybe even plan suggestions based on a heightened onboarding, where users enter what relaxes them and plans are made in accordance to that.
